title: =DJ BOC WATCH: September Rate Raise In Question After Fed Policy Shift
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--Can the Bank of Canada keep tightening while the U.S. Federal Reserve aims at staying loose?

The Fed's discrete retreat even further from monetary tightening last week has some observers thinking the Bank of Canada may have to curtail its own tightening cycle. Given how closely the two countries' economies are intertwined, it's hard for the Canadian central bank to pursue a radically different policy track for very long, they argue.

Others believe some key aspects of the two countries' economies have diverged so markedly the bank has the ability to continue tightening policy independently of the U.S.

The market appears to be taking the first view into account. Tuesday morning, the overnight-indexed swaps market was pricing in about a 60% chance of a rate increase at the bank's next announcement date on Sept. 8, down from the near certainty discounted earlier in August. The decline also reflects some weak Canadian and U.S. data in the intervening period.

Expectations for the Bank of Canada may have been more volatile than usual in recent weeks in part because markets know the bank is acutely sensitive to both external and domestic developments.

The bank has raised its key overnight target rate by 50 basis points since June, and remains the only central bank among the G7 group of industrialized economies to embark on tightening in the period following the global financial market crisis in 2008.

Since launching its tightening, the bank has underscored what a cautious and context-sensitive tightening it is. The question now is how the Fed's reassertion of monetary easing alters the context for the bank.

One reason that policy cannot diverge from the Fed's on a sustained basis is the Canadian dollar's acute sensitivity to interest rate differentials between the U.S. and Canada. If the bank continues to raise rates while the Fed abstains, the Canadian dollar will likely appreciate. In a trade-oriented economy like Canada's, the net result is monetary tightening that could easily exceed what the bank would like.

Another is that the close ties between the Canadian and U.S. economies mean the renewed weakness the Fed is worried about could easily spread to Canada.

"If we do get into a much weaker-than-expected U.S. environment, that is going to spill over into Canada one way or another," said Doug Porter, deputy chief economist at BMO Capital Markets.

Housing is one sector where Canada had clearly diverged from the U.S., with Canada's market shutting down for a few months immediately after the global financial crisis and then picking up steam again through 2009 and into this year. In recent months, however, it's been sputtering.

"We've got pretty clear evidence that housing has stalled, and the best days are behind it, already," said BMO's Porter.

While the gap between the U.S. and Canadian housing sectors has narrowed somewhat, another key divergence remains. Consumer borrowing in Canada has remained healthy. Business borrowing has as well, although to a lesser degree.

A recent report from Scotia Capital said that's the single biggest reason the Bank of Canada can part company sustainably with the Fed and stay on a tightening track.

While the U.S. is deleveraging and stuck in a liquidity trap that means monetary policy is not working to stimulate demand side of the picture, Canada is leveraging and monetary policy is arguably working too well, Scotia said.

Within six months, Canadian households will be more heavily indebted than Americans on a debt-to-income basis, Scotia says.

"The BOC has to be concerned about facing the same tag applied to the Fed in keeping rates too low for too long when looking out at risks over the coming years," Scotia said.

"Yes, the uncertainty has risen. But the fundamentals are still supportive of a continued pace of tightening," it said.

(Don Curren, a reporter based in Toronto, has covered Canadian currency and fixed income markets for more than 10 years. He can be reached at 416-306-2020 or at don.curren@dowjones.com.)

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Up, Hits 19-Month High After Jobs Data
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar ended significantly higher Friday, breaking out of its well-defined trading range and hitting its highest level in 19 months after an unexpectedly robust jobs report for February.

The rally opened the door for a run to parity with the U.S. dollar, possibly in the near term, market watchers said.

"I think that the Canadian dollar is really convincingly moving to par, now," said Aaron Fennell, senior market strategist at futures broker Lind-Waldock Canada in Toronto.

The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.0185 at 3:13 p.m. EST (2013 GMT), from C$1.0171 at 8:00 a.m. EST (1300 GMT), and from C$1.0246 late Thursday.

The U.S. dollar dropped to a daily low at C$1.0157, its lowest level since July 25, 2008, after news in early trading that the Canadian economy created 20,900 jobs in February, stronger than the 17,000 expected by economists and the unemployment rate unexpectedly fell to 8.2% from 8.3% in the previous month.

The drop took the U.S. unit through key support near C$1.0200, breaking the currency pair of out the C$1.0200 to C$1.0850 range that has held since October and setting the stage for a move to parity.

"The move we're seeing today is just directly off the labor survey, which was fantastic," said Lind-Waldock's Fennell.

"I think the key to it was we had 60,000 full-time jobs and a loss of 39,000 part-time. That just means a lot of part-time jobs are being changed to full-time," Fennell said. "I think that's a fantastic signal for the Canadian economy," he said.

Fennell believes there will be at least one correction in the U.S./Canadian dollar pair as it descends towards parity.

"I would expect as we approach par there will be a lot of profit taking," he said. "I think it will take one or two runs at par before it finally goes through," Fennell said.

A report from TD Securities said that while the pair gapped under the C$1.0170/C$1.0200 support zone Friday morning, there is not a strong sense, at the moment at least, that it is running away on the downside.

"Downside risks are certainly higher this morning, and certainly higher than we had expected at this point yesterday, but the USD is looking very oversold already," TD said.

But technical indicators suggest the U.S. dollar can only rebound more significantly if spot moves above C$1.0220 level, TD added.

The Canadian dollar is still vulnerable to bouts of risk aversion in global markets, but any losses due to that factor will likely be transitory, said Lind-Waldock's Fennell.

When the Canadian dollar appeared to be gaining momentum for a push to parity last fall, the Bank of Canadaintervened verbally in the market, with considerable success, to quell the currency's gains.

Fennell and many other market watchers believe Canada's central bank is likely to be more restrained in the coming weeks, reflecting the fact that the export sector has had time to adjust to Canadian dollar strength.

"Any manufacturer or exporter who would have problems with higher Canadian dollar values has had ample opportunities to set up hedges," he said.

The Canadian data calendar next week is characterized by a number of second-tier reports, including labor productivity for the fourth quarter and manufacturing sales for January on Tuesday, wholesale trade for January on Wednesday and international securities transactions for the same month on Thursday.

The most significant releases come Friday, when consumer price index data for February and retail sales data for January will be released.

title: Remarks by Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of Canada
text:
Release date - 11032010

Principles for Interesting Times:

I would like to thank students from universities across Canada for joining me on this special day, the 75th anniversary of the Bank of Canada.

This afternoon, I will speak about the past and the present in the hope of enticing some of you to participate in the Bank’s future.

Let me caution market participants that nothing that follows relates to the ‘near future,’ that is, the horizon relevant for monetary policy decisions, so if you are not interested in the Bank’s history, the Bank’s gift to you on our birthday is an hour of found time.

Introduction

The Bank of Canada’s mandate is to preserve the value of the nation’s currency and to promote the economic and financial welfare of Canadians. As a consequence, we focus on the major macroeconomic issues of the day. Over the past two years, these have been considerable.

With current debates ranging from the relationship between price and financial stability to the future of the international monetary system, it is an exciting time in central banking. However, I would argue that for students such as yourselves, the issues facing central banks are always intriguing since they go to the heart of how modern economies function and, indeed, how human beings behave.

The Bank in turn needs you. The Bank is a learning organization, with immense responsibilities. Our work is grounded in academia, honed by analysis, and disciplined by an unrelenting focus on our mandate. Our response to the recent economic crisis has risen to the highest standard set over our history. Guided by well-researched, policy-based frameworks, the Bank has acted decisively. As a result, the clarity and credibility of these frameworks has made action more powerful. The importance of this combination has been repeatedly demonstrated.

The formidable economic and financial challenges facing Canada today are not necessarily more intractable than those in the past. Economic forces do not change. However, the speed and scale of information, capital flows, and trade are radically different. The global economy is more fundamentally interconnected than ever before-and that means the response times for policy-makers have shortened dramatically. In this environment, the value of principles-based policy frameworks is supreme.

I am reminded of a story told to me by Jean-Claude Trichet, President of the European Central Bank. A mutual colleague, at the start of the crisis, was visiting a small village in the Scottish highlands. He was bereft of his BlackBerry and was anxious for the latest financial news. He entered a newsagent and asked for the Financial Times.

The shopkeeper said, ‘Would you like yesterday’s paper or today’s?’

Given the weight of events, he answered without hesitation, ‘I would prefer today’s.’

To which the shopkeeper replied, ‘Then come back tomorrow.’

In today’s world, policy-makers cannot wait until tomorrow. They must act immediately. To do so effectively, they need guiding principles.

Permit me to elaborate by recounting three challenges that have resonated over the years.

Monetary Policy Response to Global Economic Crisis

First, consider a severe, synchronous global recession, triggered by a financial crisis at the heart of capitalism. Commodity prices crash, protectionism is on the rise. There are bank failures around the world, although not in Canada. Nonetheless, our country is not left unscathed. Unemployment rockets and economic activity plummets. Does that sound familiar?

Triggered by the stock market crash of October 1929, the Great Depression had a devastating impact on the global and Canadian economies. By 1933, Canadian equity prices had fallen more than 70 per cent from their peak, and national output had dropped by 40 per cent, with the drought-stricken prairies especially hard hit. Nationwide, deflation was punishing, with consumer prices falling by more than 9 per cent in both 1931 and 1932. The human cost was staggering, with the unemployment rate hitting a high of 20 per cent in 1933.

By 1933, with bank lending still contracting, pressure on the federal government to ‘do something’ had become intense. Reflecting the high cost and low availability of credit, there was widespread public distrust of the chartered banks.1 Western farmers, suffering from sharp declines in both crop yields and prices, were vocal critics of the Eastern-controlled banks and strongly favoured the creation of a central bank. The Government responded with the passage of the Bank of Canada Act, and we opened our doors for business and issued our first bank notes exactly 75 years ago.

So what did the Bank do? Initially, with respect to monetary policy, the answer was, not much. The economy was already starting to recover, and the Bank maintained its Bank Rate unchanged at 2 1/2 per cent.2 As well, the notion that central banks could stabilize macroeconomic activity within their borders is relatively new. 3, 4

Moreover, the Bank retained a ‘gold mentality,’ even though Canada had officially broken the formal link between the Canadian dollar and gold in 1931. Consequently, there was a reluctance to do anything that might induce capital outflows. It was also widely believed that U.S. rates provided an effective floor for comparable Canadian rates.5

Contrast that to the recent experience. The so-called ‘Great Recession’ from which we are just emerging had the potential to replicate the dire experience of the 1930s. However, while the reverberations of the recent experience are far from finished, the aggressive and timely actions of global central banks, including the Bank of Canada, have not only averted the worst, but also created the prospect of a sustained recovery.

Recognizing the strong headwinds caused by the seizing up of financial markets, the Bank has dramatically eased monetary conditions and provided significant liquidity to the financial system. The Bank’s actions were guided by its forward-looking inflation-targeting framework, which prompted easing before the recession began and accelerated stimulus once the crisis intensified.

Between December 2007 and April of last year, the Bank lowered the overnight target by a total of 425 basis points, cutting it to a historic low of 1/4 per cent, its lowest possible level. Once we reached that effective lower bound, we developed and published a framework for unconventional monetary policy. Our conditional commitment is the only element of that framework that we have activated. While the Bank’s unconventional policy framework demonstrated to Canadians that we were not out of bullets, the use of the conditional commitment reassured them that we were not trigger happy but, rather, disciplined by the pursuit of our inflation target.

Action alone is not sufficient. It must take place within the proper context. Once again, I stress that the Bank places supreme importance on policy measures within a well-developed framework.

The Bank’s monetary policy response to the current crisis has been consistent with Ben Bernanke’s mea culpa to Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, regarding the lack of action by the Federal Reserve during the Depression: ‘You’re right, we did it. We’re very sorry. But thanks to you, we won’t do it again.’

Bernanke’s admission underscores the importance of research and learning - something the Bank has long understood. In-depth, comprehensive, and impartial research has always been critical to our success. One of the first steps taken by our first governor, Graham Towers, was to create a research and statistical department.6 Through aggressive recruitment of promising young academics and co-operation with university-based researchers and international colleagues, innovations have included leading macro models (such as RDX and ToTEM), work on price-level targeting, and cutting-edge research on payments systems.7

The Bank has also learned from the conduct of policy, including from our mistakes. Gerald Bouey famously recognized that ‘we did not abandon M1, M1 abandoned us,’ before initiating a search for a new monetary anchor. More recently, the Bank has been determined not to repeat the errors of the 1970s, when we overestimated the rate of potential growth in the wake of a major global shock.8

Most significantly, the Bank is now guided by the discipline of an inflation target. Canada helped pioneer inflation targeting, having adopted it in 1991 under the Governorship of John Crow.9 During the Great Recession, its value was clear. By disciplining our objectives and promoting transparency and accountability, the target has anchored inflation expectations, thereby ensuring that reductions in our overnight rate drive down real interest rates and stimulate the economy.

Financial System Stability and the Provision of Liquidity

Consider now a second challenge that has echoed across the decades. In the midst of an economic crisis, a mid-sized financial institution fails, potentially triggering a host of counterparty defaults across financial systems. The shock spreads globally, threatening market functioning and financial stability.

This is the story of Bankhaus Herstatt, a mid-sized German bank, active in foreign exchange markets, that failed in 1974 during the first oil shock. It was shut down at the end of the business day, when many banks still had foreign exchange contracts for settlement. The international impact was substantial, even in the ‘less-connected’ world of the 1970s. As the repercussions from failed transactions mounted, gross funds transferred in New York fell by 60 per cent over the next several days.

The Herstatt failure exposed how inadequate market infrastructure and more open capital accounts transmit shocks globally. It led to a deliberate, global process to address these shortcomings.

That same year, governors of the central banks of G-10 countries, including Bouey, established the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which continues to serve today as an important forum for co-operation on banking supervisory matters. In 1980, a second group on payments systems was established; later upgraded to the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS).

Following smaller episodes of settlement and other financial failures, the work of these committees eventually led to the establishment of CLS Bank.10 CLS links national payments systems and simultaneously settles on its books the foreign exchange transactions submitted by its member banks.

Although the response to the failure of Herstatt was slow, it did eventually develop market infrastructure to remove daylight payment risk. It also promoted the deepening of institutional structures such as the G-10. Crucially, this work paid off during the recent crisis. The G-10 has coordinated some of the most important central bank initiatives. The foreign exchange payments system itself was rock solid, despite the enormous financial turmoil. However, new channels of contagion were revealed in new markets.

Following the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a mid-sized U.S. investment bank, in September 2008, the cost of interbank borrowing spiked up to unprecedented levels. The functioning of repo, stock, loan, and derivatives markets seized as collateral values plunged and a panic over counterparty risk swept the financial system. Within days, other storied institutions either collapsed or were pushed to the brink. The seizure of the entire global financial system was a very real possibility.

The virulence of open global capital flows meant that the response, this time, had to be crafted in days, not decades.

G-10 central banks, including the Bank of Canada, acted swiftly, by conducting a coordinated 50-basis-point interest rate cut. Then, in a historic meeting, G-7 countries, including Canada, committed to:

use all available tools to support systemically important financial institutions and prevent their failure; and

take all necessary steps to ensure that banks and other financial institutions have broad access to liquidity and funding.

The G-7 actions - while absolutely necessary - left the system awash in moral hazard. The need for principles-based policy frameworks once again became clear.

The Bank’s extraordinary liquidity operations met this standard. As the crisis intensified, we introduced facilities anchored to a principles-based framework developed in the spring prior to the Lehman failure. Total outstandings peaked at $41 billion. These are now being unwound consistent with market conditions and our principles.11

The crisis also revealed grave shortcomings in market structure and regulation. On the former, rather than wait three decades, the Bank has already assisted an industry-led process to develop a central counterparty for Canadian repo markets. This initiative, which will go live later this year, will help keep core funding markets functioning continuously, including in times of stress. The Bank is also very active through the BIS in advancing reforms of global margining practices in order to dampen liquidity spirals, consistent with both the findings of academic literature and practical experience.12

Finally, through the G-20 and the Financial Stability Board, the Bank is helping to create a more resilient global financial system. In this regard, imperatives include a new bank capital regime, the development of a more systemic approach to regulation; and a series of initiatives to create a system that can withstand failure.13

In all of these initiatives, the Bank is relying on a combination of academic research, in-house analysis, and pragmatic judgment.

International Monetary System

Finally, consider a third challenge. The international monetary system frustrates adjustment and builds stresses. Current account surplus countries accumulate massive reserves, forcing a deflationary response on others. As a consequence, global economic growth is both more volatile and suboptimal. There is a need for a new international architecture, one that promotes timely and symmetric adjustment.

This challenge bedevilled the global economy during the 1930s. It could only be addressed after World War II, during the career of Louis Rasminsky, our third governor. Allow me to provide a little history. In the 1930s, the combination of fidelity to gold and tight Federal Reserve monetary policy meant that the deflationary pressures from the United States spread quickly, further weakening the global economy. Unable to adjust, countries were forced to abandon the gold standard, which had been adhered to for more than a hundred years. Though deficit countries experienced the crisis first, all countries suffered from the eventual collapse of the rules of the game.

In 1944, to avoid revisiting the problems of the 1930s, 730 delegates from 44 nations gathered in the village of Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Rasminsky was prominent in these efforts.14 During three weeks in July, he and his peers hammered out a new international monetary order aimed at establishing a system that allowed for a symmetric adjustment of balance of payments problems and a liberalized trading regime.

The Bretton Woods system of pegged, but adjustable, exchange rates was a direct response to the instability of the interwar period. Bretton Woods was very different from the gold standard: it was more administered than market-based; adjustment was coordinated through the International Monetary Fund; there were rules rather than conventions; and capital controls were widespread.

Despite these institutional changes, surplus countries still resisted adjustment. Foreshadowing present problems, countries often sterilized the impact of surpluses on domestic money supply and prices. Like today, these interventions were justified by arguing that imbalances were temporary and that, in any event, surpluses were evidence of virtue rather than ‘disequilibria.’ In contrast, the zero bound on reserves remained a binding constraint for deficit countries, which eventually ran out of time.

In 1950, Canada faced adjustment problems of its own, and the Bank, as a learning institution responded. Large capital inflows threatened to drive up inflation in Canada in the context of our then-fixed exchange rate. In an effort to maintain price stability, the decision, unpopular internationally, was taken to float the Canadian dollar, which duly appreciated. While this was inconsistent with the rules of Bretton Woods, it was consistent with their spirit, as a floating dollar allowed both for domestic stability and for the market to determine the rate, rather than being set by government for national advantage. Canada’s move to a flexible exchange rate was a precursor to the breakdown of the Bretton Woods system 20 years later.

Fast forward to today.

The intensity and scope of the recent crisis reflected unprecedented economic disequilibria among national economies. Integral to the buildup of vulnerabilities in many asset markets were large, unsustainable current account imbalances across major economic areas. Once again, the international monetary system failed to promote timely and orderly economic adjustment. Some emerging markets today face challenges similar to those of Canada in the 1950s.

Last November, the G-20 launched an important process to address the challenges. Countries committed to promote strong, sustainable, and balanced growth in global demand and agreed on a framework that stresses the shared responsibility of member countries to ensure that their policies support the commitment.

In short, the success of these discussions is critical for sustainable medium-term, global growth. Canada brings to the table one of the soundest financial systems in the world and a macroeconomic strategy that contributes to sustainable and balanced global growth. Our economy is among the most open, and our policy response to the crisis has been one of the most aggressive. We also have a long experience with floating exchange rates and a deep understanding of how to best manage domestic policies in that environment.15

Conclusion

In conclusion, the Bank of Canada has faced formidable challenges over the past 75 years. These experiences have led us to innovate and to become a more effective institution.

As the global crisis revealed, the stakes are high. Canada is a small open economy subject to immense global economic forces. Shocks can be large and response times short. This reality places a premium on the disciplined application of principles-based policy frameworks. The Bank must combine the best of academic research, empirical analysis, and practical experience to manage in such a world.

This means that we will need people such as you: to take the torch and join our effort to maintain an environment in which Canadian households and firms can invest and plan for the future with confidence.

1. The traditional rate for prime commercial loans was 6 per cent in the early 1930s, implying real interest rates (after inflation) of as much as 15 per cent or more.

2. Indeed, the first cut in the Bank Rate did not occur until 1944.

3. See D. Dodge, ‘70 Years of Central Banking in Canada,’ Bank of Canada Review (Winter, 2005-2006): 3-5.

4. The Bank believed that since chartered banks rarely, if ever, borrowed from the central bank, its Bank Rate had little impact on commercial rates. It did not apparently consider whether banks would change their policy if the Bank Rate were dropped. The Bank Rate was seen as a lender-of-last-resort rate as opposed to a monetary policy tool.

5. The Bank was active on other fronts. In April 1936, Alberta defaulted on its provincial debts and unilaterally reduced the rate paid on bonds. Other Western provinces threatened to follow suit. As monetary policy is national in scope, it could not address such regional problems. Fearing a second provincial default, Towers instead advanced $3 million to Saskatchewan. This was an extraordinary move, unique in the history of the Bank.

6. See D. McQueen, ‘Economic Research at the Bank of Canada, 1935-65,’ Canadian Business Economics 5, No. 2-3 (Winter/Spring 1997): 89-95.

7. See J. F. Helliwell, ‘From Flapper to Bluestocking: What Happened to the Young Woman of Wellington Street?’ Bank of Canada Review (Winter, 2005-2006): 31-39.

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Ends Higher, But Retreats From High
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar ended higher Wednesday as it followed through on strength from Tuesday and benefited from broader weakness in the U.S. dollar.

But the Canadian unit was unable to maintain the six-week high it hit in earlier trading and retreated from it in quieter afternoon trading.

The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.0312 at 3:35 p.m. EST (2035 GMT), from C$1.0340 at 8:00 a.m. EST (1300 GMT), and from C$1.0362 late Tuesday.

In late morning trading it touched a low at C$1.0276, its lowest level since Jan 19, according to EBS via CQG.

The Canadian unit rallied on Tuesday after the Bank of Canada left its overnight target rate at 0.25% but issued a policy statement with a more aggressive tilt on monetary tightening than many had anticipated.

At least some of the strengthening Wednesday was attributable to an extension of that rally.

"I would say it's probably more follow through from yesterday in terms of the more hawkish tone that came out of the statement," said Kevin Chau, foreign exchange analyst at IDEAGlobal in New York.

The Canadian dollar's gains Tuesday also came in association with a broader retreat by the U.S. dollar and shift back into the euro and other risk-oriented currencies after some Greek austerity measures were well received by markets.

"It's basically just a risk acceptance story. All the majors are appreciating against the dollar," said Tyson Wright, senior foreign exchange trader at Custom House, a global payments firm in Victoria, British Columbia.

IDEAGlobal's Chau said the market is waiting for monetary policy meetings at the Bank of England and the European Central Bank and critical February nonfarm payrolls data in the U.S. on Friday.

In the meantime, the U.S. dollar will likely trade in a range between C$1.0250 and C$1.0350, he said. "I don't see it going below C$1.0200," Chau.

Longer-term, the U.S. dollar will head back higher against its Canadian counterpart, he said.

Custom House's Wright also said the U.S. unit could head towards the C$1.0200 area, but believes a break below that is unlikely.

Wright said strength in the currency could ultimately prompt verbal intervention from the Bank of Canada.

In its Tuesday policy statement, the bank said the persistent strength of the Canadian dollar and the low absolute level of U.S. demand continue to act as significant drags on economic activity in Canada.

In domestic data Wednesday, Canada's official international reserves rose $365 million in February, the federal Finance Department reported.

At Feb. 26, the reserves of foreign currencies, gold and other monetary assets totaled $57.342 billion, up from $56.977 billion a month earlier.

On Thursday, building permits data for January and the Ivey Purchasing Managers Index for February will be released, and the federal budget for the 2010-11 fiscal year will be unveiled.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Extends Gains; US Data Encouraging
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)-- The dollar marched higher against the euro and U.K. pound Tuesday as a U.S. economy increasingly outpacing its peers contrasted with weaker-than-expected euro zone economic data and lingering concern over Greek debt.

Data released Tuesday showed the freefall in U.S. home prices had been eased, with aid from government efforts.

"You could argue there's a vein of thinking that the U.S. is pulling out [of recession] slightly ahead of Europe," said John McCarthy, manager of currency trading at ING Capital Markets in New York.

The small improvement in home price data only cements the idea of the U.S. leading the way out of the economic doldrums, McCarthy said.

The U.K. recovery, meanwhile, could lag as the euro zone sputters, a Bank of England official said Tuesday, putting pressure on the pound.

Tuesday morning in New York, the euro was at $1.3558 from $1.3597 late Monday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at Y90.78 from Y91.13, while the euro was at Y123.08 from Y123.94. The U.K. pound was at $1.5435 from $1.5480. The dollar was at CHF1.0814 from CHF1.0761.

The ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the greenback against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, was at 80.705 from 80.552.

The S&P Case-Shiller home-price indexes showed continuing improvement in December, according to the report released Tuesday. The 10-city and 20-city composites saw annual declines of 2.4% and 3.1%, respectively. Economists had expected the 20-City index to fall 3.2%.

The two indexes have seen improvements in their annual rates of change every month since the beginning of 2009. On a seasonally adjusted basis, both the 10-city and 20-city indexes rose 0.3% in December over November.

"Even in the areas that are still soft, the declines in price are much reduced," said Alan Ruskin, global head of currency strategy for RBS Securities in Stamford, Ct.

The slow-but-steady improvement in many measures of the U.S. economic recovery contrasted a slip in Germany's Ifo business expectations survey index, which unexpectedly fell, casting a pall on the pace of a euro-zone recovery. The February index fell to 95.2 from 95.8 in January, its first drop in 11 months; analysts had expected the Ifo business-sentiment index to have risen to 96.4.

The U.K. pound also slipped as Bank of England Governor Mervyn King said weaker euro zone growth could dent a nascent U.K. recovery. Giving evidence to U.K. lawmakers Tuesday, King said recovery in the euro zone "appears to have stalled."

Asked whether the BOE would restart its bond-buying program, called quantitative easing, King said: "I don't know, but we stand ready to do whatever seems appropriate."

A restart of the bond-buying program would likely weigh on the pound.

Separately, the euro spiked against the Swiss franc during Asian trading to CHF1.4684 from CHF1.4630. Five dealers in Tokyo said speculators bought amid talk in the market the Swiss National Bank had been buying. The SNB, as is its policy, wouldn't comment.

The SNB is thought to have intervened in the currency markets on three occasions this month, including an unusual move late afternoon Feb. 12 just as the U.S. markets were heading into a long holiday weekend.

The SNB has been intervening regularly since March 2009 in an attempt to stave off the threat of deflation, or a persistent decline in consumer prices, and to bolster the Swiss exports; the euro's broad weakness since the beginning of the year, due in part to concerns over the fiscal health of the weaker members in the euro zone, has forced the Swiss central bank to step up its interventions.

Canada Morning 
 

The Canadian dollar was lower Tuesday morning as it remained under the sway of broader fluctuations in risk appetite without any significant economic data or other domestic factors to provide guidance.

The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.0439 from C$1.0423 late Monday.

News that Canadian property company Brookfield Asset Management Inc. is readying a bid to take a large stake in U.S. mall owner General Growth Properties Inc. could put some pressure on the Canadian dollar in coming sessions, although details of the proposed deal haven't yet been released.

BMO Capital Markets said the move higher by the U.S./Canadian dollar pair in earlier trading was mainly players with short positions in the U.S. dollar bailing out as that currency rallied last night.

"So far we have seen some small sellers around 1.0450 but our gut tells us that overall risk aversion will push this pair higher," BMO said.

"We expect to see decent offers at 1.0480 and then 1.0530, but it appears the pair will remain range bound today," BMO said.

-By Bradley Davis, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2654; bradley.davis@dowjones.com

title: Forex  Focus: The Loonie Will Likely Take Off Again
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada may well need to clip the Canadian dollar's wings more if it wants to stop the currency from rising.

If the bank doesn't, the loonie dollar could make it back up to parity against its U.S. counterpart in a matter of weeks.

The last time the loonie made a sustained break of that level was back in May 2008.

See the Canadian dollar's recent gains against the U.S. dollar

http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/3310 ("http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/3310")

At the moment, the currency is under a little pressure -- hurt like other commodity currencies by talk that China is putting its foot on the economic brake to slow its rampant growth.

Fear that demand from China itself, as well as demand from other economies that depend on Chinese growth, will fall has helped to dampen recent investor interest in the Canadian currency.

The Bank of Canada also helped to remove some support when its policy meeting this week proved to be even less eventful than forecast.

The market had expected the central bank to leave rates unchanged at 0.25% but some analysts had been looking for it to be a little more hawkish and suggest that rates could be lifted before the second half of the year.

In the event, the bank didn't. Its statement on the outlook was as dovish as the last one in December.

However, the bank did appear to be a little more tolerant of the Canadian dollar's recent rise. The bank repeated that the currency's persistent strength puts a drag on the economy but it failed to be any more critical than it was in its December statement, even though the U.S. dollar has fallen about 3% against the loonie since then.

In December, the bank downgraded its opposition to the currency's appreciation.

"We believe this signals increased confidence in the ability of the Canadian economy to weather currency 'strength' and may indicate that the Bank of Canada's 'pain threshold' on U.S. dollar/Canadian dollar is drifting lower," said Todd Elmer, currency strategist with Citigroup.

In the meantime, despite the central bank's caution on the economy, some analysts are starting to bet that the first hike in interest rates will come sooner than expected as the Canadian economy continues to recover.

Much could depend on just how quickly inflation pressure starts to pick up. The latest price data on Wednesday showed annual consumer price rises accelerating to 1.3% in December from 1.0% in November.

Some market participants think that the Bank of Canada could still resort to market intervention to prevent any rally in the currency. Others reckon that with rates down at 0.25%, the loonie could well prove popular as a funding currency as carry trades that favor currencies with higher yields return.

Chances are that the loonie, which has steadily pushed the U.S. dollar down from nearly CAD1.28 a year or so ago, will continue pushing ahead, especially if central banks elsewhere start looking at it as a reserve currency, now that both the U.S. dollar and the debt-troubled euro are falling out of favor.

Early Thursday in Europe, the dollar was a little lower at CAD1.0471 from CAD1.0478 late on Wednesday in New York, according to EBS.

The dollar was mixed elsewhere as well as news that China's GDP grew by 10.7% in the fourth quarter of last year, up from 8.9% in the previous quarter, and that inflation rose to 1.9% from 1.7%, which left investors concerned that the country will soon slam on the monetary brakes to prevent overheating.

The dollar was up at Y91.56 from Y91.23, while the euro was down a little at $1.4090 from $1.4102. The euro was also up at Y129.06 from Y128.69.

title: UPDATE 1-POLL-Most Canada dealers see bank keeping rate pledge
text:
* No rate change expected in Dec and Jan

* Slim chance of BoC intervening in currency markets

* Dealers say quantitative easing also unlikely (Adds comments)

By Frank Pingue

TORONTO, Dec 4 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada is likely to stick to its conditional pledge to keep its key interest rate at near-zero levels through the second quarter of 2010, most of Canada's primary securities dealers predicted on Friday.

Most also saw only a marginal chance the central bank would opt to intervene in currency markets or introduce some form of 


quantitative easing -- effectively printing money to buy market
securities -- at some time over the next 12 months.
 "The inflation outlook is fairly subdued, especially with
the (Canadian) currency possibly headed towards parity," said
Sal Guatieri, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.
 "Everything is on track ... I don't think the Bank of


Canada will adjust its economic outlook. Inflation is likely to get back to target in third quarter 2011."

All 12 of Canada's dealers, surveyed by Reuters after better-than-expected jobs data for November, forecast the central bank would stay committed to its pledge of low interest rates at its Dec. 8 policy announcement.

The central bank said in April it would keep the overnight rate at a record low 0.25 percent, as long as inflation remains in check, until at least the end of June 2010. It has reiterated its intention to do this many times.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Pares Losses As Dubai Debt Fears Remain
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The dollar recovered some of its earlier losses Monday morning in New York as investors continue to fret over Dubai's debt crisis despite the United Arab Emirates' move to provide funds to local banks.

While safe-haven buying has once again lent support to the greenback, the U.S. currency remains down on the day versus most major rivals.

The greenback will likely take further cues from U.S. stocks, as weaker equity prices tend to erode demand for riskier assets, including the euro and other higher-yielding currencies. Futures on the Standard & Poor's 500 index indicate a slightly lower open.

In Monday morning trading, the euro was trading at $1.5010, from $1.4955 late Friday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at Y86.46, from Y86.75, while the euro was at Y129.80, from Y129.71. The U.K. pound was at $1.6470, from $1.6487. The dollar was at CHF1.0037, from CHF1.0064.

The Dollar Index, which tracks the greenback against a trade-weighted basket of six currencies, was at 74.774 from 75.034.

European equities have turned lower as caution overtook optimism after statements from a Dubai Finance Ministry official indicated that state-run Dubai World's liabilities aren't guaranteed by the government.

"There's still concern that (Dubai's debt problems) could spiral into something worse, so you have the domino effect," said Jacob Oubina, a currency strategist at Forex.com in Bedminster, N.J.

"As long as stocks remain in negative terrain in New York, the euro will continue to struggle with the $1.51" level, he said.

The euro rose as far as $1.5085 during Asian trading in the wake of news that the UAE's central bank will provide funds to banks with exposure to state-run Dubai World's debt, after the conglomerate announced last week a six-month payment standstill on its debt.

Dubai World, an investment company in property and financial services, accounts for about $60 billion of the city-state's $80 billion in liabilities.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi are two of the seven emirates that make up the U.A.E. The Central Bank is mainly backed by Abu Dhabi.

News of the UAE's financial support to Dubai's banks "does little to convince foreign bond holders that they're not going to take a hit," said Chris Turner, head of foreign exchange strategy at ING Financial Markets in London.

After stocks in Asia rose on improved sentiment, European equities fell into the red as concerns increased over Dubai's debt problems after statements made by Abdulrahman Al Saleh, director general of Dubai's Department of Finance to state-run Dubai TV Monday.

"The company received financing based on its project schedule, not a government guarantee...they [the lenders] have deemed Dubai World as part of the government and this is not true," Al Saleh said.

Losses in European bourses "imply ongoing jitters with the Dubai fallout, especially as U.K. banks have yet to unveil their exposure to the Gulf markets," said Ashraf Laidi, chief strategist at CMC Markets in London.

Meanwhile, the dollar recovered some of its earlier losses against the yen after Japanese Strategy Minister Naoto Kan said the government had agreed to measures to stop the yen's rise. Kan didn't specify what measures would be used.

The greenback had fallen as far as Y85.96 during Asian trading.

Also, Japanese Finance Minister Hirohisa Fujii Monday denied saying that intervention in foreign exchange markets was unthinkable for the time being.

"I never said anything like that," Fujii told a group of reporters.

Earlier in the day, a report in the Mainichi Shimbun quoted Fujii as saying: "(We're) now at the stage of monitoring the (currency market) situations and (intervention) is unthinkable."

Canada Morning 

The Canadian dollar is modestly higher Monday morning, reflecting the general, moderate retreat by the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar is trading at C$1.0598 from C$1.0612 late Friday.

The Canadian dollar retreated slightly after Statistics Canada reported the economy emerged from the first recession in almost 20 years in the third quarter, though the recovery was slower than expected and lagged behind the U.S.

StatsCan said gross domestic product expanded an annualized 0.4% in the third quarter after three consecutive declines, weaker than the expected 1.0% gain.

BMO Capital Markets said liquidity in the currency is expected to return to more normal levels after last week's diminished liquidity contributed to fairly volatile treading conditions.

Monday's price action is likely to be determined by month-end flows, BMO said. The short to medium-term outlook for the pair has it confined to roughly a C$1.0425 to C$1.0750 range, BMO added.

title: FOREX  VIEW: Only Fleeting C$ Boost From Russian Interest
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--News that Russia's central bank is edging closer to adding Canadian dollars to its reserves will likely have only a fleeting impact on the currency, with overall U.S. dollar gyrations playing a bigger role in its short-term movements.

The Canadian currency rallied sharply in overnight trading Wednesday, extending earlier gains after the Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian central bank's head of open market operations, Sergei Shvetsov, said in comments to the State Duma the central bank is undergoing "technical preparations for operations in Canadian dollars."

In late morning trading, the U.S. dollar had recovered to the C$1.0500 area from an intraday low at C$1.0452, but remained down significantly from C$1.0592 late Tuesday, according to EBS via CQG.

Analysts cautioned against attributing too much significance to the news, linking instead the Canadian dollar's gains to the pervasive weakness in the U.S. dollar.

"On a day when the dollar has fallen to new lows [for 2009] against the euro, fallen below par against the Swiss franc, is down over a cent against the British pound, [and at] new lows against the yen since January, I don't know if we really need the Russians to be buying the Canadian dollar to signal a Canadian dollar rally," said Marc Chandler, chief currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

"If we were to talk about the Canadian dollar in a vacuum, I would say it's as good as any story out there, but I would say it probably gives a news item too much credibility," he said.

"The Canadian dollar was already stronger ahead of those comments on the back of the U.S. dollar being sold generally," said Adam Cole, head of currency strategy at RBC Capital Markets in London.

"It's partly CAD-specific and it's partly just the dollar looking very sad [against] all the majors," he said.

Another reason not to exaggerate the significance of the Russian news is that the Russian central bank's intention was already known. In September, the central bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said that Canadian and Australian dollars could be added to reserves in the future.

Russia have also acknowledged liquidity issues associated with expanding into currencies such as the Canadian dollar.

"In the past, when the Russians have talked about the Canadian dollar, they've acknowledged...the lack of sufficient supply," Chandler said.

More broadly, the Canadian dollar has limited prospects as a reserve currency globally, in part because of liquidity constraints with the currency and the country's bond market.

"There doesn't seem to be a whole lot of room for the Canadian dollar as a reserve asset," Chandler said.

In the meantime, the Canadian dollar will continue to be driven by overall U.S. dollar movements, and in recent trading the greenback has been moving lower against the euro and other key currencies.

The U.S. dollar is under pressure and risk-oriented assets and currencies are prospering because of the abundance of liquidity in global financial markets, Chandler said.

RBC's Cole said the Canadian dollar appears poised to strengthen further, but its potential appreciation could be curbed by fears among traders that the Bank of Canada could once again intervene verbally against it.

"I think there is a general sense that the Bank of Canada is not comfortable and will try and talk the currency down. That will slow the pace of appreciation, but ultimately won't stop it," he said.

RBC expects the Canadian dollar will again test parity against its U.S. counterpart, but not likely until the New Year.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Remains Under Pressure On Asian Data
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The dollar remained near 15-month lows against a basket of major currencies in morning trading Wednesday, as positive Asian economic data continued to boost optimism into the North American session for a global economic recovery.

The euro overnight gained strongly on the positive data, hitting $1.5049, close to its 2009 high of $1.5064. If the euro breaks through its 2009 high in New York trading, it could rally beyond $1.52, according to Citigroup analysts.

U.S. stocks are expected to open higher. With no important U.S. economic data on tap and with the U.S. and Canadian Veterans Day holidays keeping trading subdued, higher-yielding currencies are likely to extend their gains if stocks rally.

In early morning trading, the euro was at $1.5016 from $1.4978 late Tuesday, according to EBS via CQG. The dollar was at Y89.88 from Y89.84, while the euro was at Y134.98 from Y134.58. The U.K pound was at $1.6643 from $1.6728. The dollar was at CHF1.0057 from CHF1.0083.

The Dollar Index, a trade-weighted basket of six currencies, was at 74.943 from 75.052.

"The momentum and the conviction that the Fed will not raise rates any time soon, coupled with the fact that the major central banks continue to provide liquidity liberally, the fundamental force weighing on the dollar persists," said Marc Chandler, global head of foreign exchange for Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

The dollar fell to its lowest level against the euro in more than two weeks in overnight trading; the euro remained well above $1.50 after failing Tuesday to muster the strength to rally past the psychologically important level as U.S. stocks wavered.

But the positive Asian economic data bolstered risk appetite, leading to gains in commodities, most Asian stocks and in European bourses so far Wednesday, though the slow trading day--with U.S. bond markets closed--could also stall the euro's gains.

"The China news is stirring the stock market higher, but without any kind of further news [in the North American session], I have a feeling we're more likely to see a stall," in the euro's gains against the dollar, said Brian Dolan, chief currency strategist at Forex.com in Bedminster, N.J.

The data showed China's industrial output for October surged 16.1% from a year earlier, outpacing a 15.5% rise forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires survey of economists.

In Japan, machinery orders rose by 10.5% in September, which UniCredit economists said was a good sign for "the sustainability of growth," and which was much stronger than the 3.2% increase predicted by a Dow Jones survey of economists.

Also overnight, sterling lurched sharply lower after Bank of England Governor Mervyn King said in a press conference accompanying the BOE's quarterly inflation report that recent sterling weakness would be supportive to an export-led recovery.

The weakness reflected expectations that U.K. interest rates will remain super-low for a long period, as well as investors' anxiety about the U.K.'s expanding debt burden, which could hamper the country's economic recovery.

This is not the first time that King has referred to sterling weakness in these terms. Nonetheless, the pound sank from a spike to $1.6798 against the dollar to the $1.6650 area. It has since recovered slightly, but remains weaker on the day.

Meanwhile, China came under new pressure from Pacific Rim countries Wednesday to let it currency rise, even as the U.S. stepped up its commitment to a strong dollar ahead of a regional summit.

As finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum were preparing to call for more currency flexibility--generally code for a rise in the yuan--U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, gave a particularly spirited defense of the U.S. currency.

"I believe deeply that it's very important for the U.S. and the economic health of the U.S. that we maintain a strong dollar," Geithner said in Tokyo before joining fellow APEC finance ministers in Singapore.

"We bear special responsibility for trying to make sure that we are implementing policy in the U.S. that will sustain confidence not just among American investors and ... savers but investors around the world" that the U.S. will fix its budgetary problems as its economy improves.

In Beijing, China's central bank made a rare change to the official language of its exchange-rate policy, giving a nod to concerns about the declining dollar and surging capital inflows.

The People's Bank of China said in a quarterly report it will take into account "changes in international capital flows and the trends of major currencies" in exchange-rate policy.


 
  Canada Morning 
 

The Canadian dollar was up sharply Wednesday morning and was outperforming a broad range of other currencies in response to strength in equities and crude oil futures and a general interest in riskier assets.

The U.S. dollar was at C$1.0453 from C$1.0500 late Tuesday. It dropped to a session low at C$1.0434, its lowest level since Oct. 22, according to EBS via CQG, before rebounding modestly.

TD Securities said the Canadian dollar is the top performer in the overnight session, and it looks for more Canadian dollar strength against the U.S. dollar, and more Canadian dollar outperformance generally, as the risk environment remains positive.

"I think you're seeing a little bit of momentum, technical type (U.S. dollar) selling, as well, over the last 24 hours or so," said David Bradley, director of foreign exchange at Scotia Capital.

Market players appear to be targeting a move toward the C$1.0325-50 area, he added.

A move toward that area could prompt more verbal intervention against the Canadian currency's strength by Bank of Canada and government officials, but actual intervention in the market by the central bank remains extremely unlikely, Bradley said.

There are no significant Canadian data releases Wednesday, and bond trading is closed for the Remembrance Day holiday.

Trading in the Canadian dollar has been notably light so far Wednesday, Bradley said.

(Don Curren in Toronto, Katie Martin in London and William Mallard in Singapore contributed to this article.)

title: WRAPUP 1-Bank of  Canada  says China  FX  policy "great risk"
text:
* BoC FX intervention would be linked to inflation target

 * Studying of price targeting merits further study

 By David Ljunggren and Randall Palmer

 OTTAWA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - China's foreign exchange policy poses a great risk and it is a top priority of global policy makers to work toward a change, Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney said on Wednesday.

 "They are running a great risk with this policy. It is a cause of some of the imbalances in the global economy. It is a contributing factor to some of the vulnerabilities that have existed and were realized," Carney told a Senate committee.

 "It is a top priority I think for all policy makers to work with the Chinese and develop a suite of policies across all major economies, including China, that are consistent with moving off of this policy."

 The Chinese yuan has been virtually repegged against the dollar since mid-2008, contributing to the further buildup of the country's massive foreign exchange reserves.

 Making his second appearance before a parliamentary committee this week, Carney repeated the central bank's view that the possibility of intervening on foreign exchange markets should be seen in the context of achieving the central bank's 2 percent inflation target.

 "We should only use our tools that we have, which include foreign exchange intervention, in a manner that is consistent with achieving the inflation target. And that would be the objective of any policy action that we would take," he said.

 Carney also repeated that the central bank does not target a specific rate for the Canadian dollar and has options, including credit and quantitative easing, if it feels further easing is needed after cutting interest rates to a record low.

 He said the Bank of Canada believes it is worth studying further the possibility of switching from its current inflation target to one of targeting price levels.

 The distinction is a fine one, but under price-level targeting the bank would aim for a specific numeric value in the consumer price index and would try to reverse any past deviation from that target.

 If the target were overshot, this would mean temporarily tighter monetary policy than otherwise would have been warranted.

 Under the central bank's current policy, which expires at the end of 2011, it tries to keep inflation at 2 percent and ignores any past deviations.

 "It's too early to come to any conclusions. I would say the price-level targeting research merits continued focus," Carney told the Senate committee.

 He would not say whether the bank thought it was useful, if inflation targeting were retained, to lower the target from 2 percent.  (Writing by Jeffrey Hodgson; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: UPDATE 2- Intervention  no good unless policy backs it-BoC
text:
* Needs complementary policy moves to work

* Says current policies are appropriate (Adds quotes)

OTTAWA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Foreign exchange intervention usually does not work without complementary policy moves, Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney said on Tuesday.

The central bank has said direct intervention remained an option, but Carney said it rarely worked long-term: "History has shown that intervention in and of itself, without backing policy moves, or policy moves that are consistent with the direction of that intervention, seldom is effective over the longer term."

He pointed out that the Bank of Canada only targets inflation, not the Canadian dollar, though it does watch the currency closely.

"What is important ultimately is that we have sufficient instruments to achieve our inflation target ... The objective of the Bank of Canada is to conduct, across a suite of policy options that we have, all those policies in order to achieve the 2 percent CPI inflation target," he said.

"In that context, the exchange rate is an important factor."

Carney repeated that the strength in the Canadian dollar had more than fully offset favorable developments in the economy since July and was a risk to recovery.

"The recent movements have caused a shifting out in the profile of when we will return to our inflation target by one quarter, and within that context the bank retains considerable options to provide additional stimulus, were it required, in order to achieve that," he said.

He said the central bank's policies, including its conditional commitment to keep interest rates unchanged through the middle of next year, were appropriate to meeting its 2 percent inflation target over the medium term.

The Canadian dollar -- which has retreated on the central bank's recent remarks -- dropped to its lowest level in almost three weeks this week as commodity prices fell and risk-averse investors moved back into the perceived safety of the U.S. dollar.

title: Bank of  Canada  needs to look at  intervening  in extreme circumstances to keep loonie from over appreciating: CIBC World Markets Inc.
text:
TORONTO, Oct. 27 /CNW/ -- 
    <<
    Over inflated Canadian dollar risks hollowing out the country's
    manufacturing base
    >>


TORONTO, Oct. 27 /CNW/ - The Bank of Canada should look to intervene at extreme times to keep the value of the loonie stable and protect Canada's manufacturing base, finds a new report from CIBC World Markets.

The report argues that by not intervening in the foreign exchange market when speculators are pushing the dollar to heights it does not believe are fundamentally sound, the Bank risks a hollowing out of the country's industrial base.

"Canada could consider what might be called a bounded float," says CIBC's Chief Economist Avery Shenfeld in the bank's latest Economic Insights report. "By intervening only at extremes, the central bank could help chase away speculative flows that take the currency, in its considered judgment, beyond fundamentally driven levels."

Mr. Shenfeld notes that Canada has let markets decide where the currency should trade since 1998, effectively leaving the intervention tool to gather dust in the central bank's basement. The policy of the Bank is not to target the exchange rate, but rather to take any net stimulus or drag associated with an under- or overvalued loonie into account in setting interest rates. He adds that in the current environment, that means leaving interest rates at rock bottom for longer than would otherwise be the case.

"Anyone who has watched the Canadian dollar's performance in the last 15 years would have a tough time arguing that foreign exchange markets are the perfectly rational, calculating machines that the textbooks suggest," says Mr. Shenfeld. "Clearly, it's not simply trade flows and commodity prices, but also wildly fluctuating expectations and the hot money flows they generate, that set the tone for currency movements. The Bank of Canada admits as much when it points out the dangers of recent Canadian dollar appreciation."

One of the concerns in not intervening in the rapid appreciation of the Canadian dollar is that the Canadian economy is made up of many different sectors that react very differently to changes in currency values and interest rates. "If one thinks of GDP as simply an undifferentiated lump of output, then foreign exchange bubbles would not seem to be too consequential for Canada," adds Mr. Shenfeld.

"In the current context, the drag on overall growth and inflation could be largely offset by the Bank of Canada's decision to keep rates on hold for an extended period. This month's interest rate announcement sent a clear message that to the extent that the Canadian dollar will delay re-attaining the two per cent inflation target, it will help keep rates low for longer, giving an offsetting boost to output."

While this may keep the country's GDP numbers on an upward slope, it's the composition of growth that concerns Mr. Shenfeld. "In the real world, the mix of output also matters. Putting people into larger houses because mortgage rates are lower than otherwise generates economic output in the construction industry, and leaves the economy with a larger stock of housing.

"But if the loonie is overvalued for a few years, we may be sacrificing business plant and equipment on the altar of a strong currency. Plants that close because they are unprofitable at current exchange rates might permanently relocate elsewhere. They won't suddenly come back if currency later cheapens. We are hollowing out our industrial base by letting speculative foreign exchange market forces, in effect, dictate the mix of monetary conditions."

Given this, he believes it may be time for the Bank to shift policy gears and intervene in foreign exchange markets when it believes the loonie is overvalued. "To those who say intervention never works, China has steered the Yuan exactly as it pleases, while Swiss intervention earlier this year stopped the franc's appreciation against the euro dead in its tracks. Intervention is a powerful tool for those who opt to use it."

What he doesn't want to see is a fixed exchange rate, "which forever hands over our interest rate policy to the (U.S.) Federal Reserve (Board), and fails to allow any adjustment to longer swings in commodity prices."

title: CANADA  FX  DEBT-C$ nears 3-week low as commodities, stocks fall
text:
* C$ eases more than 1 cent to C$1.0698 to the U.S. dollar

* Stock reversal, commodity drop drive currency lower

* Canadian bonds mostly weaker, but outperform U.S.

By Frank Pingue and Jeffrey Hodgson

TORONTO (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar fell to its lowest level in nearly three weeks Monday, as a drop in commodity prices and retreating global stocks added to losses triggered by recent central bank comments on the currency.

North America stocks had initially opened higher, but reversed direction as commodity prices fell and risk aversion increased, prompting investors to look to the safety of the U.S. dollar.

"The whole world got very unsafe very quickly this morning," said Steve Butler, director of foreign exchange trading at Scotia Capital.

"Stock markets turned around very dramatically and in the same breath the U.S. dollar turned around very dramatically and so we've seen a big shoot-up in the U.S. dollar and it's hurt almost every currency ... Canada was no exception."

The Canadian dollar often trades based on the risk appetite of global investors and prospects for the country's commodity exports.

Oil fell more than 2 percent to below $79 a barrel on concerns that a sluggish economic recovery will keep global demand low. Gold also hit a 10-day trough.

At mid-afternoon, the Canadian dollar fell to C$1.0698 to the U.S. dollar, or 93.48 U.S. cents, its lowest since Oct. 6, and down from C$1.0519 to the U.S. dollar, or 95.07 U.S. cents, at Friday's close.

The currency had already taken a hit last week after the Bank of Canada and Governor Mark Carney warned that a rally toward parity with the greenback was a risk to growth and mentioned the possibility of intervention.

"Obviously, Carney's comments and the Bank of Canada statement have taken a little bit of wind out of the sail of the Canadian dollar near term," said Firas Askari, head of foreign exchange trading at BMO Capital Markets.

Carney echoed the comments in a speech in Montreal on Monday, repeating the central bank's view that the current strength in the Canadian dollar would more than fully offset favorable economic developments since July.

Canadian government bond prices, with no domestic data to consider until later this week, were mostly weaker, mirroring losses in U.S. Treasury bonds, which investors sold ahead of a record round of new debt auctions.

The two-year Canadian government bond fell 1 Canadian cent to C$99.42 to yield 1.533 percent, while the 10-year bond fell 30 Canadian cents to C$101.65 to yield 3.545 percent.

Canadian bonds mostly outperformed U.S. issues, with the 10-year yield 3 basis points below its U.S. counterpart, compared with 2 basis points above on Friday. (Editing by Rob Wilson)

title: CANADA  FX  DEBT-C$ lower as BoC warnings on strength linger
text:
* C$ falls to overnight low of C$1.0535 to the US$

* Bond prices pinned lower across the curve

By Frank Pingue

TORONTO, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar fell versus the U.S. greenback on Friday as another warning from the Bank of Canada in the previous session that the currency's rally is a risk to growth continued to weigh on sentiment.

The central bank said earlier this week a surging Canadian currency was undermining Canada's economic recovery, which killed thoughts of an early interest rate hike and raised some concerns the bank might signal it would intervene in foreign exchange markets.

On Thursday, Governor Mark Carney said in a news conference that intervention in currency markets was an option but also stressed the bank's main concern was controlling inflation. [ID:nN22502163]

The comments sent Canada's dollar to a slightly lower close on Thursday, and the sentiment carried on through the overnight session where the currency fell as low as C$1.0535 to the U.S. dollar, or 94.92 U.S. cents.

"It's definitely underperforming against most of the crosses," said David Bradley, director of foreign exchange trading at Scotia Capital in Toronto. "Just a follow through from the comments made by Carney and the Bank of Canada over the last couple of days."

Bradley also said the Canadian dollar would have to rally through its 2007 high when it topped US$1.10 to convince the Bank of Canada to intervene.

At 7:40 a.m. (1140 GMT), the Canadian unit was at C$1.0530 to the U.S. dollar, or 94.97 U.S. cents, down from C$1.0478 to the U.S. dollar, or 95.44 U.S. cents, at Thursday's close.

Domestic bond prices, with no Canadian data to influence a move, were pinned lower across the curve alongside the bigger U.S. Treasury as overseas equities rallied and sapped demand for more secure government debt. (Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: =DJ BOC WATCH:  Central Bank  Keeps Policy Toolkit Wide Open
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada has made clear its determination to use all the tools at its disposal to achieve its goal of bringing inflation back to its 2% target as the strong Canadian dollar threatens to impede the nation's fragile recovery.

That's a key message from the bank's monetary policy report published Thursday, which fleshed out the steady policy stance affirmed by the bank earlier this week, but also made clear the bank still has a lot of flexibility when it comes to policy.

It also dispels any notion that the central bank could back away from its commitment to keep its benchmark rate at 0.25% until the end of June 2010.

Although not specifically mentioned in the report, the bank's toolkit does include foreign exchange intervention. That was made clear in the subsequent news conference by Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney, who said intervention is "always an option."

The bank hasn't intervened to manage the Canadian dollar since 1998, despite the local currency's rush to well above parity with the U.S. dollar in late 2007, though it did participate in the 2000 round of interventions to support the euro. That suggests it would be very reluctant to use that tool. On the other hand, as Carney made clear Thursday morning, it can never be completely ruled out.

Carney said the bank has been unusually transparent in laying out what it judges to be the most appropriate path to achieving the inflation target: its conditional pledge to keep the overnight target rate at 0.25% until the second half of next year.

But if it has to change that, it will. "Depending on the sum of the events that happen going forward, we will adjust policy as required to achieve that target, and markets shouldn't underestimate that," he said.

With currency intervention unlikely, some form of quantitative or credit easing as laid out by the bank in April looks to be the more likely response if the Canadian dollar's negative impact on the economy exceeds the bank's fears.

But the exchange rate is only one variable among many that affect the economy. What's important are the ultimate results in terms of growth and inflation, and that's what the bank seeks to influence through its policy tools.

As things stand now, the bank sees the risks against its forecast of inflation returning to target in the third quarter of 2011 as tilting slightly to the down side. That's only because if it was forced to adopt unconventional easing policies, it would have to do so prudently and that might keep inflation lower than target.

It's interesting reasoning, and it's clearly not that of a central bank that has definitively moved beyond the possibility of some form of quantitative easing.

But it's also important to remember that the bank sees the underlying macroeconomic risks as balanced, and from where it sits now, the bank's preferred course would be to keep rates at their lowest possible level until halfway through next year, in accordance with its conditional commitment.

title: 2nd UPDATE:BOC's Carney Says  FX Intervention  "Always An Option"
text:
(Updates throughout with more detail.)

OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney said Thursday that intervention in the foreign-exchange market is "always an option" to lower the value of the Canadian dollar, and markets shouldn't underestimate the central bank's determination to set policy to achieve the 2% inflation target.

Carney made the comments in a news conference after the central bank released its October Monetary Policy Report.

"Markets should take seriously our determination to set policy to achieve the inflation target. Markets sometimes lose their focus, we don't lose our focus," Carney said. "We will deploy the tools at our disposal appropriately in order the achieve the inflation target." He added that the Bank retains "considerable flexibility" to conduct monetary policy.

He said the persistently high Canadian dollar is a major downside risk to the economy and, because of the lag effect, the impact will be especially felt in 2010 and 2011, particularly the latter year.

"It's a risk, it's more than offset the positive developments that have happened since July, which have been considerable," he said. "It is the major downside risk - continued persistence of the (Canadian) dollar."

If not for the currency's spike, the Bank's new forecasts would have been higher than in July, he said.

Although the story of the strong Canadian dollar isn't new - the currency briefly reached parity with the U.S. unit in late 2007 - the situation this time is different, Carney said. The global economy is emerging from a deep recession and recovery is expected to be modest.

"I don't think we should downplay the scale of the challenge just because we've been at this level before," he said. "It's a very different situation today."

Carney repeated the Bank's commitment to keep the overnight rate at a record low 0.25% to the end of June 2010 provided inflation remains tame.

He said consumer demand will be even more at the heart of the economic recovery than expected in July, partly because the strong Canadian dollar makes exports more expensive.

He said there's a "tremendous amount of slack" in the economy which will offset inflationary pressures. The headline and core consumer price index are both now forecast to return to 2% only in the third quarter of 2011, three months later than predicted in July.

Carney said there are few parallels between Canada and Australia, which recently became the first G20 country to hike rates.

Among other things, Canada's economy is more open, it's emerging from a deep recession, and its biggest trading partner is the U.S. Australia, by contrast, didn't have a recession and its largest trading partner is China. Canada also has a bigger manufacturing sector than Australia.

There's "much less slack in the Australian economy than there is in the Canadian economy," Carney said.

He said pent-up demand and greater affordability has helped boost Canada's housing market in recent months.

He said the Bank's forecasts take into account "some strength" in housing and "we will continue to watch this closely".

He said the Bank is concerned about people who use low borrowing costs to get into the housing market who may face problems when rates eventually rise.

"We do have some concerns about it," he said. "Obviously consumer borrowing cannot grow faster than the economy forever."

He noted, however, that Canadian consumer balance sheets are starting from a much stronger position than in the U.S., and that debt-service ratios remain below historic averages.

He said the Bank is watching the growth in consumer credit.

"We expect prudence from lenders," and also consumers, he said.

Carney also said global current account imbalances are an important medium-term risk to the outlook for Canada and globally and there will have to be "further adjustments to structural monetary and exchange rate policies in some G20 countries". Talks on that have already begun at the G20 level, he said.
