title: 4th UPDATE:BOC Carney:Fundamentals Can't Account For C$ Volatility
text:
(Updates with more quotes, more details.)   

OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Mark Carney, the incoming governor of the  Bank of Canada, Wednesday said fundamental factors alone can't account for the volatility of the Canadian dollar in recent months.   

Carney, who is currently adviser to Governor David Dodge, also said he doesn't favor pegging the Canadian dollar to the U.S. unit, or a monetary union. He said the  Bank of Canada must focus on inflation targeting in conducting monetary policy.   

He made the remarks in an unprecedented appearance before the House of Commons finance committee. It's the first time a governor designate has testified before the committee prior to formally assuming the post.   

"Certainly we have seen substantial volatility in exchange rate markets recently, including the Canadian dollar," Carney said. "Certainly the volatility that we have seen in the Canadian dollar cannot be accounted for purely by changes in fundamentals."   

He said the best contribution the Bank can make in dealing with the volatility is to focus on its "principal and sole" objective of achieving low, stable and predictable inflation, and it was important to communicate this point.   

"The way to inject more volatility is to be perceived to change between targets. And I would submit that what we need to do at the Bank is retain the focus on the inflation target..." he said.   

He said people tend to forget the costs of inflation. He pointed out that Canada has had 15 years of low and stable inflation, coinciding with the Bank's adoption of inflation targeting.   

"That's what we risk putting in peril if we take our eye off the ball. I want to assure you I will not take my eye off the ball," he said.   

Carney said inflationary booms always end badly and it requires "Herculean effort" to get it back on track.   

Carney said the central bank hasn't intervened in the currency market to control the level of the Canadian dollar since 1998. The Bank only does so under exceptional circumstances. He said any decision to intervene is made jointly with Canada's department of finance.   

Carney said the central bank's quarter-point rate cut Tuesday, the first since April 2004, has made the yield curve less steep. He said the yield curve from the overnight to three-month rate is unusually steep.   

"The change in the overnight rate yesterday has a resulted in a lowering of that curve. So while the curve is still steep, at least it's moving with the overnight rate," he said.   

He said the Bank is trying to ensure that issues in the financial system don't spill over into the broad economy. He said market participants must bear the consequences of their decisions, but he said that securitization must continue.   

Carney becomes governor Feb. 1 after Dodge retires Jan. 31. He told the committee that he applied for the position.

title: Opening statement by Mr. Henri-Paul Rousseau, President and Chief Executive Officer of the  Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, on the occasion of the review of the commercial paper crisis by the Committee on Public Finance of the National Assembly of Québec
text:
QUÉBEC CITY, Nov. 28 /CNW/ -- 
    <<
                           Check against delivery

                              November 28, 2007

    Opening statement by Mr. Henri-Paul Rousseau, President and Chief
    Executive Officer of the  Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, on the
    occasion of the review of the commercial paper crisis by the Committee on
    Public Finance of the National Assembly of Québec
    >>
   

QUÉBEC CITY, Nov. 28 /CNW Telbec/ -   


    <<
    -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Mr. President,
    Madam Minister,
    Members of the National Assembly,

    Thank you for your invitation.

    Before going any further, there are a number of things that I should like
to state quite clearly.

    The Caisse is in excellent financial shape.

    The same is true of its depositors.

    Over the past four years, the Caisse has made a great deal of money, with
returns of 15.2%, 12.2%, 14.7% and 14.6%.

    Since December 31, 2002, depositors' net assets have increased by
$65.8 billion, going from $77.7 billion to $143.5 billion at the end of 2006.
Our returns account for 84%, or $55.3 billion, of that growth. Simply put,
this is a return of $13.8 billion a year.

    Our depositors have received very substantial amounts of money.

    Those were very good years. The Caisse outperformed the market and
outperformed its Canadian peers.

    It is important to make as much money as possible in good years, because
in the world of finance, some years are good and others are not so good.

    Moreover, each year for the past four years, I have said and written that
returns like the ones we were earning were not sustainable over the long term.

    The depositors' long-term target return is 7%, and the average return for
the past four years is 14.15%.

    The financial health of the Caisse and of its depositors is therefore
good, even very good. Québec's contributors and retirees do not have to be
concerned.

    The current problems on Canada's commercial paper market are not going to
change that.

    There are at least four reasons why I can make that statement:

    - First, the assets underlying the ABCP held by the Caisse are of very
      good quality; that has been confirmed by the work of the Pan Canadian
      Committee overseeing the restructuring of this market;

    - Second, the Caisse's exposure to the well-publicised U.S. subprime risk
      is limited, and the eventual provisions regarding these investments
      will not change the depositors' financial equilibrium;

    - Third, there is no liquidity crisis at the Caisse. We have classified
      all our holdings of third-party ABCP as medium-term investments. We
      have re-established the necessary liquidity to meet our depositors'
      needs and to continue making investments. The Caisse therefore has no
      need to liquidate its investments in ABCP.

    - Fourth, the Caisse is a long-term investor and fully has the means to
      wait until it investments in ABCP produce the expected return. That is
      not true for all the investors, but it is for the Caisse.

    Finally, I would like to point out that commercial paper is a quality
financial product. It is true that Canadian ABCP includes subprime mortgages,
but in a very limited proportion. We now know that Canadian ABCP appears to
correspond more or less to what it was deemed to be, namely assets of very
good quality.

    We will see, however, that Canada has a specific variation of this global
crisis. The mechanisms that were supposed to maintain the market did not work,
essentially because the international banks that were supposed to provide
liquidity lines in such a situation did not do so.

    From the outset, the Caisse assumed leadership in Canada by bringing
together investors to put in place a solution to the problem. The
restructuring of the market by the Pan Canadian Committee that is overseeing
this project is well on its way and will ensure an orderly resolution of what
was a crisis and is now being put into proper perspective.

    That is the essence of my comments.

    Now let's take a look at some of the details.

    First, I am compelled to state clearly and unequivocally that at no time
during my tenure as head of the  Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec have I
encountered any direct or indirect interference from anyone who has held the
position of Premier or Minister of Finance or any other political or
administrative position in the government, whether in this government or the
previous government.

    The Board of Directors and senior managers are legally responsible for the
Caisse's management and results, and we are always surprised when this
responsibility is attributed to politicians who are not and must not be
involved in these decisions.

    As the most senior officer, I am fully accountable for the Caisse's
results and the quality of its management, and I assume my responsibilities.

    You will therefore understand that I was impatient to meet with you in
order to respond to your questions and concerns.

    In addition to ABCP, I know that economic development is of interest to
you and I can also answer your questions on that matter.

    In the normal course of its operations, under its incorporating Act, the
Caisse prepares audited financial statements as at December 31 of each year
and makes a full accounting in its annual report, made public in the spring.
The Caisse's financial statements are audited by the Auditor General of
Québec.

    Under the Act and the agreements with its depositors, Caisse senior
managers also report regularly to the Board of Directors and to the
depositors, on both its results and its management.

    But you will say that the commercial paper crisis is not part of the
normal course of things.

    So why has the Caisse not disclosed the figures pertaining to its
investment in third-party ABCP?

    If we have not done so until now, it is because we decided, with the
agreement of the Board of Directors, that it was not in the depositors'
interests to do so.

    Here is the explanation.

    Canada's commercial paper crisis does not stem above all from the problem
of subprime mortgages in the United States, even though this problem was one
cause of the crisis.

    We now know that subprimes represent only a small percentage of the total
ABCP that is being restructured, and that 97% of this paper consists of
high-quality assets, as recently established by the Crawford Committee as well
as by DBRS.

    The Canadian crisis is therefore not a credit crisis but a made-in-Canada
liquidity crisis, caused essentially by the large international banks, which
realized that, as a result of a loophole in Canadian regulation, they possibly
could not be legally obliged to honour their liquidity undertakings in Canada
and thus could use their liquid assets elsewhere in the world.

    The result was a complete standstill for transactions involving this paper
and the crisis we know. After making many telephone calls in Canada and
outside the country and realizing that the lack of liquidity could have
repercussions not only for the investors concerned but also for the Canadian
market as a whole, the Caisse quickly took the initiative of bringing together
other investors to find a solution.

    That is how we ended up, August 15, 2007, in the middle of the night, in a
meeting room at the Caisse, with other Canadian investors, namely the federal
 Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP), the Desjardins Group, National
Bank, CIBC, Scotiabank and the rating agency DBRS, negotiating with the large
international banks.

    These meetings gave rise to what is now referred to as the Montréal
Accord. Although CIBC and Scotiabank refused to sign on, the agreement binds
the international banks involved in Canadian ABCP. The signatory banks are
ABN AMRO, Barclay's Capital,  Deutsche Bank,  Merrill Lynch and  UBS.

    Since September 6, 2007, the agreement has been overseen by a Pan Canadian
Committee chaired by Purdy Crawford. In addition to the original members, a
number of other Canadian investors have joined the Committee. They are Alberta
Treasury Board Financial, Canada Post,  Credit Union Central of British
Columbia, Credit Union Central Alberta, Credit Union of Ontario, Credit Union
of Saskatchewan, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation,  Credit Union Central
of Canada,  Canaccord Capital Corporation,  NAV CANADA, Northwater Capital
Management, University of Alberta and  Magna International.

    The agreement was initially concluded until October 14, 2007, but has
since been extended until December 14, 2007.

    Between August 15 and September 6, the objective of all the parties was to
progress from crisis management to control over the situation.

    The initial period was complex and difficult, because we had to gather the
investors around the table and ensure that the interests of the various
stakeholders converged.

    It meant increasing the percentage of support for the Montréal Accord by
ensuring that the Canadian banks, which had not signed the agreement,
contacted their clients and persuaded them to join the agreement. It also
meant co-ordinating numerous stakeholders on a completely private basis,
including investors, distributors, trustees and limited partners. Lastly, it
meant obtaining from the large international banks the information needed for
an orderly negotiation.

    And Québec's Minister of Finance was instrumental in helping me and the
Québec signatories to the agreement accomplish the three things I just listed.

    Her initiatives with respect to the  Bank of Canada and the federal
Department of Finance were very important in enabling us to stabilize the
situation. She did so tactfully because she had to respect the confidential
and strategic nature of the information I provided her with, while respecting
the Caisse's independence in accordance with the applicable rules of
governance and while playing her role as the ultimate fiduciary. Her
interventions to the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the federal Deputy
Minister of Finance contributed to the successful creation of the Crawford
Committee and our obtaining the support of 84% of Canada's third-party ABCP
investors.

    You should know that, from the outset of the negotiation, we planned to
make public the amounts invested by the Caisse in third-party ABCP.

    We rapidly saw, however, that our counterparts at the large international
banks were not prepared to disclose the information required to negotiate
solutions.

    Given the extreme difficulty of these talks on access to information, we
decided, like the other members of the Committee, that it would not be in the
interests of the investors to disclose our own information until the
negotiations on access to information were complete and all the parameters
were known. In other words, there was no question of showing our hand
prematurely. That would have weakened the position of the Committee, which had
to speak with a single voice during the negotiation, which was crucial to the
success of the restructuring.

    Moreover, the Committee adopted a very strict framework for the control
and confidentiality of information. Each investor and each trust disclosed its
information on a confidential basis to Ernst & Young, which acted as an
information intermediary between the various parties. Ernst & Young in turn
provided the information in aggregate form to  J.P. Morgan, the financial
adviser selected by the Committee.

    To give you an idea of the complexity of the situation, the negotiations
with the large international banks regarding access to information took two
months, lasting from August 15 to mid-October, 2007.

    This long period was due to the fact that, under the Montréal Accord, the
signatories retained their right to take legal action against the
international and Canadian banks. Yet, to negotiate an orderly solution, we
had to obtain strategic information from the banks that had signed the
agreement, although this information might be useful in an eventual lawsuit.
To say that it was a very complicated situation is an understatement.

    Once these steps were completed, the quality of the information obtained
from the banks was analyzed by the adviser to the Crawford Committee,  J.P.
Morgan, which confirmed its validity at the end of October.

    When the Board of Directors met on October 25, 2007, it reiterated the
relevance of respecting the Caisse's annual reporting framework and the
agreement with the Crawford Committee.

    With the agreement of the Board, however, I informed the Minister of
Finance that the Chairman and I were prepared meet with the members of the
Committee on Public Finance if they deemed it advisable.

    The Minister suggested such an invitation to the National Assembly on
October 30. On Thursday, November 22, we received your invitation to today's
meeting.

    In short, from August 15 to late October, the Caisse could not contemplate
disclosure without running the risk of jeopardizing the negotiation and
protection of the holdings of the depositors and the Crawford Committee
members.

    Of the 17 members of the Committee, only four have officially disclosed
their position in the ABCP market, namely National Bank, the Desjardins Group,
Alberta Treasury Board Financial and  Magna International. These four members
were obliged to do so because of various obligations applying specifically to
them.

    With issues access concerning to and analysis of the information resolved,
Caisse senior management and the Board have decided to make public today the
level of our investments in third-party ABCP and the level of our exposure to
U.S. subprimes. The members of the Crawford Committee have been informed of
this decision and did not object.

    Now let's look at the figures.

    At the end of 2006, the Caisse had total assets of $207.9 billion. This
amount consisted of $143.5 billion of depositors' net assets and $64.4 billion
of assets financed by borrowing.

    As at December 31, 2006, the total assets were diversified among the
following investment categories: bonds, publicly traded equities, private
equity, real estate holdings, real estate debt and investment funds. The
assets also included short-term investments amounting to $33.6 billion, or 16%
of total assets. These short-term investments constitute the Caisse's liquid
assets, in other words investments deemed to offer a high degree of liquidity
and a low level of risk.

    The Caisse maintains liquid assets for three main reasons:

    First, to meet the requirements of the depositors, which, in their
investment policies, allocate a portion of their funds to this investment
class;

    Second, being liquid means we can rapidly take advantage of business
opportunities to enhance depositors' returns;

    Finally, the sale of investments, the receipt of dividends and interest,
and the proceeds of financial engineering operations increase the Caisse's
liquid assets.

    The Caisse manages all these liquid assets centrally, regardless of the
specialized portfolios they belong to.

    Since the start of the crisis, third-party ABCP has not been included in
the Caisse's liquid assets.

    Despite this change, the Caisse was able to re-establish a solid liquidity
position.  Standard & Poor's issued a press release on September 28 confirming
our AAA rating and strong liquidity position. The two other rating agencies
were also informed of the situation and maintained their AAA ratings.

    What is even more important, the Caisse continues to carry out its
business plan and it has the necessary liquid assets take advantage of all
investment opportunities.

    The Caisse has a total of $13.2 billion invested in third-party ABCP.

    This amount may seem high. Moreover, it is correct to say that, in dollar
terms, the Caisse is the investor that holds the most third-party ABCP in
Canada. But as a percentage of its equity, if we compare it to those who have
disclosed their positions to date, the Caisse is the least exposed. The Caisse
was therefore not the only Canadian investor with a strategy that assigned an
important role to third-party ABCP.

    Now let's talk about subprimes.

    Of the $13.2 billion, the Caisse's exposure to subprimes is slightly less
than $1 billion.

    But let me make this clear: not all of the one billion dollars of exposure
to subprimes will eventually be subject to a provision.

    Currently, the provisions taken by the large international banks represent
from 30% to 50% of their subprime exposure.

    Assuming a provision as high as 50%, for the Caisse that would mean a
provision of $500 million. Such a provision would have an impact of 30 basis
points on the Caisse's return, or 0.3%, which is not likely to affect the
financial equilibrium of the Caisse and its depositors.

    To cite another point of comparison,  Goldman Sachs estimated in a recent
study that the provisions of the large international banks for their U.S.
subprime exposure were equivalent to 8% of their equity. For the Caisse, as I
have stated, this ratio appears to be 0.3% of net assets as at December 31,
2006.

    The remainder, namely $12.2 billion, consists of assets of very good
quality, as confirmed by  J.P. Morgan, the adviser to the Crawford Committee.

    Now let's look at another important matter.

    As you know, a few publicly traded companies recently had to state the
fair value of the third-party ABCP they hold. It is important to note that
these companies had no choice but to do so now, in light of their obligation
to publicly disclose their financial results and generally accepted accounting
principles in Canada.

    The timing of this valuation could not have been more poorly chosen,
however, because the market is experiencing a liquidity crisis and the
Crawford Committee has not yet finished its work.

    We must draw a clear distinction between a valuation that establishes a
liquidation value rather than an ultimate recovery value. It is necessarily
the recovery value that must apply in the case of a solid investor prepared to
wait for repayment of the underlying debt when nothing indicates that such
repayment is in jeopardy. The quality of the assets is the essential
criterion.

    For example, more than a third of the Caisse's assets are not liquid, such
as private equity and real estate holdings. But these assets are not recorded
at their liquidation value.

    Thus far, investors holding up to $10 million of third-party ABCP have
taken writedowns ranging from 0% to 40%. Those holding from $10 million to
$100 million have taken provisions ranging from 0% to 15.4%. Those holding
$100 million to $1 billion have taken writedowns ranging from 0% to 19.3%. The
decrease in value for the three investors with direct exposure exceeding
$1 billion is 6.5%, 8.4% and 25%.

    There are several reasons for these differences:

    - First, there is the degree of subprime exposure;
    - Second, there is the fact that the restructuring of the market is not
      complete;
    - Third, the write-downs taken by certain institutions may be greater
      because they simultaneously played several roles on the ABCP market,
      acting as trustees, distributors and advisers as well as suppliers of
      assets and liquidity. That is not true of the Caisse;
    - And, fourth, there is diversification. Unlike the Caisse, certain small
      investors did not have the same degree of diversification among the
      various trusts, which also explains the differences observed.

    The Caisse will therefore determine the fair value of its third-party ABCP
as at December 31, 2007, according to the context and the circumstances
prevailing at that time. Now that we know what our subprime exposure is,
what's left is to do a valuation of the other assets as at December 31, 2007.
We will do so rigorously, but since the quality of the assets has been
demonstrated and the Caisse is a patient investor, none of the scenarios
contemplated is likely to change the financial equilibrium of the depositors,
given, among other factors, the amounts earned in the past four years.

    As he does each year, the Auditor General of Québec has already filed his
audit plan for 2007, and it includes a review of the ABCP valuation. The
Caisse's overall audited results for 2007 will be made public in February
2008.

    At this point, I should like to state that I have agreed with the main
depositors that I would inform them of, and that I would make public today,
the allocation of the $13.2 billion of third-party ABCP to their respective
accounts. These amounts are generally speaking in close proportion to their
relative weight in the net assets of $143.5 billion.

    The total $13.2 billion of ABCP held in the accounts of the various
depositors breaks down as follows:

    - RREGOP        $4.0 billion
    - RRQ           $2.8 billion
    - FARR          $2.7 billion
    - CCQ           $854 million
    - CSS           $779 million
    - RRPE          $671 million
    - SAAQ          $634 million
    - Other         $650 million

    In passing, I should like to thank the depositors for their continuing
support for the Caisse in recent months, their understanding and their
patience. I know, because I have spoken with the representatives of many of
them, that they understand the situation and that they support the Caisse's
actions in this matter.

    You may ask why the Caisse invested in this financial instrument when
other Canadian investors did not.

    We must bear in mind that the Canadian ABCP market has two components.
That of the Canadian banks is estimated at $83 billion and that of third
parties is estimated at $33 billion.

    The Caisse, like many other sophisticated investors in Canada, believed
that a liquidity crisis on a market of more than $116 billion was highly
unlikely for three reasons:

    - First, a standstill on the Canadian ABCP market as a result of
      contamination by U.S. subprimes, while not impossible, was unlikely;

    - Second, international and Canadian banks were expected to provide the
      necessary liquidity to the market in such a situation, which they did
      not do as a result of a certain interpretation of Canadian regulation;
      that also appeared to be unlikely;

    - Third, we were convinced that if the one component of the market
      experienced a liquidity crisis, the other would also be affected and
      that, since the market represented $116 billion, the  Bank of Canada
      would provide liquidity not only to the Canadian banks but also to the
      entire market. We now know that the  Bank of Canada assisted the bank
      component of the market but could not assist the third-party market.

    Moreover, the Deputy Governor of the  Bank of Canada, Pierre Duguay, stated
in an address he gave in Québec City on November 20, and I quote: "This raises
the question of whether some market failures might be better dealt with if the
central bank established mechanisms that would provide liquidity at terms
longer than overnight, collateralized with a possibly wider range of
securities."

    Beyond the matter of ABCP, I believe it is important to say a few words
about the year in progress.

    The 2007 returns earned by Canadian pension funds will be strongly
influenced by the four following factors: the appreciation of the Canadian
dollar against the world's main currencies, the impact of the credit crisis
caused by subprime loans in the United States, the extreme volatility of the
financial markets and, lastly, the liquidity crisis affecting Canada's
non-bank ABCP.

    For example, figures available on the performance of pension funds in the
third quarter of 2007 showed that currency-hedging strategies have had a
determining impact during the year in progress. In this respect, the Caisse's
hedging strategy alone will have a positive impact of several billion dollars
on its 2007 results.

    We will obviously have to wait until year-end to measure precisely the
impact of the markets and the Caisse's investment decisions in 2007 but I
remain confident about this matter.

                                    (xxx)

    In conclusion, I would like to address another matter raised by the
situation, namely: "Does the Caisse assume too much risk in its fund
management?"

    The answer to this question is most definitely no. In fact, in recent
years the Caisse has assumed less risk and has obtained better results.

    The Caisse's objective is to produce value added, namely a performance
superior to that of the markets alone. The Caisse's basic value-added target
is 90 basis points. Since 1986, or for 20 years, the only consecutive
three-year period in which this value-added target was exceeded and when the
Caisse also ranked in the first quartile of large Canadian pension funds was
from 2004 to 2006. That is shown in table 1 appended to the text of this
statement. We achieved this historic performance while reducing the level of
risk in relation to our peers, as shown by the figure in appendix 2.

    It would therefore be wrong to state that the Caisse assumes too much
risk. On the contrary, it succeeds, while assuming less risk, in producing
better returns than its Canadian peers.

title: 2nd UPDATE:Cda To Tell G20 C$ Bearing Brunt Of US$ Weakness-Official
text:
(Updates with more details.)   

OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Canada has borne the brunt of the U.S. dollar's adjustment as the latter weakens against global currencies, a senior Canadian finance official said Tuesday.   

That is one of the key messages that Finance Minister Jim Flaherty will deliver to his G-20 counterparts and central bank governors when they meet in Cape Town, South Africa this weekend, the official said at a briefing, speaking on condition of anonymity.   

He said the Canadian dollar and the euro have each accounted for about one-third of the U.S. dollar's effective depreciation. But Canada has been bearing a disproportionate share as its about one-10th the size of the euro area.   

The official refused to speculate on whether the G20 will discuss currency intervention.   

Canada itself has no need for a targeted level of exchange rate and will only intervene in the most exceptional circumstances, he said.   

He said Canada has been doing its part to stimulate domestic demand as the U.S. economy slows, but other countries, notably China, haven't been doing their fair share.   

He said China needs to take greater steps to make its currency more flexible to encourage domestic demand and rely less on exports. But while China has taken some small steps, they haven't been enough, as evidenced by its growing current account surplus. The U.S. deficit, meanwhile, remains huge and is likely to remain so for some time, the official said.   

He said the risks of global imbalances have increased. The G20 is a good forum for countries to have informal and frank discussions about the role they have to play to make adjustments work better for the global economy, he said.   

The key issue is about sharing the burden of adjustments to ensure they take place in a more orderly way with less volatility, he added.   

The G20 ministers will also discuss high energy prices, which are a challenge for many countries. They will also discuss the need for sovereign wealth funds to be more accountable and transparent.   

Flaherty will hold bilateral meetings with U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, Mexican Finance Minister Agustin Carstens and U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer Alistair Darling.

title: UPDATE: Canada Ponders The Causes And Effects Of Loonie/Greenback Parity
text:
By Lisa Twaronite   

SAN FRANCISCO (Dow Jones) -- To Americans who live in northern states, it seems like only yesterday that they had to check their change carefully, to make sure the person at the register didn't try to slip them any of those annoying Canadian quarters.   

For one thing, not every U.S. vending machine, coin laundry or parking meter would accept them. For another thing, as recently as 2002, they were worth about 60% less than American quarters, leading to all those "Canadian peso" jokes.   

No one is joking now.   

This week, for the first time since Jimmy Carter was U.S. president-elect, Canada's dollar traded at parity to its south-of-the-border counterpart.   

The Canadian dollar -- known colloquially as the "loonie," because of the bird, the common loon, on the coin -- was already on a rising trend on the back of surging commodity prices.   

Rising prices tend to lift the currencies of commodity-producing countries, and Canada is a major producer of crude oil and metals. Crude futures closed slightly lower Friday, but the new benchmark contract gained almost 5% for the week.   

According to currency strategists at  Brown Brothers Harriman, currencies of Canada, Norway and Australia -- all major commodity-producing countries -- have appreciated by 16.5%, 13% and almost 10% respectively against the U.S. dollar this year. Those rises are significantly more than the euro's gain of about 7%.   

"The loonie's assent since 2002 has come alongside rising commodity prices, consistent with a solid fundamental basis for the stronger currency," wrote Ryan Brecht at Action Economics. "Granted, the most recent run toward parity appears to have a notable speculative component."   

The loonie has appreciated against the U.S. dollar despite the fact that interest rate differentials favor the greenback. In general, funds tend to flow out of lower-yielding currencies, as investors seek higher-yielding assets.   

The  Bank of Canada last hiked its benchmark rate a quarter basis point in July to 4.5%, and is expected to hold steady at its next meeting on Oct. 16. That rate remains below the U.S. Federal Reserve's federal funds rate of 4.75%, following the central bank's surprise half-point cut on Tuesday this week.   

The Fed's move exacerbated an already weakening dollar, and sent it to its 31-year low against the loonie, a new 15-year low against a basket of six currencies, and an all-time low against the euro since it began trading in January 1999.   

The drop led some strategists to refigure their loonie forecasts.   

"We are revising our U.S. dollar/Canadian dollar forecast lower with two quarters below parity. However, the increasingly undervalued status of [the U.S. dollar] raises questions over the sustainability of the downtrend," wrote Matthew Strauss, senior currency strategist at  RBC Dominion Securities Inc.

"In the absence of improving underlying Canadian dollar fundamentals, we see [the U.S. dollar] returning to above parity by mid-2008," Strauss said.   

Canada's economy appeared solid, according to the latest figures. It grew at an annualized 3.4% rate from April to June, above the  Bank of Canada's 2.7% estimate, after growing at a 3.9% rate in the first quarter.   

But economists are still gauging whether or not U.S. growth will slow in the coming months, after the meltdown of the subprime mortgage market. The Canadian economy is likely to feel the pain of any U.S. slowdown.   

Worryingly, Statistics Canada reported Friday that the country's retail sales fell 0.8% in July from June to about C$34.3 billion, mainly due to a decline in the automotive sector.   

Consumers not benefiting   

Canadians have not unanimously cheered the loonie's ascent.   

Canada's prices have not fallen in line with the loonie's rise, which is normally one of the benefits a strong currency brings to consumers.   

Canada's core CPI inflation rate of 2.2%, is within the  Bank of Canada's target range of between 1% and 3%, but it is still the highest of major industrialized economies .   

By comparison, U.S. core prices are up 2.1% according the latest data -- the lowest in 17 months and close to the Federal Reserve's target zone.   

"Canadian CPI inflation for goods has been running on average 1% below its U.S. counterpart for the past three years. That's a tidy sum for sure, but well below what one may have expected given the average increase of 8% annually in the currency over that time frame," wrote Doug Porter, deputy chief economist at BMO Capital Markets.   

Canadian retail prices "have responded to the loonie's moonshot with all the speed and alacrity of a three-toed sloth on a hot summer's day," he noted.   

For example, Porter said, former U.S. Fed chief Alan Greenspan's recently released memoir, "The Age of Turbulence," is now selling for about 26% more in Canada than at U.S. book discounters.   

Manufacturers call for cut   

A strong currency brings its own set of problems as well.   

In an echo of yesteryear, when American manufacturers disparaged the U.S.'s strong dollar policy for making their products more expensive in international markets and leading to layoffs at home, Canada's manufacturers are now urging their central bank to bring the loonie back down to earth.   

On Friday, Canada's largest labor group urged the  Bank of Canada to cut its key interest rates by half a point in line with the U.S. Fed's move, to prevent layoffs at manufacturers that export to the United States.   

"The  Bank of Canada recently intervened in financial markets to mitigate the credit crunch," Canadian Labour Congress president Ken Georgetti said in a letter to Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge, which was posted on the labor group's Web site.   

"In doing so, it demonstrated the capacity to successfully pursue objectives other than inflation control. The  Bank of Canada should be as willing to act in response to the manufacturing crisis as it has been in response to the financial crisis," Georgetti said.   

Other Canadians acknowledged that loonie's appreciation does have a bright side, in addition to relief from being the butt of currency jokes.   

"I love the [U.S. dollar/Canadian dollar] at parity. We are all truly richer, as the money we earn and the money we invest is worth more," wrote Sherry Cooper chief economist at BMO Capital Markets.   

In a research report published this week, Cooper put into words what some of her fellow Canadians are probably thinking right now.   

"The confluence of events of the past two years -- a collapsing housing market stateside and a strong currency here -- just might mean that the house on the beach with the palm tree out the window may not be as out-of-reach as I thought," she said. [ 09-21-07 1643ET ]

title: FACTBOX -  Foreign exchange  powers of G7 countries
text:
July 13 (Reuters) - France wants euro-zone politicians to have a stronger say over the value of the euro currency.   

European treaties and agreements have left somewhat fuzzy the exact responsibilities for who controls foreign exchange policy, giving some leeway for French President Nicolas Sarkozy to press his case.   

The broad outlines however are clear -- it is a joint task of the European Central Bank and finance ministers, price stability must be the paramount concern, and while finance ministers can give general directions, the ECB decides upon actually conducting FX intervention.   

Below is a look at how the euro zone and other Group of Seven countries manage their FX policies.   

EURO ZONE   

Decisions on foreign exchange policy are a shared responsibility of the European Central Bank and European Union finance ministers. Like ECB monetary policy, the primary objective of FX policy is to maintain price stability. Secondarily, the purpose is to support economic growth, as long as this does not conflict with the price stability objective.   

Finance ministers, with advice from the ECB, can reach agreements on an exchange rate system -- as they do in agreeing to admitting new members to the euro zone. They also can give general directions on FX policy, although EU leaders have agreed only to exercise these powers in exceptional circumstances and without threatening ECB independence.   

The ECB has the sole competence for carrying out FX interventions. Nothing specifies that they require advance approval from EU finance ministers, although in practice it may consult them. It has its own FX reserves and can call upon additional reserves held by member state central banks.   

No single European policymaker represents the euro in international fora. Group of Seven meetings are attended by finance ministers and central bankers from member countries France, Germany and Italy. ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet also attends with Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who represents the Eurogroup of euro-zone finance ministers. European Commissioner for Economic and Monetary Affairs Joaquin Almunia also attends some sessions.   

The ECB, in coordination with other G7 central banks, intervened in late 2000 to support the value of the euro.   

For factbox on treaties, please click on [ID:nL13739517]   

UNITED STATES   

The U.S. Treasury has primary responsibility for international financial policy and the U.S. Treasury Secretary speaks for the U.S. dollar. In practice, decisions on U.S. foreign exchange policy are made in consultation with the Federal Reserve. Occassionally, they decide to intervene in FX markets to counter disorderly market conditions. They use foreign currencies equally from the reserves held at the Fed and from Treasury's Exchange Stabilisation Fund.   

JAPAN   

Japanese law requires that the Ministry of Finance "shall endeavour to stabilise the external value of the yen through foreign exchange trade and other measures". The MOF has regularly intervened to smooth the value of the currency, although not recently. When markets are considered too volatile, MOF gives the Bank of Japan explicit directions on FX intervention -- the amount, currency pairs and the method. The central bank acts as its agent implementing the FX policy. UNITED KINGDOM   

The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for currency policy and controls most of the UK's foreign exchange reserves. The Bank of England has the right to intervene but only for monetary policy purposes.   

UK policymakers have avoided making any explicit reference to FX management since the debacle in 1992 when sterling was forced out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism. They did, however, take part in the G7 coordinated intervention to boost the value of the euro in 2000.   

CANADA

The government establishes an FX intervention policy in close consultation with the  Bank of Canada. The central bank intervenes on a discretionary basis, and currently acts only in the most exceptional circumstances. The bank has not intervened in the market since 1998 during the Asian crisis. Signs of a serious near-term market breakdown or the risk of extreme currency movements that seriously threaten sustainable long-term economic growth in Canada might be conditions that could warrant intervention.   

The  Bank of Canada conducts the FX intervention as agent for the government, using reserves held in the government's Exchange Fund Account.

title: BOC'S Dodge: Some Upward Pressure On C$ From Corporate M&A
text:
ST. JOHN'S (Dow Jones)--The upward trajectory of the Canadian dollar since the first quarter of 2007 has been harder to explain in terms of historical precedents, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said Wednesday.   

Dodge stopped short of calling the currency's recent rise speculatively driven and ruled out direct currency market intervention to slow its rise.   

"Since April, the upward movement in the Canadian dollar is harder to explain on the basis of the kind of historical evidence we've seen," Dodge said in response to an audience question following a speech to a business luncheon in Canada's easternmost city of St. John's, Nfld. [ 06-13-07 1316ET ]   

In later remarks to reporters, Dodge expanded on that assessment. He said that the Canadian dollar's appreciation from the end of 2002 up until about April of this year was, in general, solidly fundamentally based on increased demand for Canadian goods and services, such as commodities.   

He declined, in response to another question, to term the Canadian dollar's 8% rise since early April as speculative, but he said the move nonetheless has some questionable aspects to it.   

"The only comment I'd make is that the movement we've had over this period, on the face of it, appears to be a little more than one might have expected, based on historical relationships," he said.   

However, Dodge said "the terms and conditions" that govern when the Bank of Canada would consider direct currency market intervention to temper a Canadian dollar movement have not been violated.   

"We haven't had disorderly markets," Dodge said, referring to conditions that motivated the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's recent intervention to slow the rise of the New Zealand dollar.   

"Nor we have seen conditions where somehow currency alignments have gotten way out of line," he said. [ 06-13-07 1334ET ]   

Dodge acknowledged foreign corporate interests in acquiring Canadian-based companies, primarily resource firms, has had a role in driving the Canadian dollar higher, though he said such influence is "almost inherently impossible to precisely quantify."   

"On a net basis, there has probably been some upward pressure," Dodge said. "Some of the upward impact on the Canadian dollar has come from that," he said.   

Dodge also noted that some of the rise in the Canadian dollar has been a direct result of the downward global pressure on the U.S. dollar in an attempt to diminish global imbalances as represented by the large U.S. current account deficit.   

Dodge said this process has played out to a degree in the appreciation of currencies such as the Canadian dollar, the euro and other widely traded currencies, though not yet to the proper extent against currencies of countries with large trade and current account surpluses against the U.S.   

"What we haven't seen is very much of any U.S. dollar depreciation against currencies of countries that are building up big surpluses," he said, citing nations such as China, Japan and some countries in southeast Asians.   

"The depreciation hasn't been as big as would be warranted by this global rebalancing," Dodge said, suggesting that "there is more depreciation of the U.S. dollar to come."   

Despite recent evidence of a more hawkish Bank of Canada policy bias that has led many financial market players to price in assumptions of at least one Bank of Canada interest rate hike in coming months, Dodge didn't tip his hand as to what the central bank will do at its next scheduled interest rate decision on July 10.   

He also declined to rule out the possibility that the Bank of Canada might at some point depart from its now customary preference for interest rate adjustments in quarter-percentage-point increments.   

"Central banks around the world seem to have gone more to moving in 25-basis-point" increments, Dodge said.   

"But there's no rule on the amount of adjustment in any direction," he said.

title: WRAPUP 2-Canada mulls why C$ so strong, set to raise rates
text:
ST. JOHN'S, Newfoundland, June 13 (Reuters) - A booming economy and stronger than expected inflation will prompt higher Canadian interest rates, the head of the central bank said on Wednesday in an address that pondered, without conclusion, just why the Canadian dollar has soared so high.   

Speaking in the Atlantic province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge admitted the Canadian dollar had risen further and faster than the central bank had expected.   

But he said inflationary risks were rising too, pushing inflation above the bank's 2 percent target, and the economy was growing a full percentage point faster than the central bank expected.   

"At our last fixed announcement date we said that some increase in the target for the overnight rate will be required in the near term to bring inflation back to the target," Dodge said, giving no hint that anything had happened to change that view.   

Many economists now expect the  Bank of Canada will raise rates on July 10 for the first time in over a year. A quarter-point rise would bring the benchmark overnight rate to 4.5 percent, still well below the corresponding U.S. Fed Funds rate of 5.25 percent.   

Dodge, who retires in January, said the Canadian dollar's rise since April has been faster than past experience would suggest. But he stopped short of pinning the gains on speculative trading.   

The currency hit a 30-year high last week and is up 7 percent since the end of March. On Wednesday afternoon it was at C$1.0661, or 93.80 U.S. cents.   

Markets had been watching Dodge's remarks closely for clues to his thinking about the currency's precipitous rise.   

Dodge said there was no cause for the central bank to sell Canadian dollars to depress the currency because factors that would trigger that -- disorderly markets or extreme volatility -- were absent.   

He said  Bank of Canadaintervention policy, posted on its Web site, is different from that of the New Zealand central bank, which recently sold New Zealand dollars to drive the currency lower.   

But despite his obvious surprise at the domestic dollar's strength, Dodge said the bank did not have enough data yet to conclude whether there was more behind the rise than just strong demand for Canadian commodities and for its goods and services.   

"One needs to be very careful not to interpret this day-to-day, week-to-week (Canadian dollar move) as a long-term trend," he said.   

He declined to comment on some economists' forecasts that the Canadian dollar would rise to parity with the U.S. currency.   

"Some of those same economists are the ones who predicted the Canadian dollar would go to 50 (U.S.) cents, so I think you take those predictions for what they're worth," he said.   

The manufacturing sector has complained that the strong dollar makes it hard for firms to compete abroad. Government officials admit that's true, but say it also lowers the cost of machinery and raw materials, which businesses need to be competitive.   

Asked if he was worried about the rise in the Canadian dollar, Dodge sounded almost mournful.   

"We worry about everything. We're paid to worry at a central bank," he sighed.

title: Canada dlr to hit parity with USD by end '07-CIBC
text:
TORONTO, June 1 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar will reach parity with the U.S. currency by the end of 2007 with the help of high commodity prices, ongoing merger-related interest and higher interest rates, CIBC World Markets said on Friday.   

CIBC said the Canadian dollar, which was last at par with the U.S. dollar in November 1976, will maintain parity with the greenback into at least the first quarter of 2008.   

"Between red-hot commodity and energy markets and huge capital inflows associated with an avalanche of M&A deals, the Canadian currency has plenty of octane left to take a concerted run toward parity against the greenback," CIBC World Markets chief economist Jeff Rubin, said in a statement.   

Rubin also said he does not expect the  Bank of Canada to intervene with a rising Canadian dollar and that the central bank would actually welcome a higher domestic currency.   

"With the national jobless rate plumbing 30-year lows and core inflation now bobbing above the  Bank of Canada's target range, our earlier assumption of the  Bank of Canadaintervening against a further rise in the Canadian dollar with rate cuts, no longer seems tenable," Rubin said.   

According to Rubin, the Canadian dollar will also benefit from expectations for the U.S. Federal Reserve to cut its key lending rate in the fourth quarter of 2007.   

At 8:35 a.m. (1235 GMT) the Canadian dollar was at C$1.0655 to the U.S. dollar, or 93.85 U.S. cents, which marked its highest level since July 1977.

title: Bank Of Canada Has No Specific Tgt For C$, Says Dodge
text:
OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Canada's central bank doesn't have a specific target for the local dollar because it believes the value should be determined by market forces, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said Friday.   

The Bank hasn't intervened to influence the currency since 1998, Dodge said in a speech that he will deliver shortly to the ACI-The Financial Markets Association in Montreal.   

"The Bank of Canada today still has no specific target for the dollar, because we believe that market conditions should determine the currency's value," he said.   

Interventions in the currency market are restricted to "exceptional circumstances."   

"Canada hasn't intervened to influence the Canadian dollar since 1998," Dodge said. "A flexible exchange rate is crucial if a country is to pursue an independent monetary policy aimed at price stability."   

The text of his speech was released early under embargo to reporters in Ottawa.   

Web site:   http://www.bankofcanada.ca  ("http://www.bankofcanada.ca") [ 05-04-07 0902ET ]   

Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge touted Canada's success with a floating currency, though he acknowledged it can be hard for businesses to deal with big moves such as the Canadian dollar's 35% gain since early 2003.   

"But a fixed exchange rate is no panacea," he said. It can heighten uncertainty and add to volatility over time and limits how central bankers act because monetary policy must be aimed at protecting the fixed exchange rate.   

Dodge said it's important for Canada to maintain its flexible exchange rate rather than peg the Canadian dollar to the U.S. unit. Although the U.S. is Canada's biggest trading partner, the structures of the two economies are different and often require different adjustments and different polices in reaction to shocks.   

"Canada's floating exchange rate facilitates these adjustments without forcing our economy through some very difficult changes in the overall level of output, wages, and prices," Dodge said.   

A fixed exchange rate can be the right choice for small economies where it's difficult to have an independent monetary policy, he said.   

"For systemically important countries, we should be promoting floating rates supported by well-developed and well-functioning domestic financial markets," he said.   

However, until such well-developed markets are in place, these economies may need to manage capital flows and intervene in currency markets   

"These capital controls and foreign exchange interventions are awkward, and over time, they can lead to a lot of problems. So they must be eliminated as quickly as possible," Dodge said.   

But to the extent they are making progress, Canada and other developed economies must tolerate such awkwardness, he added.

title: Some Canadian manufacturers unfazed by C$ parity
text:
TORONTO, May 8 (Reuters) - After being battered for the past four years by a high-flying Canadian currency, Canada's manufacturers aren't much fazed by the prospect of parity with the U.S. dollar for the first time in three decades.  

"The real damage to the Canadian currency happened two years ago, when it went from 65 cents (U.S.) to 85 cents. That was a 30 percent jump," said Robert Hattin, president of Edson Machinery in Hamilton, Ontario.  

With the currency now around 90 U.S. cents, the head of the packaging machine company said: "If it goes to par, it's (only) 10 percent."  

Hattin said he expected it would rise to 95 U.S. cents then to parity. He added that those manufacturing companies to survive would be those "who have an attitude to be constantly changing and dealing with issues."  

In many cases, manufacturers have managed to adjust to the higher costs and more difficult export climate created by the Canadian dollar's 40 percent rise from record lows.  

The sector lost some 71,500 jobs in the last year but it added about 24,500 in April to stir hopes of a rebound.  

Hattin said there was little need for the Bank of Canada to intervene and curb the currency's gains.  

"People who control Canadian companies, especially manufacturing have to become less narrow minded and short-sighted," he said.  

But central bank Governor David Dodge was not reluctant to talk down the currency last week when he said its recent rapid gains were a "Type 2" move -- central bank speak for a rise that was not driven by fundamentals and could generate a policy response. The comments briefly tamped down the currency's headlong rush past 90 U.S. cents.  

Dodge also played down predictions from some market analysts that the Canadian dollar could hit parity with the U.S. dollar, a level it has not seen since 1976.  

Mel Svendsen, chief executive of Calgary-based auto parts maker Standen's Ltd., said he considered the currency to be the greatest hurdle for his sector to overcome, but he also saw an upside.  

"It's a gloomy outlook for manufacturers, but those who do survive will be extremely strong in the future," he said.  

The Canadian dollar's rise is just one of several headwinds facing the manufacturing sector.  

"Manufacturers are kind of caught in the vise right now because they are faced with the high dollar, but some of the reasons the dollar is high are high energy costs, high commodity costs," said Jayson Myers, chief economist at the Canadian Manufacturers & Exporters.  

Because Canada is a major oil and gas exporter, the currency often pushes higher with the price of crude, which climbed to record highs around $75 in recent weeks, before easing to about $70.  

The Bank of Canada reiterated as recently as Friday that business sectors were adjusting fairly well to both the rising currency and energy prices, according to deputy governor David Longworth.  

The federal agency Export Development Canada, which provides financing and risk management services to companies exporting goods and services or investing in other countries, says on its Web site that "one of every three jobs in Canada depends on export trade.  

EDC deputy chief economist, Peter Hall said, "Any economy that has to sustain 35-40 percent (rise) in its key exporting price over such a short amount of time has an enormous amount of hurdles to overcome.  

"What's amazing to me as an economic forecaster is that the carnage hasn't been worse than it is," Hall said.  

"What's very exciting ... is that we have actually managed to grow exports through this period of time and we're continuing to do that."

title: ANALYSIS-BoC moves to talk down C$ with statement
text:
TORONTO, March 7 (Reuters) - The wording of the Bank of Canada's statement on Tuesday shows it's concerned about the Canadian dollar's push to 14-year highs, but the bank is opting to try to talk the currency down, rather than resorting to the last-ditch tool of currency intervention.  

After raising its overnight interest rate to 3.75 percent from 3.50 percent, the bank suggested its current tightening cycle may be drawing to a close, and noted the Canadian dollar has risen more than it had expected in its most recent economic assessment.  

The weight of the two points prompted traders to unwind Canadian dollar bets which had factored in one or two more rate hikes over the next two meetings.  

It also calmed some muted market speculation that the bank might take direct market action to rein in the loonie, which hit 14-year highs last week.  

"The fact that the dollar was even raised in the statement, I think at the very least, suggests the bank is keeping a close eye on it," said Doug Porter, deputy chief economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns.  

The Canadian currency has strengthened 11 percent over the past 10 months against the U.S. dollar, propped up by rising interest rates, surging commodity prices and foreign takeover interest in Canadian companies.  

However, the most recent advance has come despite doubts about how aggressively the Bank of Canada plans to raise rates, and with less support from oil and gas prices which have eased from recent highs.  

Analysts say this has fueled worries at the bank that the currency's rise has been in part driven not by economic fundamentals, but by investors betting on its continued momentum.  

"The idea in the marketplace that (the Canadian dollar) is a one-way trade is possibly drawing unwanted investor attention with potential implications affecting the fabric of an economy in the midst of a resource reallocation process," said HSBC Canada's Stewart Hall in an e-mailed comment.  

INTERVENTION?  

This prompted some to wonder last week whether the central bank might take the ultimate step and intervene -- or sell Canadian dollars on foreign exchange markets to depress the currency -- if it continued to push higher.  

Serious talk of intervention last swirled in 2002 when the currency was stagnating around 62 U.S. cents.  

But the bank has not actually taken the step since 1998, when it changed its policy to allow for intervention in exceptional circumstances.  

Despite hefty layoffs in the manufacturing sector and speculation about a 90-cent loonie, analysts don't believe the situation warrants such drastic action.  

"I don't think it's the sky-is-falling scenario just yet," said George Davis, chief technical strategist at RBC Capital Markets.  

He said that if economic data began to weaken alongside a rising currency, the Bank of Canada might take action, but by altering monetary policy rather than by direct intervention.  

One Toronto-based foreign exchange trader said the central bank has been much more transparent in its actions in recent years, and would clearly telegraph an intervention if it was thinking of it.  

However, given the sharpness of the Canadian currency's move following the bank's statement, any intervention concerns will likely be shelved for the time being.  

By mid-afternoon, the loonie was at C$1.1493 to the U.S. dollar, or 87.01 U.S. cents, about 1-1/2 U.S. cents below last week's highs.  

"We've seen how the currency reacts today just to a very slight toning-down on the 'hawk-o-meter,' so there's a lot the bank can do before they resort to intervening," said BMO Nesbitt's Porter. (Additional reporting by Amran Abocar)

title: GATA: European  Central Bank  Gold Sales Repeatedly Cap Price around $440
text:
DALLAS - (BUSINESS WIRE) - July 7, 2005 - The price of gold has been capped at $440 per ounce since last December by repeated selling of gold reserves by European central banks and the European Central Bank itself, the Gold Anti-Trust Action Committee disclosed today.  

GATA's finding was based on the research of its consultant, gold market expert John Brimelow of Aegis Capital in New York.  

"The ECB reported on Wednesday a sale of 360 million euros in gold last week, 996,592 ounces at the bank's new book value for gold, or 31 tonnes," Brimelow said today. "This is a huge amount, matched only by the sale of 47 tonnes announced at the end of March (but reported only in May) and a 31.9-tonnes sale last December last year."  

Each of these sales corresponded with gold's penetration of the $440 price level, as can been seen at the one-year gold price chart here:  http://www.kitco.com/ .  

"An indisputable pattern has now developed for the ECB to step forward as a massive seller when gold approaches the $440s," Brimelow said. "Curiously, the euro price of gold does not seem to be as sensitive an issue with the ECB."  

The massive selling of gold in recent months by European central banks, Brimelow added, suggests that they will be obliged to suspend sales in September if they are to keep within the volume limits they set for themselves in the renewal of the Washington Agreement on Gold.  

The latest ECB gold sales were shown on the bank's consolidated financial report for July 1, posted this week on the Internet here:  http://www.ecb.de/press/pr/wfs/2005/html/fs050706.en.html ("http://www.ecb.de/press/pr/wfs/2005/html/fs050706.en.html").  

Brimelow's research echoed comments made Tuesday by John Embry, chief investment strategist for Sprott Asset Management of Toronto, during an interview with Report on Business Television in Canada. Embry, who will speak at GATA's Gold Rush 21 conference in Dawson City, Yukon Territory, Canada, from August 7 to 9, likened the current intervention of central banks against the gold price to their coordinated selling of gold in the 1960s via what was called the London Gold Pool. Embry noted that market demand for bullion eventually overwhelmed central bank supplies then and he predicted a similar outcome soon.  

GATA Chairman Bill Murphy today repeated the organization's belief that, because of their sales and leasing of gold and their false accounting of leased gold as gold still in the vault, central banks possess only a fraction of the gold they claim to have. Murphy added that the purpose of central bank gold sales and leasing is not really what is represented by the banks -- to raise money from a "dead asset" -- but rather to manipulate the currency and precious metals markets and deceive them about reckless government monetary policies.

title: UPDATE 1-ANALYSIS-Is China heading for G7 clash in London?
text:
(Clarifies central bankers not attending, paragraphs 17-18)  

BEIJING, June 2 (Reuters) - Who would want to be the Chinese finance minister? Jin Renqing is about to fly halfway round the world for an English breakfast and a polite but firm lecture on the need to scrap the yuan's decade-old peg against the dollar.  

China's national pride alone guarantees that public arm-twisting at a June 11 meeting in London of finance ministers from the Group of Seven rich democracies would backfire.  

Beijing has declared its currency regime to be a matter of sovereignty and pointedly did not send Jin to the last G7 talks.  

Yet even while officials from Premier Wen Jiabao down assert they will not bow to pressure, economists say the diplomatic calendar and more benign financial markets are opening a new window of opportunity to abandon the peg -- if Beijing chooses.  

Bill Belchere, chief Asia economist at Macquarie Securities in Hong Kong, said Chinese policy makers recognised that a more market-driven exchange rate would make a lot of sense.  

"But this one is going to be more about political concessions that need to be made," Belchere said. "The U.S. has showed its hand and turned this into a very big political issue. So there must be a negotiated agreement on various issues -- a grand political bargain."  

BAD LISTENER  

U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow has given China an ultimatum to reform its currency regime or face trade penalties within six months. U.S. law-makers are preparing sanctions of their own if Beijing does not revalue soon.  

Stephen Roach, Morgan Stanley's chief economist, said this protectionist pressure had changed the terms of the yuan debate.  

Speaking during a recent visit to Beijing, Roach urged China to take action to defuse the threat. The magnitude of any yuan move was less important than the act of changing.  

But Roach admitted to worries that China's leaders had backed themselves into a corner. "For a country with an open development model, China has a hard time coping with global feedback," Roach said. "How do you negotiate if you've defined it as a question of national sovereignty?"  

The rising political temperature has certainly muddied market thinking. Frank Gong, JP Morgan Chase's chief economist for Asia, says the risks have increased of both a bigger initial revaluation and of no move before the end of June.  

Gong says rising U.S. pressure and the imposition of textile curbs last month, just as China seemed to be gearing up for change, had been counterproductive. By the same token, further delay by China would increase the danger of a trade war.  

On balance, Gong still sees a significant chance of a shift before President Hu Jintao attends the annual G7/G8 summit in Scotland in early July, while a delay beyond August could sour Hu's planned visit to the United States in September.  

"The exact time is hard to predict now since the decision is with Prime Minister Wen himself and it is a one-man show now with all the new political complications," Gong said in a client note.  

FEAR OF FLOATING  

The economics are also getting more complicated. China's trade surplus is soaring, reinforcing the case for a stronger yuan. Call it a coincidence, but there has been a flurry of comments by influential economists in official media this week reflecting unease that China is relying too much on exports.  

Yet does it make sense to throw sand into the export engine when investment growth is slowing, property prices are falling and consumers -- worried about precarious jobs, poor pensions and rising healthcare bills -- are saving rather than spending?  

Officials later said that central bank chiefs were not expected to attend next week's meeting.  

But one of the regular G7 club, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge, was in Beijing on Thursday describing Canada's positive experience when it floated its currency in 1950 and then, after eight years of being fixed against the dollar, again in 1970.  

On both occasions Canada was intervening massively to preserve a fixed exchange rate, just as China is now. On both occasions, the central bank was pleasantly surprised how quickly speculators went away once the currency was floated, Dodge said.  

The toughest part, he said, had been to overcome the initial fear of floating. Without giving any direct advice, Dodge's message to Chinese policy makers grappling with the political and economic pros and cons was clear:  

"What is perhaps the most important thing is somehow to overcome the fear one has," he said. "One gets used to using controls to maintain the fixed exchange rate, and one really worries that the market system will not somehow be able to handle things when you float and you relax those controls."

title: Canada Bonds End Mostly Higher In Subdued Trading
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--Canadian bonds ended mostly higher in relatively quiet trading on Monday as North American bond markets contended with an array of influences, including concerns about whether the Bank of Japan will continue its foreign exchange-related buying of U.S. Treasurys.  


   3.00s 2005   101.19   unch      2.28% vs 2.28% 
   4.25s 2008   103.99   up 0.09   3.28% vs 3.30% 
   5.25s 2013   107.54   up 0.12   4.25% vs 4.27% 
   5.75s 2029   110.93   up 0.20   4.98% vs 5.00% 
   10-Yr Spread To U.S. 10-Yr: +49 vs +49 
   CGB JUN 04   112.26  up 0.10  volume 3,393   

Shorter-dated maturities showed little movement on Monday, while longer-dated bonds managed to eke out some modest gains.  

Canadian bonds outperformed their U.S. equivalents in most maturities Monday.  

"(It's been) fairly quiet. Most of the action is at the longer end of the curve," said David Watt, financial markets economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc.  

One factor roiling bond markets on Monday was a press report that the Bank of Japan is considering reducing its large-scale currency market intervention by the end of March.  

Such a move would coincide with the end of Japan's fiscal year and remove a crucial prop from the U.S. Treasurys market.  

Watt said the disruptive effect of the report on a potential end to intervention-driven buying of Treasurys by the BOJ was more of a factor in the U.S. bond market than in Canadian bonds Monday.  

But concern about the issue will intensify in coming weeks, he added. "In a couple of weeks and a couple of months, it's going to be something that we're going to be paying a lot more attention to," he said.  

Another development on the minds of bond market players on Monday was the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting open market committee meeting on Tuesday.  

While the U.S. central bank is expected to leave its key federal funds target rate at 1.00%, market players will be scrutinizing the accompanying statement for any indication of the timing of interest-rate increases from the Fed.  

"The event itself is going to be a nonevent, but people are worried about what the Fed might say in its statement," Watt said. "They have been inching closer and closer to moving to a formal neutral bias."  

Data released earlier Monday by the U.S. Treasury Department showed a surge in foreign purchases of U.S. government debt during January. Foreigners recorded $92.0 billion in net purchases of U.S. securities, the biggest monthly buying spree since May 2003, and up from $75.8 billion in December.  

Purchases by Japanese investors spiked 31.9%, reflecting massive amounts of BOJ intervention to support the dollar.  

In Canada, new motor vehicle sales in Canada totaled a seasonally adjusted 118,779 in January, up 1.3% from 117,211 in December but down 7.1% from 128,838 in January 2003, Statistics Canada said.  

The median forecast of analysts surveyed by Thomson Financial/IFR was for new motor vehicle sales to fall 3.6% in January from December.  

On Tuesday morning, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge will speak in Buenos Aires on the topic "Adjusting to Global Economic Change."  

The speech bears the same title as an address Dodge gave in Brazil last week which did not directly address the current economic or monetary policy situation, and is not expected to have any direct impact on markets.  

On Thursday, Canadian consumer price index data for February will be released. Economists surveyed by Thomson IFR Bonddata expect that overall inflation was at 0.9% on an annual basis in February, while core inflation as defined by the Bank of Canada was 1.2%.  

"It's probably going to show that inflation is waning even more in Canada," Watt said.

title: Bush says yuan unfair, yen to be issue at G7.
text:
PHUKET, Thailand, Sept 5 (Reuters) - U.S. President George W. Bush said that Beijing's currency peg was unfair while Canada said on Friday Japanese currency intervention to weaken its yen would be discussed at this month's Group of Seven meeting.   

 Asian currency policy has become a thorny political issue following U.S. calls, carried by U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow to Tokyo and Beijing this week, for Asia to allow its heavily protected currencies to rise.   

 Following inconclusive talks between Snow and Chinese policymakers in Beijing on whether the yuan should be allowed to appreciate, Bush said Washington would "deal with it accordingly".   

 In a CNBC interview, Bush said Snow used meetings in Beijing to "deliver a strong message from the administration that we expect our trading partners to treat our people fairly - our producers and workers and farmers and manufacturers - and we don't think we're being treated fairly when a currency is controlled by the government."   

 U.S. patience with Japan's ongoing intervention to rein in the strengthening yen also appears to be wearing thin.   

 Canadian Finance Minister John Manley told Reuters that Snow would be keen to discuss Japan's intervention policy at this month's meeting of leading industrialised countries in Dubai.   

 "I think he'll want to talk about the Japanese. We know that one of the purposes of his trip to Japan was to include some discussion on that," said Manley, who, like Snow, is in Phuket for an Asia-Pacific finance ministers' meeting.   

 DETERMINED INTERVENTION

 Dealers reported determined intervention by the Bank of Japan on Thursday to prevent the yen from approaching the key level of 115 to the dollar. The Japanese central bank has spent nearly $80 billion this year, a record, to brake the yen's rise.   

 Manley's comments pushed the yen higher in late morning trade but gains were capped on concern that the Japanese would intervene again if the yen rose too far. At 0300 GMT the dollar was at 116.81.   

 The latest round of intervention came just days after Snow left Tokyo, his first stop on a regional tour seen by many analysts as a bid to respond to claims by U.S. manufacturers that Asian currency policies make the region's exports unfairly cheap.   

 The Bush administration is under domestic pressure to stem the loss of U.S. manufacturing jobs in the run-up to the 2004 presidential election. Manufacturing is an important political and fund-raising base for the president.   

 Snow has been less critical of Japan than China in recent months, despite massive Japanese intervention, possibly reflecting a Washington view that a fragile Japanese economic recovery could be derailed by a stronger yen, economists say.   

 JAPAN MUM   

 Japan's top financial diplomat, Zembei Mizoguchi, declined to comment on Friday on whether authorities had intervened in the currency market a day earlier, saying only that the government's foreign exchange policy was unchanged.   

 "I have no comment, but there is no change to our stance," Mizoguchi, vice finance minister for international affairs and the leader of Japan's delegation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in Phuket, Thailand, told reporters.   

 Asia has a mix of foreign exchange regimes. China and Malaysia peg their currencies to the dollar, while some others float their currencies but intervene periodically to prevent destabilising lurches.   

 The dispute over the yuan is not expected to result in trade sanctions, partly because around half of China's exports come from foreign firms operating there that take advantage of cheap labour to produce shipments of everything from computer keyboards to toys.
