title: Canada  dollar caught by  intervention , bonds down.
text:
Bank of Canada: CANADA OPEN 1.5045 PREVIOUS CLOSE 1.5122 - 

 By Ka Yan Ng 

 TORONTO, June 28 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar wilted from a near 17-month high on Friday, caught in the cross-fire of intervention by Japan and others in foreign exchange markets, but analysts said the softness in the currency will not likely be sustained. 

 The Canadian dollar on Friday leaped to its highest mark since early February 2001 against the embattled U.S. dollar, at C$1.5028, but failed to end above the psychological 66 U.S. cent level for a second session in a row. 

 The Canadian dollar finished at C$1.5162 to the U.S. dollar, or 65.95 U.S. cents, down modestly from C$1.5122 to the U.S dollar, or 66.13 U.S. cents, at Thursday's close. 

 The currency remained steady after news that Canada's economy grew at a very healthy clip in April, but could not sustain the rally as the Bank of Japan sold yen with the help of U.S. and European monetary authorities. 

 "The Canadian dollar became a victim of the intervention... That's the main reason why the Canadian dollar lost some ground, but quite frankly, this kind of weakness is temporary," said Benjamin Tal, senior economist at CIBC World Markets. 

 The Bank of Japan sold yen for U.S. dollars with the help of the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, trying to stem a crisis in confidence in U.S. assets amid accounting woes in Corporate America. 

Intervention is typically seen as a way of buying time for a currency and has little lasting effect. The medium-term outlook for the Canadian unit is still one of optimism. 

 "At this point, it will be very difficult to change sentiment against the U.S. dollar," added Tal, who sees the Canadian dollar trading around C$1.5050 in the near term. 

 Earlier, a report showed Canadian growth soared in April as its gross domestic product rose 0.8 percent, its single largest monthly gain since early 2000. 

 April's strong advance in the economy was the seventh straight monthly one, and suggested it could perform better than the U.S. economy in the second quarter. 

 The report also signals that the Bank of Canada can continue raising interest rates to cool the red-hot economy. 

 Canada's stronger economy has led the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates twice this year, even as the U.S. Federal Reserve has yet to begin - giving Canada a 75-basis point rate premium over the United States. 

 BONDS DOWN ON CANADIAN GDP 

 Meanwhile, domestic bond prices pushed lower on news of Canada's economic strength, despite issues of corporate governance weighing on the minds of investors. 

 Office equipment maker Xerox Corp. was the latest U.S. company to say it had to restate revenues, but U.S. stock markets took the news in stride to seal the first weekly gain for the broad market since mid-May. Toronto stocks also capped a dismal month with an impressive gain on Friday. 

 Still, analysts generally see equities on a negative trend, and government debt could win the day as investors struggle between economic reports and corporate governance. 

 "It's really the U.S. economy against corporate governance. At this point, corporate governance is winning," Tal said. 

 "As long as this is the case, we'll see a flight to safety. What we've seen today is a temporary reaction to the better than expected numbers, but the overall tone is still negative for the equity markets." 

 Canada's two-year bond slipped 10 Canadian cents to C$99.22 to yield 3.926 percent, while the 10-year bond lost 26 Canadian cents to C$103.97 to yield 5.431 percent. 

 The yield spread between the two-year and 10-year bond was 150.5 basis points, compared with 153.1 basis points at the previous close. 

 Canada's 30-year bond, due 2029, fell 30 Canadian cents to C$99.15 to yield 5.812 percent. In the United States, the 30-year treasury yielded 5.517 percent. The three-month when-issued T-bill yielded 2.80 percent, up from 2.78 percent at the previous close. 

 Canadian financial markets will be closed on Monday for a national holiday.

title: Firm Yen Raises  Intervention  Specter But Policy In Doubt
text:
OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- With the dollar under pressure again Friday in response to a terrorist bombing in Pakistan,  disappointing U.S. economic data and another sharp drop in stocks, traders are once again on alert for the Bank of Japan - concerned that a stronger yen could derail Japan's fragile recovery - to resume its intervention. 

 The dollar briefly dipped below Y124.00 during the New York session and hovered just above that level through late afternoon trading. Analysts say this renders it very possible that the BOJ would step in to the market if the dollar continues to slide when Asian trading starts up Monday. 

 "I think they'll make a token intervention around Y123.70," said Glenn Stevens, managing director at GAIN Capital in Warren NJ, suggesting that such a move is essential to head off a major new step higher for the yen. 

 But coming out of a meeting of finance ministers from the Group of Seven this weekend in Canada, other market observers believe Japan would be wary of intervening again, particularly in the wake of comments from a senior U.S. Treasury official suggesting that the Japanese authorities should focus more on stimulating domestic economic growth and less on foreign exchange intervention. 

 "The changes needed for sustainable long-term growth in  Japan are linked to productivity growth, not foreign exchange rates," said U.S. Treasury Undersecretary John Taylor ahead of the G7 meeting in Halifax, Nova Scotia. 

 Taylor's words were seen by some as a thinly-veiled attack on Tokyo's intervention in currency markets - which it has carried out on four occasions in the any weeks at an estimated cost of $20 billion - to prevent the yen from strengthening too much. 

 "This was a very blunt statement...(showing that) the U.S. is becoming more hostile to Japan's attitude," on foreign exchange intervention, said Hans Redeker, head of global currency strategy at BNP Paribas in London. 


    Remarkably Comfortable With Policy



But U.S. analysts doubt that Taylor's comments signify any real U.S.
opposition to Japanese policy.



"I don't think this will have any impact," said Jason Bonanca,
currency strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston in New York."The U.S.
has shown a level of comfort (with Japanese policy) that's quite
remarkable,"  he said.



Keeping the intervention threat at the forefront of traders' minds are
renewed comments from Japanese policy makers, reiterating their
determination to continue fighting  the strength of the yen. "Japan's
foreign exchange policy hasn't changed whatsoever," said Haruhiko
Kuroda, Japan's vice minister for international affairs. "We will take
decisive action against excessive rises in the yen."



So traders continue to assume that the BOJ is closely monitoring
currency markets, with some suggesting the central bank could make its
presence felt not far below current levels. Currency analysts also
believe Japan's Ministry of Finance - the country's guardian of foreign
exchange policy - wouldn't hesitate to order further intervention if
faced with rapid appreciation of the yen.



"Their tactic is to look at sharp moves and smooth them  out," said
CSFB's Bonanaca. "They're not level sensitive - but they would be very
concerned if the yen approached Y120."



Late Friday in New York, the dollar was at Y124.14, above its lows for
the day at Y123.98, but well lower than Y124.90 late Thursday in New
York.



There is a chance, however, that the BOJ might not feel compelled to
take action to weaken the yen, given that market trends may be starting
to point to a weaker yen in any case. The driving force behind recent
yen gains - a major rally in Japanese stocks - now looks a bit shaky,
which analysts say is reducing the market's interest in buying
yen-assets. On Friday, the Nikkei 225 surrendered 2.0% to close at
10920.63, below 11000 for the first time in  two months.



-By  John Hardy, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-2122;
john.hardy@dowjones.com

title: Central bankers say economies looking up - but wary.
text:
MONTREAL, June 4 (Reuters) - The world's top central bankers offered a cautious assessment of a reviving global economy on Tuesday, but played down the risks of an inflationary spiral that could destroy the recovery. 

 Speaking to a high-ranking group of leading commercial bankers, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and his counterparts from Europe, Canada and Japan agreed that things were looking up after a global slowdown deepened by the Sept. 11 attacks on the United States. 

 But, like any central bankers, they also highlighted uncertainties and risks, including the stubborn need for structural change in Europe and Japan and the probability of a slow recovery in the United States. 

 "It's not going to be a dramatic upswing, but events look increasingly positive," Greenspan told the bankers, who were meeting in Montreal for three days of discussions about the state of the global economy. 

 Noting that neither housing nor consumer spending had dropped during the recent U.S. economic downturn, Greenspan said the upturn was likely to be "pedestrian", rather than the sharp rebounds that followed previous recessions. 

 The panel discussion with central bankers was the focal point of the annual International Monetary Conference of chief executive officers and other top officials from the world's leading financial institutions. 

 Topics ranged from growth and currency intervention to what Argentina should do to clamber out of its economic morass - follow the recommendations of the International Monetary Fund, improve banking and bankruptcy legislation, and straighten out messy financial ties between central government and provinces. 

 But the economies of the United States, Japan and the zone of 12 countries using the euro took center stage. 

 "Our expectations for a turnaround in real GDP growth in the euro area has been confirmed by recent published estimates, said European Central Bank President Wim Duisenberg, who is responsible for monetary policy in the zone. 

 "Looking ahead, available forecasts all paint a picture of a continued, but slow, strengthening in both foreign and domestic demand." 

 Duisenberg said he expected euro zone inflation to stay around 2 percent for the rest of this year, falling slightly next year. 

 Europe's big economies have by and large underperformed those in north America over recent years, but they remain far stronger than recession-plagued Japan. 

 Yukata Yamaguchi, deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, said a recovery in exports was finally stabilizing economic activity in Japan and industrial output was likely to show a "moderate rise" in the second quarter. 

 He called for fiscal restraint to cement a recovery, but conceded it would be difficult to lower taxes substantially at present. 

 "We believe that once the structural headwinds weaken, sometime in the future, then the present monetary policy has the potential to help support sustained economic growth in the future," he said. 

 The Bank of Japan, worried that a rise in the yen will choke off its recovery, has been intervening in foreign exchange markets to lower the value of the currency. 

 But other central banks have stayed on the sidelines, and David Dodge, governor of the Bank of Canada, made it clear that he did not think that intervention worked. 

 "The experience with floating exchange rates, given that there is going to be some volatility, has been an extraordinarily good one, and the best experience is for governments and central banks to keep their hands off," said Dodge, whose own experience of helping the Canadian dollar has been limited to strong words as the currency tumbled to record lows at the start of this year. 

 The Canadian dollar, bolstered by rising domestic interest rates and a surprisingly strong economy, has recovered well from its January low, shrugging off Sunday's dismissal of Finance Minister Paul Martin, who was credited with eliminating federal budget deficits and winning Canada back its prized Aaa rating from Moody's Investors Service. 

 (Additional reporting by Amran Abocar in Toronto and Tim Ahmann, Joanne Morrison and Glenn Somerville in Washington).

 Yukata Yamaguchi, deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, said a recovery in exports was finally stabilizing economic activity in Japan and industrial output was likely to show a "moderate rise" in the second quarter. 

 He called for fiscal restraint to cement a recovery, but conceded it would be difficult to lower taxes substantially at present. 

 "We believe that once the structural headwinds weaken, sometime in the future, then the present monetary policy has the potential to help support sustained economic growth in the future," he said. 

 The Bank of Japan, worried that a rise in the yen will choke off its recovery, has been intervening in foreign exchange markets to lower the value of the currency. 

 But other central banks have stayed on the sidelines, and David Dodge, governor of the Bank of Canada, made it clear that he did not think that intervention worked. 

 "The experience with floating exchange rates, given that there is going to be some volatility, has been an extraordinarily good one, and the best experience is for governments and central banks to keep their hands off," said Dodge, whose own experience of helping the Canadian dollar has been limited to strong words as the currency tumbled to record lows at the start of this year. 

 The Canadian dollar, bolstered by rising domestic interest rates and a surprisingly strong economy, has recovered well from its January low, shrugging off Sunday's dismissal of Finance Minister Paul Martin, who was credited with eliminating federal budget deficits and winning Canada back its prized Aaa rating from Moody's Investors Service. 

 (Additional reporting by Amran Abocar in Toronto and Tim Ahmann, Joanne Morrison and Glenn Somerville in Washington).

title: UPDATE 2-Bank of Canada's Dodge says recovery has started.
text:
(Adds details, analysts comments, market reaction, changes to Update 2) 

 NEW YORK, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said on Wednesday that both Canada and the global economy seem to have turned the corner, and said modest growth in Canada would pick up sharply in the second half of 2002. 

 But the recovery will be gradual. The Canadian economy may not get back to full speed before 2003, the governor said in a speech before the Canada Society of New York. 

 Dodge, who last month expressed concern about the Canadian dollar's tumble to record lows against the U.S. dollar, did not play up those worries on Wednesday. 

 "With the improvement since the fall in the geopolitical climate and in consumer confidence in North America and Europe, there are increasing signs that the global economy has turned the corner and will firm as the year progresses," Dodge said. 

 "Still it could be late 2003 before the actual level of output in the Canadian economy will again reach its potential level," he said. 

 Dodge gave no hints about the central bank's next interest rate decision, set for March 5. The Bank of Canada has responded aggressively to the global economic downturn, cutting its overnight rate by 3.75 percentage points since 2001 to 2.00 percent in January. 

 But analysts said Dodge's upbeat assessment of the economy suggested the Bank of Canada may be ready to lift rates from the highly stimulative levels they are currently at. 

 While warning that risks to a recovery remain, Dodge stuck to upbeat predictions he made last month, saying the economy will gain momentum from an annualized rate of 1 to 2 percent in the first half of 2002 to around 3 to 4 percent in the second half, and strengthen further in 2003. 

 "The kind of numbers he's talking about at the end of this year are exceptionally strong, signaling that yes, rates will probably have to rise, but they're not in any rush to do so," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at, Bank of Montreal in Toronto. 

 Core inflation, excluding volatile elements like food and energy, should move back up to the government's target level of 2 percent in about two years, Dodge said. Inflation will average just under 1-1/2 percent in the second half of 2002. 

 Bond and foreign exchange markets showed little reaction to his comments, detecting no shift in the central bank's policy. 

 CANADA MAY SKIRT RECESSION 

 Citing a recent string of positive economic reports, Dodge said the Canadian economy, "may well" show slightly positive growth for the fourth quarter of 2001 and the first quarter of 2002. 

 "Recent economic indicators for Canada support the view that a recovery is starting," he said, pointing to stronger-than-expected household spending, signs of revival in Canadian exports, indications that inventories are being drawn down and a bottoming out in non-energy commodity prices. 

 But Dodge warned that recovery prospects would be hurt if capital investment and business confidence do not pick up as expected this year. 

 "What we see as a significant risk to the outlook of a reasonably strong second half of the year is that investments, particularly investments by large businesses in fixed capital, will in fact not really pick up, and we may have to wait a little longer for that pickup in investment," he said. 

 Canada's economy shrank at an annualized rate of 0.8 percent in third quarter of 2001, and could skirt recession if it ekes out growth in the fourth quarter. That interpretation is based on the simple rule of thumb that defines recession as two consecutive quarters of contraction. The government is due to release Gross Domestic Product data on Feb. 28. 

 Dodge said a flexible exchange rate was important for Canada, but he did not repeat the concern he expressed last month about the Canadian dollar's recent depreciation. 

 "I have no view as to an appropriate level," Dodge said in response to questions, but said the bank's inflation-targetting monetary policy should underpin the Canadian currency. 

 "The route to a strong currency is low inflation and high real economic growth," Dodge said. 

 In January, Dodge, along with Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin, warned that Canadian currency's fall was not helpful for economic confidence in Canada and said intervention to stem the currency's losses a tool in the central bank's arsenal. The Canadian dollar has recovered from record lows hit against the dollar last month.

title: Canadian dollar drops for fourth day, bonds mixed.
text:
Bank of Canada: CANADA OPEN 1.6023 PREVIOUS CLOSE 1.5978 - 

 By Ka Yan Ng 

 TORONTO, Feb 6 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar dropped through the psychologically key C$1.60 level on Wednesday to end lower for a fourth day in a row. 

 Canadian bonds also fell as new supply met with soft demand. 

 The Canadian dollar ended at C$1.6047 to the U.S. dollar, or 62.32 U.S. cents, down from C$1.5973 to the U.S. dollar, or 62.61 U.S. cents, at the previous close. 

 "Frankly, I didn't think the recent rally that we got was going to be sustainable in any event," said Marc Levesque, senior economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank. 

 Four days of declines have pushed the currency toward its record low and have almost unwound all the gains the fragile Canadian dollar made after Canadian officials began a campaign of talking up the currency three weeks ago. 

 "(Canadian officials) may have talked up the currency and tried to convince people it should be stronger than it is, but they haven't backed up their words with anything more concrete than that," said Levesque. 

 On the backburner is the threat that the Bank of Canada may intervene on behalf of the currency. But most observers do not see the central bank coming in around C$1.60. Recent data showed Canadian foreign reserve holdings were US$33.64 billion for January. 

 In economic news, the Canadian help-wanted data for January suggested the year-long decline in labor demand is stabilizing, while building permits for December fell. In the United States, a report suggested solid economic recovery as the productivity of U.S. workers grew at a brisker-than-expected pace in the fourth quarter of 2001. 

 CANADIAN BONDS MIXED, LONG END LAGS AFTER AUCTIONS 

 Canadian bonds started in positive territory on Wednesday, and ended mixed. Long-dated maturities lagged because of poor demand for 10-year notes after an auction by Canadian and U.S. governments. 

 "Supply is knocking the market back and today's 10-year auction results reflected lackluster interest," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 The U.S. Treasury sale of $13 billion in 10-year notes produced poor results because of fears of higher interest rates later in the year and dealers dumped inventory once the results were known. 

 The Bank of Canada's 10-year bond auction resulted in an average yield of 5.397 percent at an average price of C$98.842. 

 The benchmark 10-year bond shed 15 Canadian cents to C$104.88 to yield 5.326 percent. The U.S. 10-year Treasury was down 8/32 to yield 4.929 percent. 

 Despite weakness in the stock markets, bonds couldn't convincingly pull themselves from the negative column as concerns about accounting practices still had a hold on the market. 

 The two-year bond gained 1 Canadian cent to C$103.22 to yield 3.154 percent. The yield spread between the two-year and 10-year bond moved to 217.2 basis points from 214.5 basis points at the previous close. 

 The 30-year bond, due 2029, dropped 30 Canadian cents to C$101.70 to yield 5.627 percent. 

 The three-month when-issued T-bill yielded 1.99 percent, unchanged from the previous close. 

 ($1=$1.60 Canadian).

title: Canadian dollar dips, bond rally fizzles.
text:
Bank of Canada: CANADA OPEN 1.5987 PREVIOUS CLOSE 1.5967 - 

 By Ka Yan Ng 

 TORONTO, Feb 5 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar edged lower on Tuesday, after splashing about in a modest range, uncertain of what to make of concerns about corporate accounting irregularities and waiting for direction from economic news. 

 Meanwhile, domestic bonds ended mixed after poor U.S. auction results and news that U.S. lawmakers appeared ready to give up on an economic stimulus package.

title: FORUM-France's Fabius rules out target ranges for euro.
text:
NEW YORK, Feb 2 (Reuters) - French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius on Saturday ruled out the idea of setting informal floor and ceiling targets for the euro-dollar exchange rate to be defended by the U.S. and European central banks. 

 "If you think about the euro against the dollar, it's decided on by the markets, and it's fair," Fabius told Reuters, when questioned about a suggestion made at a World Economic Forum session that the Group of Seven industrialised nations set and defend a target exchange rate range to avoid excessive currency instability. 

 Central banks should manage their own monetary policy properly and leave the markets to determine exchange rates, Fabius said. 

 Nobel Prize-winning economist Robert Mundell, an expert on monetary union, said a table of businessmen and policymakers he led proposed the next G7 finance ministers' meeting should set a de facto floor of about 85 cents to the euro and a ceiling of about $1.15 to limit damaging currency fluctuations. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve Board, the European Central Bank and the central banks of Japan, Britain and Canada intervened jointly in September 2000 to support the euro after it fell to 84.40 cents from a January 1999 launch value of $1.17. 

 Fabius brushed aside concerns about the European currency's current exchange rate of 86 cents, saying it was better to not focus on short-term fluctuations. 

 "Obviously, some people say it's weakening if we compare it to the U.S. dollar, but you have not to pay too much attention to a situation of one month or two months. I think it will be a success because it's a worldwide currency," he said. 

 Fabius declined to say whether European Union finance ministers would endorse on Feb. 12 a recommendation by the European Commission, the EU's executive body, to warn Germany because its budget deficit is nearing an EU limit of 3 percent of gross domestic product. 

 But he said: "I think the stability agreement is a very important element and all of us - France, Germany, Spain and different countries - agree on that. 

 "I think it's part of the rules of the club and you must not change that." 

 He said he was confident the German economy would recover because the German government was "a serious government". 

 Fabius said he expected Britain to decide, maybe in 2003, to join the euro because it would want to be one of the "ins" making key decisions rather than one of the historical "outs". 

 "(Prime Minister) Tony Blair is in favour of the euro and I think if people share the view of Tony Blair, it will good for Great Britain and for the rest of the euro," he said. 

 EU finance ministry officials discussed on Friday whether to formally warn Germany over its burgeoning budget deficit but failed to reach agreement, sources said. 

 "It was a totally inconclusive meeting. My reading is that there will be a reprimand for Germany but not in the form that the Commission is expecting," one source said. 

 The Commission sparked controversy by proposing on Wednesday to issue an "early warning" to Berlin. 

 Germany's deficit was 2.6 percent of GDP in 2001 and is forecast by the EU executive to hit 2.7 percent this year. Under the bloc's Stability and Growth Pact, which Germany designed, governments can be fined if deficits exceed 3.0 percent.

title: Canada Finance Min Martin Talks Down US Dollar Adoption
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Many business leaders north of the  49th parallel think their government should consider junking the long-ailing Canadian currency and hooking up with the U.S. dollar. 

 But they won't find an ally in Finance Minister Paul Martin, who's been actively talking up the Canadian dollar in recent days after it sank to a new historic low around 62  U.S. cents in mid-January. 

 "We have every advantage in maintaining our own monetary policy," Martin told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview here at the World Economic Forum. 

 The Canadian dollar, which was worth more than the greenback a few decades ago, has lost around 30% of its relative value in the past 10 years. The slide seemed to build up speed after the country's mint introduced a dollar coin bearing a rendering of a loon, a local bird celebrated for its diving prowess. 

 A recent poll by Compas Inc. showed more than half of Canadian business leaders think the country should weigh adopting the U.S. dollar, and 55% are in favor of a common currency. 

 After years of implicit suggestions out of Ottawa that a  depreciating Canadian dollar was good for the export-oriented economy, Martin and Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge have fought back in recent days with a spirited verbal campaign. 

 Last week, Martin said the currency is undervalued and blamed its woes on a "perception problem." And on Thursday, Dodge told investors in New York that the Canadian  dollar's recent depreciation is hurting consumer and business confidence and is "clearly not helpful" for the economy. 

 That aggressive talk has had an effect, creating a floor  of sorts for the currency, which was trading Friday afternoon at C$1.5907-17 to the U.S. dollar, a little under 63 U.S. cents. 

 Martin said on Friday that monetary officials aren't targeting any trading range for the Canadian dollar. 

 "It's very important to be clear the (central) bank has  said, and we share that view, that we don't talk about a level. Our comments were aimed at the direction of the currency," he told Dow Jones. 

 He said that Canada's "underlying" economic trends - including a declining debt load, a current-account surplus and a tentative recovery in domestic demand - were "not reflected" in the currency in recent weeks. 

 "We are very well-positioned for recovery," he added, pointing out healthy growth in housing statistics. 

 Canada reported Thursday that the economy edged 0.2% higher in November from October. It advanced 0.3% in October, the first positive reading since May. 

 Martin said he "fully expects" the country's ratio of debt to gross domestic product to decline further this year.  The government is aiming to cut the ratio to 40% in the next four years from the current 50%, with an "ultimate target" of 25%. 

 Monetary policy officials haven't said what they'll do if the loonie dips again in the coming days or weeks. 

 But Marc Chandler, head of currency strategy at HSBC in New York, predicted in a report Friday that "the Bank of Canada would 1) likely intervene but not 2) raise rates to defend the currency" if the U.S. dollar returns to the highs seen earlier this month. 

 Chandler, who met with Martin and Dodge, is forecasting that the Canadian currency will be trading in a broad range of C$1.58-1.61 to the U.S. dollar in the near term, but didn't rule out new pressure down the road. 

 -By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026 mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Aussie slips to one-month low vs yen, greenback.
text:
LONDON, Jan 30 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar slipped to a one-month low against the yen on Wednesday on expectation of repatriation of funds by Japanese investors ahead of their fiscal year-end book closings. 

 That in turn pushed the Aussie down to a one-month low against the dollar with investors focused on a key interest rate decision by the Federal Reserve later in the session. 

 "(Fed chairman Alan) Greenspan's statement is the key. If we have more signs of a U.S. recovery the Aussie can do better but at the moment the move in the cross is impacting the Aussie more than anything else," said Jane Foley, currency strategist at Barclays Capital. 

 The Fed is expected to leave its fed funds rate unchanged at 1.75 percent. 

 By 1030 GMT the Aussie stood at 67.06 yen , off its 23-week high of 70.14 set late last week. Against the dollar, it lost nearly two thirds of a percent on the day to stand at US$0.5061 . 

 The Aussie has been on a steep uptrend against a generally weak yen since late September partly because Japanese investors have been buying Australian bonds to seek higher yields, analysts said. 

 But Japanese investors are expected to repatriate their funds ahead of their fiscal year-end book closings in March to boost their balance sheets. 

 "... if Japanese repatriation continues then the cross may continue to be sold aggressively to the detriment of the Aussie against the U.S. dollar as well," UBS Warburg said in a note to clients. The New Zealand dollar fell against the U.S. dollar in sympathy with the Aussie. It stood at US$0.4148 from levels just above $0.42 on Tuesday. The Canadian dollar stood at C$1.5877 , pulling itself off its one-month high set on Tuesday against the greenback as investors took profits ahead of a rate decision by the Fed. 

 The Canadian currency gained sharply in the previous session, drawing support from comments made earlier this week by Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge that intervention in the currency market is a tool in the central bank's toolbox.

title: Canada Dlr Seen Benefiting From Perceived Policy Shift
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 TORONTO -(Dow Jones)- The veiled threat of intervention and a nervous currency market combined to inject a burst of strength in the anemic Canadian dollar Tuesday, but there's no guarantee the currency's vigor will be sustained, analysts said. 

 Beginning with a sharp improvement late Monday, the Canadian dollar rocketed higher Tuesday as market players scrambled to get out of short positions in the embattled currency. 

 "It's definitely been the currency of choice today," said Tim Mazanec, senior foreign exchange strategist at Investors Bank & Trust in Boston. 

 "Right now, the new trend is for a stronger Canadian (dollar). We'll have to see if momentum players push that strength even further," he added. 

 The U.S. dollar, which reached an all-time high of C$1.6194 on Jan. 21, tumbled almost 200 points from its Monday close of C$1.6027 to an intraday low of C$1.5841 on Tuesday before recovering substantially in busy trading. 

 It was at C$1.5903 in early afternoon trading. 

 While a mass exodus from short Canadian dollar positions was seen as a primary cause for the move, analysts said another round of verbal intervention from Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge - along with the implicit threat of direct market intervention - likely played a role. 

 Repeating comments initially made last Wednesday, Dodge said in a speech Monday that the Canadian dollar's recent weakness was "not helpful" for the Canadian economy and that economic recovery in Canada "does not hinge on the current low levels of the Canadian dollar against its U.S. counterparts." 

 He repeated the comments again in a separate speech on Tuesday. 

 Dodge also referred to currency market intervention as one of the tools available to the central bank last week, but since then has not elaborated on the likelihood of intervention, or any other aspects of it. 


   STOPPING SHORT OF A "STRONG DOLLAR POLICY"



However cautious the remarks from Dodge and Finance Minister Paul
Martin might be, they are seen by many analysts as a decisive shift away
from the implicit sanctioning of a lower currency that seemed to emanate
from Ottawa in the past.



"This is a clear sign that there has been a potential policy shift
away from the perception that the government wants a weaker currency to
boost exports and toward something more supportive," said a report from
John Johnston, chief economist for the Americas at RBC Capital Markets
in Toronto.



"However, the government has stopped short of a 'strong dollar policy'
along the lines of the U.S. strong dollar policy and its is unlikely to
announce any major change in macroeconomic policy designed to
specifically support the currency," the report said.



But Ottawa's move does constitute a serious policy shift, and changes
the impact of politics on the currency from negative to neutral, the
report said.



Benjamin Tal, senior economist at the Canadian Imperial Bank of
Commerce, said the verbal intervention by Canadian officials helped
buttress the currency by inducing fear of market intervention among
currency traders.



"Clearly, yesterday we saw some technical factors," he said. "But in
the background, the verbal intervention by the Bank of Canada, and
(Finance Minister Paul Martin) clearly helped."



With about $34 billion in the bank's foreign exchange reserves, the
threat of intervention is taken seriously by currency market players,
Tal said. "Clearly, fear regarding intervention is the main factor here
- it's not the fundamentals," he said.



If the currency starts selling off again, market players may begin to
test the bank's resolve and its willingness to actually intervene to
defend the currency, analysts said.



"At one point the Bank of Canada will have to deliver in order to
support the currency. You cannot support this kind of equilibrium where
the bank talks, and the market reacts, without seeing any action," Tal
said.



"You can't just be saying stuff like that, and not backing it up,"
Investors Trust's Mazanec said.



The U.S. dollar could test as low as C$1.5820, but is likely to head
back up to the C$1.6110 area, he said.



If current levels prove unsustainable and the U.S. dollar climbs back
to C$1.6130 (a Canadian dollar level of $0.62), the bank may intervene,
Tal said.



On other hand, the currency's recent strength may create an opportune
time for the bank to intervene, he added. "I would not surprised if the
Bank of Canada would take advantage of the current improved sentiment -
at least temporarily improved sentiment - and give it an extra push," he
said.



But Tal and other analysts suggest another option for the bank is to
wait for the currency to reach its natural low and then start improving
as the economy improves. The bank may use that opportunity to intervene
to support its natural appreciation, Tal said.



He puts the probability of intervention at no more than 50%, and adds
that any intervention would likely be coordinated with the U.S. Federal
Reserve. "We definitely need the Fed on our side on this one. The Bank
of Canada cannot do it by itself," Tal said.



RBC's Johnston suggested in his report that the probability of
intervention remains fairly low.



"Mr. Dodge hinted last week that foreign exchange intervention as a
possibility, though we believe that the BOC will only use this tool if
the currency were to weaken substantially in very disorderly markets,"
the report said.
   -By Don Curren, Dow Jones Newswires; 416-306-2020;
don.curren@dowjones.com

title: Canadian bonds close higher in flight to safety.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds rallied to a higher close on Tuesday as investors fled equity markets and sought the safe haven of government securities. 

 North American stock markets fell sharply in late afternoon action as investors fretted about corporate profits and the soundness of corporate financial statements in the wake of the Enron debacle. 

 Canada's two-year bond jumped 18 Canadian cents to C$103.23 to yield 3.169 percent, while the 10-year benchmark bond rose 46 Canadian cents to C$104.48 to yield 5.382 percent. 

 "It started with the equity mess today," said Hank Cunningham, director of fixed income at Correspondent Network. 

 "I think the bond market actually was a little bit oversold too so it didn't take much of a spark. It's an FTQ day: flight to quality." 

 The Toronto Stock Exchange's main index finished down 77 points, while the Dow Jones industrial average slumped 240 points and the Nasdaq composite fell 51 points. 

 Earlier in the session, bonds got off to a weak start in the wake of sturdy U.S. economic numbers, but spillover sentiment from a resurgent Canadian dollar helped cap losses. 

 Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge renewed his verbal support of the currency this week, expressing his concern about the weak dollar in speeches in Western Canada on Monday and Tuesday. 

 Dodge reiterated that intervention is still a tool in the central bank's arsenal but he would not elaborate on what circumstances it would take for the bank to move to support the faltering currency. 

 Dodge's comments sent the Canadian dollar surging to one-month highs against the U.S. currency, though it came off those highs through the session. 

 "If the Canadian dollar can regain a firming trend, given that spreads to the U.S. are comfortable, it could see international investors looking at Canada more favorably," said Dawn Desjardins, bond strategist at J.P. Morgan Canada. 

 "That would be good news for the bonds and for the currency." 

 Also released on Tuesday were U.S. data that showed consumer confidence rose for the second straight month in January, while durable goods orders also came in higher. 

 That reinforced the market's view that the U.S. Federal Reserve's easing cycle is likely over but that interest rates will remain low for several months. 

 The vast majority of Wall Street bond dealers believe the Fed is done cutting the overnight rate, but will not begin boosting interest rates again until at least the second half of the year, according to a recent Reuters poll. 

 "They've already built in no rate change into the marketplace so I don't think that will cause any action," Cunningham said. "If (the Fed) decides to go for an insurance cut, that would cause some interesting action, that's for sure." 

 The Fed's policy-setting arm started its two-day meeting on Tuesday and is expected to keep rates steady at the conclusion of its meeting on Wednesday. 

 On the Canadian data front, the December composite index rose a better than expected 0.4 percent in December, topping forecasts for an 0.2 percent rise. 

 The 30-year bond, due 2029, rose 45 Canadian cents to C$101.20 to yield 5.663 percent while the U.S. 30-year treasury gained a full point to yield 5.401 percent. The yield spread between the two-year and 10-year bond moved to 221.2 basis points from 216.5 basis points at the previous close.

title: SPECIAL REPORT-Weak Canadian dollar leaves markets guessing.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 29 (Reuters) - A new deluge of supportive words has stemmed the Canadian dollar's tumble to new lows, but the currency is still fragile and another plunge could leave the central bank few options. 

 Officials have so far ducked the question of whether the Bank of Canada will add the big gun of central bank intervention to the dollar's defense after the small-arms fire of verbal support, but the markets seem determined to test the bank's resolve. 

 They are looking to see if the bank will walk the walk - purchase Canadian dollars on foreign exchange markets to drive the currency up - as well as talk the talk. 

 "It's the old story of the boy who cried wolf," said Andy Busch, senior foreign exchange advisor at Bank of Montreal in Chicago. "It's really a question of 'show me some action'. If you're concerned about it, fine, we understand that. We know you don't like it. But do something about it." 

 Canada's prime minister, finance minister and central bank governor last week shed a long history of indifference toward the dollar, loudly lamenting its decline to a record low of C$1.6194 to the U.S. dollar, or 61.75 U.S. cents. 

 They all said the dollar should be higher, based on the Canadian economy's solid fundamentals - a large current account surplus, a budget surplus and falling government debt. 

Central bank Governor David Dodge went so far as to chide markets for ignoring Canada's strong fundamentals. He said intervention, when central banks buy their own currency to drive the price up, was "a tool in our tool chest." 

 The officials renewed their offensive this week, launching a second barrage of supportive comments that helped push the Canadian currency to one-month highs against the greenback. 

 But the tough talk hardly has dealers quaking in their shoes. 

 WORDS ARE NOT ENOUGH 

 "My experiences over the years is that politicians are best not talking about the currency because the market likes to take them on," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of foreign exchange at CIBC World Markets, who does not expect intervention. 

 "Once everyone starts throwing their 10 cents in about the currency, I think it generally leads to an adverse reaction." 

 While the market may be calling the central bank's bluff on intervention, Bank of Montreal's Busch said there was still some uncertainty about what the bank's next step might be, given its relationship with the government. 

 "They're much more politically biased than other central banks," he said. "Even the Japanese have now a degree of independence from the elected government, which is a good thing. "It depends on how much pressure (Prime Minister Jean) Chretien wants to put on Dodge." 

 Sharing the view of several other dealers, Busch said he did not expect the bank to defend the dollar unless it dropped to C$1.65 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts say there is little the Bank of Canada can do to stop the fall. Intervention is a short-term cure that could escalate into a game of chicken as the market eyes Canada's $34 billion in foreign reserves and bets that central bank action won't go on indefinitely. 

 Meanwhile, raising interest rates just as Canada struggles out of recession would be "economic suicide," one dealer said. 

 That leaves the central bank with a less palatable choice: let the market do what it will with the currency and wait for the dollar to recover once the economy rebounds. 

 At that point, the central bank could intervene on a small scale and give a tide of positive sentiment toward the Canadian dollar a push. Battling against a market sour on the currency is futile, according to senior economist Benjamin Tal of Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. 

 Tal said the market is more interested in sentiment than fundamentals and in Canada's short-term economic prospects in relation to its biggest trading partner, the United States. 

 "That's the only thing on the investors' mind...so let's leave the fundamentals to the academics," he said. 

 The Canadian dollar has fallen on the view that Canada will lag a U.S. recovery, and because the U.S. dollar is strong. 

 Tal said the verbal defense is preferable to actual intervention because it keeps the market guessing. 

 "No intervention is better than a failed intervention," he said. "You use your last bullet by intervening and then you're really powerless against the market, which will continue to test you." 

 ($1=$1.59 Canadian).

title: Canadian dollar rallies after  intervention  warning.
text:
LONDON, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Canada's dollar remained firm on Tuesday, extending sharp gains against its U.S. counterpart made in Asia and in the previous session as Canadian officials continued to support their currency verbally. 

 Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge repeated on Monday his warning that intervention in the currency markets is a tool in the central bank's toolbox. In recent days, the finance minister and even the prime minister have also been supporting their currency, which hit record lows last week, with their words. 

 Traders said the loonie, as the Canadian dollar is known, also drew support from news on Monday that British energy retailer Centrica Plc is buying the home heating serrvices arm of Canada's Enbridge Inc for C$1 billion. 

 "We've had quite a move. The Centrica M&A deal was Canada positive," said Francesca Fornasari, currency economist at Lehman Brothers. 

 At 1113 GMT, the Canadian dollar was trading around C$1.5907 per dollar compared with the previous day's Bank of Canada official closing rate of C$1.5976 (at 2230 GMT) and levels around C$1.6120 earlier earlier on Monday. 

 Analysts said some retracement of the Canadian dollar had been inevitable as the latest IMM data (as at January 22) indicated that non-commercial net-short positions in the loonie were at their highest level since November 27, 2001. 

 "It seems the world and his wife had been shorting Canada and people started pulling out," said a trader at a U.S. bank. 

 Canada's December composite index is due for release at 1330 GMT but of more interest will be November's gross domestic prooduct report on Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, the Australian dollar was weaker against its U.S. counterpart in line with the euro's weakness against the greenback. 

 "The Australian is lower because of the weakness of the euro even though we've had some good data," said Fornasari.

title: Bk Of Cda's Dodge: F/X  Intervention  Still In Toolbox
text:
WINNIPEG -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge continued his cautious talking up of the Canadian dollar Monday, telling reporters here that the Canadian unit's recent slump to all-time lows is "not helpful" for the Canadian economy and that the central bank still considers possible direct intervention in foreign exchange markets as a tool in its arsenal. 

 In a news conference after a luncheon speech in Winnigeg, Dodge didn'ot go substantially beyond comments originally made last week following the release of the latest update to the central bank's monetary policy report. 

 But he stressed again that the declining Canadian dollar could pose a potential confidence issue for the Canadian economy. 

 "As I've said before, the current recent depreciation of the Canadian dollar is certainly not helpful to economic confidence or the process of adjustment here in Canada," Dodge said. 

 The Canadian dollar in recent weeks has sunk to new all-time lows near the level of C$1.6200 for one U.S. dollar, raising calls from some quarters of the Canadian financial community that the central bank should dip into its estimated foreign exchange reserves of more than C$34 billion to intervene in the Canadian dollar's support. 

 However, when pressed several times to explain the central bank's views on direct intervention in foreign exchange markets to support the sagging Canadian dollar, Dodge declined to elaborate on statements last week that intervention remains an option for the central bank. 

 "The intervention tool stays in the tool box," Dodge said. "Because it's in the toolbox, that's where, in a sense, it stays, and you wouldn't expect me to comment on when we might take it out of the tool box, if we might take it out of the tool box, and how many of those tools we might use." 

 Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said there are several factors already in place - notably a pick-up in world demand for Canadian exports and rising foreign and domestic investment - pointing to an eventual rebound for the Canadian dollar. 

 "Clearly, for an economy that relies on trade as much as we do, strengthening world demand is very important," Dodge said. "That factor is there, already." 

 Dodge said that investment will likely pick up somewhat more slowly as this influence on the Canadian dollar's value has been hurt by disappointing earnings results for both domestic and foreign firms. 

 Dodge also said that, as the impacts of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks continue to modify risk assessments and investment behavior of domestic corporations, this could affect the Canadian economy's level of potential output in 2002. 

 The Bank of Canada has in recent years estimated that the Canadian economy's level of potential annual output growth is about 3.0%. However, under the influence of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Dodge said the bank's assessments are pointing to a slight lowering of this potential growth rate in 2002. 

 "Our thinking is that during the course of 2002, some of these adjustments will be made, and that probably will mean that the rate of output growth and potential could be a bit less," Dodge said. 

 "But it's a one-time effect that won't last long, and will likely be measured in quarters," he said.

text:

     It received short-lived support from kind words last week, 

 but a second round of government defense in as many weeks 

 caught the market's attention on Monday.

 the market is starting to take notice of it," said Paul Briggs, 

currency trader at Investors Bank and Trust in Boston. 


      The three officials had made various attempts last week



and came out with a renewed and spirited defense on Monday,



declaring the dollar weakness to be unhelpful and unjustified



by Canada's economic fundamentals and by signs of a pickup, but



all the officials stopped short of promising any immediate



action to come to its aid.

still a tool in the central bank's arsenal but would not be



drawn on whether it would be used to support the faltering


currency.

Pyle, senior financial markets analyst at Scotia Capital



Markets.

sand on (the Canadian dollar), but it is clear that interest

emerge."

title: Bk Of Canada's Dodge: Recent C$ Slump 'Not Helpful'
text:
OTTAWA -(Dow Jones)- At a press conference Wednesday, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said the recent devaluation of the Canadian dollar is "not helpful" to the country's economic recovery and raises questions of confidence in the overall economy. 

 Dodge agreed with earlier comments made by Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin that Canada's currency has been hurt, in part, by a perception problem and that the current value of the dollar doesn't reflect the underlying fundamentals of the Canadian economy. 

 Canada's dollar recently closed at a record low of 62.02 U.S. cents, though it has since risen slightly. 

 Dodge went on to say that recent economic indicators have shown that Canada's economy is stronger than had been anticipated, with exports rising, the manufacturing sector lowering inventories and receiving new orders, factory orders and retail sales rising, and household spending more robust than expected. Dodge said that, over time, this positive economic news should be reflected in the dollar. 

 "As I've always said, the best medicine for the dollar is a strong economy," Dodge said. 

 Dodge reiterated the Bank of Canada's assessment that the Canadian economy will start slowly this year, but that economic growth should steadily gain momentum throughout the year and finish 2002 with annualized growth between 3% and 4%. 

 "There's much more certainty today than there was three months ago that a recovery will be well underway" by year-end, he said. 

 Dodge said the Canadian economy, which has been slowing since the middle of 2001, is now at a "turning point." However, he stressed that a degree of uncertainty remains in the outlook, mainly that business confidence in North America still remains weak, though it should rebound later this year. 

 Dodge wouldn't say whether the central bank would consider a currencyintervention to bolster Canada's falling currency. "That is a tool in our tool chest," the governor said, refusing to comment further on the likely hood of a currency intervention.

title: Bk Of Canada Offers Rosy Outlook, But Talks Tough On C$
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 TORONTO -(Dow Jones)- The Bank of Canada continued to hammer home an optimistic view of Canada's 2002-03 economic prospects on Wednesday, and in the process, appeared to be telling currency markets that it's time to stop hammering the Canadian dollar. 

 Though it slightly pared back some earlier growth estimates and forecast a "somewhat greater" degree of economic slack in 2002, the central bank's first-quarter update to its November monetary policy report (MPR) offered a generally benign view of the way forward in which economic growth steadily gains momentum and culminates in above-potential growth of between 3% to 4% in the second half of the calendar year. 

 The inflation outlook, and by extension the monetary policy outlook, was similarly rosy, with the Bank foreseeing yearly core inflation rates below 1.5% in the second half, and all-inclusive inflation rates lower still until late in the year. 

 The MPR update's economic forecasts had been largely foreshadowed in the central bank's limited quarter-percentage point interest rate ease and accompanying commentary last week. 

 It struck many analysts as reasonable given recent domestic data and global economic and geo-political developments, even though financial markets have likely exaggerated the extent of Bank of Canada optimism by pricing in a return to monetary tightening as early as the beginning of the third quarter. 

 "I take away a signal that interest rate easing is pretty much done, but also a sense that there won't be any tightening for quite a long time," said Andrew Spence, global head of currency and credit market research at TD Securities in Toronto. "That's a world I can live with under the circumstances - I wouldn't disagree with the Bank's assessments." 


   End Of Official BenignNeglect Of C$ May Be At Hand



Of considerably more interest was Bank of Canada governor David
Dodge's subsequent commentary on the Canadian dollar, which many saw as
finally offering signs of a break with the recent central bank policy of
discussing the currency only in vague, anodyne terms.



Though he predictably refused to be drawn into discussions of specific
levels or tactical prescriptions for reviving the ailing currency, Dodge
stressed repeatedly at a post-MPR press conference that the Canadian
dollar's recent slump to new historical lows is "not helpful" and raises
confidence issues for the Canadian economy.



Dodge also echoed Monday's remark by Canadian finance minister Paul
Martin that the Canadian dollar is suffering from a perception problem
and that its value doesn't reflect the improving fundamentals of the
Canadian economy.



The Bank, Dodge said, is "closely monitoring" foreign exchange
developments.



As RBC Capital Markets chief economist of the Americas John Johnston
pointed out, "in G7-speak this is usually seen as a threat of
intervention."



While active Bank of Canada foreign exchange intervention is
considered unlikely under current conditions, even such tempered remarks
are seen by currency watchers as long-overdue signs that an implicit
policy of benign official neglect of the Canadian dollar may be over.



Steve Demers, director of foreign exchange at National Bank in
Montreal, termed this week's remarks by Dodge and Martin as an
"important first step in the right direction" that could have positive
implications over the long-term for the Canadian currency.



"One of the key factors negatively impacting the Canadian dollar since
at least 1998 has been this belief that the Canadian authorities are
comfortable with their weak currency, or even that they have a weak
currency policy," Demers said. "With the Canadian dollar being so weak
recently, it's very important for them to state that this isn't their
policy - we had a tiny bit of that from Mr. Martin, and Mr. Dodge made
it much more clear today."



Active Bank of Canada intervention in defense of the Canadian dollar
still isn't considered likely unless the currency starts to crumble
rapidly and in a volatile fashion under the pressure of a speculative
assault, or if renewed weakness spills over to disrupt activity in
Canadian fixed-income and equity markets.



And Dodge himself appeared to extend the foreign exchange market a
period of grace in which to adjust to Canada's improving fundamentals
with his acknowledgement that financial markets always find it difficult
to deal with turning points in the economy, such as the one the Bank
believes is in progress now.



But to many observers, the underlying message of Dodge's remarks is
that the Bank of Canada will no longer be as tolerant as it has been of
a Canadian dollar whose weakness violates any conception of fundamental
value.



"What was telling is that the Bank of Canada views what has happened
to the exchange rate as not being fundamentally driven," said Spence of
TD Securities. "So we've got to think  that Dodge is signalling that the
authorities are prepared to take some action with respect to the
exchange rate if this goes on - that seems to me to be the implicit
suggestion."



The Canadian dollar distanced itself further from its C$1.6194 record
intraday low in the wake of Dodge's remarks, moving to the C$1.6025 by
late afternoon Wednesday.



- By Paul Evans, Dow Jones Newswires; (416) 306-2022

title: UPDATE 2-Canadian officials speak out in dollar's defense.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Canadian officials rallied to the defense of the dollar on Wednesday, boosting the currency's short-term prospects as markets pondered the possibility of tougher measures, such as intervention. 

 In unusually direct comments, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said the Canadian dollar's decline was a source of concern, and its depreciation was not helpful because it raised issues of confidence. 

 He was the second Canadian official to defend the dollar this week - Finance Minister Paul Martin spoke out on Monday after the currency slumped to record lows. 

 Prime Minister Jean Chretien joined the chorus within hours, saying he shared Martin's and Dodge's concerns and said the currency did not reflect the strength of the economy. 

 "Dodge has put the foreign exchange market on alert although he's basically given a stay of execution," said Rob Palombi, senior analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. "The threat of foreign exchange intervention is real. It's up to the market now and it sounds like the Bank of Canada is going to give it some time to digest all the improving economic news. 

 "If at that point, the Canadian dollar continues to depreciate, that's when we might see intervention." 

 The Bank of Canada has not intervened directly to support the Canadian currency for several years, although it admits intervention could be part of its arsenal. 

 "It's always a tool in our tool chest but you wouldn't expect me to come before you and say if we would use it, when we would use it or how much we would do," Dodge said on Wednesday. "So since you wouldn't expect it, I won't give you the answer." 

 On Monday Martin stopped the sliding dollar in its tracks when he signaled his displeasure with its weakness and said markets were ignoring Canada's strong fundamentals. 

 RETHINKING DOLLAR VIEWS 

 Startled market players, unaccustomed to policymakers expressing such spirited concern about the exchange rate, began to reconsider their view on the currency. 

 "Whether the verbal support alone can really accomplish anything for more than a week is up for debate," said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns. 

 "But the more stridently Ottawa tries to quash the sense that they favor a weaker dollar, I think that has a more positive effect on the currency ultimately." 

 The Canadian dollar ended at a one-week high of C$1.6026 to the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, well above the record low of C$1.6194 set Monday and slightly above the C$1.6060 level seen before Dodge began to speak. 

 Dodge also said the dollar's weakness was not an argument for a North American monetary union and he shrugged off prospects of pegging the Canadian unit to the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the rescue missions should help the currency in the very short term. But ultimately the currency is linked to factors outside central bank's control - a Canadian economic recovery that in turn hinges on an end to the recession in the United States, Canada's biggest trading partner. 

 Alan Ruskin, research director at 4Cast Ltd. in New York said strength in the Canadian dollar would come if there was a shift in sentiment toward the greenback, the currency of choice for safe-haven seekers. 

 "The idea that the economy will turn the currency around has been tried, tested, and has failed," he said. "To see the Canadian dollar strengthen, you will more likely need to see a turn in (U.S.) dollar sentiment. 

 "And you will need a turn in euro sentiment, in particular, before you get that turn in the dollar sentiment." 

 Dodge would not comment on whether Ottawa would intervene, but he didn't rule out the possibility either. 

 "He didn't count it out and I guess he wants to hold it over the market's head as a possibility if it weakens off dramatically or too quickly," said Ronald Pancer, director of foreign exchange sales at Societe Generale. "But he certainly didn't suggest that he was looking at it any time soon either." 

 The central bank, which has $34 billion in foreign exchange reserves, last intervened directly to support the Canadian currency during the Asian crisis, spending some $4 billion. 

 The Canadian dollar has slumped as the economy grapples with the global downturn and a belief that Canada will lag the U.S. recovery. A modest interest rate cut by the Bank of Canada last week proved a disappointment for some people who had hoped for a heftier move to stimulate the economy. 

 (With additional reporting by New York financial desk) 

 ($1=$1.60 Canadian).

title: Bank Of Canada Policy Update Seen Reticent On C$ Slide
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 TORONTO -(Dow Jones)- Canadian dollar watchers hoping for a clear response to the currency's recent plunge in the Bank of Canada's monetary policy update Wednesday will likely be disappointed, analysts said. 

 While the Canadian dollar's recent dive deeper into record low territory has heightened expectations for the update, both the timing of its preparation before the currency's latest slump and the central bank's typical reticence on the subject may preclude any lengthy discussion of it, analysts said. 

 Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge will likely address the currency's decline in his news conference after the report is released, analysts said. 

 "I would be surprised if it was emphasized in the report, but I would be equally surprised if it didn't come up as the main topic in the press conference after," said Mark Chandler, senior economist at Goldman Sachs Canada. 

 The report will be released at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT), with the news conference following at 11:15 a.m. EST. (1615 GMT) 

 The report will only include information up to the bank's last interest-rate adjustment on Jan. 15, before the Canadian dollar's most recent plunge into record-low territory. 

 The U.S. dollar, which  closed at C$1.5888 on Jan. 15, surged to an all-time high of C$1.6194 on Monday. The Canadian currency recovered somewhat on Tuesday, and was hovering around C$1.6075 in early afternoon trading. 

 The scheduling of the update means that anybody looking for a "big, lengthy discussion" on the dollar is going to be disappointed, said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc. in Toronto. 

 The fact that the last monetary policy report in November contained little discussion of the currency also suggests that any comments on it will be limited, he added. 

 "They really avoided the topic in the November report, so I'd be surprised if there's anything really illuminating in the update on the dollar front," Porter said. 


   Martin's Remarks Heighten Expectations



Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin's supportive comments on the
Canadian dollar on Monday have fostered speculation Dodge may make some
strong statements of his own at the news conference on Wednesday.



In a conference call to reporters, Martin said the Canadian dollar is
undervalued and suffering from a "perception problem."



Market players credited Martin's comments with contributing to the
Canadian dollar's modest recovery on Tuesday.



Martin's comments have also fueled conjecture that the Bank of Canada
may intervene in foreign exchange markets on behalf of the beleaguered
Canadian dollar, another subject Dodge is likely to be asked about at
the news conference.



Analysts said they expected the economic outlook in the update to be
broadly consistent with the forecast in the November report, which
called for 1.5% gross domestic product growth in both 2001 and 2002.



"I think it will just firm up the economic outlook they had in the
first place," Porter said.



While the report emphasized the economic uncertainties following the
Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. and pointed out its forecast was
based on a number "working assumptions," the update may indicate that
the level of uncertainty has diminished, analysts said.



Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at the Bank of Montreal, said
the update's economic forecast could be slightly more upbeat than the
November report



Ferley said the bank may suggest some upside risk to its forecasts of
1.5% growth in 2002, and point out that 2001 appears to have ended on a
stronger note than earlier anticipated.



The update may address the question of the Canadian dollar's decline
by emphasizing that the economic data has improved recently, and
implying that will provide support to the currency, Ferley said.



But the policy update is unlikely to have a significant impact on the
currency, he added.

title: Canadian dollar fights back as market heeds Martin.
text:
LONDON, Jun 22 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar clawed back some ground on Tuesday from recent record lows against its U.S. counterpart after Canada's finance minister said late in the previous session he was worried about the currency's weakness. Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Monday the country was "not happy" with the low level of the Canadian dollar but that the currency would eventually reflect the country's good economic fundamentals. 

 His warning followed the Canadian dollar sliding more than three Canadian cents in recent sessions, hitting an all-time low just shy of C$1.62 per greenback on Monday, as investors bet on a quicker U.S. recovery and speculation of negative merger and acquisition flows. 

 "Dollar/Canada's come off a bit after we had those overnight comments by Martin," said Kamal Sharma, currency strategist at Commerzbank. 

 At 1134 GMT, the Canadian dollar was trading around C$1.6090 , about a cent stronger than the record lows set on Monday. 

 Analysts said Martin's comments had put them on alert for any intervention by the Bank of Canada though they added that the central bank was unlikely to step in unless the currency's decline became less orderly. 

 Attention was therefore focused on Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge's Monetary Policy Report Update on Wednesday. 

 Traders paid little attention to news that Canadian consumer prices rose 0.1 percent on the month in December and 0.7 percent on the year. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected prices to fall 0.1 percent on the month. 

 Meanwhile, the Australian dollar was steady in Europe after rallying in Asia, once again flirting with the US$0.52 level , as large domestic and Japanese funds found a renewed appetite for the currencies as growth hopes revived the world over. 

 New Zealand's dollar was trading at US$0.43 , little changed from levels seen in Asian trading when it had rallied nearly half a cent.

title: Martin defense lifts Canada dollar after close.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 21 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar hit its 

 highest level of a dismal day after the close on Monday as 

 Finance Minister Paul Martin said Canada was worried about the 

currency's stubborn decline. 

 At 5:25 p.m., the Canadian unit was trading at C$1.6102 to 

 the U.S dollar, or 62.10 U.S. cents, up from its closing level 

 of C$1.6115, or 62.05 U.S. cents, and well above the record of 

 C$1.6194, notched early in the day in European trade. 

 Martin said the government was "not happy" with the low 

 level of the dollar but that the currency would eventually 

 reflect the country's good economic fundamentals. 

 Martin said the market's perception of the Canadian economy 

 was not in sync with the reality, citing the balanced budget, a 

 falling debt-to-GDP ratio and a large current account surplus. 

 "If one thing stands out, it's the very flat statement that 

 the government is not happy with the falling Canadian dollar," 

 said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns. 

 "I think that was an important statement. Anything that 

 helps dispel the perception that Ottawa welcomes an ever 

 falling dollar is helpful at this point." 

 The Canadian dollar, which plumbed record depths against 

 the greenback in overnight trading, had recovered slightly to 

 end on a firmer note on Monday but dealers brushed aside the 

 gains and braced for more weakness. 

 Volumes were tepid during the session in the absence of 

 U.S. market players because of the Martin Luther King Day 

 holiday. 

 "It's just corporates taking advantage of a strong U.S. 

 dollar and locking in some gains," said Reid Farrill, executive 

 director of foreign exchange at CIBC World Markets. "I wouldn't 

 confuse that with a Canadian dollar rally." 

 The Canadian currency slumped to a record low after 

 automatic sell orders were triggered in Europe, erasing the 

 previous record set only last Thursday. 

 Steve Demers, director of foreign exchange at National 

 Bank of Canada in Montreal, said the domestic currency would be 

 stuck in "no man's land" as it groped around to establish firm 

 new lows and the market would have to rely on medium- to 

 long-term technical indicators for guidance. 

 Those indicators suggest C$1.6225 is a level at which the 

 Canadian dollar could hold against the U.S. currency for a few 

 days. The Canadian dollar could potentially trade as low as 

 C$1.6500 to C$1.6600 level, Demers said. 

INTERVENTION SPECULATION 

 As the Canadian dollar slumps to one low after another, 

 talk of intervention by the Bank of Canada has become more 

 pronounced. 

 Considering the Canadian unit's orderly decline, the 

central bank is not likely to step in unless the currency loses 

 ground rapidly but that has not dampened speculation. 

 BMO Nesbitt Burns' Porter said Martin's comments could be 

 the prelude to a more aggressive stance. 

 "This is the first step. It might be laying the ground work 

 for some actions rather than words," Porter said. "But I think 

 it's obvious that policymakers aren't quite ready or aren't at 

 that stage yet." 

 Martin declined to be drawn on whether the central bank

 might step into foreign exchange markets to defend the 

currency. 

 With intervention on so many minds, attention is riveted on 

 Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge who will present the 

 Monetary Policy Report Update on Wednesday. 

 Elsewhere, Canadian retail sales rose 1.4 percent in 

 November against October, driven by strong auto sector sales 

 prompted by zero-financing deals. Excluding autos, retail sales 

 fell 0.6 percent in November. 

 The Canadian unit, which opened at C$1.6175, moved in a 

 range of C$1.6110 to C$1.6184 during the session, according to 

 Reuters data and traders

 Australian dollar , it was at A$1.1983, compared with 

 A$1.2031 at the previous close. Against the euro , the

title: Canada  Dollar's Latest Debacle Stirs  Intervention  Talk
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 TORONTO -(Dow Jones)- The plight of the battered Canadian dollar has become so grave as to raise calls from some quarters for Bank of Canadaintervention on its behalf in foreign exchange markets. 

 A few large U.S. dollar orders from fund accounts and follow-up stop-loss selling propelled the Canadian dollar through a generally illiquid market to a new historical low of C$1.6170 to a U.S. dollar overnight, extending a three-month spiral of futility for the currency. 

 And while intervention is a weapon that has been gathering dust in the central bank's arsenal since it was last used in August 1998, the Canadian currency's sudden and rapid plunge had some currency watchers and market players waiting in vain for signs of Bank of Canada activity entering Thursday's North American session. 

 The Canadian dollar has been wallowing in record low territory ever since it first fell through its previous C$1.5850 all-time low in late November, but the speed and extent of its latest plunge has convinced some that its weakness is no longer a credible reflection of Canadian economic fundamentals. 

 Senior economist David Rosenberg of Merrill Lynch Canada in Toronto said that while it's natural to expect a weaker Canadian dollar in a period of North American recession and slumping global growth, recent activity has seen a troubling delinking of the Canadian dollar from the behaviour of other global asset classes. 

 "The Canadian dollar stands out more than any other  piece of paper on the planet in terms of still pricing in a global recession - every other security has moved on," he said. "But the Canadian dollar hasn't, and if it's broke then it's time to fix it - I think we've crossed that line in the past day or so." 

 Over the past month or so, said Rosenberg, other value indices that, like the Canadian dollar, are sensitive to global growth expectations  - such as gold prices, yield spreads between government and higher-risk corporate bonds, and commodity prices, to name a few - have all strengthened. 

 Yet the Canadian dollar's relentless weakening has suddenly accelerated, a development that Rosenberg says "breaches any semblance of fundamental value - the Canadian dollar's got no business being down here." 


   Widespread Bemusement As To Reasons For Latest Plunge



It's a telling indication of how baffling the Canadian dollar's
underperformance has become to the experts to see the growing list of
factors advanced to explain its latest midadventure.



Merrill Lynch's Rosenberg earlier Thursday put out a top-10 list of
reasons covering everything from expectations of poor fourth quarter
2001 earnings for Canadian corporations to delayed adverse reactions to
a spike in Canada's unemployment rate and Tuesday's 25 basis point Bank
of Canada cut in short term interest rates, a move that some suggest
didn't go far enough for the sputtering Canadian economy.



Other currency watchers cited factors as diverse as Japanese fund
repatriation ahead of the March 31 Japanese fiscal year-end, and
disappointment over recent developments in Canadian federal politics.



Whatever the reasons, Rosenberg said it's time for the Bank of Canada
to inject a dose of clarity by dipping into the record $34.2 billion in
foreign currency reserves that Canada has built through much of the
1990s to at least steady, if not reverse, the Canadian dollar's course.



"Now that the Bank of Canada's been out of the intervention game for
so long, it's no longer a standard procedure and would likely carry some
clout because of its rarity," said Rosenberg. "Intervention right now
would be a pretty big stick - use it!"



Though most currency watchers are taking the Bank of Canada at its
word that intervention will only come as a result of a volatile,
disorderly, or panic-driven assault on the Canadian dollar, there is
some sympathy for Rosenberg's contention that official intervention on
the Canadian dollar's behalf is now necessary to stave off a calamitous
plummet.



Some have argued that the abandonment in September 1998 of symmetrical
intervention tactics by the central bank, and only tepid supportive
remarks on the currency since then by government and Bank of Canada
officials alike, amounts to a policy of official benign neglect of the
Canadian dollar.



Unless government and central bank policy-makers begin talking up
their desire for a stronger currency, according to this view, the
Canadian dollar has no hope of halting the long-term downtrend that
began in late 1991, when the currency was trading at around C$1.1200.



"It depends on who talks it up - it would be setting a precedent if
(Canadian finance minister) Martin or (Prime Minister) Chretien were to
talk it up - that would probably have a positive impact," said Steve
Demers, director of foreign exchange at National Bank in Montreal. "If
(Bank of Canada governor) David Dodge makes a vague statement, it would
help the Canadian dollar in the short-term as a first step, if the
second step were to be a clear intervention."



Still, Demers said that central bank intervention is unlikely unless
the Canadian dollar falls rapidly to about the C$1.6350 area over the
next few days.



"We would need to be in an extreme situation where the Canadian dollar
has appreciated very quickly, it's a one-way street, and speculators are
dominating the market," Demers said. "There's no risk of intervention
until C$1.6350 for now, but if we move up there we need to be careful -
the Bank has double the amount of foreign reserves it had three years
ago, and if it could put through about $10 billion, it would have a
significant impact in the short-term."



The Canadian dollar steadied somewhat after its overnight descent, and
by mid-day in Toronto and New York had returned to trade around
C$1.6100.



- By Paul Evans, Dow Jones Newswires; (416) 306-2022
