title: Bank of  Canada  sees only rare  forex intervention .
text:
OTTAWA, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge said on Thursday that the central bank would only intervene in foreign exchange markets in extraordinary circumstances. 

 Dodge told the Senate banking committee that the Bank of Canada used to operate daily in the market to avoid major fluctuations, hour to hour or day to day. 

 "We stopped doing that. The market is deep and robust enough that it takes care of it itself," he said. 

 "So our policy, clearly enunciated, is that we don't normally intervene in markets, and it would only be in extraordinary circumstances that we would consider using the tool. It is there. It can be used, but it would have to be absolutely extraordinary circumstances."

title: FX  problems seen taking back seat to growth at G7.
text:
NEW YORK, July 4 (Reuters) - G7 finance ministers are unlikely to hammer out a coordinated currency policy when they meet in Rome on Saturday despite market speculation about central bank intervention, currency analysts say. 

 Sluggish global growth - and how to kick-start it - will take centre stage at the meeting of the Group of Seven major industrialised countries, while foreign exchange concerns will be relegated to the sidelines, they say. 

 This view was reinforced after a U.S. Treasury official said on Tuesday there were no plans for any special discussion of exchange rates at the G7 meeting and Haruhiko Kuroda, Japan' top financial diplomat, reiterated the point on Wednesday. 

 "Currencies are part of the story, but the centerpiece is really growth," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief economist at Royal Bank of Scotland in New York. 

 "STRONG DOLLAR" PINCHES U.S. 

 With the euro dangling near record lows and recession-hit U.S. manufacturers bemoaning the dollar's strength, exchange rate imbalances have become a thorn in the side of policymakers on both sides of the Atlantic. 

 The dollar's rise this year to 15-year highs against a basket of its major trading partners' currencies has sparked vociferous complaints from U.S. manufacturers, who say their competitiveness overseas is being damaged. 

 But in the run-up to the G7 meeting, the U.S. Treasury has repeatedly insisted it will keep its inflation-busting "strong dollar" policy intact. 

 "A lot of companies were burned by the strong dollar, but the Treasury has implied that it's their internal issue - i.e. don't blame the central bank," said foreign exchange adviser Bernard Tsui at Union Bank of California. 

 Rather than intentionally weaken the dollar to fuel exports, analysts say, Washington would prefer to see the euro zone and Japan pump up their economies by easing monetary policy. 

 "It's hard to imagine the U.S. is ready to discuss currency misalignments at all," said currency strategist James McCormick at J.P. Morgan Chase. 

 "The more pressing issue is that domestic demand in these two large regions, Europe and Japan, is quite weak - and the U.S. would like to see some policies put in place to support it." 

 The dollar's rise has been boosted by global investors' expectations that a series of aggressive U.S. interest rate cuts this year will help turn around America's economic slowdown. 

 EUROPE AT A LOSS TO STEM EURO SLIDE 

 In Europe, meanwhile, officials are perceived to be loath to see the euro continue to decline, as its depreciation is viewed as psychologically damaging and also as it helps feed inflation. 

 Still, the weakness of the currency is helping European exporters' competitiveness at a time when the region's economy is showing signs of slowing. 

 At any rate, the ECB has repeatedly dampened down expectations of possible intervention, and may be resigned to living with a weak euro for the time being - especially if the United States is unwilling to help out with intervention. 

 "They're paying lip service to a strong euro, but privately they're acknowledging that the chances of it turning dramatically between now and when they introduce notes and coins (on January 1) is limited," said Standard Chartered currency strategist Tim Fox. 

 "So, I don't see them moving to force the issue in the period before the end of the year." 

 The euro is currently within three cents of its record lows set last October, and below levels at which the G7 countries - Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States - intervened jointly on the eve of their September gathering to halt its persistent decline. 

 But the economic backdrop has changed dramatically since then. The U.S. economy has slowed dramatically, and euro zone economic growth has underperformed expectations. 

 Meanwhile, Japan, is verging on recession and facing a dearth of policy options to rev up its economy. 

 The market still suspects that the Japanese may have to weaken the yen, but last weekend's U.S.-Japanese summit gave traders few clues about yen policy. The G7 may have little to add. 

 This week, Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi said he had no intention of consciously bringing the yen lower. 

 That's in line with the White House view that the U.S. will tolerate a softer yen if that weakening results from badly needed structural reforms, but that a deliberate yen depreciation would be unacceptable. 

 The U.S. administration's reluctance to tweak currency policy artificially suggests that the G7 is unlikely to issue any kind of explicit currency statement, analysts said. 

 If anything, the G7 may repeat what it said at its previous meeting in April, that exchange rates should "reflect economic fundamentals".

     TORONTO, March 28 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar closed

 by Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge to a Senate banking

 falling Canadian dollar may leave less room for interest-rate

 have been bullish on more rate cuts, dealers said.

 favor of the Canadian dollar over time. 

     Talk of a possible intervention to support the flagging 

 dollar - hovering at 2-1/2 year lows and edging ever closer to 

 its record low of C$1.5850 - had rippled through the market 

 earlier, following comments by deputy Bank Governor Sheryl 

 Kennedy. 

 Kennedy said the bank is watching the weakening Canadian 

 dollar to gauge its impact on "total demand and inflation," 

 comments reiterated by Dodge in his speech. 

 While some market players inferred the central bank may be 

 signaling an intervention, others noted the comments were taken 

 out of context and threw cold water on the chances of the bank 

 stepping in to prop up the dollar. 

 "The market may have speculated that the bank was going to 

intervene but I think that's probably overplaying it," said 

 David Ebata, managing analyst of Canadian markets at Thomson 

 IFR. "There's absolutely no indication that the bank was going 

 to do anything. As a result, after the initial move down to the

 "I think it was more an excuse for dealers to take out

 Helene Moermen, senior advisor of foreign exchange at

 likelihood of an intervention, noting the bank has stated it 

 will only step in "if there is panic and I really don't think

central bank may not lower interest rates aggressively at its

 generally been tracking North American equities markets," said 

 Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns. 

 "And given that we had the added weight of yet another huge 

 pullback in Nortel, I have to say today's performance by the

title: Bank Of  Canada 's Dodge Says No  Intervention  To Help C$
text:
OTTAWA -(Dow Jones)- During a question and answer session at the Senate Committee on Banking Wednesday, Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge fended off questions about the weakening Canadian dollar and what, if anything, the central bank could do to bolster the currency. 

 When asked if the Bank of Canada would intervene to prop up the dollar, Dodge said the central bank would only intervene in extraordinary circumstances or if there was a global currency crisis. 

 He said the Canadian dollar has been weakening against the U.S. dollar, along with other world currencies, but that the Canadian currency has not been falling against other world currencies, which would be of greater concern to him and the central bank. 

 Dodge also refuted suggestions that Canada may be heading into a recession, saying the first half of this year would be "rough" for the economy, but that there should be a positive economic rebound in the second half of the year.

title: ANALYSIS-Europe seen pushing exchange rates up G7 agenda.
text:
LONDON, Jan 30 (Reuters) - Exchange rates are set to rise up the Group of Seven nations' agenda as European policymakers indicate the euro is close to the bottom of their preferred trading range just days before G7 officials meet. 

 French Finance Minister Laurent Fabius on Tuesday pinpointed $0.95 as a reasonable exchange rate for the euro, which is currently three cents weaker, and said economic fundamentals should allow a move towards dollar parity. 

 His comments come a day after Heribert Zitzelsberger, a German deputy finance minister, said rates between $0.90 and $1.00 represented a "healthy middle ground" which was acceptable to exporters and would also help contain inflation pressures. 

 Their comments have got analysts expecting exchange rates to feature at Thursday's gathering of G7 deputy finance ministers, which will lay the groundwork for the meeting their chiefs will hold later in February. 

 "The Europeans will be somewhat disappointed by the euro's performance in the past fortnight and if it goes below $0.90 they will want to revive the spirit of G7 cooperation," said Jim O'Neill, currency strategist at Goldman Sachs. 

 "It is frequently the deputies that agree all the nitty gritty details so these meetings can be important." 

 STOPPING RETREAT TURNING INTO ROUT 

 The G7, which comprises the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, Britain, and Canada, intervened jointly to buy euros in September 2000 and expressed shared concern about the potential implications of its weakness for the world economy. 

 While the euro went on to plumb record lows in the months that followed, repeated rounds of solo intervention by the European Central Bank and mounting evidence of U.S. economic slowdown succeeded in boosting the currency by the end of 2000. 

 But investors' enthusiasm has begun to flag in recent weeks, mainly on growing confidence that the U.S. Federal Reserve is acting swiftly enough to prevent a protracted slump which has revived demand for U.S. stocks and dollars. 

 This has meant the euro never got beyond $0.96 in the first week of January before turning tail. It is now nearly eight cents away from the dollar parity rate which France's Fabius said on January 14 it would be scaling within weeks. 

 European officials' comments this week suggested they would be keen to stop the euro's retreat before it turned into a rout, traders said. 

 "The euro failed to grasp the chance to get to parity and the risk now is that it will go back below $0.90," said Colin Clarkson, chief foreign exchange dealer at Sumitomo Bank. 

 "If we fall much below there, it will get people thinking about the record lows so I would expect rhetoric from both Europe and the G7 and people will probably start muttering about intervention again if we break below $0.85." 

 WHAT IS UPPER LIMIT TO EURO'S COMFORT ZONE? 

 But if currency traders are now keeping a watchful eye on forthcoming G7 meetings, some investors were more concerned by Zitzelsberger's suggestion that dollar parity might mark the upper boundary of Germany's preferred range for the euro. 

 "The market's perception had been that parity was not a boundary and so I am slightly disquieted by the comments," said Tim O'Dell, fund manager at Investec Asset Management in London. 

 He said his firm had bought euros at the end of 2000 and already taken profits in the first month of 2001. He said his firm was on the lookout for opportunities to buy the single currency but added: 

 "If, on the euro's next upleg, we saw more such comments about parity, it would be a very powerful impediment to the euro's progress."

     TORONTO, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended down 

 slightly after choppy trading on Friday as the Canadian 

 election campaign began to cast a larger shadow over the 

 volatile currency, market watchers said. 

     The Canadian dollar closed at C$1.5327 (65.24 U.S. cents) 

 against C$1.5317 (65.29 U.S. cents) at the previous close. 

     It strengthened to the C$1.5285 area in early North 

 American trading after broadly supportive job news from both 

 Canada and the United States. It then pared some of its gains

     "It was pretty whippy this morning," said one New 

 York-based currency trader with a major Canadian bank. 

     News that employment in Canada rose 20,200 in October, 

 slightly exceeding the 20,000 expected by analysts, was 

 modestly positive for the currency, market watchers said. 

     The unemployment rate rose to 6.9 percent from 6.8 percent 

 in September. 

     "I think the employment data was good. It should have 

 picked up a bit there, it should have picked up a bit more on 

 the U.S. numbers, the nonfarms being a little soft," the 

currency trader said. 

     U.S. nonfarm payrolls increased by 137,000 in October, 

 defying expectations of a 184,000 increase. 

     But the U.S. report was mixed, with some analysts pointing 

 to news that average hourly earnings rose 0.4 percent as 

 evidence that inflationary pressures are still percolating in 

 the U.S. economy. 

 The Canadian federal election on Nov. 27, which most market 

 watchers say has had only a limited impact on the currency in 

 recent volatile trading, may be starting to play a more 

 prominent role, the trader said. 

 "I think people are still looking at (the Canadian dollar), 

 still a little uncertain with the election coming up," he 

 said. 

 The fact that the incumbent Liberals are slipping a bit in 

 opinion polls, while the opposition Canadian Alliance party is 

 gaining support, may be eliciting some concern from market 

 players, the trader said. 

 A poll by Environics Research Group said the Liberals were 

 ahead of the right-wing Canadian Alliance party by 45 percent 

 to 29 percent, compared with a 44-25 spread in a poll by the 

 same company last week. An Ipsos-Reid poll this week put the 

 spread at 42 percent to 29 percent for the Liberals, compared 

 with 45-28 last week. 

 "I don't think it puts any real uncertainty into the 

 market, but it probably makes any international investor a 

 little concerned," the trader said. 

 EURO STRENGTH SAID DETRIMENTAL 

 Gains in the euro, which was boosted by currency market 

intervention by the European Central Bank on Friday, are also 

 detrimental for the Canadian dollar, he added. "Obviously, the 

 stronger euro goes a little bit against Canada, too," the 

 trader said. 

 The Bank of Canada joined in on the concerted intervention

 on behalf of the common European currency on Sept. 22, but 

 analysts believe it's unlikely the central bank will join in 

 any more efforts to defend the currency in the short term. 

 The Canadian currency is likely to drop as low as C$1.5400, 

 or even C$1.5500 in coming weeks, although a Liberal victory 

 could help inject some new strength into the anaemic currency, 

 he added. 

 "I think if the Liberals get back in, we'll get some 

 stability back here and wouldn't be surprised to see us... down 

 to C$1.5100 to C$1.5200 after the election," he said. 

 Katherine Beattie, technical analyst at Standard & Poor's 

 MMS, agreed that adverse poll results for the Liberals could 

 hamper the Canadian dollar. 

     "If the Liberals continue to slide in the polls, that's 

 another negative," she said. 

     On the top side, the Canadian unit was unable to make it 

 through congestion in the C$1.5275 area during the session, she 

 said. 

     "Technically, tools are a little mixed, but there's no 

 denying that the trend is towards a higher (U.S. dollar spot 

 rate), so we're going to watch C$1.5392, this week's high," 

 Beattie said. 

     A break through that area could see the U.S. dollar climb

title: Canadian role in joint euro defense seen as "token".
text:
(Figures in U.S. dollars unless noted) 

 TORONTO, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Canada made only a "token" contribution to the joint defence of the euro last month and may not join further actions on behalf of the embattled currency, some analysts say. 

 Official international reserve information for September released on Wednesday revealed Canada contributed only $97 million to the joint defence of the European currency on September 22. 

 With the total intervention from central banks amounting to an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion, Canada's contribution was little more than a symbolic gesture, some analysts said. 

 "I would actually classify that kind of intervention as token," said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc. 

 The $97 million revealed in the monthly release on Canada's international reserves was smaller than the $140 million estimated by some analysts after the intervention originally occurred, he said. "It's a little less than expected, but it's in the ballpark," Porter said. 

 The Bank of Canada's participation in the joint rescue for the beleaguered euro seems to have been triggered by a desire to show solidarity with the European Central Bank and other G7 monetary authorities, said Porter and other analysts. 

 "I think everyone was a bit taken by surprise by that decision. You could make the case that they were probably asked directly by the ECB or by the Europeans, and being good global citizens, they did see it as one of the most pressing concerns for the global economy and did join in the effort," Porter said. 

 The Canadian dollar has put in a wobbly performance since the intervention - it dropped 245 points from its close of C$1.4865 (67.27 U.S. cents) on September 21 to its low of C$1.5110 (66.18 cents) on Monday before recovering to C$1.4966 (66.82 U.S. cents) on Wednesday afternoon. 

 While analysts have pointed to a variety of factors for the decline, the weakness may give the Bank of Canada grounds to hesitate before joining another intervention, Porter said. 

 "I think it was a show of solidarity to support the euro, but given how the Canadian dollar has fared since that first intervention, I suspect they won't jump in willingly, again," he said. 

 Porter also said some observers were raising questions about why the bank used Canadian dollars to buy euros instead of drawing on its reserves of U.S. dollars. "I think a lot of people still scratching their heads over why they used Canadian dollars, and just didn't buy the euros with some of their U.S. dollar holdings," he said. 

 The decision to use Canadian dollars might have been prompted by a desire to make a broad-based statement of support for the euro, but that could be accomplished as well by selling U.S. dollars, Porter said. 

 Jeoffrey Hall, managing analyst at Thomson IFR Bonds, said the Canadian central bank's involvement in the intervention was "a little more than a token gesture." 

 "It seems small to me. Certainly, if it were done alone, it would have been laughed at," he added. 

 But Canada has economic justifications for supporting the European currency, he added. "Canada has a vested interest in this because Europe is a major and growing partner of Canada, and some of the value added that Canada exports to the U.S. is ultimately bound for the European Union, as well," he said. 

 "It's not surprising to have found Canada as part of the concerted intervention, whether they're a G7 nation or not," Hall said. 

 The intervention prompted selling of the Canadian dollar against the euro, perhaps correcting some overvaluation of the Canadian unit against the European currency, he said. "It rebalanced the global foreign exchange framework, a little bit," he said. 

 "I don't think it did great damage to the Canadian dollar with respect to the U.S. dollar, either," he added. 

 Further intervention will depend on the level at which euro trades in coming weeks, Hall said. 

 Porter said that further intervention is likely. 

 "I don't think any of the central banks realistically expected that one small round of intervention was going to be the final word on the subject," he said. 

 "Meaningful intervention is a long process. It's a war, not a battle. I think we're bound to see more intervention in the weeks ahead," Porter said. 

 ($1=$1.49 Canadian).

title: Press Release: Flat returns for Canadian DB pension plans in Q3 amidst equity market losses
text:
Flat returns for Canadian DB pension plans in Q3 amidst equity market losses

Canada NewsWire

TORONTO, Oct. 31, 2022

Aggressive central bank interventions and uncertain economic outlook cited as headwinds

TORONTO, Oct. 31, 2022 /CNW/ - Canadian DB pensions in the RBC Investor & Treasury Services All Plan Universe gained 0.5% in Q3, bringing the year-to-date return to -13.7% for the period ending September 30, 2022.

Niki Zaphiratos, Managing Director, Asset Owners, RBC Investor & Treasury Services, said, "Pensions experienced a temporary reprieve in July as the global markets rallied sharply. This rather short-lived change in market sentiment was based mostly on the assumption that the central banks' actions would help control inflationary pressures. We then saw losses over the rest of the quarter, primarily due to concerns that additional aggressive measures would be taken by the central banks."

"As we head toward year-end," Zaphiratos continued, "we are facing various headwinds: the emergence of new COVID-19 variants, the fear of upcoming central bank interest rate hikes and quantitative tightening to combat high and persistent global inflation, and the implications of the Russo-Ukrainian War and US-China tensions. Economic uncertainty remains high and pension fund managers are preparing for ongoing market volatility as the weight of these pressures continues to be felt."

DB pension plans' foreign equities returned -1.1%, slightly behind the MSCI World Index, which returned -0.1%. Growth stocks significantly outperformed value stocks in July, but ended the quarter only slightly ahead (MSCI World Growth CAD +1.1% versus MSCI World Value CAD -1.2%). Within the MSCI World benchmark, weakness in the Communications (-7.3%) and Real Estate (-6.0%) sectors were offset by strength in the Consumer Discretionary (+6.8%) and Energy (+5.0%) sectors. Pension plans with unhedged US dollar exposure benefitted from the rapid appreciation of the US dollar versus the other major trading currencies, driven by investors flocking to that safe haven option.

Canadian equities held by Canadian DB plans returned -1.2% over the quarter, slightly ahead of the TSX composite's -1.4% return over that period. In the benchmark, weakness was noted in the Communication Services (-7.5%) and Energy (-5.3%) sectors, whereas the Industrials (+4.2%) and Consumer Discretionary (+4.2%) sectors outperformed. On a year-to-date basis, Canadian equities led their global counterparts owing to their large exposure to the Energy sector, and were the top performing asset class (-8.8%) in the peer universe.

Fixed income securities held by Canadian DB plans returned 1.1% for the quarter, but were down 17.5% on a year-to-date basis. The FTSE Canada Universe bond index meanwhile returned 0.5% in Q3, compared to -5.7% in Q2. As central banks around the world continued to aggressively raise short-term interest rates to stem inflation, long-term bonds (FTSE Canada Long Term Bond Index +1.5%) outperformed their short-term counterparts (FTSE Canada Short Term Bond Index -0.3%) for the quarter. However, the reverse was true on a year-to-date basis, with short-term bonds returning -4.7% and long-term bonds returning -21.0%.

title: Bank of Canada says it will start providing a summary of rate deliberations next year
text:
OTTAWA, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada said on Wednesday it would begin publishing a summary of its monetary policy deliberations starting next year, accepting a key recommendation from a transparency review by the International Monetary Fund.

The "Summary of Deliberations", similar to meeting minutes released by other central banks, will be published roughly two weeks after each interest rate decision, starting with the Jan. 25 meeting, Canada's central bank said.

"We do expect it to provide a high-level summary of the issues discussed by Governing Council, as well as insight into the key points of focus in their deliberations on economic developments and the risks," said Managing Director of Communications Jeremy Harrison.

The summary will not provide attribution for comments, nor will it include votes, as the Bank of Canada makes decisions on a consensus basis and does not hold votes, Harrison said.

The IMF released its 98-page report on Wednesday, which followed a voluntary review with the Bank of Canada. The report included 10 recommendations, including that the bank publish summaries of its rate decisions and provide more transparency on its "bilateral collaborations" with government.

The IMF also recommended enhancing its disclosures in the case of intervention in the foreign exchange markets. The Bank of Canada said providing more information was not a "priority", in part because the bank has not intervened on the foreign exchange markets since 1998. (Reporting by Julie Gordon, editing by Steve Scherer)

title: UPDATE 2-Bank of Canada to start releasing rate decision summaries next year
text:
(Adds analyst comments, Canadian dollar)

By Julie Gordon and Steve Scherer

OTTAWA, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada on Wednesday said it would begin publishing a summary of its monetary policy deliberations starting next year, accepting a key recommendation from a transparency review by the International Monetary Fund.

The "Summary of Deliberations," similar to meeting minutes released by other central banks, will be published roughly two weeks after each interest rate decision, starting with the Jan. 25 meeting, Canada's central bank said.

"We do expect it to provide a high-level summary of the issues discussed by Governing Council, as well as insight into the key points of focus in their deliberations on economic developments and the risks," Managing Director of Communications Jeremy Harrison told reporters.

"Given our consensus-based decision-making system, the summary won't provide attribution to individual Council members, nor will it record votes because there are no votes in our system," he added.

The Bank of Canada has come under a rare attack from critics over its response to the pandemic, including misjudging inflation, which led to renewed calls for it to release minutes and be more transparent on its decision-making process.

The decision to release summaries comes as worries mount that the pace of rate increases - the central bank has lifted its policy rate by 300 basis points in six months - could lead to a recession.

Economists said providing summaries, similar to minutes released by the U.S. Federal Reserve and Bank of England, could help avoid unnecessary market volatility.

"They could add valuable context on how the Governing Council came to the decision, which would fill a gap that has been evident for some time," said Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins Group.

However, much will depend on how much new information is included, added Mendes.

The bank already includes some details on its talks in the news conference opening statement at its quarterly Monetary Policy Report and in speeches after other decisions.

"Even a basic overview can be useful in correcting or clarifying potential misunderstandings. And at very least, it won't be a negative for markets," said Andrew Kelvin, chief Canada strategist at TD Securities.

The IMF released its 98-page report on Wednesday, which followed a voluntary review with the Bank of Canada. The report included 10 recommendations, including that the bank publish summaries of its rate decisions and provide more transparency on its "bilateral collaborations" with government.

The IMF also recommended that the bank enhance its disclosures in the case of intervention in the foreign exchange markets. The Bank of Canada said providing more information was not a "priority," in part because the bank has not intervened on the foreign exchange markets since 1998.

The Canadian dollar was trading 0.3% higher at 1.3684 to the greenback, or 73.08 U.S. cents. (Reporting by Julie Gordon and Steve Scherer in Ottawa; Additional reporting by Fergal Smith; Editing by Jonathan Oatis)

title: Canadian Policy Makers Shouldn't Rush to  Intervene  in Housing Market -- Market Talk
text:
1111 ET - Canada's hot housing market has prompted calls for government intervention to curb price growth and speculative activity, but Bank of Nova Scotia chief economist Jean-François Perrault says those calls might be premature. He argues the main factor behind recent price acceleration is a divergence between sales and new listings. Since new listings should rise soon because of the spring season and higher prices, he says, policy makers should wait a few weeks before taking action. Perrault added that any short-term changes should be focused on limiting excessive speculation--possibly through a tax on those who flip properties--while longer-term moves should look at easing obstacles to building various forms of housing. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1103 ET - Economists polled in March by the Bank of Mexico raised their median GDP growth estimate for 2021 to 4.5% from 3.7% in February, and lifted expectations for year-end inflation to 4.1% from the previous 3.9%. A recent uptick in inflation led the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged at its March meeting, and expectations are that it will keep the overnight policy rate at the current 4% for the rest of this year. The Bank of Mexico projects GDP growth of 4.8% this year, following an 8.2% contraction in 2020, and the Finance Ministry recently raised its forecast to 5.3% from 4.6%. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1058 ET - The Brazilian central bank 's decision to allow Facebook to offer users a service to make payments between individuals will put pressure on banks' fee earnings from their own payments services, according to Moody's . The service will be available using the WhatsApp messaging application and be linked to Facebook Pay, and no starting date has been set yet for the offering. Brazilian banks have profited from offering payment services to clients for a fee, and also make money from card-payment processing, according to Moody's . The central bank launched its own electronic-payments system, called PIX, in November and that has already led to a sharp drop in fees from money transfers, Moody's says. If the bank permits Facebook to start processing payments to businesses from individuals, that would put even more pressure on banks' fee income, Moody's says. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1055 ET - Peru's presidential election Sunday is shaping up to be one of the most uncertain in memory, political analysts say, as six candidates vie for a spot in a second-round runoff amid widespread rejection of the political class by Peruvians hit hard by the coronavirus pandemic. An Ipsos poll released Sunday has Yonhy Lescano at 14.7% support, followed by Hernando de Soto at 13.9%, Veronika Mendoza at 12.4%, George Forsyth at 11.9%, Keiko Fujimori at 11.2% and Rafael Lopez Aliaga at 8.2%. Meanwhile, an Institute for Peruvian Studies poll has Fujimori and De Soto tied for first, each with 9.8% support. Lopez Aliaga is third at 8.4%. Lescano is at 8.2% and Mendoza at 7.3%. Forsyth has 5.7% backing. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1051 ET - New orders for factory goods in the U.S. declined by 0.8% in February compared with the previous month, data from the Commerce Department shows. The reading misses the 0.3% increase expected by economists polled by The Wall Street Journal and follows a 2.7% rise in January. The decline in factory orders in February disrupts nine consecutive months of increase, and can be attributed partly to bad weather across the country in the month as well as increased supply-chain challenges for manufacturers. New orders for manufactured durable goods fell by 1.2% in February, according to revised figures, compared with the previous estimate of a 1.1% drop. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

1050 ET - The vigorous services-sector activity in the U.S. suggested by the ISM PMI data sets the stage for a robust expansion in the second quarter, Oren Klachkin , lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, says. "All the right pieces for a faster services recovery--expanded vaccine eligibility, reopenings and historic fiscal expansion--are falling into place," he says. The American Rescue Plan will boost the recovery while the American Jobs Plan will also have positive knock-on effects for services as well, Klachkin says. Supply-chain disruptions are likely to hinder activity in the short-term, but they should dissipate as health conditions improve, he says. March's ISM Services PMI came in at a record-high 63.7 from 55.3 the prior month. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

1048 ET - Americans haven't saved too much money during the coronavirus pandemic, the New York Fed says. "Although large by historical standards, the savings accumulated by US households during the pandemic do not appear to be 'excessive' when set against the extraordinary need of many American families and the unprecedented government intervention to support them," wrote Florin Bilbiie, Gauti Eggertsson, Giorgio Primiceri and Andrea Tambalotti for the bank. The authors say it's possible Americans might start spending some of this $1.6 trillion in cash once the pandemic abates, but add they only expected a limited increase in spending out of the savings. The authors note that their view on savings doesn't preclude a strong recovery, while adding "spending out of excess savings won't be one of its major drivers." (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1013 ET - The oil industry has gone through years of weak investment in exploration and drilling of new oil fields due to low prices, and these upstream projects kept dropping in 2020 to a 15-year-low due to coronavirus. But Simmons Energy says the current environment is looking good for a bounceback of activity, even as many uncertainties remain. "The confluence of reflating economic activity and oil demand and redefined E&P capital allocation, should lead to tightening market balances, normalizing OPEC-plus spare capacity and the inception of an upstream reinvestment cycle," the firm says. "This isn't a bad combination for conventional energy, for now." (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

0901 ET - Columbia Threadneedle's "Return to Normal Index" for April climbs to 66% from 60% last month. All components show improvement in the wake of mass vaccination. "The monthly jump has made it clear that widespread vaccination can fuel behavioral and economic recovery," the asset management firm says. The index's components include return to school, travel, entertainment, workplace and brick-and-mortar shopping. Columbia Threadneedle says the greatest rise is happening in in-person schooling. The firm says it's optimistic, but is monitoring infection rates. "If we see a large spike in cases, the momentum carrying the U.S. to our normal range could slow." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0758 ET - US stock futures are sharply higher as investors react to Friday's stronger than expected March jobs report showing the US added 916,000 jobs while the unemployment rate dipped to 6%. Markets were closed for Good Friday. GameStop is off 15% premarket after the videogame retailer announced plans to sell up to 3.5M shares of its common stock. Later this morning the Institute for Supply Management is expected to release its March Services report measuring economic activity in services. On Friday the government is due to release its look at inflation on the wholesale level with the March producer price index. Inflation has been a concern on Wall Street in the wake of the $1.9T stimulus plan recently signed into law by President Biden, and current plans for a $2T infrastructure package. S&P futures are up 23 points. (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

0423 ET - The USD/JPY could trend upward this week thanks to the faster pace of Covid-19 vaccine distribution in the U.S. relative to Japan, IG says. Rising risk-taking sentiment is also likely to help the currency pair, the U.K. broker says, adding that projected growth in first-quarter U.S. corporate earnings should limit any falls in U.S. stock markets despite President Biden's tax-increase plan. The USD/JPY may break 111.00 this week if both U.S. stocks and Treasury yields advance, IG says. The USD/JPY is at 110.58. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0417 ET - Gold prices are calm on a day of reduced trading volumes. The precious metal is down 0.1% at $1,726.40 a troy ounce. After sliding during March, gold's recent drop may have run its course, say analysts at Fitch Group . Meanwhile, "the likely rise in inflation in March and April could support gold prices in the coming weeks, especially if it rises faster than bond yields," they say. The same could be the case if the U.S. dollar remains weak, and that "will keep a floor under prices and feeds into our view that 2021 prices will overall average on par with 2020," they say. The WSJ Dollar Index--which measures the currency against a basket of others--is flat on the day. (david.hodari@wsj.com; @davidhodari)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

April 05, 2021 11:11 ET (15:11 GMT)

title: Bank of  Canada  Says Its Market  Interventions  Are Working -- Market Talk
text:
1304 ET - The Bank of Canada 's efforts to stabilize rocky financial markets are showing early signs of success, a top central bank official says. Senior Deputy Gov. Carolyn Wilkins said the BOC 's interventions--which have so far expanded the central bank's balance sheet to around C$385B, compared with C$120B in early March--have resulted in more activity and narrower spreads. As an example, Wilkins cites the bankers' acceptance market, where she says spreads relative to overnight index swaps have fallen from a high of 120 basis points to around 20 basis points. "It's early days, but we can already see the benefits of these programs," Wilkins said. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1144 ET - A disconnect between the global-growth outlook and market pricing means the safe-haven dollar should continue to appreciate in coming months, TD Securities says. Federal Reserve 's "unbounded" balance sheet in response to coronavirus is unlikely to weigh on the dollar without a "robust" global economy, which will "get worse before it gets better," TD analysts say. Fiscal support from the U.S. government also leaves the dollar "better placed on the growth theme," they say. "A rise in US-China tensions poses additional risks." The dollar index rises 0.5% to a four-day high of 99.5990, according to FactSet. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1116 ET - Investors' withdrawal of about $140 billion from taxable bond mutual bonds and $28 billion from municipal bond funds dragged bond prices further down during the coronavirus-led selloff, which shows the growing role of mutual funds and exchange-traded funds in the U.S. credit market, says S&P Global Ratings. "These record outflows added to the pressure on bond prices during the recent credit market dislocations as fund managers sold assets to meet redemption demands," says the rating agency. Mutual funds, money market funds, and ETFs held nearly $6 trillion in corporate, government, and municipal bonds as of the end of 2019, making up 16% of the U.S. bond market, it adds. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1101 ET - Joe Gruber is joining the Kansas City Fed as its research director, the bank said. Gruber currently serves as deputy director of the International Finance Division for the Fed's Board of Governors in Washington. While at the Board, Gruber was a special advisor for then Vice Chair Stanley Fischer and then for Vice Chair for Supervision Randal Quarles . Gruber has a long central bank tenure, having joined the board in 2001. The Kansas City Fed , based on the public comments of its last two leaders, has been one of the more reliably hawkish regional central bank branches, with its leaders frequently worried about low rates, inflation and financial stability risks. The bank also hosts the Fed's premier research conference each year in Jackson Hole, Wyo., although that's in doubt this year due to the coronavirus crisis. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1058 ET - Investors have increased their bets against sterling due to renewed worries about U.K.-EU trade deal talks, ING says, citing CFTC data for the week to April 28. Sterling net positions in the futures market fell for the ninth consecutive week, which is "likely a function of the resurgence of some shorts related to Brexit uncertainty," ING analysts say in a note. "GBP net positioning is now at -4% of open interest, but the risk of additional downside in the gauge is quite material, especially when adding the rising concerns about the economic fallout of extended lockdown measures in the U.K." GBP/USD falls 0.6% to 1.2424 and EUR/GBP declines 0.1% to 0.8779. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1055 ET - The shape of the economic recovery will have little impact on company defaults over the next three years in Europe, say Societe Generale 's credit strategists. In a an equally sharp fall and rebound in economic activity-- the so-called V-shaped recovery--as well as an U-shaped recovery, which takes longer for the economy to recover, the damage is done by the initial economic contraction, they say. "The real question for credit investors, then, is not so much the shape of the recovery but rather the pace of the initial drop. The bigger the economic contraction in 2Q, the higher the realised defaults will be under any future economic scenario," they add. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1052 ET - After almost 50 days in lockdown, Peru is planning to start to reopen the economy even though the number of Covid-19 cases continues to rise sharply. A decree was published over the weekend allowing mining, and some construction and fishing to resume operations. Authorities say the reopening will take place in stages over the next four months, and require companies to adhere to strict health rules to reduce the spread of the coronavirus. Pollster Datum says the plan is backed by 70% of Peruvians, many without jobs due to the economic collapse caused by the lockdown. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1051 ET - J.P.Morgan doesn't expect any rating action on Italy by Moody's Investors Service and DBRS Morningstar at their scheduled reviews on May 8. On April 24, S&P Global Ratings affirmed Italy's rating, while Fitch Ratings last week downgraded Italy in an out-of-schedule review. "Also in their rating announcement statement Fitch highlighted that the risk for further action comes if the government does not implement a credible economic growth and fiscal strategy that enhances confidence that general government debt-to-GDP will be placed on a downward path over time," J.P.Morgan says. "Therefore, suggesting no imminent risk of further action," J.P.Morgan says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1047 ET - As eurozone governments ramp up government bond issuance to cover the fiscal costs of the coronavirus pandemic, they raised a record EUR123 billion via conventional government bond issuance in April, says J.P.Morgan . This is the highest monthly conventional issuance amount since the inception of the euro, they say. The strong pace of issuance is set to continue, says J.P.Morgan . It expects EUR100 billion-EUR110 billion of gross conventional issuance in May. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1043 ET - The euro could fall to $1.05 this summer from $1.0911 at present if EU leaders continue to disagree over how to support the eurozone's most vulnerable economies through the coronavirus crisis, Rabobank says. "While the Eurozone's huge current account surplus may continue to lend support, sentiment in the EUR will be eroded if politics turn sour on the issue of fiscal coherence within the region," Rabobank FX strategist Jane Foley . In coming weeks, EUR/USD could drop to 1.08 on safe haven demand for the dollar as U.S.-China tensions resume and global economic data shows the "scale of the demand side crisis that the world economy faces," she says. After that, a drop towards 1.05 over the summer "cannot be ruled out," she adds. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1029 ET - Relatively low yields on local debt issued by emerging markets, relative to the selloff during the 2008 global financial crisis, shows EM outflows aren't material, says Jan Dehn , head of research at Ashmore Group . Commenting on IMF data last week showing that the coronavirus pandemic triggered the worst outflow in the history of EM debt, with $100 billion fleeing the asset class, Dehn says that EM local bond yield stood at 4.87% as of Friday, while yield on EM local currency sovereign debt spiked to briefly 8.99% in 2008. The softer selloff is driven by lower inflation rates, lighter positioning among foreign investors due to 10 years of U.S. dollar strength, and more developed central bank tools in emerging countries. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1022 ET - New orders for manufactured goods drop 10.3% to a seasonally adjusted $445.8B in March as efforts to contain the coronavirus disrupted supply chains and quashed demand. That was the biggest monthly fall in records dating back to 1992. Economists surveyed by WSJ had expected a decline of 9.2%. New orders for durable goods--items designed to last at least three years--decreased 14.7%, compared with a preliminary estimate of a 14.4% fall. That was the second-biggest decline on record. (jeffrey.sparshott@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

May 04, 2020 13:04 ET (17:04 GMT)

title: Liquidity Dries Up in Canadian Corporate Bond Market -- Market Talk
text:
1745 ET - Investment funds are having trouble finding bids for corporate bonds in Canada's fixed-income market, with risk aversion keeping buyers at bay. "Liquidity in the secondary bond market is worse than it was in the fourth-quarter of 2008," says Ian McKinnon, Chairman of the Canadian Bond Investors' Association. Many funds are suffering redemption requests, he says, which is causing them to sell bonds in their portfolios to meet the demand for money. In many cases, the lack of bids is causing the funds to take losses. "There's now a cost to the withdrawals," he says. CBIA wrote a letter to the Bank of Canada Tuesday asking for central bank intervention in the bond markets to help get things moving again. (vipal.monga@wsj.com; @vipalmonga)

1734 ET - Westpac says some 200,000 people in New Zealand will lose their jobs and the economy will contract at least 10% in 2Q as pandemic-control measures bite. The bank estimates economic activity will drop by a third during the four-week national lockdown that began mid-week. Westpac 's New Zealand chief economist Dominick Stephens says the job losses will push the unemployment rate to high single digits from 4% now while the estimated contraction in the economy is "completely unprecedented in our lifetimes." Finance Minister Grant Robertson yesterday acknowledged the economic downturn will be much worse than the GFC and that job losses will be substantial even with government measures such as generous wage subsidies. (stephen.wright@wsj.com)

1649 ET - Borrowing at the Fed's discount window nearly doubled over the last week. Discount-window borrowing stood at $50.77B as of Wednesday and was at $28.22B on March 18. That's a lot compared with negligible interest in recent years, but it's still well below the $400B taken in late 2008. Separately, Fed currency swaps with other central banks have exploded amid dollar pressure: On Wednesday they hit $206.1B from near-zero levels the week before. The Fed has been extending the counterparties and terms of its liquidity swaps to ensure no shortage of dollars among major central banks. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1628 ET - The US dollar weakens broadly against other major currencies as jobless claims rise an unprecedented 3.28M, even as a more than 6% gain by the Dow puts the index in a bull market. US currency weakens about 1.5% against the euro and 1.6% against the yen. "With the number of new policy measures likely to slow, and economic numbers like these starting to roll in, we still think it is too early to call a trough in broader risk or a top in the Dollar, even as some asset classes that have seen significant government intervention start to find their footing," Goldman Sachs says. (jonathan.vuocolo@wsj.com; @jonvuocolo)

1333 ET - Sterling's rise to a nine-day high of $1.2181 Thursday is driven by a pick-up in market sentiment following efforts by global leaders to tackle the coronavirus pandemic, says John Goldie, FX strategist at Argentex Group . "The pound's assumed dynamic as a risk currency was in prime evidence today as stocks were up, volatility down, U.S. dollar down, all in sync with sterling appreciation--essentially risk is back on, for this afternoon at least," Goldie says. Recent central bank and government action in response to coronavirus "may have placated investors' fears for the time being" but it seems "very unlikely that the difficulties are over in financial markets," he says. In coming weeks, the "choppiness in markets will remain." (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1322 ET - The coronavirus has dramatically lowered the human race's ecological footprint and could have a lasting effect on shopping habits, says David Utley, consumer analyst at GlobalData. For instance, Utley says, U.K. shoppers are now buying seasonal vegetables grown in the U.K. instead of ones imported from other European countries due to the border lockdown. He says the virus could alter the shopping habits of the 41% of U.K. consumers who say they want to buy environmentally friendly goods but don't. "This will have to be reinforced by government and corporate policy if it's going to stick in the long term, especially after the pandemic ends," Utley says. (dieter.holger@wsj.com; @dieterholger)

1311 ET - There is "still no trace" of green stimulus in any of the current government plans to fight the economic fallout from the coronavirus, says consultancy Sustainable Market Strategies. Even in Europe, where leaders have previously pledged to use the next crisis to boost the green economy, no funding has been announced to fight climate change as part of planned spending or actions, SMS says. "While we are still counting the human and economic damage associated to this crisis, one can look at another, long-term silent killer yet to be tamed by governments: climate change," it says. (dieter.holger@wsj.com; @dieterholger)

1307 ET - European stocks rise on optimism over global efforts to offset the economic impact of the coronavirus pandemic. The Stoxx Europe 600 gains 2.5%, the FTSE 100 increases 2.2%, the DAX adds 1.3% and the CAC-40 is up 2.5%. The U.S. Senate on Wednesday passed a $2.2 trillion rescue package to provide relief to citizens and businesses affected by coronavirus. Meanwhile, G20 leaders on Thursday said they were willing to do whatever it takes to tackle coronavirus. "The united front from the world leaders helped market confidence, because as far as the west is concerned, the battle is in its infancy," CMC Markets analyst David Madden says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1253 ET - Canadian PM Trudeau says senior officials are pressing chartered banks and credit-card companies to offer relief for income-strapped individuals and households, either through extended grace periods or lower interest rates. At a press briefing, Trudeau says high credit-card interest rates pose "a significant challenge for many Canadians at this point. That is why we are encouraging [the financial sector] to take action and alleviate the burden for Canadians." Canadian households are among the most indebted in the developed world, based on a share of after-tax income. In Canada, nonmortgage personal debt outstanding as of January stood at roughly C$630B. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1242 ET - Thursday's rise in U.S. jobless claims to a record high of 3.2 million signal a potential global recession, says Unigestion. The asset manager says its analysis points to a 5% contraction in GDP across 2Q in the U.S. and in Europe, bringing 2020 GDP estimates to falls of 2.6% in the U.S. and 3.5% in Europe respectively. The jobless claims mean its readings now are consistent with a global recession. "The fiscal answer outside the U.S. is insufficient and there remains a global imbalance as the situation appears to be getting more serious by the hour," says Unigestion's Head of Macroeconomic Research Florian Ielpo. "For now, we remain concerned at market liquidity which may be at risk." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

1238 ET - The Federal Reserve 's recent efforts to ease the U.S. dollar funding squeeze should particularly benefit the Norwegian krone and sterling, ING says. "NOK has been the key victim of the latest market rout as the krone low liquidity heavily exaggerated the currency downfall," ING analyst Petr Krpata says. The pound "suffers from the worst current account position" in the G10 FX space and the external funding needs make the currency vulnerable, he says. "Both currencies may still decline further versus USD, but the tentative signs of an improvement on the USD funding front suggest a reducing risk of GBP and NOK meltdown during risk-off days." GBP/USD rises 1.6% to 1.2073 and USD/NOK falls 2.5% to 10.4707. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1230 ET - The euro could fall as low as $1.05 if the coronavirus pandemic worsens and boosts demand for the safe haven dollar, says Bhanu Baweja , chief strategist at UBS . However, "once the dust settles" and the coronavirus crisis eases, the dollar should "begin to weaken" and EUR/USD could rise to $1.15, he says. "We're not expecting much depreciation of the dollar as we need to see the rest of the world recovering and we don't think that growth will improve significantly any time soon." EUR/USD rises 1.2% to a one-week high of 1.1028 as the dollar falls for the fourth consecutive day after Federal Reserve action to reduce the dollar funding squeeze and a sharp rise in weekly U.S. jobless claims. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

March 26, 2020 17:45 ET (21:45 GMT)

title: Currency Intervention  Not In  Canada 's 'Active Toolkit' -- Market Talk
text:
1431 ET - A senior Bank of Canada official reiterated during a press conference that it is not the central bank's practice to engage in currency intervention. Deputy Governor Lynn Patterson was asked during a press conference in Hamilton, Ontario, if the BoC would step in to support the Canadian dollar if it fell below a certain level. "We don't typically do any currency intervention. It's not part of our policies that we would focus on," Patterson replied. She said that if the loonie fell dramatically the central bank would want to understand the reasons behind the change, but currency intervention "is not part of an active toolkit that we use." The BoC has not intervened in foreign exchange markets to affect movements of the Canadian dollar in more than 20 years. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1206 ET - The U.S. Senate 's banking committee has advanced nominees to fill vacancies at the U.S. Export-Import Bank to the full chamber for approval. A favorable vote would allow ExIm to resume its proper work, including what Boeing CEO Dennis Muilenburg says is $40 billion in a backlog of deals--many for planes. But that is only one hurdle ExIm faces. Mr. Muilenburg says that in September, the export credit agency comes up for reauthorization, which could stir new political battles about the institution. (robert.wall@wsj.com)

1124 ET - European financial and mining stocks are on the back foot after the European Central Bank 's rate hold and dovish outlook on the economy offset any potential lift from its announcement of a cash injection for banks. German, Italian and Spanish banks are among the biggest pan-European fallers, while in London, Fresnillo, Glencore and Rio Tinto are among the biggest mining losers. "The move initially propelled the major eurozone equity markets into positive territory, but it was short-lived," says David Madden at CMC Markets . "The underlying message from the ECB was negative, and that played out in the stock market." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

1102 ET - The European Central Bank has been pre-emptive rather than reactive, says Seema Shah, senior global investment strategist at Principal Global Investors . By announcing new liquidity operations earlier than the market was anticipating, the ECB has moved ahead of the curve and provided strong reassurance to the banking sector, and to the real economy to some extent that it will provide support if required, Shah says. The ECB announced a new series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations but these TLTROs themselves are unlikely to provide strong stimulus, but demonstrating its intent to act is half the job done, Shah says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

1054 ET - Shares in European banks fall sharply after the European Central Bank said Thursday that it would leave interest rates unchanged at least until the end of the year, longer than investors had expected. Banco de Sabadell shares, which fall 7.7%, and Deutsche Bank stock, which is down 5.3%, are among the worst performers. UniCredit , Societe Generale , BNP Paribas , Credit Agricole, Commerzbank and UBS , among others, fall between 3.3% and 4.9%. (pietro.lombardi@dowjones.com; @pietrolombard10)

1053 ET - The European Central Bank 's stimulus announcement is having a ripple effect in the federal-funds futures market, where traders are pricing in higher odds of a Federal Reserve rate cut by year-end. Futures recently showed a 14% chance of the Fed lowering short-term interest rates by the end of the year, a jump from 5.9% Wednesday and 6% a week ago, according to CME . The futures, while volatile, have over the past few months pointed to growing conviction among traders that the Fed will either leave rates unchanged throughout 2019 or lower them. The ECB 's move, spurred by weakening growth in the eurozone and the rest of the world, gives traders more reason to believe that yields across developed markets will remain lower for longer. (akane.otani@wsj.com; @akaneotani)

1052 ET - The ECB 's current strategy clearly follows the idea of "if you can't beat it, try to avoid it for as long as possible," says ING economist Carsten Brzeski . A severe downswing in the economy would now require unprecedented measures. But whatever the outcome, "today's ECB meeting clearly means that Mario Draghi will be the first ECB president who never hiked interest rates during his term in office," says Mr. Brzeski. (nina.adam@wsj.com; @Nina_Adam_)

1046 ET - The initial market reaction to ECB 's announcement that it is keeping interest rates unchanged until next year as well as launching another round of targeted longer-term refinancing operations is underwhelming, David Riley , chief investment strategist at BlueBay Asset Management , says. European government bonds have rallied but equities, including bank stocks, in the region are down and the euro is modestly weaker, which suggests investors appear to be more focused on the "substantial" but realistic downgrade to the ECB 's forecasts for Eurozone growth in 2019 to 1.1% compared with 1.7% forecasts in December. "The fear that investors have is that despite President [Mario] Draghi's talk of optionality, the reality is that the ECB has limited monetary ammunition to offset downside risks," he says. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1030 ET - European Central Bank President Mario Draghi once again managed to "over deliver" relative to market expectations but the structural headwinds for the eurozone remain the same as before, says Marc Ostwald , global strategist and chief economist at ADM Investor Services International . The structural headwinds will continue to ensure that as long as euro-area governments continue to "under deliver" on reforms and in broader policy terms, the impact of ECB policy measures will continue to be heavily muted," Ostwald says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

1026 ET - Euro "bears have fresh ammunition" after European Central Bank 's monetary policy decision on Thursday, says Audrey Childe-Freeman, chief strategist at FX Knowledge, as the euro falls to a 16-week low of $1.1229. Postponing the first interest-rate increase and cutting eurozone economic growth forecasts to such an extent was surprising, Childe-Freeman says. The euro could fall to $1.10 if it drops below $1.12, she adds. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

1025 ET - Even though the European Central Bank changed its forward guidance and lowered economic growth forecasts, the main driver for the euro is likely to be the U.S. and China trade discussions, says Audrey Childe-Freeman, chief strategist at FX Knowledge. The euro fell to a 16-week low of $1.1229 on Thursday after the ECB announcement, but "the ECB-driven euro bearish case that we identify today is a short-term story," says Childe-Freeman. "Over the next few weeks though, the euro outlook will be more a function of international considerations than of domestic and ECB factors," she says. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com)

0954 ET - The fall in eurozone government bond yields accelerate as European Central Bank President Mario Draghi holds his press conference, giving insight into the Governing Council's decisions and slashing 2019 growth and inflation forecasts. Italian bond yields continue to lead eurozone peers lower, trading 10 basis points lower at 2.52%, according to Tradeweb . German Bund yields trade 3.7 bps lower at 0.091%. French, Belgian, Spanish, Portuguese and Irish bond yields trade lower by between 5 and 6 basis points. The ECB delayed its forecast for when it expects to raise interest rates. It now sees interest rates staying at current levels at least through the end of 2019 and announced a new series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Market Talk Roundup: Latest on Trump, U.S. Politics
text:
The latest Market Talks covering President Donald Trump and U.S. politics. Published exclusively on Dow Jones Newswires throughout the day.

1129 ET - The Institute for Supply Management says its nonmanufacturing index for November will be released on Thursday instead of Wednesday this week. The index-tracking a wide range of US industries such as health care, finance, construction and agriculture, will come out at 10am ET on Thursday, December 6 after President Donald Trump declared Wednesday to be a National Day of Mourning to pay tribute to former President George H.W. Bush. The New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq will close in his honor, and Fed Chairman Jerome Powell 's testimony before Congress on Wednesday was also canceled. (harriet.torry@wsj.com; @HarrietTorry)

1040 ET - The US-China trade spat has rocked soybeans prices this year and Chicago futures are still down 11% over the past six months. It will take more than vague agreements to spark a sustainable soy rally, investors say, and soybeans' global trade flow has also irreparably shifted, with China having upped its imports from Brazil and Argentina in anticipation of US tariffs. "Even if China came back to the US market in a huge way... they would have to buy record amounts every week from now until the end of the marketing year in August," says Zaner Group's Brian Grossman. Soybeans are up 1.8% at $9.11 a bushel. (david.hodari@wsj.com; @Davidhodari)

1027 ET - A major seafood group says it's pleased by the US-China tariff truce, but warns American jobs are still at stake. Both US importers and exporters of seafood have been caught in the trade dispute: China in July slapped 25% duties on a range of imported American fish, in response to tariffs imposed by Washington. Dozens of varieties of fish imported to the US from China -- including some caught in America and processed in China -- were then hit by 10% tariffs from the Trump administration. The National Fisheries Institute says it's pleased the US will not boost those tariffs but that more progress is needed. "Whether it's imports or exports the jobs impacted are here in the U.S.," the group's spokesman said. (jesse.newman@wsj.com; @jessenewman13)

0956 ET - BMO Capital Markets has revised downward its economic growth forecast for Canada in 2019 after Alberta ordered crude-production cuts, equal to 325,000 barrels a day or nearly 9% of output. BMO now anticipates 2019 growth in Canada of 1.8%, versus earlier estimate of 2%. In particular, growth in 1Q next year is now expected to slow significantly to 0.7% annualized. "This is a modest downgrade to the growth call but there's plenty of uncertainty heading into next year," BMO told clients. Firm doesn't expect Alberta cut to affect Bank of Canada rate-policy plans, although cautioning BoC's tone may change about outlook when central bank issues latest rate decision Wednesday and Gov Stephen Poloz delivers speech Thursday. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

0937 ET - Bank of Nova Scotia said Alberta's decision to cut crude production by nearly 9% in 2019 should lead to price spread between Western Canadian Select and WTI to narrow by "a couple of bucks" from Friday's $29 level. Firm's economists, though, indicate the production cut in Alberta comes at a time when other factors are already working to compress the spread, which hit a high of $50 in October. Those factors include US refineries coming back online, increased use of rail to ship crude, and the completion next year of Enbridge's Line 3 pipeline replacement project. Scotiabank says now spread could shrink to the $15 to $20 once everything is accounted for. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

0916 ET - Rising political uncertainty ahead of the European Parliament elections in May 2019 could further undermine recent positive economic-growth dynamics, says Fitch Ratings . "Slower GDP growth, higher interest rates and pressures to increase capital expenditure will pose a challenge for debt dynamics in highly indebted sovereigns," says Michele Napolitano, senior director at the ratings firm. He says that changing policy mixes will make fiscal consolidation more challenging, while politics becomes less conducive to tight fiscal policies and reforms. Among the 22 Western European countries in Fitch's report, Austria and Finland have positive ratings outlooks, while Italy, the U.K. and San Marino are on negative outlook. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0853 ET - Imperial Oil's CEO Rich Kruger says Alberta's mandatory 8.7% oil output cut, announced Sunday, is risky and could lead to unintended consequences. title: Trump Administration Considering Adding  Currency  Rules to Nafta, Sources Say--2nd Update
text:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration has told senators it is considering adding rules barring currency manipulation to the North American Free Trade Agreement , according to congressional aides, a departure from past U.S. policy that could set a precedent for other trade deals.

U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer said in a Senate meeting Wednesday that he is looking at currency rules as a part of planned renegotiation of Nafta, the 23-year-old trade agreement that connects the U.S. economy with Canada's and Mexico's, the aides said.

An administration official confirmed the U.S. is looking at some sort of currency disciplines but didn't say whether the rules would be binding and enforceable through Nafta's dispute-settlement procedures.

Canada and Mexico haven't been the focus of U.S. criticism over currency, but adding currency rules to Nafta could set a precedent for including them in future negotiations with Asian trading partners.

Currency rules weren't in a previous draft of the administration's Nafta negotiating blueprint plan reviewed by The Wall Street Journal in March.

"It is highly controversial, but I think it does make sense," said Fred Bergsten, founding director of the Peterson Institute for International Economics and co-author of a forthcoming book this year on currency manipulation.

"The link between exchange-rate movements is very clear and very substantial. It's a lot more important than many of the other things that have been linked to trade policy," he said.

While U.S. manufacturers have complained about currency manipulation, groups representing sprawling multinational businesses say they are more concerned about tariffs and commercial rules of the road than currency levels, which fluctuate up and down over time.

In the past two years, critics of U.S. trade policy have generated opposition to Washington's trade agreements by saying China and other countries manipulate their currencies in ways that have a bigger effect on their export competitiveness than tariff levels set by trade deals.

Former President Barack Obama's administration didn't include enforceable currency rules in the Trans-Pacific Partnership, the 12-nation deal that Congress never ratified and President Donald Trump exited in January. At the time, U.S. officials said trading partners were opposed to the rules, and some worried such guidelines, even if carefully tailored, could tie the hands of U.S. monetary policy in the future.

Instead, the TPP countries agreed to nonbinding guidelines and transparency procedures outside the agreement.

The issue of currency rules wasn't unexpected as a part of the new administration's trade policy. Mr. Trump has frequently blamed China for manipulating its currency, although his Treasury Department declined to declare Beijing a currency manipulator this year. Economists say China has actually been intervening to support the value of the yuan of late, rather than pushing it weaker to gain a trade advantage.

title: Trump Administration Considering Adding  Currency  Rules to Nafta, Sources Say--Update

An administration official confirmed the U.S. is looking at some sort of currency disciplines but didn't say whether the rules would be binding and enforceable through Nafta's dispute-settlement procedures.

Canada and Mexico haven't been the focus of U.S. criticism over currency, but adding currency rules to Nafta could set a precedent for including them in future negotiations with Asian trading partners.

Currency rules weren't in a previous draft of the administration's Nafta negotiating blueprint plan reviewed by The Wall Street Journal in March.

"It is highly controversial, but I think it does make sense," said Fred Bergsten, founding director of the Peterson Institute for International Economics and co-author of a forthcoming book this year on currency manipulation.

title: Canadian Dollar Falls for 10th Straight Day to New Multiyear Low
text:
TORONTO--The Canadian dollar fell against the U.S. dollar for the 10th consecutive day as plummeting oil prices continued to weigh on the commodity-linked currency and push it to new multiyear lows.

The U.S. dollar was recently at C$1.4530 from C$1.4358 late Thursday, according to data provider CQG. The greenback rose as high as C$1.4555 or 68.70 U.S. cents, during the Friday trading session, a level it hasn't reached since April 29 2003.

The loonie fell early during the overnight trading session as a sharp drop in oil and market expectations of a looming Bank of Canada rate cut next week pulled investors away from the currency.

With an uncertain outlook in oil prices and several troubling economic indicators, some economists expect the Bank of Canada to cut interest rates during its rate meeting next week.

"It's very rare to see these moves extend in this way," said Scotiabank chief currency strategist Shaun Osborne. "We're well overdue a rebound in the Canadian dollar at this point."

Other market watchers, like BMO Capital Markets chief economist Doug Porter, believes the Canadian dollar should trade around current levels until oil prices bottom out.

"Lower oil prices are still a net negative for the Canadian economy and for the Canadian dollar," Mr. Porter said.

While Mr. Osborne expects the Canadian dollar to recover from its recent lows, he also doesn't expect to see the Bank of Canada cut rates next week. The Canadian dollar has depreciated enough that the central bank may want to take a wait-and-see approach to gauge whether the weaker currency may drive foreign business investment into the country over the next several months before making a move on monetary policy.

A rate cut will also "convey to the market casual disregard to the currency's performance going forward," he added.

The sudden move in the loonie has also brought to light the slim chance the Bank of Canada may intervene in currency markets, the first such time it would do so since 1998. Mr. Osborne doesn't believe it'll happen, but given the extraordinary moves, it isn't outside the realm of possibility, he said.
