title: =DJ  FOREX  VIEW: Canada Dollar Strength Could Collide With BOC Rhetoric
text:
A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN

TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar hasn't faced many serious hurdles as it has firmed to a two-and-a-half year high in recent trading. But continued strength could bring into play a formidable adversary: the Bank of Canada.

Canada's central bank has been subdued in recent statements about the currency, citing it as a potential risk to the recovery in exports but not emphasizing the threat. But the bank has used rhetoric as a tool in combating currency strength in the past and some analysts think it will do so again in the coming weeks.

The Canadian dollar has rallied since the bank's last policy statement in December, pushing above the psychologically significant parity level with the U.S. dollar and staying there for its first extended stretch since May 2008.

The U.S. dollar was trading at C$0.9862 Wednesday afternoon, considerably below the C$1.0200 average the Bank had assumed for its two-year forecast period in its most-recent quarterly monetary policy report in October.

Supported by the rally in commodity prices, favorable short-term yield differentials against the U.S. and Canada's superior fiscal situation, the currency looks poised to continue its rally.

If the bank is worried that this situation will be a threat to Canada's export sector, it has a perfect opportunity to voice those fears in the coming days. The bank has its first policy announcement of the year scheduled for next Tuesday. The following day, the bank releases its quarterly monetary policy report and Governor Mark Carney is expected to hold a news conference.

"I suspect he'll say something about the Canadian dollar being too high and the Bank of Canada's willingness to intervene," said Aaron Fennell, senior market strategist at futures broker Lind-WaldockCanada in Toronto. But any reference to intervention in currency markets will be "noncommittal"; a reminder of the bank's capacity to intervene rather than a commitment to take action, he said.

That was the pattern the bank followed in the fall of 2009, when an appreciation in the currency prompted some effective sabre rattling from the bank, but no actual intervention. The bank last intervened in currency markets in a joint effort to bolster the euro in the fall of 2000. The last time it intervened on its own was in 1998, and that was to prop up the Canadian dollar, not bring it down.

Some other analysts believe the bank will refrain from escalating its rhetoric. They think it will instead take the view the currency's rise is justified by the strength in prices for the commodities which make up a big portion of the country's exports, and the dampening effect on export volumes will be offset by the higher prices of the commodities exported.

"Although the currency's a little bit stronger than it was the last time they spoke about it, commodity prices are also stronger, so on a net basis, it hasn't become a worse issue since the last time they spoke," said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC World Markets.

Doug Porter, deputy chief economist at BMO Capital Markets, agrees the bank could take the view that the broadly based rise in commodity prices explains the increase in the currency so far. But any further move higher could elicit concern from the bank, he said.

"I think the bank is probably somewhat concerned about the currency taking another big step higher from current levels," Porter said.

-Don Curren, Dow Jones Newswires; 416-306-2020; don.curren@dowjones.com

title: GROWING APPEAL OF CANADA TO FOREIGN CENTRAL BANKS MAY BE OVERHEATING THE LOONIE: CIBC WORLD MARKETS INC.
text:
TORONTO, Dec. 17 /CNW/ -- Exchange rate hampering Bank of Canada's ability to slow growth in household debt

TORONTO, Dec. 17 /CNW/ - CIBC (CM: TSX; NYSE) - The growing appeal of Canada to foreign investors, including central banks, may be overheating the value of the loonie, further hurting an already battered Canadian manufacturing sector and making it difficult for the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates to slow growing household debt, finds a new report from CIBC World Markets Inc.

While Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney recently warned of a "death grip" on the U.S. dollar, given that over 40 per cent of America's trade is now with countries with managed exchange rates against the greenback and more than a dozen countries seeing double-digit growth in their reserves, the report notes the Canadian dollar may also be in a "death grip" of its own.

"Reasonable decisions by central banks to diversify their reserve holdings, including added weight in the Canadian dollars, may have been a key factor in driving our currency to parity vs. the U.S. unit, offsetting a large trade deficit," says Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC. "Precise data on such flows aren't available, and much of the foreign ownership of Canadian bonds is likely in private sector hands. But a significant share of the growth of late, and it's been massive, appears to be linked to central bank reserves and other sovereign funds."

The CIBC report found that foreign investors added more than $72 billion to their Canadian dollar bond holdings in the past 12 months, nearly enough to finance last year's entire federal and provincial deficit. The majority of that has been in Government of Canada issues, the favoured vehicle for central bank reserves.

Canadian dollar central bank holdings are lumped into an "other" category in IMF data that would also include the Australian dollar and a few others, with most emerging economies not reporting on the composition of their holdings. Mr. Shenfeld believes these non-reporters are following a similar allocation. Using a reasonable estimate of Canada's share of that "other" group, he estimates central banks might be accounting for a third-to-a-half of the net new foreign buying, which is also in line with anecdotal evidence from market participants.

"Those central banks are not, of course, trying to control their currency's cross against the Canadian dollar, since the bilateral trade flows that would be affected would be modest," adds Mr. Shenfeld. "Nor are they directly aiming at driving the loonie up against the U.S. unit. But that is still the outcome."

The elevated value of the loonie has hamstrung the Bank of Canada in its efforts to stem the rapid growth in consumer debt through interest rates hikes. A CIBC Economics analysis in the report shows that Canada's current debt load is not problematic, but if maintained, the present pace of borrowing could put a squeeze on household finances five years out.

The Bank can't move to raise interest rates to deter additional borrowing for fear of sending the loonie even higher and putting further drag on exports. Already, the Canadian dollar's appreciation has contributed to Canada losing more than a quarter of its 2001 share of the U.S. import market.

While many are now looking to the federal government to put the brakes on household borrowing, the report suggests Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney has another option.

"There is one weapon yet to be touched: fighting fire with fire," says Mr. Shenfeld. "Canada could match foreign central bank intervention in favour of our currency with an offsetting intervention, selling an equivalent volume of loonies. That would simply move back to market determined exchange rates, and would loosen the death grip on the Canadian dollar."

Mr. Shenfeld notes that while global policy makers have devoted a great deal of time and effort to developing financial sector reforms based on the lessons from the past economic crisis, Canadian policy makers may want to pay a little more attention to the impacts of an imbalance in trade tied to misaligned currencies, another key factor in the recent troubles that tripped up the global economy.

title: UPDATE: BOC's Carney: Interest Rates In Canada "Abnormally, Exceptionally Low"
text:
(Updates to include additional comments from Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney beginning in paragraph 10.)

TORONTO (Dow Jones)--Interest rates in Canada remain abnormally low even though they have been raised from the emergency levels reached after the collapse of Lehman Brothers in the fall of 2008, Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney said in an interview with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

The interview is scheduled for broadcast on Sunday morning but was released in advance by the publicly owned national broadcaster Friday afternoon.

Carney said Canada's central bank has raised its key policy rate from the record low of 0.25% reached during the financial crisis "because the Canadian economy is back at the level we were before the crash."

"We've recovered all the jobs we'd lost during the crash. I mean, things have moved quite positively for Canada, but [interest rates] are still at exceptionally low levels," he said. There's a risk some Canadians will take on more debt on the assumption "that interest rates will always be this way," Carney said.

Asked about a recent media report that Royal Bank of Canada is on an international list of banks deemed "Too Big to Fail", Carney said the largest Canadian bank was "absolutely not" on the list.

"Let me first clarify that RBC is not on that list. There's a report that it might be, but that was an unsourced report," he said.

While governments and central banks had to stand up and provide capital and liquidity for banks during the global financial crisis, it's important that the concept of "too big to fail" does not become established in markets, Carney said.

"This isn't how a market economy should work," he said. "There needs to be discipline on the financial institutions and there's a variety of things that we're doing to end 'Too Big to Fail,' not to enshrine 'Too Big to Fail'," he said.

Asked if Canada could get "caught in the crossfire" as nations around the world engage in competitive devaluation, Carney said the Bank of Canada has "a number of tools" available.

"We can intervene in currency markets if extreme movements in our dollar seriously threaten economic outcomes in Canada," Carney said. "Those are decisions taken by the Minister of Finance and the Governor," he said. "They are extreme."

The bank has policy flexibility and would use it, if appropriate, to achieve its 2% inflation target, he said.

Carney said efforts to manipulate trade through fixed currency policies could be damaging to the global economy. "You can cause damage to the global system in the short-term, but it doesn't work in the long term because ultimately those adjustments to currencies will come through relative inflation differentials if nothing else," he said.

The global financial system came within about 36 hours of a "seize up" in October 2008, Carney said in the interview. "[The] Minister of Finance and I entered a G7 meeting - it was at the time on a Friday afternoon in Washington...at that point I think it was clear that we were going to have nothing less than a seizure of the global financial system if certain decisions were not taken," he said.

The international banking system is "without question" more secure now than it was two years ago, Carney said.

Globally, the situation has improved because there have been big adjustments to policy, including monetary policy, he said. Additionally, major banks around the world have built up substantial amounts of capital over the last two years, he added.

title: UPDATE 1-Unilateral  FX intervention  rarely effective: BOC
text:
* BoC would prefer to intervene along with others - Carney

* Carney gives no indication bank ready to act now

* Says rates abnormally low, must be vigilant on debt (Adds quotes, details)

By Louise Egan

OTTAWA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Unilateral intervention in foreign exchange markets is rarely effective and if the Bank of Canada wanted to act, it would look to do so with other countries, Governor Mark Carney said on Wednesday.

Carney noted that the central bank's long-established policy is to intervene only in cases of disruption in foreign exchange markets or when extreme movements in the value of the Canadian dollar threatened the economy.

"Unilateral intervention without backing policy actions seldom works sustainably. If conditions warranted we would look to act with our partners in advanced economies and emerging economies if necessary," he told the Canadian Senate's banking committee.

"We would always work to ensure that underlying policy was consistent with the action," he said.

Carney did not suggest such action was imminent. The last time the Bank of Canadaintervened in foreign exchange markets to influence the level of the Canadian dollar was in 1998.

Many major world economies, shaken by three years of financial turmoil, have recently taken steps to cap or weaken their currencies in a fight over fragile global demand for exports. These include Japan and Brazil. China also faces widespread calls to let the yuan appreciate more quickly.

The Canadian dollar <CAD=D4> briefly shot past parity with the U.S. dollar earlier this month, putting currency strength firmly back on the bank's radar amid signs the export-reliant economy's recovery is losing steam.

The Canadian currency retreated on Wednesday as the greenback rose broadly on speculation the U.S. Federal Reserve would take a measured approach to adding further stimulus through asset purchases, or quantitative easing. [CAD/]

Carney, who has openly fretted about high levels of household debt in Canada, once again reminded Canadians that interest rates are "abnormally low" and that individuals should ensure their debt load will be sustainable when rates inevitably rise.

"Our role is limited. At this stage our role is principally to identify the issue rigorously," he said.

"There is an element of ... identification of the issue to the public, to ask people to be aware, to remind people that we're living in abnormal times."

He also said authorities must be vigilant about the possibility of a build of up of excessive debt as a result of keeping interest rates low for an extended period of time.

The central bank kept its benchmark overnight target rate unchanged last week at 1 percent, following three successive hikes between June and September. Markets do not expect the bank to raise rates again until well into 2011. (Additional reporting by Ka Yan Ng and David Ljunggren; Editing by Jeffrey Hodgson)

title: 4th UPDATE: Bank Of  Canada 's Carney:  Forex Intervention  Would Be Joint Move
text:
(Updates with further comments from Carney on currencies.)


 
   By Nirmala Menon 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Bank of Canada Gov. Mark Carney said Wednesday unilateral intervention in the foreign-exchange market "seldom works."

If the central bank intervenes, it would do so in cooperation with other countries, Carney said in testimony to the Senate banking committee.

Senior Deputy Governor Tiff Macklem also spoke.

Carney said the Bank and the federal government would contemplate intervening in two scenarios. One is if there was a "disruption" in foreign exchange markets, which he said was relatively rare.

The second situation, he said, is if "extreme movements" in the currency market "seriously imperiled conditions that would support sustainable long-term growth."

"Unilateral intervention without backing policy actions seldom works sustainably," Carney said. "If conditions warranted, we would look to act with our partners in advanced economies and emerging economies if necessary. And we would always work to ensure that underlying policy was consistent with the action."

Carney said the Bank of Canada's economic forecasts assume additional monetary stimulus by the U.S. Federal Reserve. He said it was "no secret" that the Fed is discussing additional quantitative easing.

"The point is obviously to avoid further disinflation and deflation, and given the debt dynamics in the United States, not just at the government level but very importantly at the personal level, it would be unhelpful to move into a deflationary environment," he said. "That's a downside risk obviously for the Canadian economy and it's one we watch closely."

Carney said conditions in Canada are very different from the U.S. In the U.S., he said there is "considerable challenge" over access to credit. The U.S. job market is in "very difficult shape", and there has been limited progress in closing the output gap. He said U.S. conditions warrant additional monetary stimulus.

Although the Bank doesn't have direct experience with quantitative and credit easing, its reading of such non-conventional policy measures is that "they're most effective when markets are not functioning well as was the case during the crisis," Carney said.

Macklem, meanwhile, said it was important for countries to have greater currency flexibility. Carney said currency inflexibility has serious longer-term impact on the global economy.

"Ultimately, exchange rates should find their natural level, their appropriate level, that's consistent with fundamentals," he said, adding that Canada has benefited "tremendously" from having a flexible exchange rate which has acted as a "shock absorber" for the economy.

"It has made Canada a wealthier country as a whole when combined with a host of other factors," he said. "It is ultimately unsuccessful to resist fundamental adjustments to currencies."

Carney said the adjustment will be much more difficult if it comes through relative inflation rates rather than through the nominal exchange rate.

"What we are seeing now is disinflationary pressures in the United States, and increasing inflationary pressures in China, which is one of the reasons why Chinese authorities raised interest rates last week for the first time since the crisis," he said. "This dynamic is much more difficult adjustment, it brings ultimate costs in growth."

He said there are mechanisms that countries can put in place to address the speed and sharpness of adjustment that are still consistent with market-based rates. He noted that the G-20 had committed over the weekend in Gyeongju, South Korea, to move towards market-determined exchange rates, and that he expected to see progress on the matter.

Carney also said that returning to a gold standard is "not viable at all."

"But certainly the discussion of adjustments to the international monetary system of a different form will be increasingly prevalent over the coming years, we believe," he said.

He also said there's a need to remain "vigilant" on household debt in Canada. He said credit for small businesses is improving "quite considerably."

-By Nirmala Menon, Dow Jones Newswires; 613-237-0668; nirmala.menon@dowjones.com [ 10-27-10 1939ET ]

title: UPDATE 2- Canada  says  FX  concerns on G7 meeting agenda
text:
* Currency intervention, flexibility to be on G7 agenda

* Flaherty says Geithner "has a point" on IMF reform, forex

* Ottawa will bring strong stance on currencies to table

By John McCrank

OTTAWA, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Concerns about currency market intervention and inflexible currency regimes will be on the agenda at the upcoming meeting of Group of Seven policymakers, Canadian Finance Minister Jim Flaherty said on Wednesday.

"There are concerns about interventions in currency markets. There are concerns about inflexibility, relatively speaking, of certain currencies in the world. This is a topic that I'm sure we will be discussing," he told reporters in Ottawa.

Group of Seven finance ministers and central bankers will gather informally on Friday ahead of the International Monetary Fund's twice-yearly meetings in Washington this weekend. Finance chiefs from the main global economic forum, the G20 emerging and industrialized nations, are scheduled to meet on Oct. 22 in South Korea.

Currency tensions have risen to the top of the agenda for these meetings as policy makers deal with a drive by many of the world's economies to cap the strength of their currencies.

In pointed remarks earlier on Wednesday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said that the problem of undervalued currencies in some emerging economies was "inherently a multilateral problem" that would take a cooperative effort to solve in the form of an effective multilateral mechanism to push countries with big current account surpluses to abandon export-oriented policies. [ID:nN06208024]

He suggested the IMF should have more capacity to "make a difference" in these issues. IMF member countries are negotiating governance reforms that would give emerging economies more clout in the organization.

"It's worthwhile making sure those reforms to governance, which we deeply believe in and support, are complemented by more effective ways for the IMF to play a greater role in helping change behavior on the exchange rate front and encourage surplus countries to shift to more domestic demand led growth," Geithner said.

"That's the basic deal on offer," he added.

Asked about Geithner's comments on IMF reform and exchange rate policy, Flaherty said Geithner "has a point."

"He and I have had discussions of late on that and other subjects," he said.

China's reluctance to let its currency appreciate more quickly has prompted stronger rhetoric from the Canadian central bank and government in recent weeks.

A senior Canadian finance official said on Wednesday that Ottawa would bring to the multilateral table a strong stance in favor of flexible currencies, but he declined to comment on the nature of any possible negotiations for an agreement on currencies or intervention policies.

Flaherty urged against a "distortions in currency values or distortions in trading relationships."

"There is a danger here that countries that do have currencies that trade in a market, that trade freely, are disadvantaged by certain interventions that are made by other countries and by inflexibility of other currencies," he added. title: UPDATE: Canada  Fin Min: Freely Traded  Currencies  Could Be Affected By  Interventions , Inflexible  Currencies
text:
(Updates throughout with quotes, detail.)


 
   By Nirmala Menon 
   OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Canadian Finance Minister Jim Flaherty said Wednesday there is a danger that freely traded currencies will be "disadvantaged" by interventions and currency inflexibility.

Flaherty made the comments ahead of meetings in Washington of Commonwealth Finance Ministers and G-7 finance ministers and central bank governors that he will chair.

Several key nations this week took steps to arrest their soaring currencies. Flaherty said there are concerns about interventions in currency markets and about currency inflexibility.

"This is a topic that I'm sure we'll be discussing in the next several days," he told reporters after the weekly caucus meeting of the governing Conservative Party.

He said Canada has always made it clear that it believes in freely traded currencies.

"There is a danger here that countries that do have currencies that trade in a market, that trade freely, are disadvantaged by certain interventions that are made by other countries and by inflexibility by certain currencies," he said. "So we don't want these kinds of distortions in currency values or distortions in trading relationships. It's a very important topic."

Flaherty said U.S. Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner "has a point" in proposing to link International Monetary Fund reform and currency practices.

"He and I have had discussions of late on that and other subjects," he said.

Flaherty said G-20 countries have to keep the Toronto G-20 Summit Framework "in the forefront." He said one of the purposes of the meetings this weekend is to make sure countries stay on track to fulfill the commitments made at the Toronto Summit.

Flaherty reiterated that economic growth is fragile. But he said the Canadian economy doesn't need further stimulus "at this point."

"We watch carefully of course and will continue to watch. The economic recovery is fragile so we have to be prepared to be nimble but there's no intention now to extend stimulus programs," he said.

Flaherty said the private sector has to pick up the slack as governments in Canada and other G-20 countries ease out of stimulus. Canada's two-year stimulus program is scheduled to end in March 2011. Flaherty said the IMF's latest figures on Canada's economic growth are "encouraging."

title: WRAPUP 3-BoC says C$ volatility a concern, eyes yuan
text:
* Would only intervene in C$ in extreme circumstances

* China must allow greater flexibility in its currency

* BoC has flexibility if Fed eases further

* G20 has the right plan, must implement it (Adds closing C$ level, further details from speech)

By Louise Egan

MONTREAL, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Volatility in the Canadian dollar is a concern for the Bank of Canada, but it would only resort to market intervention in extreme circumstances, the central bank's second-in-command said in an interview on Tuesday.

Tiff Macklem, senior deputy governor of the bank, also predicted negative consequences for the global economy if China does not allow its currency to appreciate more quickly, ramping up the rhetoric on foreign exchange policies ahead of G7 and G20 meetings this month.

Macklem spoke as the Canadian dollar, boosted by commodity prices after the Bank of Japan cut rates, jumped more than half a U.S. cent to hit its highest levels since Aug. 6. It closed at 98.30 U.S. cents.

Bouts of Canadian dollar strength have traditionally exacerbated problems for exporters, who have already been hurt by waning demand from the United States, Canada's biggest export market.

"Clearly, we absolutely need to take into account where the dollar is, why it is where it is when we take monetary policy decisions and, yes, we do get concerned about the exchange rate, particularly if it's volatile, if it's moving quickly," Macklem told Reuters in Montreal, following his maiden speech after starting his new job in July.

The Bank of Canada rarely intervenes in foreign exchange markets and has a policy of resorting to such action only if there is a near-term market breakdown or extreme currency movements that threaten the Canadian economy.

The comments by Macklem, formerly Canada's G7 and G20 finance deputy, come as a drive by many countries to cap the strength of their currencies is gaining momentum and causing tensions. [ID:nLDE69308R]

The other big threat appearing on the central bank's radar is the possibility of further easing by the U.S. Federal Reserve, widening the policy gap after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark rate three times since June to 1 percent.

Governor Mark Carney has said recently that there are "limits to the divergence" in policy between the Bank of Canada and the Fed, given Canada's trade reliance on its neighbor.

Macklem said the bank has more flexibility to react now that it has moved away from emergency measures such as near-zero interest rates, a conditional commitment to keep rates at a low level for a specific period of time and extraordinary liquidity facilities.

"Having moved off our extraordinary conduct ... we have more flexibility," he said when asked how the bank would respond if the Fed engaged in further asset buying, or quantitative easing.

"Having said that, a 1 percent interest rate is still a very low interest rate. Broader financial conditions remain very expansionary and that is appropriate, given the fact that we continue to have a very significant output gap." <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

For a graphic comparing Bank of Canada and G7 rates see:

http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/F/09/CA_RATE0910.gif("http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/F/09/CA_RATE0910.gif") <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Macklem said the Bank of Canada is developing models that could help it expand its mandate in the future to "lean against" financial imbalances rather than a single-minded focus on inflation targeting.

"When you get into a situation where either the financial system isn't working normally, or you get into a situation where there are distortions in the financial system, you need to look under the hood ... We need to start putting money and credit and the key institutional features of banking systems into our models, so we have started to do that," he said.

Macklem said in his speech that the issue of using monetary policy to tackle imbalances is an important one to consider as the bank approaches the renewal of its inflation-targeting mandate with the government at the end of 2011.

Under the terms of an agreement with Ottawa, the bank aims to keep inflation at the midpoint of a 1 to 3 percent range. It has been looking at possible alternatives since 2006.

But Macklem said it was not clear if the bank and the government would be ready for that change just yet.

"Clearly, as we get towards the end of 2011 and the renewal of the inflation targeting regime, there will be some decisions to be taken jointly by the government and by the BoC."

CHINA MUST TAKE MORE STEPS

The Bank of Canada has been escalating its calls for China to let the yuan appreciate more quickly and Macklem said there will likely be considerable discussions about this at upcoming Group of Seven and Group of 20 meetings.

If China does not make the necessary changes, the adjustment will be made more messily: through inflationary pressures in China and deflationary pressures in the United States, Macklem warned.

"That is not going to be good for China and the United States and it's not going to be good for the rest of us either."

G20 leaders agreed to more currency flexibility at their June summit in Toronto and should be held accountable to that agreement, Macklem suggested.

"Go back, read the agreement, its quite a detailed agreement ... I think it's the right plan."

Macklem declined to say whether he though policy makers would reach an agreement by a November summit in Seoul on a mechanism that would allow systemically important banks to fail without resorting to taxpayer-funded bailouts.

Canada has been pushing for including contingent capital, which could be converted to equity in times of distress, as a key element of any resolution regime for globally important banks.

"(The idea) is gaining traction ... it is now very much part of the main agenda," he said. (Reporting by Louise Egan; editing by Rob Wilson and Jeffrey Hodgson)

title: Forex  Focus: Aussie Should Outshine The Commodities
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Gold may be heading even higher but don't expect the precious metal to take all the commodity currencies with it.

As we have seen this week, both the Canadian and New Zealand dollar are being constrained by their own problems for now.

This leaves only the Australian dollar to follow gold higher.

As concern over the global recovery has risen, the price of gold has been pushed to new record highs over $1,250 an ounce.

With little sign of any turn in sentiment and with longer-term investment funds expected to join the fray, the price could well make it up as high as $1,500 or more by the end of the year.

For commodity currencies this should be good news. More often than not a rally in the price of gold indicates a rise in global demand that should be reflected in commodity prices as a whole.

However, support for both the Canadian and New Zealand dollars should prove limited.

In Canada's case, there will certainly be resistance from the central bank, which is becoming increasingly wary of the recent strength in the Canadian dollar.

Earlier this week, Bank of Canada Governor Mark Carney issued a strong warning about the downside risks that the currency is posing for the economy. This was enough to even trigger talk of Bank of Canadaintervention to halt the Canadian dollar's rise, even though the chances of such a move are seen as pretty remote.

The New Zealand dollar may well have proved a better bet.

But the earthquake in Christchurch earlier this month appears to have put a stop to that.

By the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's own reckoning, the earthquake will wipe 0.3 basis points from GDP growth in the third quarter in an economy that was already flagging because of slower global growth. Th latest manufacturing purchasing managers index came in at 49.3 in August, under the key 50 level, suggesting that the economy is now contracting rather than expanding.

RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard warned Thursday that interest-rate increases will now be fewer and further apart and warned that the recent rise in the New Zealand dollar doesn't reflect fundamentals.

In other words, like Canada, New Zealand feels its currency has risen as far as it should go.

For commodity bulls, this just leaves the Aussie.

The Australian currency already rallied to a two-year high earlier this week. But, with the Australian economy going from strength to strength, especially now that China looks set to avoid a hard landing, and with Australian interest rates likely to be raised again before the year is out, more gains can be expected.

If the price of gold keeps on climbing and with the prospects of the Chinese economy still improving, the Aussie could well find itself testing its mid-2008 high of $0.9847--a level that, prior to then, it hadn't hit in about 27 years.

See how the Aussie has been performing in the last few years:

http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/4605("http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/4605")

Early Friday, commodity currencies were generally higher as risk sentiment improved ahead of the weekend. Apart from Spain's successful bond auction Thursday, the market's mood was being lifted by the lack of any disappointing economic data and a global rally in equity markets.

By 0645 GMT, the Aussie was up at $0.9446 from $0.9368 late on Thursday in New York, according to EBS.

The euro was up at $1.3145 from $1.3085 and at Y112.79 from Y112.29. The dollar was steady at Y85.80 as the market waited for any signs that the Bank of Japan will return to intervene in the market.

title: Canada  Bonds Dip After Japan  Currency Intervention
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--Canadian bonds notched a slim decline across the curve on Wednesday, but on the long end declined less than their U.S. Treasury counterparts following Japan's intervention in the currency market.

Canada's two-year bond yield was at 1.480% late Wednesday, from 1.446% late Tuesday. The 10-year bond yielded 2.963%, from 2.931%. Bond yields and prices move in inverse directions.

"The U.S. long end is down substantially this afternoon. We are following the pull there," said Sheldon Dong, vice president of fixed-income strategy at TD Waterhouse Canada in Toronto.

The intervention, through which Japanese officials bought U.S. dollars and sold the yen, aimed to prevent a surging yen from threatening the economic recovery in the world's third-largest economy.

The 10-year and 30-year U.S. maturities bore the brunt of the selling in a choppy trading session, as Japan's intervention prompted investors to pivot into the shorter-dated notes that are believed to be the favored destination of Japan when parking its dollar proceeds.

The market also is positioning ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's meeting next week, Dong said.

"The U.S. dealers are calling for a second round of quantitative easing by the Fed. So there is a bit of uncertainty," he said. "In Canada, we are just sort of muddling along."

Canada will keep watch on U.S. data releases, including the August consumer price index, due Friday. Canada's data calendar is empty for the remainder of the week.

"Canada is pretty much on hold. I think our market is watching the rest of the world," Dong said. "The Bank of Canada has pretty much stated that whether they hike rates in October depends on factors outside of our borders."

In June, the Bank of Canada became the first central bank in the Group of Seven industrialized nations to raise interest rates since the global economic crisis began two years ago. It has made three consecutive rate increases, but now cautions that "any further reduction in monetary policy stimulus would need to be carefully considered in light of the unusual uncertainty surrounding the outlook."

On Wednesday in Newfoundland, BOC Deputy Governor Timothy Lane said the recovery in Canada is continuing but will likely be more modest than in previous cycles.

In new Canadian bond supply, the Canadian Finance Department reported an average 1.556% yield at an auction of C$3 billion of 1.50% non-callable government bonds due Dec. 1, 2012.

The high accepted yield was 1.559%; the low 1.554%. The price equivalent for the average yield was 99.879. The allotment ratio at the high accepted yield was 39.62727%.

The aggregate value of the bids received was about C$7.87 billion, including C$37.1 million of non-competitive tenders accepted at the average yield.

With the new bonds, the outstanding total of 1.50% bonds due Dec. 1, 2012, is C$6.5 billion.

Canada Housing Trust is looking to raise C$6.25 billion from an issue of five-year bonds. The issue has yet to be priced, but the spread guidance is around 24.5 basis points over the government of Canada 3% December 2015 bond benchmark.

And Armtec Holdings is looking to raise C$150 million from an issue of bonds that mature in September 2017. Pricing for the bonds, which are callable in 2013, is not yet determined. The coupon is expected to be around 8.875%.

title: BOC: Declines To Comment On Japanese  Intervention
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada declined to comment on Japan's intervention in currency markets that has pushed the dollar and euro sharply higher against the yen.

Jill Vardy, acting chief of communications for the Bank of Canada, said Canada's central bank would have no comment on the intervention.

The yen was falling steeply Wednesday after Japan intervened in currency markets for the first time in more than six years.

Japanese authorities said they are prepared to extend the intervention into the North American session and possibly into Thursday, according to a Kyodo news report.

After the U.S. dollar fell to a 15-year low Tuesday of Y82.87, the initial barrage of yen-selling orders hit the market early in the Asian day; it was followed by bursts that pushed the dollar above Y85. The dollar was at Y85.63 in late morning in New York on Wednesday, from Y83.08 late Tuesday, according to EBS via CQG.

The Canadian dollar was at Y83.49, from Y81.12 late Tuesday.

Japan's Ministry of Finance overnight announced the intervention about 20 minutes after the first sales hit the market in Asia.

Only Turkey is against trend. title: Canada  Morning: C$ Down, Mkt Cautious on  Intervention  Fear
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar is down against the U.S. dollar in cautious trading early Monday, with the U.S. unit having again moved above the C$1.5200 mark in reaction to Russia's devaluation of its currency earlier. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5220 at 9:38 a.m. EDT (1338 GMT), up from C$1.5212 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) and from C$1.5171 late Friday, which was also the Bank of Canada's official closing level. 

 Traders said the Canadian dollar was pushed lower in an immediate knee-jerk reaction to the news out of Russia. Unlike the German deutschemark however, the Canadian unit failed to stage a comeback as markets digested the news. 

 "I'm kind of surprised that Canada's still so weak," said a currency trader at a major Canadian bank in Toronto. "In Canada, the pressure is now more due to natural demand for U.S. dollars on the back of the September bond maturities, and a bit of speculative interest beginning to seep back into the market." 

 The Canadian dollar has been expected to come under more pressure from a heavy government bond redemptions calendar over the next eight months, with C$12.8 billion slated to mature in September alone. 

 Some traders also suggested the Bank of Canada's recent asymetrical intervention strategy in support of the Canadian dollar may be starting to lose some of its sting. 

 "People are beginning to believe that the central bank can't hold the currency by intervention alone, as it looks less and less likely that the bank can raise interest rates," said one trader. 

 The central bank's last intervention level was at C$1.5200 on Thursday, and currency watchers said the market is looking for another intervention if the U.S. dollar begins creeping up towards C$1.5230 Monday.

title: =Bank of Canada -2: Estimates Of Amount Spent Vary
text:
The bank's recent shift to early intervention is far from unprecedented, C.T. Securities' Pyle said. 

 The bank was intervening before 70-tick moves in January, when the currency was also under acute pressure, he pointed out. 

 Bank officials have not abandoned their usual pattern of intervening at 70-tick moves despite the fact that they are coming in early then they judge it appropriate, Pyle said. 

 "If the bank feels that it is in a different type of climate where there is a lot of pressure - or undue pressure - on the currency, then it is going to leave that rule on the shelf," he said. 

 The market will continue to test the central bank's resolve, Pyle said. 

 The key question now is whether the central bank has established a level for the currency, he said. Some market watchers believe that it has targeted a Canadian dollar worth 65 cents U.S. (or a U.S. dollar level of C$1.5385) as the level it will defend. 

 Unlike some observers, who laud the bank's recent intervention tactics and believe it may have staved off an interest rate increase in defense of the currency, Pyle offers a more restrained assessment of the bank's approach. 

 "I think it was necessary for the bank to try to convince the market that there was independent policy at hand, that this simply wasn't a 'let it drift' policy co-ordinated by the Bank of Canada and the federal government," he said. 

 But the central bank may have been better served by a sudden, surprise rate hike, Pyle argued. 

 He estimates that the bank may have spent about 10% of its foreign exchange reserves - reported at US$22.5 billion in July - during the last week or so. 

 "It wasn't cheap intervention, by any stretch of the imagination," Pyle said. 

 The Bank of Canada only releases details of intervention spending on a monthly basis. The August release is scheduled for Sept. 3. 

 Estimates of the amount spent since the bank began intervening more aggressively on Aug. 7 have varied considerably, ranging from around US$1 billion to US$2 billion or more.

title: Canadian bonds open little changed, T-bills firm.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds opened little changed on Friday, with a lack of significant news keeping activity muted, even as T-bills benefited from the stabilisation of the Canadian dollar. 

 "We've been conditioned to look to international situations for signs of which way things are going. Today, it's a little bit more quiet out there," said Arve Bendiksrud, a fixed-income analyst with TD Securities Inc. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond fell C$0.14 to C$132.16 to yield 5.710 percent. Its U.S. 30-year bond rose 2/32 to yield 5.59 percent. The Canada-U.S. spread rose to 12 basis points from six basis points at Thursday's close. 

 Canada's yield curve underperformed the U.S. curve from the three year area and up. Analysts said Canadian bonds have been under pressure during the past few weeks because of weakness in the currency. 

 For the first time in years, Canadian bonds are now yielding more than their U.S. counterparts, beginning at the three-year portion of the curve. 

 Hammered by falling commodity prices, the Canadian dollar fell to the lowest point in its 140-year history on August 7, dropping to C$1.5355 ($0.6513). 

 But aggressive intervention by the Bank of Canada in the currency markets during the past five sessions benefited the money market on Friday. 

 T-bill prices rose as the Canadian dollar firmed to open at C$1.5178 (US$0.6588), up from C$1.5194 (US$0.6582) at Thursday's close.

title: =Canada Bond Redemptions -3: Bond Mkt Seen More Vulnerable
text:
However, a recent pattern of rapid, often aggressive market interventions by Canada's central bank in defense of the Canadian dollar is sending signals that Canada's monetary authorities have seen enough depreciation in the currency, and it's slide has at least been checked, if not reversed. 

 A growing number of analysts now feel that a little more currency stability may be all international investors need to keep at least some of their redemption proceeds in Canada, especially given the fact that Japan and Russia now seem poised to set off a new round of global financial turmoil. 

 "I'm not expecting major turbulence from the redemptions calendar - I think it's been overstated," said Aron Gampel, deputy chief economist at the Bank of Nova Scotia. "Investors have been shunning Canadian securities for some time and what I'm banking on is that international investors will want to at least maintain a core presence in Canada." 

 Most of the potential turbulence over the heavy redemptions period is now seen falling on the Canadian bond market, as an ever-expanding pool of excess liquidity sloshes around over the next eight months trying to find a home. 

 "It's perhaps less of an issue of what's going to happen to the currency as what's going to happen to spreads between Canada and the U.S.," said Nesbitt Burns' Porter. "I suspect we are going to see a marked deterioration of relative spreads during this heavy rollover period." 

 The case for not rolling over proceeds into other Canadian issues largely hinges on the deterioration in relative yield spreads versus U.S. Treasurys that has occurred over the past few years, most agree. 

 "The original buyers were able to get the maturing bonds at a 60 to 90 basis point yield pickup over U.S. Treasurys," noted one Toronto bond dealer. "Now there's only a small 10-15 basis point pickup in the 5-year and 10-year area. As the stuff matures, are foreigners and other investors going to be as eager to step back in - I doubt it."

title: WORLD BONDS-Australia preferred over Kiwi, Canada.
text:
LONDON, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Investors should consider Australian government bonds over their New Zealand and Canadian counterparts, but all three markets are dogged by currency weakness, analysts said on Thursday. 

 The currency turmoil created by the Asian economic crisis has in turn affected government bonds, particularly in Australia and New Zealand but also Canada as well. 

 Added to this New Zealand faces political risk from a possible break up of the country's coalition government, while Australian tax reform proposals have marred the longer term outlook for Aussie bonds. 

 In Canada currency weakness prompted the central bank to intervene on Wednesday, selling U.S. dollars to try to prop up the local currency. 

 "The intensification of the Asian crisis has hit these markets especially badly and near term I would be cautious," said Dick Howard, director of economic research at Bank Julius Baer in London. 

 "All three are perceived as commodity currencies. We've had weaker commodity prices which has led to weaker currencies and that in turn has fed through into higher bond yields." 

 At 1219 GMT, 10-year Australian bonds were yielding 24 basis points over U.S. T-notes. Aussie bonds were trading at 15 basis points through U.S. Treasuries in late May, early June. 

 The New Zealand/U.S. spread was at 96 basis points, having widened from 63 earlier this month. 

 Howard said the at these levels Aussie and Kiwi bonds offered reasonable value. "But near term so long as we continue to get bad news out of Asia the spread could widen further. So investors may yet be able to get better levels," he said. 

 But the outlook for Australian bonds over the next few years is less rosy. Tax reforms unveiled on Thursday have changed the fiscal outlook, reducing the budget surplus for 1999-2000 and 2000-2001. 

 "The market was distinctly soggy in the run up to the tax reform announcement," said Howard. "(Australian Treasurer Peter) Costello didn't announce anything that was any great surprise but even so the idea that the fiscal position going ahead is going to be nothing like as good as the market thought it was has certainly taken the shine off the Australian bond market." 

 James McKay, global market strategist at Commonwealth Bank in London, also preferred Australian debt near term. 

 "With dollar/yen heading down, you would expect that to support the Aussie dollar, which should remain supportive towards the Australian bond market," he said. 

 Dollar/yen was at 145.60, just off the day's low. 

 McKay said New Zealand debt and currency markets would suffer from political uncertainty after cabinet ministers from the New Zealand First party walked out on Wednesday. 

 "While I wouldn't expect that to amount to anything in the end, it is clearly going to have an impact on the market over the coming days," he said. 

 "Nevertheless if the market sells off too much in New Zealand, I would certainly recommend people look at the bonds particularly at the shorter end of the curve." 

 Elisabeth Afseth, fixed income saleswoman at Williams de Broe in London, said political risk had caused the 10-year spread to widen and further underperformance of New Zealand bonds could be expected in coming days. 

 "For the short term I would be quite cautious, but if it goes out to much over 100 it could be a buying opportunity," she said. "On economic fundamentals you are seeing the economy slowing down quite a lot so longer term the bond market should be relatively good." 

 The 10-year Canada/U.S. spread was at 17 basis points compared with minus 35 in mid-April. 

 "Canada is coming back onto the radar screens for investors," said Howard. 

 However, Julius Baer had a zero weighting in Canadian bonds and was not likely to buy any near term, he said. 

 But although still a risky market, Afseth favoured the longer end of the Canadian yield curve. 

 "The spread is unlikely to go negative again but if it stays at roughly current levels in a 10-20 over range for the time being, it offers reasonably good value," she said. 

 "I would either go for safe-haven buying of Treasuries or if you want a bit more risk with it Canada is starting to look quite good." ((Deepthi Wickremasinghe, International Bonds +44 171 542 4041, Fax +44 171 542 5285, uk.governmentbonds.news@reuters.com)).

title: Canada  Afternoon: C$ Steady After 6th Straight  Intervention

TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar ended nearly even with Wednesday's official closing level against the U.S. dollar, in the sixth consecutive session in which the Bank of Canada has intervened to prop up the currency. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5190 at 4:20 p.m. EDT (2020 GMT), up from C$1.5175 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) but down slightly from C$1.5204 late Wednesday. The central bank's official Wednesday close for the U.S. dollar was C$1.5193. 

 Traders described a rather lackluster session of trading Thursday, with the central bank mounting two light afternoon rounds of intervention in support of the Canadian dollar after it began edging up against the psychologically important C$1.5200 mark. 

 In the morning session, some said the Canadian dollar had a good bid on rumors that a major foreign investment house had issued a buy Canada recommendation, but the bid dwindled when the rumors could not be confirmed, and on a firming of the U.S. dollar against the yen. 

 While many feel the Bank of Canada's interventions are gradually losing their sting, some also said the bank's apparently modest goal of simply limiting further Canadian-dollar depreciation is having its intended effects. 

 "There's more accounts out there that seem to be tired of being long in U.S. dollars," said Bill Mooney, chief foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Montreal. "They're just not getting the run-up to C$1.5250 that they thought they'd get." 

 Mooney said that there is some latent buy-Canada sentiment in the market, but persistent fears of instability from Russia and Japan are keeping it in the closet. He said that for the time being, continued central bank intervention is likely to keep the U.S. dollar/Canada dollar rate confined to a relatively narrow range below C$1.5200.

 "We trading kind of tick for tick with (U.S.) dollar/yen," said one currency trader with a major Canadian bank. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5145 at 9:49 a.m. EDT (1349 GMT), from C$1.5175 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) and from C$1.5204 late Wednesday. 

 "There was some interest among IMM types early to buy some Canada," the trader added. "It's pushed (the U.S. dollar) down." 

 Some market watchers suggested the Canadian currency appeared to be settling in a range after weeks of sustained negative sentiment and then several sessions of volatility after the Bank of Canada beginning intervening at unpredictable levels and in varying amounts. 

 "We're just trading around in a range, a consolidation range. We're just bouncing around inside." the trader said.

title: Bank moves support Canada dollar, but outlook murky.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Continuing Asian turmoil and depressed commodity prices make prospects for the faltering Canadian dollar uncertain, analysts said on Tuesday, despite several recent rounds of Canadian central bank intervention that have halted what had been a steady decline. 

 The Bank of Canada launched a pre-emptive strike on Tuesday morning for the third straight business day, buying Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars in a successful bid to scare off speculators betting on further drops in the value of the domestic currency. 

 Following a turnaround prompted by the central bank's heavy intervention on Friday, the local dollar had stabilised on Tuesday at around 65.79 U.S. cents, or C$1.5200 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Canadian dollar, now in the middle of a five-month downtrend, has recovered from a record low of 65.14 U.S. cents or C$1.5355 to the U.S. dollar set last Friday. However, it is almost six U.S. cents below its level of a year ago of around 72 U.S. cents. 

 "The Bank of Canada intervention has been successful so far, at least preventing the currency from falling further," Sal Guatieri, senior economist at Bank of Montreal, told Reuters Television. "It has diverted speculators' attention to other currencies besides the Canadian dollar." 

 But the outlook for the dollar, referred to by Canadians as the "loonie" for the depiction of the loon on the golden one-dollar coin, remains clouded by a number of factors. 

 A recent slip in the U.S. dollar against the Canadian unit is "a pause in a rising trend", and is unlikely to end until the currency rises to 67.57 U.S. cents, or C$1.4800 to the U.S. dollar, a level last seen in mid-July, said Martin Autotte, technical analyst at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities. 

 The U.S. currency is being bolstered by flows of capital seeking a safe haven from such troubled regions such as Asia and Russia. 

 The U.S. dollar rose above 147 yen, an eight-year high, in Asian trading on Tuesday on growing concern about the prospects for Japan's bid to rescue its recession-hit economy through banking and tax reform. 

 And Indonesia's government said on Tuesday it had deferred some principal payments on its foreign debt in August, although that this did not involve a default. 

 In addition, confidence in Canadian securities generally could come under scrutiny by international investors if the Canadian stock market continues to plunge and bond prices fall again. Economists see a recent drop in North American stocks as a correction to sharp gains, rather than a free-fall. 

 A wave of selling on Tuesday drove the Toronto Stock Exchange's key index down by more than four percent at one point in the morning before bargain-hunting pared losses. 

 One factor helping stabilise the Canadian dollar was the release last Friday of Canada's July jobs data, which showed higher-than-expected growth and which coincided with Bank of Canada intervention in the currency market estimated to total at least US$500 million. 

 Canada's dollar has also come under pressure from soft commodity prices caused by the Asian crisis, and more recently, from worries over a slower pace of domestic economic growth. 

 The currency weathered bearish domestic economic data on Tuesday morning and news of a fall in international crude oil prices to a 10-year low. 

 Canada's housing starts fell 6.5 percent in July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 123,100 units from a revised 131,700 in June, hit partly by construction strikes in the province of Ontario. 

 "The weaker starts does suggest a further weakness in the Canadian dollar, and by and large the Bank of Canada will tolerate a weaker currency provided it's reflecting weakening fundamentals," Guatieri said. 

 For clues as to the overall strength of the Canadian economy, the market is awaiting the release on August 31 of second quarter gross domestic product (GDP) and current account data. 

 "The GDP report at the end of this month should help refocus the market," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. "In current account we could see a deterioration, but overall people are still looking at the current account deficit to GDP ratio of two percent. That's actually supportive for the Canadian dollar." 

 ((Reuters Toronto newsroom (416) 941-8107, toronto.newsroom@reuters.com)).

With destabilized financial markets potentially threatening economic growth, the bank was compelled to move, Scotiabank's Gampel suggested. 

 "I think that the central bank had decided a degree of urgency had entered into the need to introduce a two-way risk into the marketplace," he said.

 And the effectiveness of intervention is inherently limited because it ultimately does not address the global economic factors that are undermining the Canadian dollar, he said.

title: Canada bonds end weaker, 30-year spread positive.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended mostly weaker on Monday with the long end of the yield curve falling sharply and the yield on the 30-year bond now offering a higher rate than the U.S. bond for the first time since July 1997. 

 Canada's bonds failed to attract investors as U.S. dollar assets are the investment of choice at a time of global uncertainty and bearish domestic stock performance. 

 "Nobody believes that the Bank of Canada is going to raise interest rates (to protect the local currency), so the sell-off in the front end has been very marginal," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 Most sectors in Canadian bonds are now offering higher yields than U.S. bonds, reflecting currency risks. 

 The Canadian dollar has finally stabilised after Friday's massive central bank intervention and a less aggressive buy-Canada operation on Monday, and has ended firmer against the U.S. dollar for two trading days in a row. 

 "The market is basically building in the uncertainty risk premium for the currency. We've been underperforming the U.S. for two and half weeks now," Palombi said. "The 10-year and 30-year have built in a roughly 20-basis point premium." 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond (due June 1, 2027) fell C$0.94 at C$132.93 to yield 5.666 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond cut losses, rising 3/32 to yield 5.62 percent. 

 The Canada-U.S. spread in 30-years turned into positive 4.6 basis points from negative 1.6 points at the previous close here. 

 The Canada-U.S. spread could return to parity from positive if the Canadian government's 10-year bond auction later this week produces good results, Palombi said. 

 "The game is over as far as Canadian yields are trading below those in the U.S.," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. "The central bank can influence certain rates, but it can't direct the whole market." 

 The bond market has been affected by the weakness in the Canadian dollar in recent trade. 

 "The market is still waiting for some kind of signal on what the bank really wants here," he said. "Friday's intervention at least got a lot of people off guard and was very well done. Whether it's enough to keep the currency stable beyond the few days, I'm quite doubtful." 

 The Bank of Canada has refrained from raising its key short-term lending rate as a means of boosting the local dollar. Higher borrowing costs for firms and consumers could hurt consumer and business confidence, and it would take more than a rate hike to turn around the current downtrend. 

 The central bank's prime policy is to control inflation, which is still under control. The depreciation of the currency tends to push up import costs, but it has not had a major impact on the inflation front. 

 The money market was firmer in line with the appreciation of the local dollar. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill yielded 5.02 percent after 5.10 percent at the previous close here.

title: New jobs, massive  intervention  spur Canadian dollar.
text:
OTTAWA, Aug 7 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar rebounded on Friday after massive intervention by the central bank and news of slightly better than expected job growth in July surprised the market. 

 The ailing dollar, which only yesterday was prompting calls from opposition politicians for the resignation of Finance Minister Paul Martin, gained more than one U.S. cent after the Bank of Canada intervened in mid-morning trade. 

 "(The intervention) caught bearish Canadian dollar participants with their pants down," said Jeffrey Cheah, a financial market analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS International. 

 "What the bank did this morning is very effective. If anything, it changes the rules. It shows that you can no longer place a risk-free bet against the bank," Cheah told Reuters. 

 Traders said the central bank, which had been criticised by some for failing to show enough support for the dollar, was "all over" with persistent intervention. The bank's show of support - its second-straight day of intervention - halted what had become a freefall by the currency. 

 The dollar strengthened to 66.20 U.S. cents after the bank spent between $500 million and $2 billion to increase Canada's popularity. The Canadian currency lost a half a U.S. cent on Thursday to closed at record low of 65.39 U.S. cents. 

 Cheah said the dollar also got a boost from slightly higher-than-expected Canadian job growth. Although market reaction to the numbers was masked by the intervention, Cheah said the dollar may have improved on the news that 26,600 jobs were created in Canada in July. 

 Canada's unemployment rate remained stagnant at 8.4 percent, as expected, for the fourth straight month as the benefits of the new jobs were offset by a rise in the number of people actively seeking work. 

 Economists surveyed by Reuters had on average expected July employment to rise by only 4,800 after a decline of 35,900 jobs the month before. 

 Some economists downplayed the growth in new jobs because 20,300 of them were only part-time. 

 "(It is) a little bit better than expected, especially when you look at the headline number of 26,600 jobs, but the bulk was in the part-time sector. The full-time jobs were only 6,300, so the headline number was over-exaggerating the employment growth," said Harvinder Kalirai, an economist at I.D.E.A. in New York. 

 Cheah warned that the bounce in the Canadian dollar will be short-lived if Asia's financial crisis continues to worsen, strangling demand for Canadian commodity exports. 

 "Events in Asia could still pose a problem. If the yen continues to weaken significantly it might put pressure on the Chinese government maybe to (devalue) its currency...not the kind of news that I think would be favourable," Cheah said. 

 An attempt by the finance minister to talk up Canada's economic strengths prior to a speech on Thursday evening had little effect. 

 "Very few countries have the productivity record which we have got," Martin said. 

 "No Canadian, certainly no minister of finance, is indifferent in terms of the behaviour of their currency," he told reporters in Orillia, Ontario. 

 ($1=$1.52 Canadian) 

 ((Andrea Hopkins, Reuters Ottawa Newsroom, 613-235-6745, fax 613-235-5890)).

TORONTO, Aug 7 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar trimmed earlier large gains that were made on central bank intervention, but was still firmer at C$1.5230 (US$0.6579) at midday on Friday after opening at C$1.5313 (US$0.6530).



The Bank of Canada surprised traders by hitting the currency market as early as 0900 EDT/1300 GMT with massive U.S. dollar selling for Canada, continued at various levels and estimated to total US$500 million to US$1 billion. One trader put it between US$1 billion-US$2 billion.



Unlike Thursday's smoothing-out operation that failed to stop a slide in the Canadian dollar, today's action worked as many traders had been anticipating a possible rate increase at the 0900 EDT/1300 GMT window for money market operation, instead of early currency intervention.



To maximize the impact, the central bank was waiting "for the best timing" to step in, an authoritative market source said, using a different tactic than it usually does. Normally, the Bank of Canada limits itself to smoothing out fluctuations when the U.S. dollar rises more than 70 points against Canada from the previous day's close.



The first round of intervention came around C$1.5350 (US$0.6515), a record trading high for the U.S. dollar and 50-60 points above the previous close here of C$1.5294 (US$0.6539). Persistent intervention pushed the U.S. dollar down by nearly 250 points from the high to a day's low of C$1.5105 (US$0.6620).



The source said the bank considers that Canada has not lost investor confidence despite the downtrend for the currency and a bearish tone in domestic equity and bond markets. A rebound in Canada's labour market came as a relief to central bankers.



Higher-than-expected growth in Canadian job creation in July, released earlier this morning, supports the limping local currency, but overall sentiment is still bearish as traders were jittery over sliding values in Canadian stocks this week and the U.S. dollar was rising above 146 yen.



"It has become a confidence issue that forced them to do a direct intervention," said Mark Chandler, senior economist at Goldman Sachs Canada. "It may just be a matter of time now before the returning weakness in the currency leads to a rate increase to support that intervention."



"Conditions changed in the past week to where it has become more of a confidence issue. I still think that it's appropriate for them to hold off, but I also think they may be forced to raise rates," he said.



"They (central bankers) will see on Monday whether this holds, if it's at these levels, they might hold off on a rate increase. But once again history will tell us that we're not out of the woods on the currency yet just based on sterilised intervention."


Canada's employment rose 26,600 to 14.27 million in July from June. Full-time employment grew by 6,300 from the month before, while part-time employment grew by 20,300.



The jobless rate in July, as expected, was unchanged from June, for the fourth consecutive month, at 8.4 percent.



"The underlying trend in full-time jobs is around 20,000-25,000. That's faster than the growth rate in the working-age population and is still consistent with above-trend gross domestic product growth," said Harvinder Kalirai, economist at I.D.E.A. in New York.



Economists on average had expected Canada's July employment to have grown by 4,800 (forecast range: a fall of 20,000 to a gain of 20,000) after a decline of 35,900 in June.



There was little market reaction to the U.S. July jobs data, which showed non-farm payrolls rose by 66,000, higher than the consensus forecast of 35,000, after a revised rise of 196,000 (prelim: 205,000) in June.



The growth was the weakest since a decline of 48,000 in January 1996. The July data were distorted by the General Motors strike.



The average hourly earnings, closely watched by the market as an indicator for inflation, rose 0.2 percent in July against the consensus forecast of a rise of 0.3 percent and a rise of 0.1 percent in June.



The unemployment rate, as predicted, was unchanged at 4.5 percent.



   In cross trading, the Canadian unit posted a recovery. It rose to 1.1689



marks from 1.1567 marks in the early morning and 1.1598 marks at the previous



close here. Canada extended gains to 95.97 yen from 95.10 yen at the opening



and from 94.40 yen on Thursday.



    The Canadian dollar has been on a general downtrend since hitting a high of



1.3068 marks on April 1, and, in a bigger trend, slipping from a high of 1.3613



marks recorded on August 5, 1997.



    The Bank of Canada has refrained from raising its key short-term lending



rate to boost the dollar. Higher borrowing costs for firms and consumers could



hurt consumer and business confidence, and it would take more than a rate hike



to turn around the current downtrend.



    The central bank's prime policy is to control inflation, which is still



under control. The depreciation of the currency tends to push up import costs,



but it has not had a major impact on the inflation front.



    Negative factors still exist for the Canadian dollar.



    It is expected to take a long time before the public feels the effect of



the anti-recessionary measures taken by Japan's new government and the market



speculates that China will be forced to devalue its currency to maintain export



competitiveness.



    All this uncertainty encourages a capital flow to U.S. dollar assets,



which are backed by the world's biggest economy and its strongest military.



    "The market hasn't reacted particularly positively to the Japanese package,



I gather," said Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange at CIBC Wood



Gundy Securities. "If North America sells yen, that would be a signal maybe a



tough day for Canada, particularly the yen goes through 146 yen."



   Looking at the the U.S. dollar topside, the next target is around C$1.5385,



or psychological level of US$0.6500. Then comes C$1.5400 (US$0.6494).



    The U.S. dollar firmed above 145 yen, then to a two-month high of 146 yen,



from around 144 yen as the market was disappointed with an inaugural policy



speech by Japanese Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi at the start of an extraordinary



session of parliament.



Obuchi had nothing new to offer in his bid to tackle the nation's deepening



recession as he had already announced earlier plans to cut taxes and reform the



banking system.



    Japan's prime minister traditionally tries to cover so many issues in an



inaugural policy speech that the audience gets only few details on each topic.



    In addition, Japan will not come up with detailed tax reform plans, seen as



key to boosting confidence, until the year-end, after debates by the



government's advisory groups. The government is targeting a tax system overhaul



effective on April 1, when the next fiscal year starts.

title: Canada bonds end weaker despite U.S. gains.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended weaker on Friday, retaining bearish sentiment seen most of this week triggered by the weakness in the Canadian dollar. 

 A continued slide in the domestic stock market has not prompted a fund shift to Canadian bonds. Instead, investors were concerned about the overall weakness in Canadian assets. 

 In contrast, U.S. treasuries ended firmer on the back of the rising U.S. dollar and steady equity prices. 

 The short end of the yield curve pared earlier gains on the back of a jump in the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar in early morning trade. 

 Massive intervention by Canada's central bank boosted the local dollar, but its outlook is still uncertain. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond (due June 1, 2027) trimmed some earlier losses, quoted down by C$0.18 at C$133.87 to yield 5.614 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond rose 20/32 to yield 5.63 percent. 

 The U.S.-Canada spread in 30-years narrowed further to 1.6 basis points from 6 points at the previous close here. 

 "The primary question for a lot of those investors is the currency," said Mark Chandler, senior economist at Goldman Sachs Canada. "At even yields or with the potential for a stronger currency, I think we can induce some investors into Canadian assets." 

 The Bank of Canada has refrained from raising its key short-term lending rate as a means of boosting the local dollar. Higher borrowing costs for firms and consumers could hurt consumer and business confidence, and it would take more than a rate hike to turn around the current downtrend. 

 The central bank's prime policy is to control inflation, which is still under control. The depreciation of the currency tends to push up import costs, but it has not had a major impact on the inflation front. 

 Higher-than-expected growth in Canadian job creation in July, released this morning, is supportive for the local currency, which has been on a general downtrend since mid-March. 

 Canada's employment rose 26,600 to 14.27 million in July from June. Full-time employment grew by 6,300 from the month before, while part-time employment grew by 20,300. 

 The jobless rate in July, as expected, was unchanged from June, for the fourth consecutive month, at 8.4 percent.

 There was little market reaction to the U.S. July jobs data, which showed non-farm payrolls rose by 66,000, higher than the consensus forecast of 35,000, after a revised rise of 196,000 (prelim: 205,000) in June. 

 The growth was the weakest since a decline of 48,000 in January 1996. The July data were distorted by the General Motors strike. 

 The average hourly earnings, closely watched by the market as an indicator for inflation, rose 0.2 percent in July against the consensus forecast of a rise of 0.3 percent and a rise of 0.1 percent in June.

title: FOCUS- Canada  chooses dollar  intervention  over rate hike.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Canada's central bank defended its battered dollar with massive intervention in the currency market on Friday, staving off a rise in interest rates that could choke off growth in the domestic economy. 

 Economists hailed the move made by the embattled Bank of Canada - early morning selling of U.S. dollars for Canadian that took Canadian dollar bears by surprise. 

 Many traders, who had expected a rise in the bank's key short-term lending rate to defend the dollar, were caught off guard and the intervention boosted the Canadian dollar by more than two Canadian cents against the U.S. dollar at one point. 

 The central bank has held off raising rates since it pushed the key rate up by 50 basis points to 5.0 percent in January to fight currency speculators, a move that drew criticism at the time. 

 But market concern over a loss of investor confidence in Canadian securities grew this week as stock and bond prices continued to slide and pressure for a rate hike mounted. The Canadian dollar had been ending day after day at record lows. 

 The Canadian dollar closed stronger on Friday at 65.70 U.S. cents after a record low the previous day of 65.39 U.S. cents. 

 "I'm supportive of the Bank of Canada not raising rates currently," said Andrew Sharpe, executive director at the Centre for the Study of Living Standards in Ottawa. "We do have a larger output gap than in the States, we have higher unemployment. It's not appropriate to raise interest rates right now." 

 Canada's jobless rate has been stuck at 8.4 percent, compared with 4.5 percent in the United States, according to the latest data, for July, released on Friday. 

 Higher borrowing costs for firms and consumers could hurt consumer and business confidence, and it would take more than a rate hike to turn around the current downtrend for the Canadian dollar, several economists said. 

 The central bank's prime policy is to keep inflation low. Depreciation of the local currency pushes up import costs, but it has not had a major impact on the inflation front. 

 Sharpe pointed out that the central bank has no incentive to push for lower inflation right now as Canada's consumer price index (CPI) is rising only one percent year on year - the bottom of the bank's 1-3 percent target band for inflation. 

 Economist Kenneth Boessenkool, at C.D. Howe Institute in Toronto, agreed, arguing that a rate hike now could put the economy back into recession later this year. 

 He is actually calling for action in the opposite direction and recently issued a report titled, "Let's Defend the Dollar - With Lower Interest Rates." 

 Slack demand in Asia has driven the Canadian dollar down and caused the weakness in the economy, which has also been hit by strikes at General Motors plants and in the construction sector. 

 The latest data showed that Canada's economy, as measured by the gross domestic product (GDP) declined by 0.2 percent in May after no growth in April. 

 The Bank of Canada has reacted to the dollar's fall in the past by raising interest rates, which has produced more weakness in the economy. 

 "You have to get on the right track by reversing those earlier interest rate increases," Boessenkool said in an interview. 

 On suggestions by some economists for income tax cuts as a means of offsetting the impact of what they consider a necessary evil of a defensive rate hike, Boessenkool said: "We have to separate short-term and long-term issues." 

 "For dealing with what's going on in the short term, why the dollar is falling this month, we think that's related to the weakness in the economy. Long-term problems require long-term solutions," he said. 

 Canada has eliminated two thorny structural weaknesses - a huge budget deficit and a high inflation rate - but it still faces a long process in boosting productivity and lowering tax rates to give incentives to spending and investment. 

 "We are not over the hump yet. It's taking us four to five years to fix the deficit problem, it took us six to seven years to get our inflation rate down," Boessenkool said. "It takes 20 years to create those problems, you can't get out in one." 

 Canada has jumped onto the bandwagon of corporate restructuring and social welfare spending cuts, but it may not totally emulate the United States, its biggest trade partner. 

 "As far as social policy goes, we still have a preference for a generous social safety net, and that's why our debt-to-GDP ratio is not to going to decline dramatically over the near term. That's the choice Canadians have made for themselves," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. "It would be difficult for any government to introduce a new round of spending cuts and tax cuts at the same time to bring the debt burden down more quickly." 

 ((Reuters Toronto newsroom (416) 941-8107, toronto.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Canada  Afternoon: C$ Soars on  Central Bank Intervention

The U.S. unit whipsawed through a wide range between C$1.5350 and C$1.5115 in the morning session before settling in a narrower range around the C$1.5200 mark.
