 As the Canadian unit weakened off towards C$1.5350 early, several waves of U.S. dollar selling by the central bank hit the market, in a move that most analysts said was unprecedented in recent years in terms of scope and timing (see story 4238). 

 Following a volatile morning session, traders said the market was largely becalmed in afternoon trading, especially after the U.S. currency failed to extend a brief retracement of its morning losses. 

 "There was some thin corporate interest in buying U.S. dollars at lows," said a trader at a major Canadian bank. "That accounted for a bounce of about 100 ticks in the afternoon, but we came off that later." 

 Analysts said it is still too early to tell if Friday's intervention will be successful in engineering anything more than a brief turnaround in sentiment for the beleaguered Canadian currency, but a key development in its favor is likely today's closing level near C$1.5200. 

 "People will likely feel that the bank's efforts were not in vain with any close around C$1.5200 or slightly lower," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of foreign exchange at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.

title: Analyst - Cdn Imperial, Cdn Banks -5:Fund Mgr Buys CIBC Stk
text:
Royal Bank of Canada's (RY) earnings in the fiscal third quarter will be affected to some extent by the industry-wide slowdown in brokerage and underwriting businesses. However, the impact will be significantly less than the impact on Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (BCM), said Nabanita Merchant, Royal Bank's head of investor relations. 

 "We have a very different strategy" than Canadian Imperial, Merchant noted. Royal Bank is more focused on its personal and commercial business and wealth-management operations, than on the brokerage business. In addition, Royal Bank hasn't expanded as agressively as Canadian Imperial into servicing U.S. capital markets, Merchant said. 

 A spokesman for Bank of Montreal (BMO) declined to comment on the bank's third-quarter results, except to say the bank has no reason to pre-announce its results. 

 Friday's sell-off in the bank sector comes after a substantial correction in bank stocks in recent weeks. That correction resulted from fears of higher interest rates due to the weak Canadian dollar and concerns over whether planned mergers in the group will get government approval. 

Intervention Friday by the Bank of Canada to prop up the Canadian dollar against the U.S. currency heightened concerns that the central bank might be preparing to raise interest rates Monday.

 The record low was about C$1.53 to the U.S. dollar, which meant one Canadian dollar was worth about 65.4 U.S. cents. 

 The Bank of Canada is watching to see if the present weakness in Canada's currency, bond and stock markets is causing a dangerous loss of investor confidence. 

 North American stock markets have been bearish this week and the Toronto stock market was down again at midday. Canada's long-term government bond prices fell nearly a full point.

 "We've already come up 100 points very quickly today, and I think that should put a cap on the Canadian dollar's weakness for the week," he said. "Going into next week, we're definitely targeting C$1.54 (64.9 U.S. cents)." 

 The markets are bracing just in case the Bank of Canada raises interest rates to support the local currency, but a general consensus among economists is that the best policy for the central bank is to hold off raising rates unless the weak currency starts to undermine economic activity. 

 Higher borrowing costs for firms and consumers at a time of global uncertainty could further depress consumer and business confidence. 

 More importantly, economists predicted that a rate increase alone may not be powerful enough to turn around the marked downtrend in the Canadian dollar.

 The descent of the Canadian dollar, which has been hard hit by falling commodity prices, has intensified speculation that the bank of Canada may be compelled to raise rates to defend the embattled currency.

title: Toronto stocks swideswiped by more dollar weakness.
text:
TORONTO, July 31 (Reuters) - Any hopes of a sustained recovery for Toronto stocks from recent losses were smashed late on Friday as the key stock index dove 1.6 percent in light volume, sideswiped by fresh weakness in the Canadian dollar. 

 The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 Composite Index fell 114.53 points or 1.63 percent to close at 6931.43. The index rose on Thursday after dropping for nearly two weeks. Since the index's July 20 opening, at 7441.33, it has lost 6.9 percent. 

 Toronto fared worse on Friday than its U.S. counterpart, which posted a slightly smaller percentage drop, at 1.59 percent, falling 143.66 points to 8883.29. 

 Trading on Canada's largest equities market was thin at 73.8 million shares worth C$1.4 billion as players and investors skipped out ahead of a long weekend. 

 "There's no one around to trade and everybody (who's left) wanted to sell," said Craig Strachan, research services manager at TD Evergreen. 

 Canada's dollar finished the day with a record low close of C$1.5119 (US$0.6614) but was slightly higher than the new low of C$1.5130 (US$0.6609) it hit earlier in the day. Canada's central bank was forced to intervene in an attempt to slow the dollar's depreciation after months of losses. 

 As the dollar's value falls, fears increase that the Bank of Canada will be forced to raise short-term interest rates to spur investor interest in the currency. 

 "We're off another quarter cent, and that's whacking our interest-sensitive stocks," Strachan said. Interest-sensitives such as banks generally see their profits shaved once rates rise. 

 Nearly a quarter of Toronto's 300 index is composed of financial services stocks. The sector fell 1.89 percent. 

 Toronto got no help from the U.S., Strachan added, where sentiment was bearish over lower-than-expected corporate earnings results. 

 Strachan was pessimistic about the outlook for the Canadian market. "We're not going to see a bottoming in our market until we see a bottoming in our dollar." 

 All of the TSE's 14 sub-indexes fell, led by golds, off 3.89 percent, consumer products, down 3.32 percent and retail, off 2.05 percent. 

 Declines beat out advances 574 to 391 while 309 stocks closed flat. 

 Markets will be closed on Monday in most of Canada, with the exception of Quebec, for the August civic holiday. 

 TransAlta Corp.  was among the most active stocks, falling C$0.40 to C$21.50. Its New Zealand division is at a critical juncture: within three months it must decide which branch to sell to become either a lines business or an energy company in order to comply with new legislation. 

 Linamar Corp.  fell nearly 10 percent, or C$2.65 to C$25.10, because of disappointing earnings of C$0.33 a share in the second quarter versus a year-ago C$0.36. 

 ($1 = $1.51 Canadian).

*Canada's dollar ended at a record low close of C$1.5119 (US$0.6614), but off a record trading low of C$1.5130 (US$0.6609) hit in the early afternoon, at which level Bank of Canada intervened to slow pace of depreciation. *Sentiment turned bearish after news Canada's May GDP fell and U.S. Q2 GDP came in stronger than forecast. *U.S. dollar staying firm above 144 yen. *Latest U.S. dollar rise sparked by Thursday's comment by Japan's new finance minister that fate of yen and stocks should be left to markets. *Canada's markets closed, except for Quebec, on Monday for holiday.



TORONTO, July 31 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar wrapped up an eventful week sharply lower against the U.S. dollar, ending at a record low close of C$1.5119 (US$0.6614), more than 100 points weaker than a week ago.



Monica Lewinsky gave an unintentional boost to the loonie on Tuesday, when she secured immunity from prosecution in the White House sex scandal. But on Thursday Japan's new finance minister, Kiichi Miyazawa, hit the currency indirectly with comments that the market took as a hands-off policy towards the falling value of the yen.



The latest trigger pushing down the Canadian dollar was the announcement on Friday morning of the weakest economic growth data in two years. Before the Bank of Canada stepped into the currency market to cap the slide, the Canadian dollar hit a record trading low of C$1.5130 (US$0.6609) in the afternoon.



That's the level at which the central bank bought Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars. Stop-loss selling beat down the currency from C$1.5035 (US$0.6651) at the opening and C$1.5063 (US$0.6639) at Thursday's close.



"The Bank of Canada has a policy where they intervene approximately 70 to 75 points from the previous day's close. And we hit that level, so they intervened. It's regular business as usual for the Bank of Canada," Steven Butler, director of foreign exchange at Scotia Capital Markets, told Reuters Television.



Weaker-than-forecast May economic data for Canada, released this morning, ended a brief pause in Canada selling, prompting the currency to breach the previous record low of C$1.5094 (US$0.6625) set here on Thursday.



"Once we got that data out at 8:30, it really became a full-blown conclusion that Canada would break C$1.5100 (US$0.6623)," said Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities.



Until late morning, the Canadian dollar resisted one-way selling after slipping immediately after the 0830 EDT/1230 GMT release of two sets of key North American data.



Canada's gross domestic product (GDP), hit by widespread weakness in the economy, fell by 0.2 percent in May after being unchanged in April. The consensus forecast pointed to mild growth of 0.1 percent.



It marked the first time in two years the economy has failed to grow in two consecutive months.



Statistics Canada foresees GDP growth of around two percent on an annual basis in the second quarter, pulled down by strikes at General Motors' factories and in the construction sector, after 3.7 percent in the first quarter.



In contrast, the U.S. second-quarter GDP rose 1.4 percent from upwardly revised growth of 5.5 percent in the first quarter. The Q2 growth was the weakest since a rise of 0.4 percent in Q2 1995. The average forecast called for a rise of 0.2 percent in the April-June quarter.



In cross trading, the Canadian unit shed earlier gains, falling to 1.1742 marks from 1.1816 marks at the previous close here. Canada slipped a bit but was still quoted higher at 95.58 yen from 93.37 yen.



Canada's financial markets will be closed, except for Quebec, on Monday for a holiday.



The next key data, July employment figures for both U.S. and Canada, come up on Friday, August 7.



Economists on average expect Canada's July employment to have grown by 4,800 (forecast range: a fall of 20,000 to a gain of 20,000) after a decline of 35,900 in June. The jobless rate is seen unchanged at 8.4 percent. The weak June report triggered selling of the Canadian dollar.



The U.S. non-farm payrolls are seen rising by 35,000 in July after a rise of 205,000 in June. The unemployment rate is forecast to be unchanged at 4.5 percent.



Meanwhile, Canada's overall monetary condition, measured by the monetary conditions index (MCI) published and closely watched by the central bank, loosened further this week, along with the depreciation of the Canadian dollar. Traders expect the Bank of Canada to hold off raising its key lending rate unless the weak currency induces sharply higher import prices and pushes up inflation, or speculative selling of Canada's dollar causes a loss of investor confidence.



Butler said it was hard to pinpoint a specific point on the MCI scale that could prompt the bank to raise interest rates.



"At this point they seem very content to sit back and let the currency run its course," he said.



The Bank of Canada's weekly calculation of the MCI hit a record low this week, according to figures released by the bank on Friday. The bank gave a figure of -6.32 for Wednesday, going beyond the previous record low of -6.26 on June 25, 1997. The more negative the figure, the more relaxed monetary conditions are deemed to be.



The index has slipped further since Wednesday, according to Reuters constantly updated calculations, hitting -6.405 at 1330 EDT (1730 GMT) on Thursday.



The central bank has said it would expect a wider fluctuation in monetary conditions, measured through movements in short-term interest rates and the Canadian dollar's value.



"It (the weak GDP) is definitely negative for the Canadian dollar. It kind of confirms the trend we've seen in other monthly indicators... manufacturing shipments and new orders are down, exports have been down, a sign of weakness in some aspects of consumer spending," Daniel Kelly, director of financial markets at CIBC Wood Gundy, told Reuters Television.



"This just confirms that the Bank of Canada is between a rock and a hard place. They've got very low inflation in Canada, below the target, but weakening growth, so there's not much of rationale for them to raise interest rates and try to strengthen the Canadian dollar," he said.



He said Canada's consumer confidence appeared to have deteriorated recently along with the 20-week decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, but pointed out that the weaker currency, which makes Canadian exports price-competitive, has worked as a buffer against soft commodity prides, boosting profit margins for the natural recourse sector and preventing it from laying off workers.



The U.S. dollar stayed firm above 144 yen on fading fears of Bank of Japan intervention to stem the yen's slide.



The U.S. unit started its latest upward move on Thursday, when Canada's dollar fell prey indirectly to a comment by Japan's new finance minister, Kiichi Miyazawa, that the fate of the yen and stocks should be left to the markets. The U.S. dollar jumped on his comment as traders took it to mean that no currency intervention was imminent to boost the yen.



Overnight, a senior Finance Ministry official in Tokyo quoted Miyazawa as saying that Japan's foreign exchange policy was unchanged.



On the domestic front, traders generally hailed the approach to the currency market taken by Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin, who stressed the underlying strength of the nation's economy and declined comment on how the government would rescue the local currency.



Martin, in response to questions, pointed to Canada's improved economic fundamentals, telling reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday that Canada's productivity had increased, the federal budget was estimated to be balanced this year, and inflation was low.



Martin said he was not "indifferent" to the Canadian dollar's fall.



But his boss, Prime Minister Jean Chretien, did not have much luck in dealing with the market on the following day.



He stuck to the same line as Martin's, telling reporters that Canada's economy was strong with low inflation. But the timing was bad: the Canadian dollar had already been under downward pressure from stop-loss orders and slumped as he made that comment.



Chretien was in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, ahead of the annual premiers' meeting there next week.

title: Canada bonds end mixed on U.S./Canada GDP data.
text:
TORONTO, July 31 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended a shortened trading day mixed on Friday, with the long end of the yield curve slightly firmer on the latest economic data and the short end hit by a sharp drop in the local currency. 

 Trading was relatively quiet as the bond market closed early here at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT on Friday ahead of a long weekend. Financial markets will be closed on Monday in Canada except for Quebec. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond (due June 1, 2027) rose C$0.23 to C$134.63 to yield 5.572 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 2/32 to yield 5.73 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread was 16 basis points after 14 points at the previous close here. 

 Long-term bond holders were relieved by the U.S. second quarter gross domestic product (GDP) that came in stronger than some forecasts but showed price stability. That suggests that the U.S. central bank will hold off raising interest rates. 

 Canada's long bonds firmed also because the weak May GDP data for Canada prompted expectations that the market will be free of inflationary pressure for the time being. 

 U.S. treasuries suffered from selling as some players were disappointed that steady growth in the U.S. economy, albeit at a slower pace, means there is no need for the Federal Reserve to lower its key lending rate. Some economists had forecast a decline the second quarter. 

 Chicago Purchasing Managers July indices, which showed robust economic activity, also weighed on the U.S. bond market. But the price index showed a falling trend since April. 

 U.S. second-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) grew 1.4 percent after upwardly revised growth of 5.5 percent in the first quarter. The Q2 growth was the weakest since a rise of 0.4 percent in Q2 1995. The average forecast called for a rise of 0.2 percent in the April-June quarter. 

 In contrast, Canada's GDP, hit by widespread weakness in the economy, fell by 0.2 percent in May after being unchanged in April. The consensus forecast pointed to marginal growth of 0.1 percent. 

 Statistics Canada foresees GDP growth of around two percent on an annual basis in the second quarter, depressed by strikes at General Motors' factories and in the construction sector, after 3.7 percent in the first quarter. 

 "The fact that the deflator eased in the U.S. in the second quarter offers more evidence that inflation is not picking up and therefore that we're not going to see a hike by the Fed in the near term, and I think that's helping the long end of the Canadian market outperform the U.S. right now," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 The U.S. GDP price index rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter, slower than a downwardly revised rise of 0.9 percent in the previous quarter. 

 The U.S GDP deflator rose 0.9 percent in the April-June quarter after a rise of a downwardly revised rise of 0.8 percent in the January-March quarter. 

 The front end of the Canadian yield curve was weaker as the local dollar, after posting mild gains overseas overnight, plunged through key support levels and hit new lows before the Bnak of Canada intervened to buy Canada at C$1.5030 (US$0.6609). 

 The Bank of Canada's weekly calculation of its monetary conditions index (MCI) hit a record low this week, according to figures released by the bank on Friday. 

 The bank gave a figure of -6.32 for Wedneday, going beyond the previous record low of -6.26 on June 25, 1997. The more negative the figure, the more relaxed monetary conditions are deemed to be. 

 The index has slipped further since Wednesday, according to Reuters constantly updated calculations, hitting -6.405 at 1330 EDT (1730 GMT) on Thursday. 

 The central bank has said it would expect a wider fluctuation in monetary conditions, measured through movements in short-term interest rates and the Canadian dollar's value. 

 The money market was quiet, fluctuating in a narrow range along with the move in the Canadian dollar. 

 "(It was) a little bit better bid this morning when the currency was firmer, but gave up that ground as the (Canadian) dollar started to sell off again," said Walter Posiewko, money market trader at Royal Bank Investment Management Inc. "We're totally in sympathy with the currency right now." 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill yielded 5.04 percent after 5.02 percent at the previous close here. 

 The Bank of Canada on Friday set special purchase/resale agreements at 5.0 percent to take pressure off tight conditions in the overnight rate movement at the end of the quarter for the bank. It is a technical move by the central bank to keep the call rate within its target range of 4.5-5.0 percent, and has no policy implications.

title: Chastened Chretien now mum on flagging Canadian dollar.
text:
SASKATOON, Saskatchewan, July 29 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Jean Chretien sidestepped questions over the flagging Canadian dollar on Wednesday in an apparent effort to avoid a past gaffe that served only to drive the currency down further. 

 Chretien, in the prairie province of Saskatchewan to meet with Premier Roy Romanow before a meeting of provincial leaders next week, declined to comment to reporters on the dollar other than to point out that the economy was strong and inflation low. 

 "The economy is performing very well at this time. It is our role to make the economy perform very well," he said, noting that annual inflation was less than one percent last month. 

 Chretien's Liberal party government has come under increasing fire from economists and opposition politicians over what they view as a lack of action on the ailing currency, which has recently plumbed record low after record low against the U.S. dollar. 

 Many analysts and observers have said he should talk up the currency - to leave the possibility in speculators' minds that they might get burned. 

 The Canadian dollar, often called the "Loonie" because of the aquatic bird's image on the coin, slipped in value again on Wednesday. It ended at a record low close of C$1.5063 (US$0.6639) on Wednesday. 

 Chretien's last public intervention, on July 14, was to tell reporters after a cabinet meeting in Ottawa that the weaker dollar helped Canadian exports and tourist spots. 

 Asked then if he was happy with the weak dollar he said: "It's not a question of being happy. It's a reality of life." 

 Analysts said the nonchalance displayed by the comments led traders to drive the dollar's value down further. 

 During Wednesday's brief press conference behind a Saskatoon hotel, Chretien also avoided commenting on the possibility of instituting tax cuts as a way of supporting the dollar, instead inviting reporters to ask him the question again before the next fiscal budget, scheduled for February. 

 There have been suggestions from economists and politicians that the best way to boost demand for the Canadian dollar would be to cut taxes. Others have countered that this could raise concerns among international investors about the government's commitment to debt and deficit reduction. 

 Despite vague market expectations of some action, the central bank, the Bank of Canada, has refrained from currency market intervention and has held off raising key lending rates as a means of attracting investors to Canadian assets. 

 Much of Canada's weakness derives from soft commodities prices as the nation still relies on exports of oil, gas, and farm and forest products for a substantial part of national income. 

 In the eyes of currency traders, there are few fundamental factors supporting Canadian currency at the moment.

title: Canada Afternoon -2: U.S. Dlr Seen Targetting C$1.5100
text:
While the Canadian dollar had trended slowly lower throughout Wednesday's session as the U.S. dollar regained strength versus the yen, late afternoon dealings pushed the currency to the brink of the C$1.5075 level thought to be the trigger for intervention from the Bank of Canada. 

 The central bank's general policy is to intervene whenever the exchange rate moves 70 ticks in either direction from the previous day's close. 

 With Tuesday's abortive rally now seemingly exhausted, most believe that barring unforseen developments, the U.S. dollar will now resume its pattern of making moderate daily gains against the Canadian unit, with the C$1.5100 level now in sight.

title: Canada dlr crosses key C$1.50, heads to new lows.
text:
LONDON, July 27 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar fell past a key psychological barrier at C$1.50 ($0.6666) to set new record lows against the U.S. dollar on Monday, undermined by interest rates below those in the U.S and a fragile economy. 

 Dealers said the Canadian dollar set a new historic low of C$1.5022 ($0.6656) after grinding down on hawkish interest rate comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan at his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last week. 

 "That helped it and there are a lot of economists jumping on board saying the Canadian dollar can achieve really low targets," said John Glover, vice president and director of foreign exchange for the Toronto-Dominion Bank in London. "Our own economist came out over the weekend and said 50 cents (U.S.) was not out of the question." 

 Last week Greenspan warned U.S. lawmakers that the risk of inflationary pressures continued in the U.S. economy and that further strength in wage inflation could force the Federal Reserve to raise U.S. interest rates. 

 Such a rise would widen the interest rate differential between higher U.S. rates and lower Canadian ones. 

 The fall of Canadian interest rates to levels below those of the U.S in the last two years has steadily ground down the Canadian dollar. 

 On Monday U.S. Federal Reserve funds were at 5.50 percent, while the Bank of Canada's operating band for overnight funds was at 4.5 to 5.0 percent. 

 Affectionately known by Canadians as the "loonie" after the waterfowl depicted on the country's one dollar coin, the Canadian dollar has lost more than seven U.S. cents over the last two years and 22 U.S. cents in the last six years. 

 "They've got interest rates below the U.S. and while that happens why buy Canada," said one dealer at a major Canadian bank in London. "You might as well invest in the U.S.." 

 At 0945 GMT the Canadian dollar was trading at 1.5000/10 compared with 1.4984/89 in late European trading on Friday. 

 Traders said the Canadian dollar has also been left exposed by a hamstrung Bank of Canada, which cannot raise interest rates to defend the currency for fear of squelching a fragile economy. 

 They said they had expected the Bank of Canada to appear in defence of the Canadian dollar ahead of 1.50 on Friday and its failure to appear prompted more selling. 

 "We thought on Friday, the Bank of Canada would have been in early to defend this 1.50 level and there was absolutely no sign of that," said a trader. 

 They said the market would focus on the hours when the Bank of Canada begins its trading operations around 1355 GMT on Monday for a possible rate rise to defend the currency. 

 "We will see what happens at the window," another trader said. "I don't think anyone will be long dollars ahead of that." 

 The Bank of Canada last intervened to buy Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars on July 15 at the C$1.4870 ($0.0.6725) level. 

 "I spoke to them (the Bank of Canada) last week and they are not happy about where the dollar is," said Ian Amstad, economist at Banker's Trust in London. 

 But he said low inflation, weak commodity prices and a strike by General Motors Corp workers, made the central bank unwilling to raise the cost of financing. "With inflation running at 0.8 percent on their underlying measure and some of their real economy numbers looking a little bit soft they are reluctant to move," Amstad said. 

 He said the Bank of Canada is focused on its Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), as a measure of monetary policy effects and an indicator when an adjustment could be needed. 

 On Friday, the Bank of Canada reported the MCI fell to its lowest level in more than a year to -6.16. 

 The index measures the the three-month prime corporate paper rate and the Canadian dollar index against the 10 major currencies. The index base is January 1987. The more negative the index, the looser monetary conditions are deemed to be. 

 "Now it's a matter of the market deciding when the MCI is at a level where the Bank (of Canada) has got to do something and we're already through the levels where everyone had thought that would be the case now," Glover said. 

 ((Paul Casciato, London newsroom +44 171 542 8968 fax +44 171 542 5293, paul.casciato@reuters.com)).

title: No reprieve in sight as Canada dollar falls again.
text:
TORONTO, July 27 (Reuters) - Canada's dollar continued its swoon on Monday, hitting more record lows, and traders and economists expected it to weaken still further in the absence any supporting news. 

 That means Canadians will have to keep on paying more than one and a half Canadian dollars to get one U.S. dollar. 

 The new trading low was C$1.5053 (US$0.6643) against the U.S dollar, reached in afternoon trade. The Canadian dollar ended official North American trade at C$1.5032 (US$0.6652), a record closing low. 

 Despite vague market expectations of some action, the central bank, the Bank of Canada, has refrained from currency market intervention and has held off raising key lending rates as a means of attracting investors to Canadian assets. 

 The slide in the Canadian dollar has been constant but orderly. 

 Much of Canada's weakness derives from soft commodities prices as the nation still relies on exports of oil, gas, and farm and forest products for a substantial part of national income. 

 In the eyes of currency traders, there are few fundamental factors supporting Canadian currency at the moment. 

 Economic indicators have shown signs of a slower pace of growth in Canada, and investors tend to choose U.S. dollar assets as a safe-haven when uncertainty persists, as it does now in Asia. 

 The Canadian dollar is on a downtrend against the German mark, while climbing against the Japanese yen. 

 ((Reuters Toronto newsroom (416) 941-8107, toronto.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: World  Forex  -3: Canada Dlr Breaches Key C$1.5000 Level
text:
Elsewhere Monday, the Canadian dollar sank past the psychologically important level of C$1.5000 to a U.S. dollar. The next target level of C$1.6000 will be attainable, especially if the dollar manages to extend its gains against the yen, said Bank of America's Nickerson. 

 Late in New York, the dollar was quoted at C$1.5035, down from an intraday high of C$1.5053, but up from C$1.4990 late Friday. 

 Canada's central bank has accommodated the the weak trend seen in the Canadian dollar. However, "if the market starts to question if it is benign neglect as opposed to a policy," then the Bank of Canada may intervene to show it is paying attention, said Nickerson. 

 Other so-called commodity-based currencies weakened against the dollar as well. The Australian dollar and the New Zealand dollar both fell on the back of a weak yen Monday. 

 The same trend- tracking the yen- was seen in a majority of the Southeast Asian currencies Monday, with the exception of the Indonesian rupiah, which gained nearly 2% on the day. The rupiah broke the psychologically important level of IDR14,000 to a dollar after two protest demonstrations remained peaceful. 

 In intraday trading Monday, the U.S. dollar fell to IDR13,700, but has since recouped those losses and was trading near IDR14,100 late in New York, unchanged from Friday's levels. 

 Analysts say the focus is now on the two-day meeting of countries which lend money to Indonesia to take place in Paris later this week . The donor countries are expected to increase significantly the amount of loans they provide to Indonesia this year from US$5.3 billion last year.

TORONTO, July 23 (Reuters) - Canada's battered dollar resisted selling pressure most of the day, but ended at a record closing low of C$1.4956 (US$0.6686) on Thursday.



That was still firmer than a new trading low of C$1.4971 (US$0.6680) set in morning trade before unfounded rumours gave the currency a temporary shot in the arm.



The Canadian dollar rose on rumours that the U.S. Federal Reserve was selling treasury bills to raise funds for intervention by Bank of Japan and Bank of Canada to sell U.S. dollars.



Market players later sold back Canadian dollars slightly, realising that Canada's central bank would have of no need of the help of its U.S. counterpart to raise liquidity.



"It wasn't breaking the C$1.4940 level convincingly so people turned around and took back their short (U.S) dollar positions," one trader said.



The pace of the currency's 19-week slide has slowed and it is stuck in a tight range as both buy and sell orders emerged from corporate customers.



Some players have predicted that the U.S. dollar will hit the next target of C$1.5000 (US$0.6667) by the end of the week, but traders now think it might take a little more time.



The U.S. dollar was steady this afternoon after rising above 142 yen overseas on growing concern over Japan's ability to fix its financial problems and jump-start the economy.



The latest shock to the Asian markets came overnight from credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service, which has put Japan's top-notch Aaa debt rating under review for a possible downgrade, an unprecedented move for Japan.



Uncertainty about Japan also persisted ahead of Friday's election of the nation's ruling party leader, who will become the next prime minister unless any large-scale defectors undermine the party's majority in the powerful Lower House of parliament.



In cross trading, the Canadian unit, after a rebound, ended the session down at 1.1926 marks from 1.1954 marks at the previous close here. Canada gave up earlier gains and was flat at 94.35 yen after 94.34 yen.



Above C$1.5000 is uncharted territory and hard to project trend lines, but



the next price objective after that level is  C$1.5033, based on recent moves,



said Katherine Beattie, senior technical analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS.



The Bank of Canada has maintained its silence, trying to avoid any



deterioration of the exchange rate by commenting on the market, particularly



after Prime Minister Jean Chretien came under fire for saying last week that



the weak local dollar was good for Canada's exports and tourism.



The bank is looking at soft commodities prices and resulting weakness in



Canada's exports, and a low inflation rate, which has worked as a buffer for



the weak currency. It is monitoring investor confidence in Canadian dollar



assets, but its aim appears not to fight the flow of exchange rates.



On Friday, Japan's ruling Liberal Democrats will cast their votes, starting



at 1400 JST/0500 GMT/0100 EDT, and the results of the first vote will be



announced at around 1450 JST/0550 GMT/0150 EDT. If there is a winner, he will



hold a news conference at 1600 JST/0700 GMT/0300 on the same day.

TORONTO, July 21 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar drifted to new lows as the U.S. dollar rebounded against key currencies at the start of key testimony by the U.S. central bank chief.



The Canadian unit touched a record trading low of C$1.4926 (US$0.6700) after matching earlier this morning the previous record low of C$1.4920 (US$0.6702) hit overnight in technical trading.



The market is now watching for further comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan at the two-day semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony kicked off this morning.



"His comment was interpreted as slightly hawkish, the U.S. dollar is above 140 yen... there's no huge surprise there," said Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities.



Greenspan said higher U.S. inflation would outweigh the downside risk arising from the Asia's economic downturn. His comment triggered selling in North American bonds and the U.S. stock market.



"While we expect that the situation will develop relatively smoothly, the committee believes that, given the current tightness in labour markets, the potential for accelerating inflation is probably greater than the risk of protracted, excessive weakness in the economy," he said.



In cross trading, the Canadian dollar slipped from earlier levels, but was still up at 1.1975 marks after 1.1967 marks at the previous close here. Canada rose to 93.92 yen from 93.24 yen.



   Last time Greenspan testified, on June 10, North American



bond prices surged on his balanced comments and prevailing



flight-to-quality capital flows.



    On that day, the Canadian dollar came under speculative



selling pressure, which prompted Bank of Canada intervention to



buy Canadian for U.S. dollars.



    Back then, Greenspan told the Joint Economic Committee of



Congress that the Federal Reserve might have to raise interest



rates if demand were to continue to exhibit few signs of



abating noticeably, but that there was no need for a tighter



monetary policy to cool off the economy.



Earlier today after the 0900 EDT/1300 GMT daily window of



money market operation by the Bank of Canada, the Canadian unit



had firmed a bit to C$1.4881 (US$0.6720) in a technical move.



"It was sort of stop-loss driven, first (the U.S. dollar)



ran up to the C$1.4905/10 (US$0.6709/0.6707) level. I think



there was small nervousness about the bank doing something



about the rates, nothing happened, of course," one trader



said.



"I think people were going to short Canada, long (U.S.)



dollars, so as a result they didn't like it, a couple of guys



sold it (the U.S. dollar) and it fell through," he said.



Some weakness in the Canadian currency, which cuts the



nation's export prices, is needed to offset external shocks,



such as the slump in Asia and soft commodities prices, said



Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, macro economics at Bank



of Montreal.



"However, the C$1.4900 (US$0.6711), in our view, that's



getting on the weak side and maybe indicating an overshoot," he



told Reuters Television.



Canada's latest economic indicator had little impact on the



market. Canada's May retail sales came in as expected, up 0.5



percent after a revised 1.1-percent rise in April. Economists



on average had expected a 0.4-percent rise in May.



    Separately, U.S. June housing starts rose 5.6 percent after



revised a 1.0-percent fall in May.



    "Finally we've got a break from a string of data that were



coming in weaker than expected," Ferley said. "I thin the gain



is suggesting that consumer spending is still remaining



relatively healthy.



He said he was a bit concerned about the June data in light



of slow automobile sales and an expected decline in income as a



result of the General Motors strike.



"For the second quarter, we feel there's enough momentum in



the economy that we should see growth close to three percent,"

TORONTO, July 17 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended flat at C$1.4884 (US$0.6719) on Friday after scratching a record trading low of C$1.4918 (US$0.6703) on technical moves in early trade.



The currency slipped to an 18-month low against the mark as the German currency firmed versus other currencies on brighter prospects for financial reform in Russia, backed by international aid.



The Canadian unit has been sliding against the U.S. dollar constantly for the past four months from the C$1.4070/80 level (US$0.7107/0.71020), and still lacks support on the chart. Canada has weakened by 100 points this week, with the U.S. dollar firming by a full Canadian cent.



"As we go forward, I think people will sell the Canadian dollar initially and just to see if there's any continued follow-through in the weakness in Canada," one trader said. "Right now I don't think the market is terribly in love with the Canadian dollar, they prefer to short (sell) it."



On the downside of the U.S. dollar, short-term traders would buy back Canadian dollars at C$1.4845/50 (US$0.6736/0.6734), he said.



Trading is expected to remain cautious as U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, the world's most influential central banker, discusses the U.S. economy in his Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony next Tuesday.

title: Canada bonds end weaker, following U.S. market.
text:
TORONTO, July 16 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended weaker on Thursday, after fluctuating in a relatively narrow band, following U.S. treasuries. 

 The U.S. dollar's slide versus the yen on hopes of stronger Japanese leadership and growing optimism over Russia's economic reform took some shine off the safe-haven status of U.S. dollar assets, which spilled over into Canadian bonds. 

 North American bonds were unable to gain strongly on some bond-friendly data that showed a slower pace of U.S. economic growth and thus little inflationary threat. 

 U.S. treasuries ended mostly lower, also on hedge fund selling. 

 Focus is on the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan next Tuesday. 

 The Japanese currency extended overnight gains on growing expectations in the market that former chief cabinet secretary Seiroku Kajiyama will win the race for the leadership of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and succeed the outgoing prime minister, Ryutaro Hashimoto. 

 The market favours the drastic banking reform plans Kajiyama has been proposing since he quit the cabinet in the previous Hashimoto government. 

 Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi, seen as a safe choice but lacking strong leadership, is still a front runner in the LDP election, which has been delayed by three days till July 24. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond fell C$0.35 to C$135.11, yielding 5.546 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 11/32, yielding 5.73 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread was 18 basis points, unchanged from the previous close here. 

 The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia said manufacturing activity fell in July in the U.S. third economic district. 

 The monthly business outlook survey showed its business index fell to 11.6 in July from 28.2 in June. Indexes for inventories and prices fell. 

 Earlier, the market failed to react favourably to a decline in U.S. industrial output data that suggested the U.S. economic growth is slowing and poses little inflationary threat to bond holders. 

 June industrial output fell 0.6 percent from a 0.3-percent rise in May, mainly hit by General Motors strikes. Capacity utilization slipped to 81.6 from 82.4. 

 Also in the morning, Canada's June consumer price index (CPI) showed tame inflation, but had little direct impact on the market. 

 Overall CPI rose 1.0 percent year on year in June after a 1.1-percent rise in May, and the core rate (ex-food and energy prices) rose 1.0 percent from a year earlier after a 1.4 percent rise. 

 Economists on average had forecast a 1.1-percent rise for all items and an increase of 1.3 percent for the core rate. 

 "The year-over-year increase of 1.0 percent moves back down to the floor of the (central) bank's 1-3 percent target band, so there's no reason on the basis of inflation data why they should be raising rates," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 "In my view, the Bank of Canada is going to have to raise rates, but I don't think that's yet a majority view. I think they are going to have to go regardless of the CPI numbers," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. 

 He pointed to the underperformance in Canadian bonds and bills against the U.S. market on Wednesday, which means the contagion of the currency is spreading to other assets. 

 The Canadian unit, which has been sliding for the past four months, hit a record trading low of C$1.4895 (US$0.6714) on Wednesday with intervention by the Bank of Canada slowing the pace of depreciation.

I think we're a couple of weeks away or we need to have a very, very big move in the currency like when we come in tomorrow morning, and the dollar is at C$1.5000 (US$0.6667), that's a problem and the (central) bank will go."

title: Canada bonds open weaker in line with U.S. market.
text:
TORONTO, July 16 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds opened weaker in stable trading on Thursday, following U.S. treasuries. 

 The U.S. dollar's slide below 140 yen on hopes of stronger Japanese leadership took some shine off the safe-haven status of U.S. dollar assets, which spilled over into Canadian bonds. 

 The Japanese currency extended overnight gains on growing expectations in the market that former chief cabinet secretary Seiroku Kajiyama will win the race for the leader of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to succeed outgoing Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. 

 The market favours drastic banking reform plans Kajiyama has been proposing since he quit his cabinet post in the previous Hashimoto government. 

 Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi, seen as a safe choice but lacking strong leadership, is still a front runner in the LDP election, which has been delayed by three days till July 24. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond fell C$0.16 to C$135.30, yielding 5.536 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 8/32, yielding 5.72 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread was 18 basis points, unchanged from the previous close here. 

 The market failed to react favourably to a decline in U.S. industrial output data that suggests the pace of U.S. growth is slowing and poses little inflationary threat to bond holders. 

 June industrial output fell 0.6 percent after a 0.3-percent rise in May, mainly hit by General Motors strikes. Capacity utilization slipped to 81.6 from 82.4. 

 Earlier in the morning, Canada's June consumer price index (CPI) showed tame inflation, but had little direct impact on the market. 

 Overall CPI rose 1.0 percent year on year in June after a 1.1-percent rise in May, and the core rate (ex-food and energy prices) rose 1.0 percent from a year earlier after a 1.4 percent rise. 

 Economists on average had forecast a 1.1-percent rise for all items and an increase of 1.3 percent for the core rate. 

 "The year-over-year increase of 1.0 percent moves back down to the floor of the (central) bank's 1-3 percent target band, so there's no reason on the basis of inflation data why they should be raising rates," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 "In my view, the Bank of Canada is going to have to raise rates, but I don't think that's yet a majority. I think they are going to have to go regardless of the CPI numbers, said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. 

 He pointed to the underperformance in Canadian bonds and bills against the U.S. market on Wednesday, which means that the contagion of the currency is spreading to other assets. 

 The Canadian unit, which has been sliding constantly for the past four months, hit a record trading low of C$1.4895 (US$0.6714) on Wednesday with intervention by the Bank of Canada slowing the pace of steep depreciation. 

 The most recent selling came from a string of weak economic domestic economic data. 

 Consensus forecasts for key Canadian economic indicators for the rest of the week (hit ECI/CI + F9 for a full list): 

 Friday, JULY 17 

 May trade surplus C$1.22 billion (April: C$1.20 billion). 

 The money market was stable this morning after weakening sharply on the falling Canadian dollar on Wednesday. 

 "We've weakened off and that's brought buyers back into the market," said one trader. "We personally did not believe that the bank will raise rates today. I think we're a couple of weeks away or we need to have a very very big move in the currency like when we come in tomorrow morning, and the dollar is at C$1.5000 (US$0.6667), that's a problem and the (central) bank will go." 

 The Bank of Canada's signal to the market so far has been "business as usual" and its tone hasn't changed, she said. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill traded with a yield of 4.95 percent, unchanged from the previous close here.

 "It's pretty bearish. The comment from Ottawa did not help yesterday. They are not showing any particular concern in the currency," one trader said. 

 Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien told reporters on Tuesday that a weak currency actually helps exports and tourism. "It's not a question of being happy. It's a reality of life," he said. 

 And the Bank of Canada has been quiet about the loonie's performance. No intervention by the bank to sell U.S. dollars for Canada has been detected in recent trade, with the slide coming in narrow movements. 

 "There's always speculation of an interest rate hike, but they've let it go this far," the trader said. 

 Canada's economic indicators weighed on the market this morning. 

 May manufacturing shipments fell 1.0 percent after a revised drop of 0.7 percent in April, while economists had forecast a 0.6-percent rise. May car sales came in lower than expected, rising 1.1 percent after a 5.9-percent rise in April.

 monetary conditions are expected in Canada. It is watching

 In theory, if Canada raised domestic interest rates, it

title: Canada dollar breaks to record lows beyond C$1.48.
text:
LONDON, July 13 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar broke to new record lows on Monday in European trading after surpassing the psychological C$1.48 level earlier in Asian trade. 

 Dealers said Canada's currency was prodded further along its recent weakening path by Friday's unemployment numbers, which revealed an increasingly fragile economy. 

 "Friday's figures were not looking too good and overall if you look at the Canadian economy you've got the problems with the weak commodity prices and shockwaves from the Asian situation," said Derek Shewring, senior dealer at Royal Bank of Canada. 

 "The currency is going to continue to suffer and we're looking for a test towards C$1.50." 

 Statistics Canada reported on Friday that the nation's unemployment rate held steady in June at 8.4 percent, unchanged from May. But employment fell by 35,900 to 14.24 million in June. It also fell by 7,300 in May. 

 Dealers at other Canadian banks in London said they also expected the Canadian dollar to head towards a test of C$1.50 by the end of the summer, but that a sharp drop could prompt intervention from the Bank of Canada. 

 "We're still targeting C$1.50, but if this thing shoots up quickly the Bank of Canada is going to have to come in to stem the tide," said a dealer at a Canadian bank in London. 

 At 1120 GMT the Canadian dollar was trading at C$1.4785/90 ($0.6761/64) after setting a new record low of C$1.4814 ($0.6749) compared with C$1.4793/98 ($0.6757/59). 

 However, they said intervention from Canada's central bank would not be enough to staunch the flow of money exiting Canadian investments because of low interest rates and a fragile economy. 

 They said the Canadian dollar will continue on its weakening trend as long as yields in Canada remain below those in the U.S. and economic data show economic growth may be slipping. 

 Canada's three-month T-bill was trading at a yield of 4.80/77 percent on Monday compared with U.S. three-month treasuries at 4.94 percent. 

 The softer economy and dollar are likely to test the Bank of Canada's resolve, which may have to make the choice of whether it prefers to see the dollar fall further and faster or economic growth injured if the bank raised in interest rates. 

 "With the currency above C$1.48 there will be speculation that the Bank will hike, but I'm not sure the Bank of Canada can do too much given the state of the economy," Shewring said. 

 In other dollar bloc currencies, the Aussie and Kiwi dollars hit two-week lows under pressure from renewed weakness in the yen. 

 Dollar bloc's Asian partners came under renewed selling pressure against the U.S. dollar as dollar/yen soared on losses to Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in Sunday's election for the Upper House of Japan's parliament. 

 Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto resigned over the electoral defeats, which are as a major blow to the LDP party. 

 At 1135 GMT, the Australian dollar was at $0.6108/13, off a one-week low of $0.6029, but still down from $0.6142/52 in late European trading on Friday. The New Zealand dollar was at $0.5114/21, off a low of $0.5059, but still down from $0.5138/45 on Friday.

TORONTO, July 10 (Reuters) - Canada's dollar slumped on Friday to a record closing low of C$1.4783 (US$0.6765), after touching a new intra-day low of C$1.4800 (US$0.6757) in gradual selling triggered by the nation's weak jobs data.



There was no indication of market intervention or an exchange rate check by Canada's central bank to stem a further decline in the currency, which has been fairly orderly.



"We tested the C$1.48 big figure level, but did not breach it. The market is certainly poised to move through that price point next week," one risk manager said. "The basic mood is still bearish and the Bank of Canada has been noticeably quiet, or totally absent from the market not only in terms of intervention but in terms of commenting."



"There's not a real sense of panic yet in the currency being sold off," another trader said, adding that market players were leaving for home with either square or small U.S. dollar long (buy) positions in spot, short-term trading.



"I think some people may be looking out to put on long Canada positions on a longer-term basis, maybe constructing their positions for option plays," he said.



Economists and market participants expect Canada's central bank to hold off raising its key lending rate for a while. Such a move would would be expected to lure investors into Canadian assets, boosting dollar demand.



The currency took another hit in typically thin summer trading in North America as traders, who had expected some growth in job creation, renewed Canadian dollar selling on early morning news that employment in Canada fell for the second consecutive month in June.



Total employment fell by 35,900 to 14.24 million with most declines recorded in the agricultural sector, after a drop of 7,300 in May. The jobless rate was unchanged at 8.4 percent.



Canadians may see more weakness on the jobs front in July as the impact of the General Motors plant shutdowns in North America was not fully reflected in the latest data.



"The Canadian dollar story has been a global story until today. The weakness in the exchange rate was clearly reflecting the weakness in the commodities prices, which are relevant to Canada," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Bank Securities. "However, we're beginning to see signs of slowdown domestically, and the question is if that slowdown is temporary or something more permanent."



Canada's bearish jobs report came on the heels of Thursday's news of a 4.6 percent drop in June housing starts, making the third consecutive month of declines. Construction industry strikes in the key province of Ontario were blamed.



In cross trading, Canada fell to 1.2283 marks from 1.2390 marks at the previous close here, and to 95.44 yen from 95.53 yen, moving in tight ranges in response to the U.S. dollar's fluctuations against the mark and yen.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank of  Canada  joins euro  intervention .
text:
TORONTO, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada on Friday joined central banks from Europe, Japan and the United States in the fight to defend the beleaguered euro on the eve of a meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised countries. 

 "Bank of Canada joins concerted intervention. Bank of Canada buys euro versus Canadian dollars," said the central bank in a statement. 

 Bank officials declined to confirm if the bank had used its own funds to buy euros for Canadian dollars and said they will not be making any further comment on Friday. 

 G7 finance ministers are gathering in Prague this weekend for the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. 

 Analysts cheered the move by the Bank of Canada and its counterparts ahead of the meeting of G7 finance ministers. 

 "In a way, that was a brilliant stroke. I think the market was assuming we'd wait and see what came out of the G7 meeting and they were probably ready to pounce on it and say it wasn't enough," said Doug Porter, senior economist at BMO Nesbitt Burns Inc. 

 "I think it really caught the the market flat-footed," he added. 

 The intervention, the first joint central bank effort since 1995, drove the euro up sharply before relinquishing some of its early gains. 

 Analysts said the concerted move by central banks sent a positive message to euro markets. 

 "I think the Bank of Canada was just trying to show some solidarity. I don't think they were at all concerned about the specific Canadian dollar-euro exchange rate, that's not really a huge issue for the Canadian economy," said Porter. 

 "In a way it shows how strong the Canadian currency is versus units other than the U.S. dollar," he added. 

 The Canadian dollar opened at C$1.4900 (67.11 U.S. cents) on Friday against C$1.4865 (67.27 U.S. cents) at the previous session's close. Traders said early morning trading activity was "very busy," taking the Canadian dollar to 1.3194 against the euro, on news of the intervention.

title: UPDATE 1-Euro to feature in G7 communique- Canada 's Martin.
text:
PRAGUE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention to support the euro reflected concern about the currency and Canada joined in because it benefits from stable markets, Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Friday. 

 Martin, in Prague to attend Saturday's meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised countries and the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, told reporters that both oil and the euro would feature in the G7 discussions after Friday's shock central bank intervention. 

 "The possibility of intervention, abstractly, is something that always exists, but essentially it is not something that you discuss in advance," Martin said. 

 "Obviously there were concerns (about the euro), which is why the intervention took place, so I think you can assume that the communique will make some mention of this." 

 He added, "Canada participated in this intervention because we have a great deal to gain by stability in world markets." 

 Central banks sold dollars and other currencies for euros on Friday ahead of the G7 meeting after mounting concern from Europeans about the impact of their currency's apparently relentless slide. The action drained euros from the market and gave the European currency support. 

 Martin said high oil prices would also be on the agenda at the G7 meeting. 

 "We would obviously like to see the prices be of a level that do not cause the kind of disruptions we have seen. At the same time we want to see prices that are sustainable over a longer period," he said. 

 Current problems were caused both by strong demand in a booming world economy and by tight supply, he added. 

 Martin said he also planned to use his time in Prague for bilateral talks with ministers from the Group of 20 developed and developing countries. 

 The group meets in Montreal next month to review progress in reforming and improving the world financial system after the crisis which struck Asia and other regions in 1997-99. 

 It is the second meeting of the new group - the first one took place in Berlin late last year.

title: Intervention  tactics gives clues to ECB, G7 methods.
text:
LONDON, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Currency dealers got the first taste on Friday of the European Central Bank's methods of intervening on the foreign exchanges and now know what might come their way in the weeks ahead. 

 The ECB, which joined forces with other Group of Seven industrialised nations to buy euros, dealt directly with a range of banks at a time when the single currency was already rising. 

 It did so in a public operation which was immediately flagged by an official statement. This was the first time since 1995 that the U.S, Japan and Europe had intervened jointly. 

 Central banks started buying the euro shortly after 1100 GMT, when the single currency was already three cents above record lows it had set against the dollar on Wednesday and rising. 

Intervention is typically more successful if the market is already moving in the right direction and when it has the element of surprise on its side. 

 Dealers said this was the case on Friday as the market was already covering short euro positions amid fears of euro-supportive action after the weekend meeting of the G7 finance ministers. 

 In the event, they were overtaken by the central banks' shock attack before the meeting. 

 "Some large sell orders in dollar/Swiss triggered gains in the euro, and then the ECB came in," said a dealer from a UK bank in London. 

 The euro was trading under $0.8740 when dealers began to report that central banks were piling into the market. 

 European dealers said central banks had dealt from around $0.8740 to around $0.8850 in the first wave of intervention, which was followed by at least one or two more. 

 Dealers said the relevant countries intervened in their own foreign exchange cross rates - the United States in euro/dollar, the Japanese in euro/yen, the Canadians in euro/Canadian dollar and the British in euro/sterling. 

 The first round of intervention saw the euro surge to two-and-a-half week highs above $0.90. A high of $0.9040 was seen on electronic broking systems, dealers said. 

 "Whether or not you deal with central banks, you can tell when there is intervention because the two-way market dries up. EBS becomes one-sided and all the other prices have gone," said a trader from a European bank in Paris. 

 SEVERAL CENTRAL BANKS INVOLVED 

 In addition to the ECB, the Fed and the BOJ, confirmation of coordinated action came from the Bundesbank, the Bank of France, the British Treasury and the Bank of Canada. 

 The Swiss National Bank said it did not intervene, putting the responsibility for the action firmly in G7's court - the G7 powers are the United States, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Britain and Canada. 

 "There were so many central banks involved - the ECB, the Fed, the BOJ, the Bundesbank, the Bank of France - but who knows who else?" said Paul Mackel, currency analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Frankfurt. 

 "There might be other ones just sitting on the sidelines, maybe some of the smaller European central banks." 

 European bank dealers said the Bank of Italy also intervened. They said the central bank was spotted buying the single currency for yen but added it was not clear whether these purchases were on its own behalf or for Japan. 

 Euro/yen jumped as far as 96.60 yen , according to Reuters data. 

 But investors used higher euro levels as an excuse to sell, and dealers said the central banks came back into the market shortly after 1200 GMT when euro/dollar was back around $0.8840. 

 Dealers said the size of the intervention on Friday was hard to gauge, though one said it was "medium to large-sized", compared with past interventions. 

 Another suggested the intervention volumes on Friday could have amounted to at least $3.0 billion, but declined to be more specific about which central banks had spent the most money. 

 At last count, the net foreign currency reserves of the European system of central banks was 260.9 billion euros, giving them ample scope to prop up the single currency. 

 The size of Japan's euro purchases were not immediately clear but could amount to a sizeable chunk of the total if its past forays into the foreign exchanges are any guide. 

 The Finance Ministry has said in recent months that Japan sold 1.385 trillion yen ($12.88 billion) yen for dollars in currency intervention in one day alone, on April 3, 2000 when it was combatting yen strength. 

 The Bank of Japan acts as the Finance Ministry's agent in the foreign exchanges. 

 The euro fell to $0.88 by 1612 GMT, and traders said G7 powers would need to intervene again to stop the single currency's rot setting in once more. 

 "Welcome to intervention - it's a two-way trade," said a trader from a U.S. bank in London. 

 "A lot of exporters are taking their cue to sell the euro from here, but it is going to go higher again - they will have to intervene again."

title: UPDATE 1-Duisenberg sees weak euro an inflation risk.
text:
CALGARY, Sept 8 (Reuters) - European Central Bank President Wim Duisenberg on Friday expressed concern for the first time in months about the euro's sharp decline, saying it could spur inflation and undermine investor confidence in the common currency. 

 "A very prolonged position of the euro clearly below what represents its fundamental equilibrium - a prolonged position below that would have an impact on future domestic European inflation. That would be a matter of concern," Duisenberg said during a question session with business leaders. 

 It was imperative to maintain confidence in the still sliding euro, he added. The European common currency has plunged more than 25 percent since its launch in January 1999. 

 Duisenberg spoke as the euro hovered near life lows against the dollar and as European finance ministers pleaded that a strong euro is in the interest of the entire region. 

 The euro plunged some four cents this week, hitting fresh life lows several times even as euro zone finance ministers, meeting in France, said growth remained very robust in the area. 

 The ministers also said the ECB remained committed to maintaining price stability, fearing a soft euro could push up domestic prices for goods like oil, which is denominated in dollars and is already soaring. 

 Speaking thousands of miles across the Atlantic, Europe's top central banker said the ECB's monetary policy goal is to keep European inflation in check rather than to target a specific exchange rate for the single currency. 

 In his Calgary remarks, however, Duisenberg failed to address market speculation about how the ECB may act to stem the euro's persistent slide, such as central bank intervention to prop it up. 

 Members of Canada's business and political elite attending the speech said they were still in the dark about the ECB's next step. 

 "I don't take what Duisenberg said as a signal that they may or may not take action," said Tony Comper, chief executive officer of Bank of Montreal, Canada's fifth largest bank. "Like everything else, things have to unfold and markets will react as they think appropriate." 

Currency markets have been inundated with talk about the euro this week, especially after Germany's Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder said earlier this week that he was unconcerned by its fall. Though he later took back the statement, the damage had already been done, dealers said. 

 "Our objective is to maintain stable prices in the euro area and not a specific level of the euro's exchange rate," said Duisenberg, speaking on the international role of the euro to the Spruce Meadows Round-table, an annual gathering of global corporate leaders in Canada. 

 In his speech, Duisenberg said international investors would have to consider the euro to be a stable currency to hold assets in the euro zone. 

 "Only if investors outside the euro area are confident that their purchasing power will be preserved over time, will they engage in euro-denominated financial activities," he said. 

 His comments came as the euro hovered around $0.8654 - a little above its record lows against the dollar.

 At the same time, Duisenberg said it was critical to maintain confidence in the still sliding euro. The European common currency has plunged more than 25 percent since its launch in January 1999. 

 For months European leaders have said the euro's decline was more related to the U.S. economy's ongoing strong performance rather than Europe's weaker growth potential. 

 But now that European companies are pressing ahead with restructuring - and reaping stronger growth because of it - they have begun to protest that fundamentals are out of line.

 Members of Canada's business and political elite attending the speech said they were still in the dark about the ECB's next step. 

 "I don't take what Duisenberg said as a signal they may or may not take action," said Tony Comper, chief executive officer of Bank of Montreal, Canada's fifth largest bank. "Like everything else, things have to unfold and markets will react as they think appropriate." 

Currency markets have been inundated with talk about the euro this week, especially after Germany's Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder said earlier in the week he was unconcerned by its fall. Though he later took back the statement, the damage had already been done, dealers said. 

 In his speech, Duisenberg said international investors would have to believe the euro was a stable currency before they agreed to use it to hold assets in the euro zone.

title: Canadian banks confident they're ready for Y2K.
text:
OTTAWA, Nov 26 (Reuters) - The woman overseeing Y2K preparations for Canada's bankers already knows what she is going to say when the phone rings at midnight on December 31: "All is well, happy new year from Canada's banks." 

 Karen Michelle, director of Y2K at the Canadian Bankers Association, said the country's 53 banks are confident it will be business as usual when the clock ticks into the year 2000, along with thousands of bank computer chips. 

 "In Canada, the banks have been working on Y2K since 1995...they are considered to be world leaders in terms of preparation for the year 2000," Michelle said. "All of (our) systems have been tested, have been rolled over into a year 2000 environment, and they are ready for the new year." 

 The Y2K problem, or "millennium bug," refers to potential shutdowns or disruptions in computers programmed to read only the last two digits in a year. That could make them unable to tell whether the date advances to 2000 or recedes to 1900 at midnight on December 31, 1999. 

 Michelle said Canada's banking industry has cooperated to ensure that connected systems within the financial sector, those that handle direct deposits, credit card transactions and check processing, for instance, all work together. 

 In August, tests of widely used, industry-wide systems such as Interac went off without a hitch. Interac is responsible for the network that links 24,788 automated banking machines and more than 425,000 point-of-sale debit card terminals across Canada. 

 Visa and Mastercard, the credit cards issued by Canadian banks, have also passed the Y2K readiness test. 

 The banks will have an extra buffer, a long weekend, to start the new year with. Financial markets will be closed in Canada on Monday, January 3 for the New Year's statutory holiday. That will give banks more breathing room to reset any disabled systems. 

 The risk, it now seems, lies with their customers. If Canadians fear their banks are not a safe place to stash their cash over the new year, a surge of withdrawals could turn into a full-blown financial crisis if demands cannot be met. 

 The country's central bank, the Bank of Canada, has prepared for such a run on money. It is the lender of last resort to the commercial banks - and the government itself. It also prints the money and guards the nation's gold reserves. 

 While assuring Canadians that it will not be disrupted by Y2K, the central bank has quadrupled its cash reserves, printing new bank notes as usual and stockpiling old ones to ensure there is enough money to go around at year-end. Across the country, distribution centres will hold larger-than-usual stockpiles of notes, and armoured car companies will be on standby for deliveries. 

 The central bank said it routinely keeps about C$6 billion of bank notes on hand to deal with public demand in peak periods - the Christmas shopping season, for instance - and in case of extraordinary circumstances. Those reserves will be boosted to C$23 billion by year-end. 

 "Because we are expecting business as usual in the financial sector, the substantial increase in bank note supplies that we are planning should be more than enough for any increase in demand that might arise," the bank said in a release on the Y2K concern. 

 The central bank has also prepared a command centre close to its Ottawa headquarters in case disruptions to electricity or phone lines or other infrastructure hampers normal operations. An emergency generator has been installed to power the centre if regular electricity gives out. The bank already uses duplicate phone lines, from different providers, and has emergency power sources, to guard against disruptions. 

 Among the central bank's most important operations are supplying currency, settling financial transactions, and acting as a fiscal agent for the government. 

 The command centre, constructed in the Ottawa region on property already owned by the bank, will replicate systems already in place at bank headquarters to transfer large payments or intervene in financial markets worldwide. 

 The Bank of Canada will be overstaffed around the clock over the New Year's weekend, and staff have been trained in manual methods of doing their jobs - like using a pencil and paper - if the need arises.

    TORONTO, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar	



jumped to a two-month high on Friday on signs of tame U.S.



inflation and rising energy and commodities prices.



    The currency maintained most of its morning gains, drifting



around C$1.4750 at the end of the day, a key technical level



cracked in early trade.


Canada was also posting gains in cross trading as currency

intervention by Tokyo slowed the yen's upward march and the



euro continued to hit new lows.



    Following Thursday's sharp gains, market players rushed to



buy more Canadian dollars because they were relieved by



indications of benign U.S. inflation seen in wholesale price



data released on Friday and the employment report a week ago.



The data more than offset the negative impact of weak



Canadian employment numbers released early on Friday, which had



dented the currency briefly.



Now all eyes are on U.S. retail inflation data due out next



Wednesday, which should provide a good clue to whether U.S.


central bank policymakers will be inclined to raise interest



rates at their next meeting on October 5.



The overall U.S. August producer price index came in



stronger than forecast, but excluding volatile food and energy



prices, the index actually fell, calming inflation jitters.



"It's an interesting ironic mix that you see strong U.S.



economic news creates bearish asset markets and a weaker



Canadian currency, whereas weaker U.S. economic news creates



bullish asset markets and a stronger Canadian currency," said



Jack Spitz, regional manager of treasury financial markets at



National Bank.



    "But that's not necessarily a long-term view because



fundamentals will always come back," he said.



    Rising prices in energy and commodities are a cause for



concern among fixed-income investors, but Canadian dollar



buyers are paying more attention to the benefit of higher



commodities prices, which boost the value of Canada's exports



and ensure job creation down the road.



    The closely watched Commodity Research Bureau (CRB) index



has edged up above 202, at a 10-month high.



    Canada's unemployment rate rose to 7.8 percent in August



from 7.7 percent in July, the second consecutive monthly rise



after unemployment hit a nine-year-low of 7.6 percent in June.



There were 6,500 fewer jobs in Canada in August against the



average forecast for an increase of 26,000.



Economists expect the employment report, which reflects



economic conditions about six months ago, to have ups and down



in the coming months.



The first trigger for boosting Canada this week was news



from Japan. The Canadian currency gained sharply on Thursday on



brighter prospects for the Japanese economy seen in



stronger-than-expected growth data for the April-June quarter,



which promise to generate more demand for commodities exported



by Canada.



Canada's dollar has blown away the summer blues. In much of



July and August investors favoured U.S. dollar assets for higher



interest rates. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised short-term



rates twice between late June and late August, while the Bank



of Canada has maintained its easy money policy after lowering



rates twice this year, with the last cut in early May.



Inflation is no threat to the bank's policy. Canada's



August consumer price index, due out next Friday, is forecast



to have risen 1.7 percent at the core rate, the same as in



July, staying in the lower half of the official target band.



Other data should show healthy domestic economic activity



and will be mildly supportive for the Canadian dollar. New



motor vehicle sales, manufacturing shipments, wholesale trade,



all for July, are forecast to show stronger gains than in the



previous month.

 from 72.99 yen at the previous close here, and was



firmer against the euro	   at C$1.5338 after C$1.5559.

   to A$1.0405 from A$1.0351.



    The U.S. dollar popped up to around 109 yen after the Bank



of Japan intervened in the market to stem the yen's steep rise,



which could undermine exporters' profits and overall economic



growth.

title: Canada Morning: C$ Down As Rate Outlook Clouds Prospects
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar is lower amid relatively thin dealings early Friday, as the currency continues to be pressured by expectations that with U.S. interest rates poised to move higher, the Bank of Canada will hold domestic rates steady, widening the interest rate premium for U.S. dollar-denominated assets. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.4650 at 9:42 a.m. EDT (1342 GMT), from C$1.4656 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and C$1.4619 late Thursday. 

 Traders said that with financial markets having taken U.S. Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks on Thursday as confirmation of an imminent modest hike in U.S. interest rates, Friday's soft Canadian inflation data has also confirmed that there is no rationale for higher Canadian rates at present. 

 "The Canada has essentially been under pressure since Mr. Greenspan's comments yesterday," said John Nicholson, European manager of foreign exchange at the Bank of Nova Scotia in London. "The rather benign Canadian inflation numbers bring into the spotlight whether the Bank of Canada will match the Fed rate hike at the end of this month, and with inflation as low as it is, the answer is probably not." 

 Statistics Canada said early Friday that the consumer price index for all items rose 0.3% in May from April, while core CPI (excluding food and energy) rose 1.4% from the same month in 1998. 

 Traders in Canada said there was domestic interest to buy limited amounts of Canadian dollars as confirmation of the European Central Bank's buying of euros against yen made the rounds, but the move had little muscle behind it and the U.S. dollar soon returned to trade around C$1.4660. 

 "There were a few Canadians buying Canada on the intervention, which allowed the Canadian dollar to blip to about C$1.4630," said one currency trader at a large Canadian bank in Montreal. "But they didn't succeed in pushing it past there, and it came right back." 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to continue grinding higher the rest of Friday, with a decisive break of the C$1.4660 area seen favoring a move past the C$1.4700 figure.
