title: Bank of  Canada  to announce  forex intervention .
text:
TORONTO, May 12 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada will start making brief announcements when it intervenes in the foreign exchange market to both maximize the impact of such action and enhance disclosure, bank officials said on Wednesday. 

 The new procedure was authorised this week, they told Reuters. 

 Initially, the bank will notify the currency market of only the first round of intervention of the day, by sending a brief message electronically to news agencies. 

 On the Reuters Terminal, for instance, the message "THE BANK OF CANADA INTERVENES IN FOREIGN EXCHANGE MARKET" will appear on page BOFC, where the bank also announces changes in the bank rate, its short-term lending rate. No details - the level of intervention or the amount bought or sold - will be disclosed, the officials said. 

 The next step could be to notify the general public by posting information on the central bank's website at www.bank-banque-canada.ca("http://www.bank-banque-canada.ca/"). However, the bank is still "looking at" this, one official said. 

 There has been confusion about how the bank would communicate with the market on currency intervention since Deputy Governor Charles Freedman briefly announced plans for the move in a speech in Vancouver on March 25. 

 "In order to enhance the signal effect and to avoid any confusion with normal government business in foreign exchange, we plan to announce our intervention when it occurs," Freedman had said. 

 Another bank official told Reuters at the time that the disclosure would be limited to market players. 

 Last September the Bank of Canada told currency traders that it would scrap its customary method of automatically stepping into the currency market to buy or sell dollars when the market moved a certain extent either way. 

 The latest intervention by the Bank of Canada was detected last August, when it bought Canadian dollars aggressively in a largely unsuccessful effort to stop a freefall of the Canadian currency triggered by fears of a global market meltdown. The bank was then forced to jack up its short-term lending rate by a full percentage point to lure back investors. 

 The bank would intervene in the market when investor confidence was eroded, "a signal to markets that the bank was concerned about the developments and was acting to stabilise the situation, and that if the intervention was unsuccessful it would very likely to be followed up with interest rate action by the bank," Freedman had said in the Vancouver speech.

title: Canada  to let traders know of  currency intervention .
text:
TORONTO, March 25 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada plans to let currency traders know when it has intervened in foreign exchange markets to maximize the impact of the action, a senior central bank official said on Thursday. 

 "In order to enhance the signal effect and to avoid any confusion with normal government business in foreign exchange, we plan to announce our intervention when it occurs," Deputy Governor Charles Freedman said in a speech to a business group in Vancouver. 

 Freedman said the central bank would continue to intervene through currency brokers in a bid to "maintain the effectiveness of the signal." 

 The disclosure is limited to market players, a bank official told Reuters. 

 "We are not going to talk about the size (of intervention). If I get a call from one of the market participants, I will be allowed to confirm," he said. "We are not going to be pro-active, we are not going to initiate anything." 

 On September 30, the Bank of Canada told currency traders that it would scrap its customary method of automatically stepping into the currency market to buy or sell dollars when the market moved a certain extent either way. 

 The bank would intervene in the market when investor confidence was eroded, "a signal to markets that the bank was concerned about the developments and was acting to stabilise the situation, and that if the intervention was unsuccessful it would very likely to be followed up with interest rate action by the bank," Freedman said.

title: Bank of  Canada  to announce  forex intervention .
text:
VANCOUVER, March 25 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada will saywhen it has intervened in foreign exchange markets in future in order to maximize the impact of such action, a senior central bank official said on Thursday. 

 "In order to enhance the signal effect and to avoid any confusion with normal government business in foreign exchange, we plan to announce our intervention when it occurs," Deputy Governor Charles Freedman said in a speech to a business group made available to the news media. 

 He was speaking on "policy-making under uncertainty" at an annual general meeting of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association in Vancouver. 

 Freedman did not elaborate further in the speech, and no other Bank of Canada officials were immediately available for comment. 

 Freedman said the central bank would continue to intervene through currency brokers in a bid to "maintain the effectiveness of the signal." 

 Last year the Bank of Canada announced that it would scrap its customary method of automatically stepping into the currency market to buy or sell dollars when the market moved a certain extent either way. 

 The bank would intervene in the market when investor confidence was eroded, "a signal to markets that the bank was concerned about the developments and was acting to stabilise the situation, and that if the intervention was unsuccessful it would very likely to be followed up with interest rate action by the bank," Freedman said. 

 The Bank of Canada staged aggressive currency intervention last August in a largely unsuccessful effort to stop a freefall of the Canadian dollar triggered by fears of a global market meltdown. The bank was then forced to jack up its short-term lending rate by a full percentage point to lure back investors. 

 Freedman's comments were in line with a speech delivered by Governor Gordon Thiessen on Monday. Freedman said the underlying momentum of the Canadian economy is healthy and intense retail competition and excess supply in product markets have kept overall inflation in Canada "somewhat below expectations." 

 The easing of financial market crises "has made it possible to refocus attention on the medium-term policy objective of keeping the trend of inflation inside the target range" of 1-3 percent," he said. 

 On monetary policy changes, Freedman stuck to what the bank does about short-term rates in general terms - tightens credit when inflationary pressures mount and brings about easier money conditions when the inflation rate comes under downward pressures. 

 He repeated that the bank's policy is to use its monetary conditions index (MCI), which is based on movements in the Canadian currency and short-term rates, only as a "guide" to policy, and not as a short-term target.

title: Bank Of  Canada  To Announce All Future  Forex Interventions
text:
VANCOUVER (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada intends to officially announce future foreign-exchange interventions, a senior official of the central bank said Thursday. 

 Charles Freedman, deputy governor for Monetary Policy & Financial Analysis, told the International Swaps & Derivatives Association's annual conference in Vancouver that the bank will announce each intervention "when it occurs" in order to "enhance the signal effect" of monetary interventions. 

 Last September, the Bank of Canada dropped its policy of symmetrical interventions - automatically intervening whenever the Canadian dollar rose or fell a predetermined amount in a single day. These were highly predictable for foreign exchange markets, as they essentially guaranteed the Bank of Canada would step into the market once the Canadian dollar moved a fixed amount. The Bank also had a policy of asymmetrical intervention, which Freedman described as "intervening before the automatic limits were breached and/or in amounts that were larger than customary." 

 Freedman said the Bank of Canada "will continue to intervene in a discretionary manner when it is deemed appropriate." He said such an intervention "would be a signal to markets that the bank was concerned...and was acting to stabilize the situation. And if the intervention was unsuccessful it would very likely be followed up with interest rate action by the bank." 

 Freedman added that "in order to maintain the effectiveness of the signal, we intend to continue to intervene through the brokers."

title: Canada's top central banker says  currency  is undervalued.
text:
OTTAWA, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen gave a short-term boost to the Canadian dollar on Monday, departing from the cautious words of a policy report to scold investors for undervaluing the country's currency. 

 "I'm certainly not happy with the relative weakness of the currency. I think it's undervalued, and I think it should be stronger. But over short periods of time, markets do move around," Thiessen told a press conference after the release of the bank's semi-annual monetary policy report. 

 Canada's dollar strengthened to about 64.7 U.S. cents on the comments before sliding back to about 64.5 in late trade. 

 The report itself, released more than an hour before Thiessen spoke to the media, received a lukewarm response from financial markets. 

 In the carefully worded report, the Bank cut its projections for economic growth in Canada to "just below" three percent in 1998 and between 2.25 percent and 3.25 percent in 1999, citing the effects of the global financial storm. 

 Canada's central bank in May had forecast annualized growth of about 3.5 percent through the middle of 1999. 

 Thiessen said the central bank will pay "particular attention" to short-term confidence in Canada's markets, intervening to buy or sell Canadian dollars or adjusting interest rates as needed to preserve confidence. 

 "We have to use the tools that we've got if we find ourselves confronted again with an undermining of confidence in markets," Thiessen said, referring the decline of Canada's dollar to record lows in August. 

 The bank spent about US$5 billion of its foreign reserves in August to try and shore up the weak dollar. This had little lasting effect and the bank was then forced to raise interest rates a full percentage point to stop the currency's slide. 

 Thiessen said investors had exaggerated the effects of low commodity prices on Canada's economy, and oversold the dollar. 

 The central banker stressed that market flows are particularly thin because of the current global financial uncertainty, so fluctuations appear exaggerated. 

 "It doesn't take very much to move (currencies) in one direction or another. So I don't think you want to attach a huge amount of significance to short-term movements in currencies," Thiessen told reporters. 

 In its report, the bank noted that the depreciation of the dollar against the U.S. currency improves Canadian competitiveness in foreign markets and will likely boost export volumes and domestic demand, while decreasing the growth of imports. 

 The bank also expects growth of business investment and consumer demand to ease through to the end of next year. 

 Thiessen declined to offer specific projections on when Canada might achieve full production capacity. The bank noted that the margin of slack in Canada's economy has remained essentially unchanged since the end of 1997. 

 The bank had said in its May report that Canada should reach full capacity, closing its so-called output gap, during 1999. 

 Thiessen bristled at the suggestion that by immediately matching the last two interest rate cuts by the U.S. Federal Reserve, the Canadian central bank had made it easy for market players to bet against Canada's dollar. 

 "That presumes that we will always be predictable in the future, and I don't think you should presume that," he said. 

 The focus of the financial markets remains on U.S. monetary policy, with many expecting the U.S. Federal Reserve to cut interest rates on Tuesday by 0.25 of a percentage point to support the economy. 

 The Bank of Canada is widely expected to follow quickly any move to lower rates unless the Canadian dollar is faltering.

title: =Canada $2.5B Global Bond Caps Campaign To Boost  FX  Reserves
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The $2.5 billion global bond offering launched by Canada into international credit markets Tuesday was the keynote issue of an aggressive campaign to replenish an international reserve account drained by currency intervention throughout the summer, analysts and government sources said. 

 The 10-year issue, which carried a coupon of 5.25% and offered a spread of 67 basis points over U.S. Treasurys, was Canada's largest-ever public offering of foreign currency-denominated bonds, Canadian Ministryof Finance officials told Dow Jones Tuesday. 

 The issue is seen as the culmination of a recent pattern of aggressive Canadian government issuance that has also included a four-billion French franc, a 4.45% 10-year issue, and a 200 million pound sterling re-opening of Canada's 6.25% medium-term note. Canada also mounted a four billion deutsche mark-denominated 10-year issue in late June. 

 All proceeds from these issues have been applied to boosting the government's foreign exchange reserves, in accordance with long-standing government practice with regard to foreign currency-denominated issues. 

 Canada's official international reserves were seriously depleted by repeated Bank of Canada currency market intervention in support of the Canadian dollar through the summer. Intervention cost the government $5.8 billion in the month of August alone, bringing reserves down to $17.9 billion by the end of August. 

 At the time, the finance ministry indicated it would seek to top boost reserves "to reflect increased flows and volatility in foreign exchange markets," and most analysts concede that Tuesday's $2.5 billion global did the trick quite nicely, although the issue's settlement date of November 5 means that proceeds from the deal will not appear in October's reserve figures. 

 According to estimates from Standard and Poor's MMS in Toronto, the recent slate of foreign currency issuance should help boost Canada's international reserves to a new record amount of about $23 billion by November.

title: Bank of  Canada  changed  intervention  policy-dealers.
text:
LONDON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada has abandoned its policy of intervening in the Canadian dollar when it exceeds a certain range against the U.S. dollar, dealers in London said. 

 In a meeting last week, the central bank decided to abandon its policy of buying or selling Canadian dollars on moves of more than half of one percent from the close of trading in Canada to the following day's open, dealers said. 

 "The Bank of Canada has changed their policy," one dealer at a major Canadian bank in London. "It was half of one percent, but they have said they are no longer using that policy." 

 Massive spending by Canada's central bank to defend the Canadian dollar drained nearly $5 billion from the country's foreign reserves in August, leaving it looking to borrow to replenish its stores. 

 Canada's Finance Department said a record $5.82 billion was spent last month on government operations, mostly market intervention spending. 

 The Bank of Canada last intervened to buy Canadian dollars on September 17. 

Canada's dollar was under pressure on Wednesday after the Bank of Canada matched a 25 basis points cut in U.S. interest rates on Tuesday.

title: =Bank Of Canada -2: Analysts See Earlier Policy As Failure
text:
The formal change in intervention policy comes after the central bank's decision to intervene more frequently and aggressively than normal policy dictated when the Canadian dollar came under particularly intense attack in August. 

 While the central bank had previously deviated from the policy during times of acute pressure on the currency, it did so with particular emphasis during the August assault on the Canadian currency. At the same time, the Bank of Canada also sometimes intervened in accordance with its normal policy. 

 Some Canadian currency market watchers said the central bank's move was inevitable after what they described as an ultimately failed effort to contain currency market volatility through intervention. 

 "The biggest (reason for the change) is because the methodology they were working with before really didn't have a chance of working," said Mark Chandler, an economist with Goldman Sachs in Toronto. 

 Chandler characterized the policy change as a retreat from an ambitious but flawed experiment. 

 "I think it was bit of an experiment. It was an ambitious task they set themselves to see if they could control intraday volatility in such a fashion," he said. 

 But because of the predictability of the bank's intervention, it became a "near-term speed bump" that was well-recognized and wasn't effective, Chandler said. 

 Bill Mooney, chief foreign exchange dealer with Societe Generale, agreed that the predictability of the bank's old approach to intervention ended up undermining its effectiveness. 

 "It kind of defeats the whole purpose of trying to defend something when you take away the element of surprise," Mooney said. 

 Pressure on the central bank's foreign exchange reserves may also have contributed to its decision to opt for less structured approach to intervention, Mooney suggested. 

 The central bank spent a record US$5.82 billion defending the embattled Canadian dollar in August alone, taking its reserves to US$17.97 billion.

title: =Bank of  Canada  Opts For "Discretionary"  Intervention  Style
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada has abandoned its policy of regular, predictable intervention in currency markets in defense of the Canadian dollar in favor of a more discretionary approach, bank officials confirmed Wednesday. 

 The decision by the Canadian central bank and the federal department of finance marks the formal abandonment of the bank's policy of intervening in currency markets whenever the U.S. dollar moved 70 ticks against the Canadian dollar in either direction from the previous day's official close. 

 The policy, first adopted by the bank in April 1995, was intended to smooth out volatility in Canadian dollar trading. 

 An official statement on the change said it is intended to increase the effectiveness and "signaling impact" of intervention. 

 "The Bank and the department of finance have decided to make further changes to the way intervention is conducted in the market for the Canadian dollar," the statement said. 

 "From now on, the bank will intervene in a more discretionary manner, as it did in August, in order to increase the signaling impact and effectiveness of intervention. The purpose of intervention remains promotion of orderly markets," the statement said. 

 The Bank of Canada referred further inquiries on the change to a finance department who was not available for comment late Wednesday morning. 

 True to its word, the central bank stood on the sidelines Wednesday morning as the Canadian dollar tumbled through what would have been the central bank's normal intervention trigger of C$1.5175. 

 The U.S. dollar, which closed at C$1.5105 Tuesday, climbed as high as C$1.5310 before relinquishing some of its gains. It was at C$1.5259 at 12:09 p.m. EDT (1609 GMT).

title: Canada dollar hurt by Chretien interest rate gaffe.
text:
TORONTO, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A stumbling foray into monetary policy by Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien set the stage for yet another dismal day for the troubled Canadian dollar on Thursday. 

 The Canadian dollar plunged three quarters of a cent to 65.33 U.S. cents in a second consecutive day of heavy losses as investors continued to react to Chretien's call for lower U.S. and Canadian interest rates. 

 The sharp decline prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene in currency markets by buying Canadian dollars at levels from 65.74 to 65.33 U.S. cents. 

 Chretien, a former finance minister, made his remarks on Wednesday amid signs that U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was not contemplating an imminent interest rate cut. 

 The Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa yesterday that he hoped the U.S. would cut its interest rates and that this would "give room" to the Bank of Canada to do the same. 

 "Mr. Chretien's comments did raise the prospect that if the Fed were to ever lower rates, maybe the Bank of Canada not only would match but potentially could leapfrog. That is bothering the market," said Michael Gregory, senior economist at Lehman Brothers Inc. in New York. 

 Control over interest rates in Canada, as in many other countries, falls under the jurisdiction of an independent central bank rather than the government. It is the Bank of Canada's Governor Gordon Thiessen, not Chretien, who determines the direction of Canadian interest rates. 

 Aware that the prime minister had treaded in dangerous territory, Finance Minister Paul Martin told a gathering of the ruling Liberal Party in suburban Toronto on Thursday that he would not discuss the Canadian dollar or interest rates. 

 Others were less reluctant. 

 "I do think it is inappropriate. I don't think the prime minister of Canada should be calling on the Federal Reserve to ease interest rates. It gives all the wrong signals," said Sherry Cooper, chief economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns in Toronto. 

 Chretien's misstep, combined with Greenspan's failure to signal lower interest rates in the United States, abruptly halted a three-week rally in which the Canadian dollar had gained almost four percent in value against the U.S. dollar. 

 Chretien spoke to reporters shortly after a poker-faced Greenspan had failed to mention interest rates in testimony before U.S. lawmakers, kicking support out from under the Canadian dollar. 

 The troubled currency has benefited handsomely in recent weeks from growing market speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve might soon cut interest rates to cope with the threat of global financial turmoil. Lower U.S. rates would tend boost the Canadian dollar because higher-yielding Canadian instruments would become more attractive to investors. 

 Analysts said Greenspan's refusal to signal an impending rate cut had heightened anxiety over the fate of the global financial system and deflated some of the recent optimism that supported commodity-dependent currencies like the Canadian dollar. 

 "We are seeing a lingering impact of Greenspan's comments. There was a feeling out there that lower rates by the Fed were needed to turn the global economy around," Gregory said. 

 Questions about the direction and management of Canada's monetary policy were also swirling in markets. 

 Harsh criticism was leveled at Thiessen on August 27 after the central bank raised its key interest rate by a full percentage point to 6.0 percent in a bid to shore up the flagging Canadian dollar. 

 The Canadian dollar came under pressure earlier this year, first from the Asian crisis and then from concerns weakening commodity prices would impair Canadian economic growth. 

 The August rate hike flew in the face of Thiessen's earlier pledge to hold monetary policy steady and prompted many economists to lower growth forecasts for the Canadian economy. 

 Analysts said Thiessen would have a lot of explaining to do next week when he speaks in public for the first time since last month's rate hike.

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Down As Greenspan Disappoints

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5130 at 4:30 p.m. EDT (2030 GMT), from C$1.5058 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and from C$1.5020 late Tuesday. 

 Canadian currency and bond markets had firmed in recent sessions on expectations that Greenspan might hint that softer U.S. monetary policy might be in the offing, possibly as early as the Fed's next meeting on September 29.

 "A lot of people were short U.S. dollars and waiting for a big Canada rally to ensue (on the Greenspan testimony)," said Bill Mooney, chief foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Montreal. title: Canada reserves plunge after big  currency operation .
text:
(all figures in U.S. dollars) 

 OTTAWA, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Massive spending by Canada's central bank to defend the Canadian dollar drained nearly $5 billion from the country's foreign reserves in August, leaving it looking to borrow to replenish its stores. 

 The Finance Department said on Thursday a record $5.82 billion was spent last month on government operations, mostly market intervention spending. The government offset a bit of the spending by selling some gold and increasing its foreign currency debt, but reserve holdings still dropped $4.56 billion to $17.97 billion, their lowest level since last December. 

 The reserves, which provide a cushion in case of extreme exchange rate fluctuations and inspire confidence among international investors, had been climbing steadily at about $175 million a month since 1994. 

 Jeoff Hall, a market analyst at Thomson Global Markets in Boston, said he was alarmed by Canada's frantic dip into the fund. 

 "To me, what we had in August in terms of the currency phenomenon was not even a rainy day....Yes those were dark clouds (but) I don't know that that was worth spending one-fifth of the total reserve portfolio in one month," he said. 

 Canada's dollar tracked commodity prices precipitously lower in August, sliding to a record low just above 63 U.S. cents by August 27. The central bank fought a running battle throughout the decline, buying the currency 13 days out of 20 in a largely futile attempt to prop it up. The bank finally resorted to raising interest rates to stem the decline. 

 "(The intervention) ended up being a rather defensive move on their part, trying to lean against the wind to no avail. At the rate they were going, they'd be out of reserves by the end of the year, and that's alarming," Hall said. 

 Jeffrey Cheah, a financial market analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS, said the the central bank's continuous defence of the dollar in August had prepared economists for a dip in the reserves, but the degree of spending surprised many. 

 "It certainly was a lot larger than what most people were expecting. It obviously reflects that the Bank of Canada's intervention in August was a lot more aggressive than what most people had expected," Cheah said. 

 The Finance Department did not disclose exactly how much of August's $5.82 billion in government spending went to currency intervention, but one official said he expected most commentators who follow the reserve holdings would peg intervention "in the $5 billion range". 

 The previous record for spending on government operations was set in September 1992, during the European Rate Mechanism crisis, when Canada spent $2.9 billion and reserves dropped $4.3 billion. 

 In its release, Finance pledged to rebuild its stockpile of reserves and position itself to weather future market turmoil. 

 As a safeguard against a future run in the currency, Canada said on Wednesday it had extended its $6 billion standby line of credit with international banks. 

 Cheah said Canada should have no trouble borrowing in international markets to build the reserve account back up to about $25 billion, or just over 4 percent of GDP. 

 "That kind of paper (Canadian debt issues) should probably be very well received, just because a lot of people might want to diversify their portfolio and a Canadian Euro market borrowing would be considered a good credit risk," Cheah said. 

 But Hall said returning reserves to July's enviable $22.52 billion level will take months, if not years. And he frowned on the two most obvious options for refilling the reserves - selling gold or borrowing internationally. 

 "I'm not sure that this would be an appropriate long-term strategy to start borrowing against the future here.... And the practice of using gold sales to replenish the coffers (is) a caution flag for me," Hall said, comparing it with a debtor selling land - it brings a quick profit but a hard asset is gone for good once the sale is made. 

 Canada sold 296,000 ounces of gold in July and August, the first sales from its gold holdings since October 1996, boosting reserves by $99.4 million.

title: Intervention  Moves Reduced  Canada 's Monetary Reserves In August
text:
OTTAWA -(Dow Jones)-  Canadian monetary reserves fell $4.56 billion in August, the Canadian Finance Department said Thursday, as government intervention activity in foreign-exchange markets to defend the besieged Canadian dollar reduced reserves by nearly $6 billion. 

 As of Aug. 31, the official holdings of gold, foreign currencies and other monetary assets totaled $17.97 billion, down from $22.52 billion in July and down from $20.08 billion a year earlier. All reserve figures are reported in U.S. currency. 

 A survey of Canadian economists by Technical Data had estimated August reserves at $17.86 billion. 

 The department said official government operations reduced reserves by $5.82 billion in August. The Bank of Canada intervened in foreign-exchange markets repeatedly in August and Canada's central bank raised official interest rates in an attempt to support the embattled Canadian dollar. The currency has suffered from fundamental weakness stemming from lower short-term interest rates compared to those in the U.S., low commodity prices and global uncertainty stemming from economic and financial turmoil in Asia and Russia. 

 "It's not as if it's a shock that the government spent a lot of money defending the currency," said Doug Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns Inc. The largest decline in foreign-exchange holdings before August was the US$3.2 billion drop in September 1992, he pointed out. 

 "This is right off the radar screen in terms of dollar defense," Porter said. "It gives you a sense of just how vigorously the bank was trying to defend the (Canadian) dollar during the month, and it shows to what extent they were going to before they finally succumbed and raised rates." 

 The central bank raised its bellwether bank rate 100 basis points to 6.00% on Aug. 27 in a move designed to provide support for the currency, and maintain suitable monetary conditions for noninflationary growth. 

 "Canada retains a strong reserve position," the Finance Department said Thursday. It said it will continue its policy, as outlined in recent budgets, of increasing reserves to reflect increased flows and volatility in foreign-exchange markets. 

 The government plans to replenish reserves through a broad range of financing programs, it said. The management of reserves is supported by the recent extension of Canada's $6 billion standby line of credit with international banks, the department said. 

 Official government operations in August also included a loan to Thailand, which reduced reserves by $361 million. 

 While some analysts argue that Canada's reserves are adequate by international market standards, Hall said the recent developments in the account raise questions about the extent of the holdings. "Among industrialized nations, the amount of reserves that Canada had was on the low side, Japan being the very other extreme," he said. 

 While the reserve account had been building by about US$175 million a month for most of the last three years, that trend has been arrested in recent months, Hall said. 

 Ottawa must start to rebuild the account, TechData's Hall suggested. 

 Nesbitt's Porter agreed that efforts to increase the war chest are likely in the coming months. "They don't seem to have any specific target for the level of reserves,' Porter said." (But) it seems that something on the order of US$20 billion can be used as a benchmark, so one way or another they will likely try to rebuild those reserves over the next six to 12 months.'

title: Toronto stocks caught up in world wide slump.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 31 (Reuters) - The bear continued to devour investors on Monday as uncertainties in international markets and a slumping Canadian dollar fed the beast's appetite for destruction. 

 North American markets proved to be the main course on the bear's plate. 

 In Toronto, the key 300 Composite Index dived 235.67 points or 4.1 percent to 5530.64. Volume was a light 98.2 million shares worth C$1.79 billion. Declining stocks smothered advancers 855 to 261 with another 254 issues unchanged on the sidelines. 

 With today's gut wrenching loss, the Toronto market has plunged 2291.61 points from its April high. 

 And in New York, the bellwether Dow Jones Index Average suffered its second-biggest point loss dropping 512.61 points or 6.37 percent to 7539.07. 

 The technology-heavy Nasdaq also demonstrated the compounding problems as it posted its biggest point loss in history and fourth largest percentage decline, falling 140.53 points or 8.57 percent to 1499.155. 

 As has been the case often in this topsy-turvy market, the Toronto market began the day on a positive note climbing 49.14 points to 5815.45 where it hovered for much of the day before taking a shocking and destructive turn late in the day, when North American markets began their steady descent at breakneck speed. 

 In the last hour of trading alone, the TSE 300 lost more than two percent of its value. 

 "I haven't seen any news to explain that. It's just a mystery as to why this thing has fallen out of bed so fast on so little news. It just doesn't happen this way," said Conor Bill, director of retail trading at ScotiaMcLeod in Toronto 

 "This is bear sentiment turning. People just turned bearish. They looked at the weakness on the Dow and said 'There's no good news coming, take me out'." 

 Though there was nothing concrete on the day to force the international markets lower, the usual culprits - a slumping Canadian dollar, weakening demand for commodities, uncertainty in Asia and Russia, and concern over weaker than expected earnings from the United States - conspired to wreak havoc. 

 "This has been a pretty serious down day, it's being driven by its own momentum, there's no bid out there. A market will fall on its own weight. It takes serious buying to make the market go up," said Doug Davis, president of Davis-Rea Ltd. Investment Counsel. 

 Overall in Toronto, all of the TSE 300's 14 subindexes closed lower led by a 7.1 percent dip in the conglomerates index and a 5.2 percent drop in the communications and media index. The gold and precious minerals group and oils index also suffered dramatic losses. 

 The bluest of the blue chip stocks led the markets lower. Telecommunications giant BCE Inc. , which holds the most weight on the index at 6.9 percent, dropped C$1.80 to C$50.60 in heavy volume of 3.6 million shares. Northern Telecom Ltd. , the third-highest weighted stock on the index at 4 percent dipped C$3.35 to C$75.25 and Bank of Nova Scotia  fell C$0.10 to C$25.80. 

 The Canadian dollar also closed weaker at C$1.5674 (US$0.6379) after the Bank of Canada intervened in foreign exchange markets to support the troubled currency, traders said. 

 The central bank bought Canadian dollars at levels from C$1.5675 (US$0.6379) to C$1.5730 (US$0.6357) as the currency weakened past key support levels. 

 Following the intervention, the Canadian dollar stabilised and was eventually sidelined by falling equity markets. 

 As is the trend, with the devastation in the equity markets, Canadian bonds rallied for a second day, as investors fled falling shares for the safety of bonds. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond gained C$1.25 in value to trade at C$131.75 and yield 5.732 percent. 

 The difference in yields between the Canadian and U.S. 30-year bonds was 46 basis points, unchanged from Friday but down from 52 basis points on Thursday. 

 "The currency, even though we're trading at weaker levels, has seen some buying interest over the past one or two sessions," Rob Palombi, a senior fixed-income analyst with MMS International told Reuters. 

 "(The gain in bonds ) was just safe-haven interest on the back of the slide in stocks." 

 Analysts now fear the worst for the mutual fund industry where the majority of Canadians have their money invested. With massive losses people are now reconsidering their portfolios, seeking ways to stop the losses. 

 "These days are very disturbing because this is going to cause a lot of contraction in the mutual fund sector. This is where people get worried and redeem their funds. This will start some redemption activity."

title: Canada  dollar closes weaker after bank  intervenes .
text:
TORONTO, Aug 31 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar closed weaker at C$1.5674 (US$0.6379) on Monday after the Bank of Canada intervened in foreign exchange markets to support the troubled currency, traders said. 

 The central bank bought Canadian dollars at levels from C$1.5675 (US$0.6379) to C$1.5730 (US$0.6357) as the currency weakened past key support levels. 

 Following the intervention, the Canadian dollar stabilised and was eventually sidelined by falling equity markets. 

 The Canadian dollar has suffered from turmoil in international markets, particularly in Russia, which prompted fears that a global economic downturn would spread from emerging markets to more developed Western economies. 

 But that turmoil jolted currency markets more severely on Monday. 

 The Toronto Stock Exchange's composite 300 index fell by about four percent to close at 5530.66, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 6.4 percent to close at 7539.07 

 "I think obviously the stock market (the Dow) has deflected concerns about the Canadian dollar right now," said Jeoff Hall, managing Canadian market analyst with Thomson Global Markets. 

 Equity markets were spooked by news that Russia's opposition communists would reject President Boris Yeltsin's choice of Viktor Chernomyrdin as the country's next prime minister. A senior Kremlin aide also warned of possible political revolution in Russia. 

 Western nations have called on Russian President Boris Yeltsin to implement strong reforms to cope with a financial crisis that threatens to topple Russia's economy. 

 Hall said the weaker U.S. equity markets could end up haunting the Canadian dollar if economic growth slows in the United States and Americans begin buying fewer Canadian exports. 

 Analysts said the release of economic data failed to have an impact on the Canadian dollar. 

 Statistics Canada reported Canada's real gross domestic product fell 0.1 percent in June after falling 0.3 percent in the previous month. 

 The agency also said Canada's current account deficit narrowed marginally in the second quarter to C$4.23 billion from a C$4.28 billion deficit in the previous quarter. 

 A Reuters survey of economists had forecast a 0.2 percent decline in monthly GDP and a current account deficit of C$4.79 billion. 

 "The data had little impact overall. The most important piece of it was the current account and there was little change," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst with Standard & Poor's MMS International. 

 Analysts also said growing speculation the U.S. Federal Reserve might cut interest rates was helping to keep Canadian dollar buyers in the market. 

 London markets were closed today for a bank holiday. 

 In cross trading, the Canadian dollar fell to 1.1123 German marks from Friday's close of 1.1251 marks and dropped to 88.91 yen from 90.73 yen at the previous close.

title: Canada Raises Rates Sharply In Vain Effort To Defend Its  Currency
text:
TORONTO -(Dow Jones)- The widening global financial crisis hit North America Thursday, as Canada's central bank raised official interest rates sharply in a controversial attempt to support a currency bedeviled by plunging commodity prices and global volatility. Canadian stocks plummeted. 

 The Bank of Canada, the country's equivalent of the U.S. Federal Reserve, raised its benchmark bank rate by a full percentage point, to 6%, in an effort to alleviate the massive pressure stacked up against the Canadian dollar. Major Canadian banks followed by raising their prime lending rates. 

 However, the rate increase and subsequent intervention failed to stem the Canadian dollar's slide. In late trading, the U.S. dollar was trading at 1.5795 Canadian dollars, up from C$1.5655 late Wednesday in New York. On the Toronto Stock Exchange, the bellwether 300-stock index plunged 6% and the bond market also fell sharply. The yield spread between Canada's 30-year bond and its U.S. counterpart widened to three-quarters of a percentage point, from a half-point. 

 The U.S. dollar had recorded new all-time highs against the Canadian currency in nearly every session over the past week. The Canadian currency has suffered from fundamental weaknesses stemming from lower short-term interest rates compared to those in the U.S., low commodity prices and global uncertainties stemming from the renewed economic and financial turmoil in Asia and Russia. 

 These weaknesses were exacerbated in recent days by strong global flows of capital seeking the safety of U.S. assets in the wake of the Russian debt crisis and a consequent revival of intense speculative pressure. 

 Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said "Canada is being hit by a very nervous and uncertain international scene." He noted that primary commodity prices have been hurt by economic problems in Asia and Russia, and Canada's currrency has been affected. Some 35% of Canada's exports are commodity-based. 

 The finance minister claimed Canada is "strongly positioned to weather the storm," noting the country has eliminated its deficit and begun paying down debt. He said despite today's increase by the Bank of Canada, "interest rates remain low by the standards of the last 20 years." 

 Both the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England intervened to support the Canadian dollar Thursday. However, some observers said the Bank of Canada's rate increase reduced the credibility and effectiveness of its intervention tactics. 

 "Whatever the bank's spent on intervention today, trust me, they've spent far more in credibility," said one currency trader. "All the rate hike did was give offshore accounts better levels to sell their Canadian assets. Accounts are making a lot of money today at the expense of inadequate policy decisions." 

 Many said the overwhelming pressure against the Canadian dollar won't ease appreciably as long as world-wide commodity prices continue to fall, as in the mind of the market, the value of the currency is closely linked to the value of commodities. There was speculation that the central bank may soon have to institute another, smaller hike in rates to try and stabilize the currency. 

 The Bank of Canada had resisted raising rates despite the massive pressure on the currency in recent sessions. In a statement regarding its action, the central bank said the currency's recent slide reflected downward pressures on the prices of the commodity products Canada exports, and developing problems in Russia. 

 But the momentum in the currency's decline and upward pressure on long- and medium-term interest rates signaled a diminishing confidence in Canadian dollar investments, and that prompted the increase, the bank said. 

 "I don't think they expected it to be a resounding success as it was a very unpalatable option, but probably the only one open to them," said Mark Chandler, an economist with Goldman Sachs in Toronto. 

 Other analysts were more critical, saying the rate increase may end up inflicting more serious injuries to the Canadian economy. 

 "It's just a sad day for Canada and the 1.3 million jobless," said Sal Guatieri, an economist at the Bank of Montreal. "It's ineffective, it's not supporting our currency, and it's really undermining the outlook for our economy and investor confidence in our economy." 

 "The downside risks to our economy have hugely increased in light of today's rate hike by the Bank of Canada," Guatieri said, pointing to the fact that the Canadian yield curve inverted after the increase, meaning long-term securities had a higher yield than short-term ones. 

 Bill Mooney, chief foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Montreal, called the move an "unmitigated, unqualified disaster." 

 "They would have been better cutting instead of raising 100 points today. It's a total exercise in futility - people knew it was too little, too late, and they would have been better off not doing anything at all," Mooney said.

title: Canadian markets sink despite  central bank  rate hike.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Canada's financial markets suffered a bloodbath on Thursday after the central bank raised interest rates in a futile bid to bolster confidence in the sickly Canadian dollar. 

 Panicky investors dumped Canadian equities and fixed income instruments in step with the Bank of Canada's decision to hike its key rate by a full percentage point to 6.0 percent. 

 The Canadian sell-off was intensified by a financial meltdown in Russia and growing international fears that an economic downturn in emerging markets could spread to more developed Western economies. 

 Russia suspended all trading of the free-falling rouble as its economy teetered on the brink of collapse and opposition politicians stepped up demands that Russian President Boris Yeltsin resign. 

 Moscow's deepening crisis prompted an international stampede to hold U.S. dollars at the expense of most other currencies, especially the commodity-dependent Canadian dollar. 

 "The fear that is there is creating a huge flight to quality from all markets to the United States and from equities to bonds. Canada, unfortunately, is being caught in that," said Michael Gregory, senior economist at New York-based brokerage firm Lehman Brothers Inc. 

 Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin tried to reassure Canada's currency and stock markets, saying the country was "strongly positioned" to weather the economic storm. 

 "While these are turbulent times, we have no choice but to deal with them. We must not lose sight of the fact that Canada is strongly positioned to weather the storm," Martin told reporters at a hastily called news conference in Montreal. 

 "I have complete confidence in the governor and in the Bank of Canada and the action that they took today," Martin said, adding that the central bank must "act to maintain order and calm to the best extent possible in currency markets." 

 Canada's day of pain began in the currency market where the Canadian dollar fell to a new record low of 63.11 U.S. cents following the Bank of Canada's interest rate hike. 

 The troubled currency, known widely as the "loonie" but recently dubbed the "northern peso", eventually stabilised at 63.21 U.S. cents on the back of heavy central bank intervention to buy Canadian dollars. 

Canada's largest stock market soon followed the currency's decline. The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 stock index plummeted about six percent to 5799.46, wiping millions off stock prices across the board. 

 Analysts fretted that higher interest rates would hurt consumer confidence, draw investors out of high-yield blue chip stocks and topple Canada's slowing economy into a recession. 

 "You can't hold back a hurricane and the markets are essentially saying the same thing. The last thing this economy needs is dampening of consumer demand and consumer confidence," said Ruth Getter, chief economist with Toronto-Dominion Bank. 

 Canadian bonds also choked on the central bank's bitter medicine. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond due June 1, 2027 fell C$0.76 to C$130.20 to yield 5.867 percent, even as the U.S. 30-year bond rose 24/32 to yield 5.37 percent. 

 The fiasco on Canadian markets was an astonishing embarrassment for the Bank of Canada which had vowed to hold interest rates steady until Canada's slowing economy broke free of the shackles imposed by chaos in emerging markets. 

 The central bank last raised interest rates by 50 basis points in January in an equally unsuccessful attempt to bolster the weakening Canadian dollar. 

 In recent weeks, the central bank had opted to support the local dollar with a short-term strategy of sporadic, heavy intervention in currency markets. 

 The Bank of Canada continued that strategy on Thursday, repeatedly buying the Canadian dollar as audacious traders drove the unit ever lower. 

 The Canadian unit has lost about 11 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past six months. 

 "People sit up and take notice when a currency just falls out of bed like that," said Jeoff Hall, a Canadian market analyst at Boston-based Thomson Global Markets. 

 "Investor confidence has really been shaken by this currency debacle that's going on right now in Canada. There's some fear that rates may go up again as soon as tomorrow."

title: Toronto stocks suffer worst drop ever.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Toronto stocks on Thursday suffered their worst drop ever after the Bank of Canada hiked interest rates by one full percentage point in an apparently futile attempt to defend the falling Canadian dollar. 

 Gloom on global financial markets and ailing commodity prices added to Toronto's woes. 

 The TSE 300 Composite index went into a steep decline from the opening bell and had plummeted 502.70 points, or 8.14 percent, to 5669.60 by around 1140 EDT/1540 GMT. 

 Toronto Stock Exchange spokesman Steve Kee said the previous worst point drop was set on October 27, 1997, when the TSE 300 Composite Index closed down 434.25 points. 

 The largest decline in percentage terms was on the October 19, 1987 Black Monday crash, when the TSE 300 fell 11.13 percent. Key said no records are kept for intraday changes. 

 All 14 subindexes were at least four percent lower, with losses ranging from 4.41 percent for pipelines to 8.95 percent for financial services. 

 "We're a lot closer to crisis than I would have thought. I thought we'd have another year probably before we reached these proportions," said ScotiaMcLeod market strategist Peter Gibson. 

 Interest rate rises hurt stock prices because of the risk of damage to consumer confidence. Higher rates also draw investors out of high-yielding blue chip stocks into bonds. 

 "Rate hikes have a dramatic effect on the markets because people are willing to pay less for stocks when rates increase, for a number of reasons," said Todd Kappala, investment specialist at Priority Brokerage. 

 "The major impact is felt on bank stocks." 

 The substantial fall in the financial services index recently has created something of a vicious circle. Bank shares are the chief driver of the TSE and the banks themselves are dependent on strong stock markets for a good portion of their profits. 

 The financial services group was down 789.50 points, or 10.37 percent, at 6824.91. Kappala said he felt bank shares were getting to a level where they were "good value." 

 The central bank's rate rise, while damaging to equities, had little impact on the dollar which resumed its fall after a brief hiatus, hitting a further historic low of C$1.5845 (US$0.6311). It was trading at C$1.5783 (US$0.6336) after sustained central bank intervention. 

 "The Bank of Canada is leaning against a hurricane. They can't halt the slide in the currency at all. The rate hike was just a pure technicality, there had been such a significant tightening in policy led by the market before the Bank of Canada hiked rates," said Harvinder Kalirai, a New York-based analyst at I.D.E.A. 

 Equity analysts said if the dollar does not respond well to this rate hike, forcing the Bank of Canada to move rates still higher, the peril for Canadian equities will increase dramatically. 

 "It's very dangerous because...if you push the consumer into recession in Canada, then it's going to be very painful because you really do run the risk of deflation," said Gibson. 

 Following the rate rise, several Canadian banks raised their prime lending rates to 7.5 percent from 6.5 percent. 

 Commodity prices were sharply weaker. 

 Gold slid sharply to US$278.50 at the London afternoon fix, matching its low of January 12 which was itself the lowest level since June 29, 1979. 

 "Everybody's operating in a vacuum. Suddenly everybody wants to get out the same door," said Irwin Michael, portfolio manager at ABC Funds. 

 ($1=$1.58 Canadian)

title: Canadian dollar closes weaker after rate hike.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 27 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar closed at C$1.5816 (US$0.6322) in heavy trading on Thursday despite a move by the Bank of Canada to raise its key interest rate by a full percentage point to six percent, traders said. 

 The troubled currency fell to a record low of C$1.5845 (US$0.6311) before the central bank intervened to buy Canadian dollars in currency markets. 

 The Canada unit's sell-off was intensified by a financial meltdown in Russia and growing international fears that an economic downturn in emerging markets would spread to the more developed Western economies. 

 Russia suspended all trading of the wobbly rouble as its economy teetered on the brink of collapse and opposition politicians stepped up demands that Russian President Boris Yeltsin resign. 

 Moscow's deepening crisis prompted an international stampede to hold U.S. dollars at the expense of most currencies, especially the commodity-dependent Canadian dollar. 

 "People sit up and take notice when a currency just falls out of bed like that," said Jeoff Hall, Canadian market analyst with Boston-based Thomson Global Markets. 

 "Investor confidence has really been shaken by this currency debacle that's going right now in Canada. There's still some fear that rates may go up again as soon as tomorrow," he added. 

 The Bank of Canada said it raised interest rates to shore up the weakening Canadian dollar and re-balance monetary conditions. 

 "Today's increase in interest rates is aimed at providing support for the Canadian dollar in order to bolster confidence, while preserving monetary conditions that will help to sustain the present non-inflationary expansion of the economy," the bank said in a statement accompanying the rate hike. 

 Economists were left scratching their heads over the rate hike. 

 "I'm really sceptical of whether this move in interest rates will provide long-term upward support for our currency. If our economy does tumble a year from now, I think our currency will be much weaker than it is now," said Sal Guatieri, senior economist with Bank of Montreal. 

 In cross trading, the Canadian dollar dipped to 1.1370 German marks and fell to 89.05 yen.

title: FX  IN EUROPE - Yen capitalises on Russia sell-off.
text:
LONDON, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Deepening concern over Russia drove the mark and commodity-linked currencies lower on Thursday, to the benefit of the yen, analysts and dealers said. 

 Investors sold the mark and dollar to buy the yen, in a reversal of recent trades, in order to offset losses in Russia and other emerging markets, dealers said. 

 "Hedge funds have been selling mark/yen," said a trader from a U.S. bank. 

 Russia failed to restore confidence in its markets on Thursday, after disappointing foreign investors with its debt restructuring package released late on Tuesday. 

 The Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) suspended all rouble foreign exchange trade on Thursday and said trading would not resume on Friday. 

 "Today we haven't really seen any new information hit the market," said Stewart Newnham, international economist at First Chicago. "There's been a lot of speculation of course." 

 A Finance Ministry official said details of Russia's short-term rouble debt restructuring plan were likely to be announced on Friday. 

 But analysts said only hard political news on Russia could calm feverish markets. 

 "The political situation is still pretty volatile," said Patrick Foley, senior economic adviser at Lloyds Bank. 

 Rumours of President Yeltsin's resignation, later denied, were among factors hitting the mark on Thursday. 

 The mark was trading at 78.92/95 yen at 1504 GMT, from a one-month low of 78.67 and from 79.92/95 in late European trade on Wednesday. 

 The dollar also lost ground to the yen, falling to a one-week low of 142.20. It was trading at 142.73/83, from 144.37/42 in late European trade on Wednesday. 

 Verbal intervention also helped the yen on Thursday. 

 Japan's Vice Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara said he was watching moves in mark/yen carefully. 

 He also said it was important for Japanese investors to lock in profits in any foreign currency transaction. 

 The mark fell to six-week lows against the pound and 10-week lows against the Swiss franc, both safe havens from emerging market woes. 

 Commodity-linked currencies, meanwhile, felt the full thrust of falling commodity prices, amid fears that Russia would try to increase oil and precious metal output against a backdrop of declining global demand for commodities. 

 Central banks pulled their weight to support the Canadian and Australian dollars, which fell to record lows. 

 The Bank of England intervened on behalf of the Bank of Canada in the European morning to defend the Canadian dollar. 

 The Bank of Canada later raised interest rates by 100 basis points, and intervened directly to rescue the Canadian dollar from a record low of C$1.5845 to the dollar. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve, meanwhile, sold dollars for Australian dollars, dealers said, hauling the Australian dollar back above lows below $0.5500. 

 The New Zealand dollar also hit record lows below $0.4800. 

 Oil-dependent Norway's crown fell to record lows against the mark and against its Ecu index. 

 But the Norwegian central bank said it had not changed policy since Monday, when it said it was suspending use of interest rates to keep the crown steady against the European currency unit, and scaling back intervention "for the time being". 

 The dollar reached six-week highs of 1.8135 marks, but dipped to 1.8070/80 by 1527 GMT, from 1.8062/72 in late Europe on Thursday. 

 The dollar failed to make further gains because of its exposure to ailing markets in Latin America, analysts said. 

 "The dollar is not a safe haven from a global emerging market crisis," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Bank. 

 ((Carolyn Cohn, London newsroom +44 171 542 6320, uk.forex.news@reuters.com)).

title: Canada $ Plummets -2: Rate Hike Seen Totally Ineffective
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada's 100-basis
point raising of its benchmark bank rate Thursday has failed
to alleviate the massive pressure stacked up against the
Canadian dollar, with the battered currency now having
fallen more than 150 ticks from its Wednesday close against
the U.S. dollar.
   After reaching as high as C$1.5840 earlier, the U.S.
dollar was trading at C$1.5780 at 10:52 a.m. EDT (1452 GMT),
from C$1.5750 at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and C$1.5648 late
Wednesday.
   Traders said there has been sporadic and inconsistent
intervention in the Canadian unit's favor from Canada's
central bank throughout the morning, but these salvos have
so far had no effect in stemming the bleeding for the
Canadian dollar.
   The bank was seen selling U.S. dollars beginning at
C$1.5630, and at several other apparently random levels as
the U.S. dollar continued climbing higher.



   Several currency traders described the speed of the
Canadian dollar's fall Thursday as "frightening," saying
Bank of Canada intervention tactics have completely lost
their credibility and effectiveness with Thursday's
ill-timed rate hike.
   "Whatever the bank's spent on intervention today, trust
me, they've spent far more in credibility," said one
currency trader. "All the rate hike did was give offshore
accounts better levels to sell their Canadian assets.
Accounts are making a lot of money today at the expense of
inadequate policy decisions."
   Many said the overwhelming pressure against the Canadian
dollar will not relent appreciably as long as worldwide
commodity prices continue to fall, as in the mind of the
market, the value of the currency is closely linked to the
value of commodities.
   Some said there is also considerable speculation that
the central bank may soon have to institute another, smaller
hike in rates to try and stabilize the currency.

title: Bank Of  Canada Intervene  -2: Follows Rate Hike; C$ Steadies
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada intervened in the foreign exchange market Thursday morning, selling U.S. dollars at C$1.5630 in an effort to contain market volatility in the wake of the Bank of Canada's 100-basis point raising of its benchmark bank rate earlier, traders in Toronto said. 

 The intervention had only a momentary effect in halting the U.S. dollar's climb though, although traders said it had restored some calm to the market. The U.S. currency was trading at C$1.5650 at 9:28 a.m. EDT (1328 GMT). 

 Thursday's intervention took place only minutes after Canada's central bank relented in the face of overwhelming market pressure and finally led domestic interest rates higher to try and halt the Canadian dollar's recent freefall. 

 The 100-basis point raising of the bank rate initially sent the Canadian dollar surging, as the Canadian unit rapidly moved from around C$1.5760, its level immediately before the rate hike was announced just before 9:00 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT), to C$1.5590 minutes later. 

 However, traders said the U.S. currency quickly regained a strong bid to begin moving back up amid extremely volatile trading, prompting the intervention. 

 The U.S. dollar had recorded new all-time highs against the Canadian currency in nearly every session over the past week, forcing the Bank of Canada's hand in leading rates higher Thursday. 

 The Canadian currency has suffered from fundamental weaknesses stemming from lower short-term interest rates versus the U.S., low commodity prices and global uncertainties stemming from the renewed economic and financial turmoil in Asia and Russia. 

 These weaknesses were exacerbated in recent days by strong global flows of capital seeking the safety of U.S. assets in the wake of the Russian debt crisis, and a consequent revival of intense speculative pressure. 

 Many currency watchers had begun to voice misgivings about the long-term effectiveness of the bank's intervention tactics, saying they would likely be in vain unless backed by higher interest rates.

title: Canadian dollar drop raises specter of interest rate hike.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar snapped through a series of record lows like matchsticks on Wednesday, heightening pressure on the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates to restore confidence in the troubled currency. 

 The Canadian dollar, locally known as the "loonie", plummeted almost one full U.S. cent to finish the North American trading session at 63.87, its lowest closing level since the currency was introduced in 1858. 

 Derisively dubbed the "North American peso" by some observers, the Canadian dollar has lost about 10 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past six months. 

 The sell-off was triggered by financial turmoil in Russia, which prompted a worldwide rush to hold U.S. dollars, the preeminent safe haven currency. 

 Economists said the fast unravelling of the Canadian dollar made it now more likely the central bank would be forced to eat its words and raise interest rates to bolster the currency. 

 "This is very bad today. This is clearly a question of confidence which the bank said would be needed before they made the move toward a rate hike," said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs in Toronto. 

 Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen had previously vowed to hold interest rates steady until the slowing Canadian economy broke free of the shackles imposed by turmoil in Asian markets and weak commodity prices. 

 The central bank last raised interest rates by 50 basis points in January in a largely unsuccessful attempt to bolster the weakening currency. 

 Policy makers fear another rate hike could push the slowing Canadian economy into a recession. 

 Instead, the central bank has opted to bolster the Canadian dollar with a short-term strategy of irregular but heavy intervention in currency markets. 

 It repeatedly bought the Canadian dollar on Wednesday as determined currency traders pushed the currency to record lows. The central bank has spent an estimated $3.5 billion out of its $20 billion in foreign reserves defending the currency in August. 

 Canada's Prime Minister Jean Chretien said he supported Thiessen's strategy. 

 "When you look at the Canadian situation, we have all the fundamentals right," Chretien told reporters in Moncton, New Brunswick. "I have confidence in him (Thiessen) and confidence in my minister of finance." 

 Although analysts initially praised intervention as a good counterweight to excessive speculation in currency markets, it has failed to halt the general downward trend of the currency. 

 "We're caught in a downdraft and this is beyond the control of the Bank of Canada. The intervention is just providing liquidity and wasting money," said one currency trader at a Canadian bank. 

 The increasing likelihood of an interest rate hike has battered Canadian bonds, which usually take their direction from U.S. Treasuries. Even as the U.S. market firmed on safe haven flows, Canadian bond prices fell on Wednesday across the entire yield curve. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond lost C$2.09 in value to trade at C$129.83 and yield 5.844 percent. 

 The difference in yields between the Canadian and U.S. 30-year bonds shot up to 40 basis points as investors demanded a premium to account for an increasing currency risk. 

 Even so, some economists are advising the Bank of Canada to stick to its guns and resist calls for a rate hike. 

 "I think it is a very costly move. The Canadian economy is weakening and the last thing we need now is a rate hike," said Ruth Getter, chief economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank. 

 She said the Canadian dollar could not escape the selling pressure afflicting commodity-based currencies like the Canadian dollar. 

 "At this point, you've got to batten down the hatches and wait for the hurricane to pass by," Getter argued. 

 ($1=$1.57 Canadian).

title: Canadian dollar hits record lows, bank  intervenes .
text:

 The central bank bought Canadian dollars at levels from C$1.5560 (US$0.6426) and C$1.5595 (US$0.6412). 

 "They're coming in with the usual amount," said a foreign exchange trader with a Canadian bank. 

 The Canada unit has lost 10 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past six months and markets appear poised to continue the sell-off until the Bank of Canada raises interest rates. 

 Analysts said the likelihood of a rate hike had risen.

title: Canada policy makers scramble to halt dollar's slide.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Canada's government and central bank scrambled on Tuesday to halt a painful six-month slide in the Canadian dollar as currency traders continued to press for an interest rate hike. 

 The troubled Canadian dollar, derisively dubbed the "North American peso" by some observers, has lost about nine percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past six months in step with weakening commodity prices and swirling financial turmoil in emerging markets. 

 The currency finished the North American trading session at 64.50 US cents on Tuesday - its lowest close ever. 

 While edgy Canadians fret over the rising cost of imports and their declining standard of living, the architects of Canada's financial house have treated the falling Canadian dollar as one might a rabid cat. 

 Canada's policy makers, led by Prime Minister Jean Chretien, have refused to consider changes in fiscal or monetary policy to bolster the currency, nicknamed the "loonie." 

 Until yesterday, that is. 

 Chretien, one of the chief proponents of the do-nothing approach, suddenly reversed course on Monday with a pledge to support the Canadian dollar with a round of tax cuts in the federal budget next February. 

 It was the first time the Canadian government had linked tax cuts to the chronic weakness of the currency, which is trading at its lowest level since it was introduced in 1858. 

 But traders openly ridiculed Chretien's proposal as too distant to have any meaningful impact. 

 "The market thinks that Chretien has got his head in the sand. It's laughable. People are just raising their eyes in horror again," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of corporate foreign exchange with CIBC Wood Gundy. 

 "What are we going to do for the next six months? Go to C$1.6000 (62.50 US cents)?" Wateridge quipped. 

 That sentiment evoked a general feeling in the country that the Canadian government and central bank have mismanaged the currency crisis. 

 Chretien at first flippantly dismissed the dollar's fall as unimportant and a windfall for Canadian exporters. 

Central Bank Governor Gordon Thiessen has also been assailed for telegraphing months in advance his intentions to hold interest rates steady. 

 Chretien's vague promise of tax cuts yesterday followed weeks of heavy intervention by the Bank of Canada in currency markets. The central bank has spent an estimated $3.5 billion out of its $20 billion in foreign reserves buying Canadian dollars in August. 

 Although analysts initially praised the central bank's move as a good counterweight to a speculative attack on the currency, the intervention failed to halt the Canadian dollar's general downward slide. 

 "The intervention doesn't change the momentum, it just slows the decline in the currency a bit. It is also only effective when it is surprising and it is no longer a surprise," said Sherry Cooper, chief economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns in Toronto. 

 Cooper agreed that an across-the-board personal tax cut was needed, but said such a move should be accompanied by "minor" short-term interest rate hikes. 

 "There has to be a fundamental shift to ease fiscal policy and tighten monetary policy," said Cooper, who has argued for an immediate 50-basis-point hike. 

 The Bank of Canada last raised interest rates by 50 basis points in January to bolster the Canadian dollar, but the gains from that move were short-lived. 

 The central bank remains reluctant to tinker its monetary policy again for fear of tumbling the slowing Canadian economy into a recession. 

 Many Canadian economists concur. 

 "Higher interest rates are not warranted because of the likely impact on growth at this point - it would probably slow it further," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal. 

 "It's important to keep in mind that the depreciation of the currency is coming about because of weakening in commodity prices. That's a shock we have no control over," Ferley said. 

 ($1=$1.55 Canadian).

title: Canada dollar slides,  central bank  steady on rates.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar plummeted to yet another record low on Wednesday as the central bank ignored calls for an interest rate hike and continued its war of nerves with increasingly bold currency traders. 

 The beleaguered Canadian dollar, derisively dubbed the "North American peso" by some observers, fell below 64 U.S. cents for the first time since it was introduced in 1858. 

 The currency has lost about 10 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past six months as commodity prices slumped and financial turmoil roiled international markets. 

 Russia was the catalyst for the latest sell-off. 

 The Russian rouble slid by more than a third against the German mark after a 5-percent fall against the U.S. dollar triggered circuit breakers on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange. 

 Russia devalued its currency by 30 percent and suspended some foreign debt repayments 10 days ago in a desperate bid to inject some order into its crumbling economy. 

 Moscow's misery has prompted a worldwide rush by investors to park their cash in the U.S. dollar, the world's pre-eminent safe-haven currency. 

 "The Russian situation seems to be getting out of hand, so there is major nervousness and everybody is fleeing to the U.S. dollar," said Ruth Getter, chief economist with Toronto-Dominion Bank. 

 Getter said the Canadian dollar could not escape the herd mentality now prevalent in currency markets. 

 "At this point, you've got to batten down the hatches and wait for the hurricane to pass by." 

 Canada's deepening currency crisis has spurred its central bank to continue a month-long strategy of sporadic but heavy intervention in currency markets to bolster the Canadian dollar. 

 The Bank of Canada repeatedly bought the Canadian dollar on Wednesday as the currency progressively snapped through record lows. The central bank has spent an estimated $3.5 billion out of its $20 billion in foreign reserves defending the currency in August. 

 Although analysts initially praised intervention as a good counterweight to excessive speculation in currency markets, it has failed to halt the general downward trend in the currency. 

 "We're caught in a downdraft and this is beyond the control of the Bank of Canada. The intervention is just providing liquidity and wasting money," said a foreign currency trader with a Canadian bank. 

 With intervention fast losing appeal, the central bank faces a stark choice: allow the dollar to hit bottom or raise interest rates. 

 The Bank of Canada last raised interest rates by 50 basis points in January in a largely unsuccessful attempt to bolster the weakening currency. 

 The central bank fears that another rate hike could tumble the slowing Canadian economy into a recession. 

 Some economists and business leaders have called on the federal government to immediately cut taxes to help spur the economy should the central bank finally move to raise borrowing costs. 

Currency traders, however, have vowed to continue selling the Canadian dollar until the central bank makes its move on rates.

 The currency market focus has shifted away from Asia and mostly to Russia, the trader suggested.

TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar extended its freefall Wednesday, plunging more than 200 ticks in heavy trading volumes as the waves of global turmoil continue to shred the Canadian currency.

 The bloodletting took place despite steady and sizeable intervention from the Bank of Canada throughout the session, traders said, with many market players now sensing that intervention has become a doomed and futile tactic. 

 "The market is obviously disheartened," said Bill Mooney, chief foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Montreal. "People in this whole move downwards for the Canadian dollar never sensed that the bank has lost the war as much as they did today." 

 Mooney cited the extraordinary rapidity and scope of the Canadian unit's fall Wednesday, despite a rumored total of more than C$1 billion spent on intervention by the central bank, as a telling sign that the market no longer regards central bank actions as having the same weight as they carried even a week earlier. 

 Although the U.S. dollar has been on a strong uptrend against the Canadian unit owing to its safe haven status as global markets are shaken by the Russian debt crisis, many currency watchers attributed the scale of Wednesday's fall to poor sentiment spread by falling commodity prices. 

 Wednesday's massive selloff of the the Canadian dollar also coincided with a fall of the bellwether CRB futures index to its lowest level in 12 years.

title: Canadian dollar hits another low, bank  intervenes .
text:
TORONTO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar fell to a record low of 64.51 U.S. cents on Monday as financial troubles in Russia and Venezuela added to market concerns of a rising tide of separatist sentiment in French-speaking Quebec. 

 The Canadian dollar's decline prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene to try and shore up the currency in money markets, buying Canadian dollars at several levels between 64.67 and 64.62 U.S. cents. 

 The central bank has intervened heavily and regularly since August 7 in a bid to halt the decline in the Canadian dollar, which foreign exchange traders have dubbed "the northern peso" because of its chronic weakness. 

 Traders, however, questioned the effectiveness of continuing central bank intervention to try and prop up the currency. 

 "If the bank is not going to hike rates then they should stop intervening on the currency, because they're just wasting taxpayers money. It's not doing anything," argued one Toronto-based money market trader. 

 The Canadian currency has lost about 10 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar during the past six months. 

 Russia, once again, was the trigger for the latest Canada dollar sell-off. 

 Russian President Boris Yeltsin fired his entire cabinet on Sunday and replaced Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko with former Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in a desperate attempt to stabilise Russia's precarious financial state. 

 Yeltsin's move followed a recent 30-percent devaluation of the Russian ruble and a 90-day moratorium on some of Russia's foreign debt repayments. 

 Rumours of an impending devaluation of the Venezuelan peso also added to the deepening financial crisis in emerging markets. 

 Both Russia and Venezuela are exporters of key commodities, primarily oil and nickel, and their financial crises were seen as yet another reason to sell the commodity-based Canadian dollar. 

 "The Canadian dollar is falling alongside all the other commodity-linked currencies," said Sal Guatieri, senior economist with Bank of Montreal. 

 "There is further nervousness about emerging markets given the situation in Russia and Venezuela." 

 Analysts also said rising political tensions between Canadian federalists and Quebec separatists were hovering over the troubled Canadian dollar. 

 Canada's Supreme Court renewed secessionist talk in a landmark case last week when it ruled that Quebec did not have a legal right to secede unilaterally from the rest of Canada. The court, however, added that the issue was largely a political question and should be decided by a popular vote in Quebec and by negotiations among politicians. 

 Separatist Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard quickly declared the court's decision a victory and embarked on what many observers view as a pre-election tour of the largely French-speaking province. 

 Markets fear that another separatist victory in Quebec would lead to a third independence referendum in the divided province. 

 The Canadian dollar lost about four percent of its value in the month before the 1995 referendum, which Quebec separatists narrowly lost. 

 "Given that the Supreme Court has unwittingly given Bouchard a playing card, that's likely to be a source of trouble for the currency," said Mario Angastiniotis, an economist with Standard & Poor's MMS International.
