TORONTO, Aug 21 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar closed the week much weaker, hitting new lows and ending at a record low close of C$1.5417 (US$0.6486), caused by technical selling.



The currency settled at the midday rate, which was 100 points (one Canadian cent) lower than the quiet opening.



Renewed speculative selling pounded the currency below the previous record low of C$1.5355 (US$0.6513) set August 7 in mid-morning trade, sparking more stop-loss selling.



The Bank of Canada tried to defend the currency, intervening to buy the Canadian dollar for U.S. dollars from around C$1.5360 (US$0.6510), but failed to halt the slide.



The central bank was last seen intervening at C$1.5425 (US$0.6483), a new record trading low for the local dollar.



The bank has been defending the "loonie" relatively strongly over the past two weeks since after shifting to more aggressive, preemptive intervention to counter speculative selling of Canadian dollars. But the weaker trend continued.



"Full stop at the figure (C$1.5400) and took it up there. "(There were) no rumours, just stop-losses," one trader said.



In cross trading, the Canadian dollar fell to 1.1654 marks after 1.1736 marks at the previous close here, but rose to 93.85 yen after 93.35 yen as the Japanese currency lost ground against the U.S. dollar.



On the chart, there was little resistance to the U.S. dollar's upward march.



A seven-year channel shows little is in the way before the U.S. dollar climbs to C$1.5800 (US$0.6329), possibly in the next few weeks, said Mark Roberts, FX technical analyst at I.D.E.A in New York.



"Until we get up there, there's very little to hold the market," he said. "Obviously all the big figure numbers like C$1.5600 (US$0.6410) will offer some kind of resistance, but the next chart level is C$1.5800."



On the downside, the U.S. dollar is well supported around the previous ceiling of C$1.5350 (US$0.6515), and C$1.5320 (US$0.6527).



Traders are watching the direction of the dollar/yen. Despite fears of Bank of Japan intervention, the U.S. dollar rebounded to around 145 yen today after a brief fall to mid-141 yen on Thursday, and to 1.80 marks.



Russia's financial crisis and general concern over Asia's economic slump provided underlying support for the U.S. dollar and North American bonds as safe-haven, but not the Canadian dollar.



Moody's Investors Service cut Russia's country ceiling for foreign currency debt. Prime Minister Kiriyenko told parliament Russia had just entered "a serious financial crisis," while parliament demanded President Yeltsin resign over his handling of the crisis.



As the Canadian dollar remained weak, the monetary conditions index (MCI) fell to a new low. The Bank of Canada said today the MCI was at -6.88 for Wednesday. It was quoted further down at -7,048 earlier today.



When the local dollar started the day at C$1.5316 (US$0.6528), it was stuck in a tight range and appeared to be a quiet day in the absence of major market-moving events and economic indicator releases.



In assessing the political risk of holding Canadian assets, the market is looking for more reaction from Quebec separatist leaders to Thursday's Supreme Court decision.



Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard, speaking to reporters in Quebec City, said on Friday that the court ruling will not affect the provincial election schedule, but did not give any indication as to when he will call one.



Traders are seeking clues on when the next provincial election will be held and how it could raise the possibility of another popular referendum on secession.



The Supreme Court ruling that Quebec has no right to unilaterally break away from the rest of the country had only a muted effect on the Canadian market.



The release this morning of another bearish economic indicator for June had little impact on the Canadian dollar as market players had already seen a surprise plunge in June retail sales on Thursday.



Canada's manufacturers' shipments fell 2.9 percent in June month on month due to plant closures in the automotive sector related to a General Motors strike in the United States. New orders were down by 2.0 percent and inventory was up 1.3 percent.



A Reuters survey of analysts had predicted on average that shipments would fall by only 0.7 percent and new orders by 0.8 percent.



On Thursday, the Canadian dollar came under selling pressure in the morning on the June retail sales data, which show a fall of 1.7 percent against the consensus forecast of a 0.2-percent rise. This suggests consumers might be tightening their purse strings earlier than expected. Sales were still up by 1.6 percent for the April-June quarter from the previous quarter.



Canada's economic indicator calendar looks slim until August 31, when the second-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) current account data are due out.

TORONTO, Aug 20 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar opened firmer at C$1.5281 (US$0.6544) on Thursday, boosted by a gradual but continuous rise in the yen against the U.S. dollar.



Trading was cautious and choppy ahead of the Supreme Court decision, due out at 0945 EDT/1345 GMT today, on the legality of any unilateral secession of the French-speaking province of Quebec from the rest of the country, and separatist reaction to the judges' opinions.



In early trade the local dollar was also riding the wave of vague and unrealistic rumour that the Bank of Canada would raise its key lending rate to prop it up.



Then came Canada's bearish retail sales data and wiped out the early gains.



The June retail sales fell a surprising 1.7 percent against the consensus forecast of a 0.2-percent rise, suggesting that consumers might be tightening their purse strings earlier than expected. Sales were still up by 1.6 percent for the April-June quarter from the previous quarter.



"That (the retail sales figure) really hurt. It was surprising. We were looking for a reasonably good number." said Steven Butler, director of foreign exchange at Scotia Capital Markets. "It takes the off-bid of a rate hike out of the equation."



Stephen Wateridge, managing director of corporate foreign exchange at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities agreed.



"I thought the ex-auto component would be slightly better than the headline (number), but the ex-auto was actually down by two percent," he said. "A horrible number. Hardly a backdrop for raising rates."



For the average consumer in Canada recent rises in the mortgage rate, based on rising long-term interest rates in the bond market, means the cost of borrowing is already higher and resembles the effect of a tighter monetary policy by the central bank, he noted.



Douglas Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns Inc said economists may have to revise down their estimates further for Canada's second-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) to below two percent at an annual rate.



The GDP and current account data will be released on August 31. Canada will also release June manufacturing shipments on Friday.



"The market is very nervous this morning, depending on what happens with (the court) ruling. I think anything over the C$1.53 handle, the market will be a little bit nervous that the Bank of Canada may step in," Scotia's Butler said.

Traders are looking at a record low of C$1.5355 (US$0.6513) that was set on August 7 as the next key target.



Key domestic and global events had little impact on price action after the local dollar had suffered initial selling on bearish economic data, which wiped out earlier gains.



There was no sign of Bank of Canada intervention today.



"No sign of them. They're resting," one trader said. "Since the fiasco this morning, it's been fairly range-bound. The currency weakened off a little bit in the day and is expected to weaken off a little bit overnight."



The central bank had been intervening in the currency market almost on a daily basis since August 7 to stem any drastic slide in the local dollar's value against the U.S. dollar. On Tuesday, it was seen at C$1.5341 (US$0.6518).

In reaction, the Quebec government said an absolute majority of 50 percent plus one vote in the next referendum on independence would be enough to start the process of secession.

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Edges Up After Trading A Wide Range
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar is only slightly higher late Thursday from its late Wednesday levels versus the U.S. dollar, after an eventful day in which the Canadian unit broke with recent trends and traded a wide, nearly 100-point range without once drawing intervention from Canada's central bank. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5315 at 4:30 p.m. EDT (2030 GMT), from C$1.5275 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and C$1.5328 late Wednesday. It traded through a wide C$1.5245-C$1.5351 range, but this volatility was largely confined to the early morning and overnight sessions. 

 In something of a paradox, dealers said flows were very light throughout the North American session, despite an onslaught of news events throughout the day that included a key Canada supreme court decision denying Quebec the legal right to seperate unilaterally from Canada, the Quebec government's reaction to it, Canadian June retail sales data, and the U.S. attack on alleged terrorist targets in Sudan and Afghanistan. 

 Perversely, the Canadian dollar failed to react much to any of the news, with the possible exception of the morning retail sales report, which showed sales down 1.7% in June from May, and which helped the U.S. dollar to rise off its overnight lows at C$1.5245. 

 "At first glance, we still appear to be status quo here," said Bill Mooney, chief foreign-exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Montreal. "But none of the news bodes terribly well for the Canadian dollar - the trend hasn't changed, and it's going to weaken. No two ways about it." 

 Mooney said the fact that the Canadian unit exited North American trading at the low end of its daily trading range will likely bode ill for its fortunes Friday. 

 He said it will likely continue weaker in overnight trading in international markets, with a fresh test of its all-time intraday low near the C$1.5355 U.S. dollar level likely in store for Friday.

title: Canada bonds open weaker on local dollar's fall.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds opened weaker on Wednesday, under pressure from the weakness of the Canadian dollar and softer U.S. bonds, with the price of long bonds falling more than a full point in Canada. 

 What appears to be temporary easing of concern over Russia's financial system and Asia's economic slump have prompted selling of North American bonds and buying of equities in general this week. 

 U.S. treasuries, from which Canadian bonds take direction, have been softer this week as the U.S. dollar has continued to slide against the yen on growing fears of Bank of Japan intervention to stem the yen's fall. 

 "We are underperforming quite a bit in Canada. I think this has to do primarily with the continued weakness in the currency," said Arve Bendiksrud, vice president at fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. 

 "Even the U.S. market is weaker... We seem to have more confidence in the equity market for the last couple of days, whether fragile or not. Probably some of the asset allocation that had take place into bonds has been reversed, for the time being anyway." 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond (June 1, 2027) fell C$1.07 to C$130.80 to yield 5.788 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 11/32 to yield 5.59 percent. 

 The Canada-U.S. spread, an indicator for the currency risk premium for holding Canadian securities, widened to 20 basis points from 17 points at the previous close here. 

 The Canadian dollar opened weaker this morning from Tuesday's close of C$1.5282 (US$0.6544). The market is testing its downside again towards a record low of C$1.5355 (US$0.6513) that was set on August 7. 

 Buyers in the market also stayed cautious ahead of the Supreme Court decision on Thursday on the legality of any unilateral declaration of independence by the mostly French-speaking province of Quebec. 

 "It's unclear what the reaction from the Quebec government will be to the Supreme Court ruling. Until we know that I think the bond market will demonstrate preference for larger risk premiums towards a wider Canada-U.S. spread," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 The Supreme Court judges will issue their decision in a thick document at 0945 EDT/1345 GMT on Thursday in Ottawa. 

 Any rekindling of the war of words in Canadian politics between pro-unity federalists and Quebec separatists could also discourage overseas investors from holding Canadian assets. 

 This morning, the U.S. bond market came under downward pressure on strong economic data which suggest interest rates might higher down the road. 

 The U.S. July housing starts came in stronger than expected, rising 5.7 percent to an annual rate of 1.718 million units after rising a revised 5.7 percent in June. 

 In the money market, Canadian T-bills were little changed, escaping a sell-off despite the continued fall in the local dollar's value. 

 "We had a bill auction yesterday, which went more expensively than people had anticipated. So a lot of people who had tendered did not get filled and had to buy after the auction at more expensive levels," one trader said. 

 "The market has held relatively well even though the currency has weakened off. We're in a very different mind-set than we were the the last time the currency was at this level," the trader said. 

 The market has stopped pricing in expectations of an increase in the official lending rate by the Bank of Canada. In the past many market players thought the central bank would resort to credit tightening to shore up the dollar. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill yielded 4.97 percent after 4.93 percent at the previous close here. 

 North American stock markets posted modest gains this morning, while the Canadian dollar remained depressed. 

 The Bank of Canada intervened in the currency market this morning, sellintg U.S. dollars from C$1.5321 (US$0.6527) to C$1.5328 (US$0.6524) to defend the battered local currency. 

 The Canadian dollar did not benefit from the yen's steadiness overnight. The U.S. dollar has been sliding this week against the yen as traders become more wary of holding long dollar positions at a time when Japan's top policymakers are suggesting that the Bank of Japan will not tolerate a further decline in the yen's value. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted just above 144 yen this morning, down from around 147 yen a week ago. 

 Japan's Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed Mr Yen for his influence on the market, on Wednesday continued to stage a verbal intervention, warning traders of risks of keep buying U.S. dollars. "Risks of the stronger yen for investors are becoming bigger. They should be careful about that. Chances for yen-supportive intervention are drawing near," he told reporters in Tokyo.

"Overnight you had a lot of talk about a possible BOJ intervention to prop up the Japanese yen... and that benefited other commodity-linked currencies, such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars, but the Canadian dollar continued to weaken."

Economic indicators released this morning had little direct impact on price action in the market.



Canada's wholesale trade fell 1.7 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in June from May, marking the first time since the slowdown in 1995 that sales have fallen for two consecutive months.



A Reuters survey of analysts had on average forecast a decline of 0.6 percent. The drop was predominantly due to shutdowns resulting from a General Motors strike in the United States.



Canada's consumer price index (CPI), a barometer of inflation, rose 1.0 percent year on year in July, at the same rate as in June. "Given the continuing slack in the economy, the greater risk is that inflation could move below the target band... as you eliminate the impact of the exchange rate," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal. "We've had a fairly pronounced depreciation of the Canadian dollar, which is still putting upward pressure on the inflation measure. But that's only a transitory factor."



For the bigger picture, Canada's second-quarter gross domestic product and current account data will be released on August 31. Canada will also release June retail sales on Thursday and June manufacturing shipments on Friday.

In cross trading, the Canadian dollar slipped back to 1.1717 marks from 1.1790 marks at the previous close here, and extended losses to 93.84 yen from 94.75 yen.



The Canadian unit has been fluctuating in a range of 92-97 yen for the last two months. On a weekly chart basis, it has been on a general uptrend in the longer term since it bottomed out just above 60 yen in April 1995, when the Japanese currency hit record highs against key currencies.



Weakness returned to the local dollar this week as investors again bought U.S. dollars as a safe haven investment on renewed concern over Russia's financial system.



In Canada any rekindling of the war of words between pro-unity federalists and Quebec separatists might also scare overseas investors from holding Canadian assets.



"It's (today's weakness) the disappointment of the bank's actions on Monday," a senior trader at another bank said. "Yesterday they deviated from policy of metrical intervention, but the amount they spent was minimal and they had no impact at all."



"The same players, the same bank accounts decided to sell the currency this morning at C$1.5315 (US$0.6530), so we're in a very, very precarious situation. Even with good news coming out, that's not helping us," he said.



The Bank of Canada continued to intervene in the currency market this week to slow the pace of the depreciation of the local dollar, at C$1.5303 (US$0.6535) and C$1.5296 (US$0.6538) on Tuesday and at every five points from C$1.5240 (US$0.6561) to C$1.5255 (US$0.6555) on Monday.



In trading since August 7, the central bank has been launching preemptive attacks on Canadian dollar selling, sometimes by buying the local currency aggressively with large amounts of U.S. dollars. Monday was an exception when the central bank returned to its customary practice of waiting until the U.S. dollar moved 70-75 points from the previous close.



Economic indicators released this morning had little direct impact on price action in the market.



Canada's wholesale trade fell 1.7 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in June from May. It was the first time since an economic slowdown in slowdown in 1995 that sales have fallen for two consecutive months.



A Reuters survey of analysts had on average forecast a decline of 0.6 percent. The drop was predominantly due to shutdowns resulting from a General Motors strike in the United States.



The U.S. July housing starts came in stronger than expected, marking the strongest pace in 11 years of a rise 5.7 percent to an annual rate of 1.718 million units after rising a revised 5.7 percent in June.



It was the fastest rate for any month since March 1987, when new hones were built at a rate of 1.73 million a year.



Canada's consumer price index (CPI), a barometer of inflation, rose 1.0 percent year on year in July, at the same rate as in June. The core CPI (excluding food and energy prices) rose 1.3 percent year on year after a 1.0 percent rise in June. Economists on average had forecast the overall CPI would be up 1.1 percent and the core rate up 1.2 percent.



"Given the continuing slack in the economy, the greater risk is that inflation could move below the target band... as you eliminate the impact of the exchange rate," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal. "We've had a fairly pronounced depreciation of the Canadian dollar, which is still putting upward pressure on the inflation measure. But that's only a transitory factor."



Looking at the bigger picture, Canada's second-quarter gross domestic product and current account data will be released on August 31. Canada will also release June retail sales on Thursday and June manufacturing shipments on Friday.

title: Bank Of  Canada Intervenes  -2: Repeated  Interventions  Seen
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada has intervened in the foreign exchange market repeatedly Wednesday morning, also selling moderate amounts of U.S. dollars at C$1.5328 in an effort to contain market volatility, traders in Toronto said. 

 The U.S. dollar leveled off briefly after the intervention, and was trading at C$1.5325 at 10:25 a.m. EDT (1425 GMT). 

 The new round of U.S. dollar selling comes after an earlier intervention near the C$1.5320 level failed to halt the U.S. currency's ascent toward its all-time intraday high of C$1.5350. 

 Wednesday's actions also mark the ninth of the last ten sessions in which the central bank has come out in support of the Canadian dollar. 

 The bank's actions thus far Wednesday have been typical of its recent policy of random, asymmetrical intervention as opposed to its previous unofficial policy of intervening in currency markets only on intraday moves in either direction of 70 ticks or more. Tuesday's official U.S. dollar close was at C$1.5282. 

 Traders said total bank sales of U.S. dollars Wednesday morning have been somewhat higher than in previous days, and are likely intended to signal the bank's intention of preventing the U.S. dollar from advancing past the all-time high Wednesday. 

 The bank's new strategy of intervening early and unpredictably began on August 7, when it sold large amounts of U.S. dollars as the U.S. unit was trading at the C$1.5350 level. 

 While the bank has generally been successful in preventing a further decline in the Canadian currency and minimizing outright speculative pressure against it, market players in recent days have begun to have misgivings about the long-term effectiveness of the intervention tactics. 

Intervention has failed to reverse the declining trend for the Canadian currency, and many feel the strategy is doomed unless backed by a central bank move to lead interest rates higher. 

 The Canadian dollar has been under severe downward pressure in recent months, prompting the more aggressive, activist tactics seen recently. 

 Analysts say the Canadian currency has fundamental weaknesses stemming from low commodity prices and global uncertainties stemming from the renewed economic and financial turmoil in Asia and Russia. 

 The intense pressure on the Canadian dollar is expected to last until the pressures originating in Asia relent, or the Bank of Canada raises interest rates to defend the embattled currency.

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5328 at 4:24 p.m. EDT (2024 GMT), from C$1.5306 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and C$1.5275 late Tuesday. It rose as high as C$1.5343 at 2:06 p.m. EDT (1806 GMT) before being pushed back by U.S. dollar selling by the central bank.

title: Defend Canada dollar with rate cut, economist says.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada should cut interest rates, not raise them as some economists have suggested, to defend the falling Canadian dollar, a prominent Canadian policy institute says. 

 The C.D. Howe Institute's unorthodox strategy is the latest contribution to a medicine chest of prescriptions and remedies designed to treat the ailing Canadian dollar. 

 The currency has lost seven percent of its value against the U.S. dollar during the past five months as financial crisis in Asia and plummeting commodity prices continue to prompt a rush toward the safe haven of the U.S. currency. 

 Canada's dollar fell again on Tuesday to 65.40 U.S. cents as unexpectedly soft Canadian trade numbers and the impact of Russia's devaluation of the rouble triggered yet another move to hold U.S. dollars. 

 "What the plunging dollar really needs from the Bank of Canada is an interest rate cut," said William Robson, an economist with the institute. 

 "We would be well served in everything but the very shortest run if the Bank of Canada would readjust its focus firmly on the domestic economy and give us the kind of monetary expansion we need to grow the economy to its potential," Robson added. 

 That argument flies in the face of conventional wisdom which holds interest rate hikes as the first line of defence for a currency under attack. 

 Rate hikes usually make it more attractive for short-term investors to buy securities and fixed-income instruments denominated in a weak currency and almost always leads to some immediate currency gains. 

 The Canadian dollar did, indeed, gain about three percent against the U.S. dollar in the three weeks after the last Bank of Canada interest rate hike in January. The benefits of that 50-basis-points rise, however, were short-lived as the currency then weakened precipitously in early spring. 

 Robson blamed the January move as the key contributor to a subsequent slowing of the Canadian economy and warned that Canada was treading close to dangerous waters. 

 "A hike in rates large enough and sustained enough to make any difference to the dollar's performance over the next few weeks would probably also tip the Canadian economy into recession by year end," Robson argued. 

 Although some economists privately agree in principle with Robson's argument, most fear a rate cut would invite further selling of the Canadian dollar. 

 Sherry Cooper, chief economist with Nesbitt Burns in Toronto, said speculators would "trash" the currency if the central bank lowered rates in an environment of pronounced currency weakness. 

 "It would be exactly the wrong signal and it just shows a total lack of understanding of how financial markets work. Every other country in the world is raising interest rates to defend their currencies," Cooper said. 

 Cooper, who favours a 50-basis-points hike in interest rates to defend the currency, said tax cuts were the most appropriate tonic to spur economic growth at the moment. 

 Despite the calls to tinker with interest rates, Canada's central bank has opted instead to intervene heavily in money markets during the past two weeks in a bid to bolster the Canadian dollar. 

 It has spent an estimated $1.5 billion defending the Canadian currency since August 7. Analysts praised the intervention as successful in stabilising the currency, though they said intervention was not a long-term solution. 

 "Intervention only works for very brief periods. You have to see a generalized shift in policy before it begins to have a sustained effect," Cooper said. 

 ($1=$1.53 Canadian).

title: Canada bonds end weaker on  currency  anxiety.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended weaker on Tuesday, extending mild losses throughout the day as investors became nervous about holding Canadian assets. 

 The outlook for the Canadian currency is gloomy again as the financial turmoil in Russia and economic downturn in Asia are clouding global economic growth prospects. 

 "The Canadian dollar has really affected all the assets in Canada, stocks and bonds," said Sheldon Dong, manager of fixed-income research at Midland Walwyn Capital Inc. "For the foreign investor, there is not fun owning Canadian securities when you're losing money on the currency." 

 The Canadian dollar ended little changed at C$1.5282 (US$0.6544) on Tuesday, stabilising after central bank intervention in the morning, but still quoted weaker than Monday's close. 

 "The pressure on the Canadian dollar is continuing on long bonds, and probably some further small deterioration relative to U.S. markets," Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, at Bank of Montreal, told Reuters Television. "The key is the performance of the Canadian dollar." 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond (June 1, 2027) fell C$0.64 to C$131.78 to yield 5.732 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 6/32 to yield 5.56 percent. 

 The Canada-U.S. spread, an indicator for the currency risk premium for holding Canadian securities, widened to 17 basis points from 15 points at the previous close here. 

 Any rekindling of a war of words in Canada between federalists and Quebec separatists might also scare overseas investors away from holding Canadian assets. 

 Buyers were cautious ahead of the release of a ruling on Thursday by the country's supreme court on the legality of any unilateral declaration of independence by the mostly French-speaking province of Quebec. 

 The decision will be released in a thick document at 0945 EDT/1345 GMT in Ottawa on Thursday. 

 "Bonds are under minor pressure," said Katherine Beattie, senior technical analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. "The U.S. CPI data came in as expected, but we've got a continued negative bias in the Canadian dollar, which is hurting our entire yield curve." 

 A rebound in North American stock prices could be slightly negative for bonds as investors who had shied away from plunging stocks last week might be putting some money back into stocks from bonds and cash. 

 Despite recent aggressive intervention by the Bank of Canada in the currency market to stem the U.S. dollar's rise, the outlook for the Canadian dollar is bleak. 

 Beattie expects the currency to break this week the record low of C$1.5355 (US$0.6513) that was set on August 7, and fall towards C$1.5400 (US$0.6494). 

 There was little market reaction to North American economic data released this morning. 

 Canada's June trade surplus widened to C$1.54 billion from a downwardly revised C$1.33 billion in May. A Reuters survey of economists had put Canada's merchandise trade surplus at C$1.65 billion in June after C$1.67 billion in May. 

 The U.S. trade deficit narrowed by 8.9 percent to US$14.15 billion from US$15.54 in May. 

 The U.S. consumer price index rose 0.2 percent, and the core CPI (excluding food and energy prices) also rose 0.2 percent. 

 Canada still has a high employment rate, above eight percent, and a low inflation rate, which is at the bottom of the Bank of Canada's target band of one to three percent. 

 Against this background Canada has no reason to tighten monetary policy at the moment. There may be a slight reason to ease the grip on money in circulation. 

 "But the given the pressure on the Canadian dollar, I think right now interest rates will hold steady," Ferley said. 

 In the money market, Canadian T-bills were weaker. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill yielded 4.93 percent after 4.88 percent at the previous close here.

TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar is down early Tuesday against its U.S. counterpart, with trading mainly confined to a range below the C$1.5300 U.S. dollar level on uncertainty about the Bank of Canada's intervention intentions. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.5292 at 10:15 a.m. EDT (1415 GMT), up marginally from C$1.5290 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) and from C$1.5265 late Monday. 

Currency watchers said the central bank, which has intervened to prop up the Canadian currency in seven of the last eight trading sessions, must show its hand in a decisive way if it hopes to maintain the effectiveness of its tactics. 

 "The Bank of Canada has to intervene early today," said Avery Shenfeld, senior economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities. "The market will be looking for an early intervention because we're getting closer to the point where they first stepped in to support the Canadian dollar a week and a half ago." 

 The central bank's first aggressive, asymettrical intervention took place near the C$1.5350 level on August 7, and some traders noted that despite the bank's support, the Canadian dollar is now edging back to the same levels. 

 "The view on Canada is still very negative, unless the bank is prepared to do something more concrete, like raising interest rates," said one currency trader at a Canadian bank. "Intervention isn't working - the bank is just spending money for nothing." 

 To add to the negative fundamentals pressuring Canada's currency, some traders cited rumors that Russia may soon begin large-scale sales of base metals and other commodities in the wake of its de facto devaluation of the ruble, which would increase the competition for similar exports from Canada. 

 This would be expected to hurt Canada's export performance, which has already been relatively flat recently. 

 Statistics Canada reported earlier Tuesday that the nation's trade surplus widened slightly in June, to C$1.54 billion from C$1.33 billion in May, but with exports advancing only 0.1% over the previous month.

title: Bank Of  Canada Intervenes  -2: Bank Seen Defending C$1.5300
text:

the foreign exchange market Tuesday morning, selling U.S.

action, said a trader in Toronto.

U.S. dollars as the U.S. unit was trading at the C$1.5350
level.
   While the bank has generally been successful in
preventing a further decline in the Canadian currency and
minimizing outright speculative pressure against it, market
players in recent days have begun to have misgivings about
the long-term effectiveness of the intervention tactics.
   The Canadian dollar has been under severe downward
pressure in recent months, prompting the more aggressive,
activist tactics seen recently.

title: Canadian dollar closes weaker in light trade.
text:
TORONTO, Aug 17 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar closed weaker at C$1.5260 (US$0.6550) in light trading on Monday as a crisis in Russian financial markets and concerns over impending Canadian trade data placed pressure on the currency, traders said. 

 An international crisis in Russia was the key trigger for the Canada unit's renewed weakness. 

 Russia effectively devalued its rouble by as much as 30 percent and announced a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt repayments on Monday in response to a crisis of confidence in the government's ability to defend the currency. 

 Canadian analysts considered the devaluation particularly important because Russia, like Canada, has a large presence on world commodity markets. 

 The strength of the Canadian dollar is closely tied to commodity prices because the country's economy remains largely resource-based. 

 "The Russian devaluation renews concerns about emerging markets and commodity prices since Russia is a huge exporter of energy and metals and minerals. That's another negative for Canada," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns in Toronto. 

 The falling Canadian dollar pushed the Bank of Canada to intervene in the currency market, buying Canadian dollars at various levels between C$1.5240 (US$0.6561) and C$1.5255 (US$0.6555). 

 "They've been buying all the way up," said one foreign exchange trader following the intervention. The trader described the intervention as moderate. 

 But Monday's intervention appeared to be less effective than the central bank's aggressive moves to bolster the currency in the past 10 days. 

 Analysts had applauded the central bank for setting a temporary ceiling on the currency, which few speculators were willing to challenge. 

 The central bank has moved from a policy of intervening to smooth out gyrations in the currency to aggressively defending the dollar. 

 "It does look like intervention was somewhat less effective than it was last week," Porter said. 

 Analysts were also keeping a close eye on key Canadian and U.S. data due to be released later this week. 

 Statistics Canada will report Canada's merchandise trade data on Tuesday. A Reuters survey of economists predicted Canada's merchandise trade surplus would narrow to C$1.65 billion in June from C$1.67 billion in May. 

 Canada will also report key inflation data on Wednesday. 

 On the crosses, the Canadian dollar fell to 1.1742 marks from 1.1871 marks at Friday's close and dipped to 95.46 yen from 96.43 yen at the previous close.

title: Canadian dollar opens weaker in light trading.

TORONTO, Aug 17 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar opened weaker at C$1.5217 (US$0.6571) in light trading on Monday after investors sold the currency against the German mark overnight in overseas markets, traders said. 

 They said they expected the Canada unit to be sidelined in North American trading as markets focused on continuing crisis in Russian financial markets and the release of Canadian and U.S. inflation numbers later this week. 

 Russia effectively devalued its rouble by as much as 30 percent and announced a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt repayments on Monday in response to a crisis of confidence in the government's ability to defend the currency. 

 "The focus today is the Russian rouble," said a foreign exchange trader with a Canadian brokerage. "There are also a lot of numbers coming out this week, so I think the focus will be on whether those numbers show further Canadian weakness." 

 Statistics Canada will report key merchandise trade data on Tuesday and inflation numbers on Wednesday. 

 Analysts said the Bank of Canada's previous aggressive intervention had set a temporary ceiling on the currency which few speculators were willing to challenge. 

 The central bank has moved from a policy of intervening to smooth out gyrations in the currency to aggressively defending the dollar. 

 "The intervention on August 7 has been effective in creating a more stable range for the Canadian dollar," said Rob Palombi, fixed-income analyst with MMS International. 

 "They've intervened at many different levels and that basically says the bank can be in anywhere at anytime and it has derailed the more speculative activity that we were seeing prior to the intervention," Palombi said. 

 The strength of the Canadian dollar, however, remains tied closely to commodity prices because the country's economy remains largely resource-based.

title: =Bank Of Canada Tactics Win Praise, But Also Raise Questions
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--While the Bank of Canada's feisty approach to currency market intervention in recent sessions has helped bring some stability to the Canadian dollar - and has won plaudits from some market watchers - how long it will remain effective and how sustainable it is are open questions for Canadian dollar watchers. 

 After weeks of letting the currency slide and intervening only as its usual policy dictates - when the U.S. dollar moves 70 ticks or more against the Canadian currency - the bank began intervening early on Aug. 7, and followed the pattern every day last week except for Friday. 

 As a result of the bank's actions, the currency, which had been declining steadily for weeks, began to range trade. 

 Monday morning, after the Canadian currency weakened significantly in the wake of the Russian ruble devaluation - the central bank let the U.S. dollar move the full 70 ticks before intervening. 

 That apparent reversion to the bank's standard operating procedure left some market watchers wondering if the bank has abandoned its more aggressive approach to currency intervention, and will once again let the Canadian dollar slide, intervening only at 70-tick junctures. 

 Some analysts interviewed by Dow Jones Newswires believe the Bank of Canada will continue to intervene early if bank officials believe it is necessary. 

 But opinions were divided as to how long the bank's strategy will remain effective - and how long its foreign exchange reserves will permit it to keep intervening early. 

 Andrew Pyle, vice president of investment banking at C.T. Securities Inc., said the bank's early interventions may already be losing their effectiveness. 

 "Even the surprise element now, by doing this deviation tactic, isn't a lot," Pyle said. "I'd argue now that the market knows that the bank can do this, and does do this."

The bank has been heavily active in the market in recent weeks, both intervening and raising interest rates in an effort to contain the fallout from market turmoil in part connected to the Asian crisis. 

 However, when the central bank rejected calls for another rate increase Friday - the bank rate remains at 4.50% - the U.S. dollar shot through the key C$1.4285 level (70 U.S. cents), prompting heavy U.S. dollar selling from the BOC. 

 Many analysts think the Bank is now reluctant to raise rates again, particularly given news on Friday that inflation slowed to 0.9% in November, below its 1%-3% target range. 

 'The market is very thin, the bigger players are not active at the moment,' said one dealer. That may partly explain why the central bank's actions this morning had a more pronounced impact. 

 But the trader doesn't see much improvement in the days ahead with the extent of the Asian troubles still unclear. On Monday, the Nikkei stock index in Tokyo dropped another 3.4% to its lowest level since July of 1995.

title: Canadian bonds end firmer but T-bills ease on C$.
text:
TORONTO, Dec 22 (Reuters) - The Canadian yield curve flattened in light dealings on Monday, with the short end closing negative as the Canadian dollar traded at almost 12-year lows. 

 "Things just drifted down during the day," said Richard Wylie, Toronto-Dominion Securities fixed-income economist. "The people are a little bit disappointed about the currency, and the Bank of Canada isn't going to do anything in defense of it." 

 Canada's 30-year benchmark bond added C$0.16 to C$127.82 to yield 5.979 percent following its U.S. counterpart higher, as it rose 15/32 to yield 5.89 percent. 

 The positive spread between the two bonds rose to nine basis points from seven at the close of trading on Friday. 

 By contrast the three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 4.53 percent from 4.47 percent on Friday. 

 Canada's currency closed at C$1.4342 (US$0.6973) after repeated intervention by the central bank this morning. The Bank of Canada sold US$50 million blocks to buy Canadian dollars several times after the currency dipped as low as C$1.4353 (US$0.6967), levels not seen since February 1986. 

 More T-bill supply also dampened the short end, said Michael Gregory, Lehman Brothers economist. 

 The Bank of Canada auctioned C$5.8 billion of T-bills, including C$3.6 billion in new cash. The average yield of three-month treasury bills was 4.460 percent, up from 3.799 percent at the last auction. 

 Trading was light ahead of the holidays, analysts said.

title: Canadian bonds, T-bills end higher in thin trading.
text:
TORONTO, Dec 19 (Reuters) - Canadian long-term bonds and short-end T-Bills end higher in skimpy pre-holiday trading on Friday, resisting the pull of the weaker Canadian dollar as it dropped to 11-year lows. 

 "Bills held in surprisingly well," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at Toronto-Dominion Securities. Canada's currency ended the week at its weakest closing levels in 11 years, finishing at C$1.4312 (US$0.6987), softer from its close on Thursday of C$1.4265 (US$0.7010). 

 Canada's three-month cash T-bill rose to yield 4.47 percent from 4.51 percent at Thursday's close. 

 Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.41 to C$127.70 to yield 5.987 percent. The U.S. 30-year bond rose 7/32 to yield 5.92 percent. The positive spread between the two bonds closed steady at seven basis points from the close of trading on Thursday. 

 Bonds and T-bills drifted higher in the afternoon following a firmer U.S. market, after T-bills opened softer due to a tumbling Canadian currency. Investors sold the dollar after the Bank of Canada failed to hike short-term interest rates this morning as some expected. 

 "The case for a rate hike was not all that strong this morning with CPI (consumer price index) the way it was," Webber said. Statistics Canada reported that the Canadian consumer price index rose by just 0.9 percent on the year, so the central bank could not justify increasing rates to cool an overheated economy. Instead the bank tried vainly to shore up the currency by intervening heavily. 

 Dealings tapered off late in the day. 

Canada's 10-year benchmark bonds rose C$0.27 to C$111.35 to yield 5.679 percent.

TORONTO, Dec 19 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar tumbled to its lowest point in 11 years on Friday, prompting the central bank to intervene heavily to buy the currency, traders said. 

 Dealers said the central bank began buying the currency at C$1.4285 (US$0.7000), then intervened again at C$1.4292 (US$0.6997), the currency's lowest point in 11 years. 

 The intervention was ineffective, and the currency weakened further to reach US$1.4322 (US$0.6982), they said. 

 The Bank of Canada has been intervening steadily since it was first in the market. Dealers said they had last seen the central bank in at C$1.4320 (US$0.6983).

title: Canadian dollar weakens to 11-year low.
text:
TORONTO, Dec 11 (Reuters) - Canada's dollar tumbled below 70 U.S. cents on Thursday for the first time in 11 years, battered by financial turmoil in Asia and a showdown between currency traders and the Canadian central bank. 

 The Canadian dollar weakened to 69.98 U.S. cents, its weakest point since early 1986, before recovering slightly in the afternoon to end the North American trading session at 70.09 U.S. cents. 

 The dollar's all-time low against the U.S. dollar was 69.13 U.S. cents in February 1986. 

 The sell-off occurred despite heavy intervention by the Bank of Canada, which bought Canadian dollars on foreign exchange markets in an attempt to halt the decline. 

 "The pronounced weakness today I think you can trace to the renewed turmoil in Asia. It's as much a (flight to the) U.S. dollar story as a Canadian dollar story," said Doug Porter, senior economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns. 

 Many international investors have responded to the Asian crisis by moving their capital into so-called safe haven currencies, such as the U.S. dollar and German mark. More marginal currencies like Canada's have been overlooked. 

 The Asian problems have also lowered expectations for growth in that region and hurt commodity prices. Canada is a major exporter of commodities like grain and metals and its currency tends to mirror movements in global commodity prices. 

 The dollar's slide is being partly blamed on the Bank of Canada's reluctance to raise interest rates. Rate hikes tend to strengthen a currency by attracting capital from other countries. 

 After slashing interest rates to 40-year lows last year, the Bank of Canada has enacted just three rate hikes of 25 points each this year. 

 The most recent increase was on Nov. 25, when the bank raised the key bank rate to 4 percent. That move failed to arrest the dollar's decline. The bank rate is similar to the U.S. federal funds rate, which is at 5.5 percent. 

 The Bank of Canada has been reluctant to raise rates for fear of stalling the country's economic recovery. But currency traders, who expected more tightening, have sold off the dollar in the absence of more rate hikes. 

 "At the end of the day (the currency weakness) centers on the credibility of the Bank of Canada," said Andrew Spence, senior economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. 

 "They had got the market set up to look for a fairly steady tightening in interest rates..and the bank wasn't really willing to deliver," he said. 

 Analysts said another Bank of Canada rate increase was needed to halt the dollar's slide and that it could occur within days. 

 "It is impossible for the bank now to step back and totally ignore what is happening. I think the odds are basically for a 50-basis-point tightening," said Andrew Pyle, senior economist with ABN-AMRO Bank Canada. 

 "The market knows that you cannot defend levels on the Canadian dollar with foreign exchange intervention. It may work for five minutes, but it never works (in the long run)," he said.

   Currency weakness results despite a 1/4-point increase

   The bank tends to step into the market against moves

South Korea and Japan will put long-term downward pressure
on commodity prices, an important factor in the Canadian
economy.

the Asian crisis and a spillover from that to commodity
prices," says Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman
Sachs Canada. "We saw a little bit of an indication of that

   The Canadian Industrial Product Price Index fell 0.3% in
October, with the most important price declines in pork,
softwood, lumber, aluminum products and refined zinc, said
Statistics Canada earlier Wednesday.

through to a weaker than expected increase in the producer

title: Canada markets falter on sliding dollar.
text:
TORONTO, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Canadian financial markets slumped on Wednesday after the Canadian dollar fell to 2-1/2-year lows despite aggressive efforts by the Bank of Canada to defend the currency. 

 Stocks, T-bills and much of the bond market softened on concerns the currency would weaken further and force the Bank of Canada to hike interest rates again. 

 "Given the difference in action between the Dow (Jones industrial average) and the TSE (Toronto Stock Exchange), there's obviously a lack of stability in our market," said Philip Strathy, chief investment officer with Strathy Investments Ltd. 

 Canada's benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 Index, which tumbled as much as 2 percent at midday, closed the session lower, ending down about 125.12 points at 6,505.40. 

 Pulling the market lower were gold stocks and interest-sensitive banking shares. While gold producers weakened because the price of gold fell to its lowest level in 12-1/2 years, concerns about the further Canadian interest rate hikes hurt banks and much of the rest of the market, analysts said. 

 Causing the overall decline in Canadian markets was the weakened state of the currency. Canada's dollar has been in a steady decline for several weeks as the financial crisis in Asia spilled over into North America. 

 "The currency is still reacting to external factors and fears that the Japanese might repatriate Canadian and U.S. assets," said Rob Palombi, a senior fixed-income analyst with financial analysis firm MMS International. 

 In an attempt to halt the dollar's slide, the Bank of Canada on Tuesday raised its key bank rate, which is similar to the U.S. federal funds rate, by a quarter of a percentage point to 4.0 percent. 

 The central bank said it raised interest rates for the third time this year to put an end to what it called "persistent weakness" in the Canadian dollar. 

 But the Bank of Canada tightening had little effect, with the currency falling to a new 2-1/2-year low of C$1.4253 to the U.S. dollar overnight. 

 The continued slide in the dollar brought the Bank of Canada into the foreign exchange market on Wednesday. The central bank repeatedly bought Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars. Traders said the intervention was "more aggressive" than usual and the bank was trying to sent a strong signal to the markets. 

 Weakness in the currency is feeding speculation that the Bank of Canada will have to raise rates again soon to lure capital flows back into Canadian dollar assets. 

 "A lot of the scenario is pretty similar to what was happening in '94 and '95 with the Mexican peso crisis. You saw the same type of stuff going on then with the Bank of Canada raising rates and intervening heavily," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A. 

 The currency weakness reflects "a loss of investor confidence in Canadian assets," Kalirai said.

title: Canada dollar ends down on weaker employment data.
text:
TORONTO, Nov 7 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended weaker on Friday at C$1.4095 (US$0.7095) from Thursday's close of C$1.3987 (US$0.7149), after Canada reported lower than expected employment growth for October. 

 Dealers said the currency slid after Statistics Canada reported employment fell by 11,100 positions versus expectations for a rise of 37,000, and the Bank of Canada did not deliver an anticipated interest rate rise. 

 "It's definitely down because of that and the weak employment numbers," said Mario Angastiniotis, economist at MMS International. 

 The unemployment numbers stunned economists, who had predicted the jobless rate would drop below the psychologically important 9 percent level for the first time in more than seven years. 

 "Let's face it, all of us were expecting 8.9 or 9 percent unemployment, so we were extremely surprised," said David Ebata, senior Canadian analyst with Technical Data in Boston. 

 "There are some very disturbing trends in the jobs data, especially when you look at the overall drop in employment," said Ebata, who added that economists could start scaling down their 1998 forecasts for Canada's economic growth. 

 The currency's sharp decline after the job numbers were reported prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene in early morning trade, buying Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars around the C$1.4075 (US$0.7104) level.

title: Canada's Martin keeps close watch on markets.
text:
OTTAWA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said he is keeping a close eye on the market turmoil that has sent panic through Canadian stocks and the currency. 

 "We are monitoring the situation, and remain in contact with the Bank of Canada, market officials and the U.S. Treasury," Martin said in a statement released late Monday. 

 "The Canadian economy is in a position of strength, with sound economic fundamentals and the best fiscal health of the G7," Martin said, reiterating comments he made on Monday to reporters. "I feel very good about the Canadian situation and indeed, about the North American situation." 

 Martin indicated he had confidence in the safety mechanisms that shut down the Toronto Stock Exchange on Monday during late afternoon trading. 

 "Trading and settlement mechanisms and market safety measures all worked well," Martin said in his statement. 

 The TSE, battered by heavy selling through the day, closed early after its key 300 index fell 434.29 points to 6599.20, mirroring losses on the New York Stock Exchange's Dow Jones index, which fell 554.26 points and was closed 30 minutes early at 7161.15.

title: FOCUS-Toronto stocks post biggest-ever point drop.
text:
TORONTO, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Toronto Stock Exchange posted its biggest one-day point loss in history on Monday, as Canada's biggest equities market was walloped by stock losses in Asia and a 12-year low for gold prices. 

 Toronto's benchmark 300 Composite Index tumbled 434.29 points or 6.17 percent to 6599.20. The drop shattered the previous point loss record of 400.37 points set on "Black Monday," on Oct. 19, 1987. 

 Volume was 122.6 million shares, worth C$2.14 billion ($1.52 billion). Officials shut down trading one-half hour early at 3:30 P.M. EST (2030 GMT) because of the losses. Toronto trading was also suspended briefly earlier in the afternoon. 

 In New York, the Dow Jones Industrial Average also posted its biggest ever single-day loss, falling 554.26 points or 7.18 percent to 7161.15. Trading was also halted before the regular 4 P.M. EST (2100 GMT) close on the New York Stock Exchange. 

 In percentage terms, it was Toronto's fourth biggest ever decline. The record percentage loss was 11.13 percent on Black Monday in 1987. 

 "We haven't got over the Asian flu yet. We're being hit by Asia and the idea the Swiss might sell off their gold," said Fred Ketchen, senior vice president at Toronto brokerage ScotiaMcLeod. 

 Losses in Toronto were aggravated by the plunge in gold to $311.80 an ounce on Monday, its lowest price since July 8, 1985. Toronto's 300 Index has a heavy resource weighting. 

 Toronto's gold and precious metals index fell 770.06 points or 9.57 percent on Monday. 

 Gold traders said the market overreacted to a Swiss proposal last Friday to sell 1,400 tonnes of gold. The plan must be approved by parliament and a referendum in 1999. 

 Jack Geller, acting chairman of the Ontario Securities Commission, said that his agency was "closely monitoring the situation and will continue to do so in the morning when markets reopen." 

 Geller said his agency, which regulates stock trading in Toronto, Canada's biggest equities market, consulted through the day with regulators elsewhere in Canada and in the United States. 

 Montreal-based equities strategist Bill Ram said that "everybody's got to start making new computer models of global growth because of these low currencies in the Far East." 

 Weaker currencies in southeast Asia threaten to cut import demand for basic commodities. 

 The market rout also sent the Canadian dollar tumbling to a two-year closing low of 71.33 U.S. cents despite at least three rounds of intervention by Canada's central bank. 

 The only winners on the day were Canadian long bonds, which rallied as tumbling North American stock markets eased concerns that central banks would hike short-term interest rates. 

 "It's like a bungee cord market," said Hank Cunningham, director of fixed-income at First Marathon Securities Ltd. 

 "This morning investors were worried the U.S. Federal Reserve would increase rates, but after today's stunning selloff in North American stock markets, rate hikes would further scare equities players," he said.

 'The Bank of Canada has got itself into a bit of a pickle,' said a dealer with one of the major Canadian banks. Indeed, many traders said a break of C$1.4024 could set off stop-loss orders to sell the Canadian currency, and accelerate its decline. (see story on page 4346 for the intervention rounds.) 

 Markets were rocked Monday as another sharp loss in Hong Kong stocks set the stage for a similar sell off in New York and Toronto. The Dow Jones Industrials plunged 554.26 to 7,161.15 before trading was halted, while the Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 composite index was off 434.3 points at 6,599.2. 

 What's more, the market faces a key test in the third-quarter employment cost (ECI) index out of the U.S. on Tuesday. If the index is strong it will fuel talk of a near-term U.S. interest rate increase, which would likely exaccerbate stock losses and the Canadian dollar's troubles. Forecasts call for a 0.8% increase. 

 Some observers said Canadian losses resulted as speculative investors pressed for a level at which the Bank of Canada will actually raise short-term interest rates to defend the currency. It's seen vulnerable given extremely low short-term interest rates relative to the U.S. and a widening current-account deficit. (see story on page 4224) 

 The central bank made clear when it raised interest rates Oct. 1 that it would like to move gradually toward tighter monetary policy. However, many analysts think it is no rush to do so and particularly wants to avoid a move that is unlikely to have lingering impact on the Canadian currency. 'In this sort of market it's not clear how much it would help the currency,' said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada.

title: =Turbulent Global Markets Could Hasten Rate Hike In Canada
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--Tumultuous trading in global
financial markets is helping to unsettle the Canadian dollar
and could hasten the next rate increase from the Bank of
Canada, analysts say.
   The wide gap between lower yielding Canadian debt
instruments and their U.S. counterparts and a recent turn
for the worse in Canada's balance of payments leaves the
country's dollar much weaker and vulnerable to the unsettled
trading now gripping global stock and currency markets.
   As Southeast Asia's currency troubles reached the Hong
Kong dollar last week, they sparked a precipitous plunge in
Hong Kong stocks that rippled through the world's major
stock exchanges and many of its currencies. The turmoil
initially boosted the Canadian dollar, but traders say that
since then there's been some selling associated with the
action.
   "We are getting awfully close to a rate hike in this
country," said Michael Gregory, fixed-income economist with
Lehman Brothers Canada.
   The U.S.



 dollar surged against its Canadian counterpart
Monday, touching C$1.3980 and prompting the Bank of Canada
to intervene to sell U.S. dollars. Further central bankintervention will be required to keep a lid on the U.S.
dollar's rise, observers said. At mid-afternoon, the U.S.
dollar was trading at C$1.3997, up from C$1.3918 at Friday's
close.
   That's because losses by the Canadian dollar leave
monetary conditions as loose as they were on Sept. 30, the
day before the Bank of Canada last raised its bank rate, by
1/4 point to 3.75%. As part of an export-driven economy, the
Canadian dollar's trading level is an important determinant
of the level of economic stimulus and growth. The U.S.
dollar hit a low of C$1.3690 after the rate increase.
   Central bankers signaled at that time a strong desire
for less stimulative monetary conditions, so much so that
analysts say if their words are to remain credible, the
central bank will have to bump rates up again to strengthen
the currency and tighten credit conditions.

The bank habitually intervenes in the market on intraday movements of 70 ticks or more in either direction. But it steps in early sometimes, as it did June 25, just a day before it last raised interest rates in defense of the currency. 

 And its the timing of the next rate increase that will preoccupy currency dealers as speculative type players sense the potential to force the central bank to move rates again. Pyle said if the U.S. dollar closes below C$1.3755 it might keep some speculative sellers at bay. But they'll be hovering to exploit any opportunities - it's Pyle's view that if the U.S. dollar reaches C$1.3900 or over, the Bank of Canada will again raise interest rates.

 It's feared prolonged Canadian dollar weakness may eventually overstimulate the economy by fueling the huge export sector at a time when domestic demand is already surging. Some analysts say it could take a series of rate increases to reverse the trend if the bank doesn't act soon. 

 "The intervention could be an early sign the Bank of Canada is becoming uncomfortable with" the level of monetary conditions in the economy, agreed David Rosenberg, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns Inc. 

 Traders said the central bank began selling U.S. dollars around C$1.3960 just before noon EDT (1600 GMT), just C$0.0052 above Tuesday's close and well ahead of what would have been the bank's normal intervention point this session.  The monetary conditions index (MCI) sits at minus 6.26, near record lows. The index measures the aggregate impact of interest rate and currency movements on monetary conditions in the economy and is an important guide to Bank of Canada policy. The lower the index, the easier monetary conditions. 

 "I would say they are beginning to respond to the fact that the MCI is getting too easy relative to demand momentum," said Andrew Spence, senior economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

title: FOCUS-Canada dollar rallies on bank comments.
text:
TORONTO, May 15 (Reuter) - Canada's dollar rose almost one U.S. cent on Thursday in its most volatile session since Quebec's 1995 sovereignty referendum, after Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen suggested the need for a shift to a less stimulative monetary policy. 

 The dollar rocketed to C$1.3710 (US$0.7293) in late trading after opening the North American session at C$1.3846 (US$0.7222). The currency closed on Wednesday at C$1.3893 (US$0.7197). 

 The rally prompted repeated intervention during the day by the Bank of Canada, which began selling Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars at the C$1.3828 (US$0.7231) level. 

 "The bank's been in everywhere. They're coming in every five or 10 points," one trader said. 

 The dollar began to rise after the central bank released its semi-annual monetary policy report, which indicated the bank's willingness to shift to a more neutral monetary policy from a stimulative one if inflation remained stable. 

 Strong fundamentals in the economy, low inflation and improvments in Canada's fiscal policy "continue to underpin market expectations of a future appreciation of the Canadian dollar," the report said. 

 Thiessen confirmed the bank's confidence in the currency when he told a news conference, "I really believe the underlying trend is upward and I know that on balance it has tended to be weak recently after the American interest rate move." 

 The prospect that the central bank would stop resisting future U.S. interest rate hikes had an immediate effect on the dollar as investors snapped up heavy volumes of Canadian bonds and securities. 

 Canadian bonds, which typically trade in the same direction as U.S. treasuries, were sharply higher today, while U.S. treasuries slumped. 

 "The idea that the bank is going to switch to a less stimulative monetary policy comes as a relief to the foreign exchange market," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst for MMS International. 

 The Canadian dollar has depreciated by five percent since January, due mostly to concerns over diverging policies between the U.S. Federal Reserve and Canada's central bank. 

 "This rally is all about what is going right for the Canadian economy," Palombi said. 

 Analysts also said that early morning U.S. data indicating largely stable consumer prices helped prepare the Canada dollar for its impressive showing. 

 The U.S. Labor Department reported that the monthy Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.1 percent in April, as forecast last week by a Reuters survey of economists.

title: Battered Canadian dollar hits 2-year low.
text:
TORONTO, April 11 (Reuter) - The Canadian dollar was under siege on Friday, pounded to a two-year low by signs of rising U.S. inflation and signals that Canada's central bank may resist hiking domestic interest rates. 

 The currency was trading at C$1.3982 (71.52 U.S. cents) -- its lowest point since April 3, 1995 -- as investors unloaded the dollar in heavy selling. 

 Bank of Canada intervention to buy the dollar and support it at the C$1.3960 (71.63 U.S. cents) level on Friday failed to stem the markets' strong anti-Canada bias. 

 "The dollar is vulnerable right now. It could easily hit C$1.4000 (71.42 U.S. cents) before it rebounds," said John Anania, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada. 

 Friday's sell-off followed U.S. indicators showing inflation worries were reviving in the United States. 

 The U.S. Commerce Department reported that the core producer price index rose by a higher than expected 0.4 percent in March, with retail sales growing 0.2 percent. 

 Analysts said U.S. inflationary pressures could push the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates again in May and force the Bank of Canada to raise its rates in defense of the flagging Canadian dollar. 

 A 25-basis-point rate hike by the Fed on March 25 widened the spread between U.S. and Canadian short-term rates to more than 200 points, pressuring the Canadian dollar and renewing calls for the Bank of Canada to follow suit. 

 Canada's dollar has shed almost four percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since January as investors moved to buy the higher yielding U.S. short-term securities. 

 "Canada (the dollar) is going to get hurt in this environment of rising U.S. interest rates," said William Chin, vice-president of foreign exchange with ABN-AMRO Bank. 

 He added that the central bank was unlikely to raise interest rates, now at 30-year lows after 11 interest rate cuts last year. 

 Early last year, the Bank of Canada began pursuing a "made in Canada" interest rate policy aimed at revitalising Canada's lackluster economy. The bank's rate slashing last year was independent of action by the Fed. 

 Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Timothy Noel may have tipped the central bank's hand on Thursday when he told Reuters in Lima, Peru that the central bank would not react to "every wiggle" in the currency. 

 "The bank does not want to react to every wiggle in the dollar," said Noel, adding that the bank would raise interest rates only if monetary conditions warranted such a move. 

 Noel's comments triggered a slide in the Canada dollar on Thursday, forcing the bank to intervene and to shore up the currency. 

 But Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Charles Freedman appeared to step back from those remarks on Friday when he said at a conference in New York that the central bank kept close tabs on exchange rate movements. 

 But some economists said the beating of the drums for a Canadian interest rate hike flew in the face of Canada's economic situation. 

 "The Bank of Canada is focused on deflation. A cheaper Canadian dollar helps them with that battle by easing overall monetary conditions and by pushing domestic prices up," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics, in a commentary released on Friday. 

 The persistent challenging of the central bank to do something about the falling dollar "is getting boring," Weinberg said.

TORONTO, April 10 (Reuter) - Canadian bonds closed weaker on Thursday, underperforming U.S. treasuries as a sharp drop in the value of the Canadian dollar to two-year lows and a softer U.S. bond market weighed on prices, analysts said. 

 "We're starting to see slightly more aggressive selling into the close," said Andrew Pyle, head of fixed-income research with ABN-AMRO Bank Canada. "It's the weakness in the Canadian dollar and if you look to the U.S. curve, things improved a little bit, but the tone is still weak." 

 Canada's 30-year benchmark bond fell C$0.40 to C$107.00 to yield 7.390 percent. 

 The U.S. 30-year bond fell 3/32 to yield 7.11 percent. The spread between the two widened to 28 basis points from 25 basis points at Wednesday's close. 

 Canadian and U.S. bonds began the session lower as investors looked ahead nervously to the release of Friday's U.S. economic data. The U.S. retail sales and producer price reports for March were expected to provided further clues about whether the U.S. Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee would hike rates again when it met in May. 

 But Canadian bonds were also hit by a drop in the Canadian dollar to a two-year low later in the session. 

 The Canadian dollar weakened after comments from a Bank of Canada official led to a selloff and intervention by the central bank. 

 Traders said the Bank of Canada bought Canadian dollars to support the currency when it hit a new two-year low at C$1.3945 (US$0.7171). 

 The currency eased after the central bank's Deputy Governor Tim Noel told Reuters in Lima, Peru that the Bank would not react to "every wiggle" in the currency, suggesting it had no plans to raise interest rates. 

 "A lot of players here in the domestic market are going to be factoring in a possible move up to the the C$1.40 level. If that's the case, then you're going to see the entire Canadian curve really underperform the U.S., regardless of what kind of data comes out tomorrow morning," said Pyle. 

 In other prices, the Government of Canada's 10-year benchmark bond fell C$0.30 to C$100.80 to yield 6.884 percent while the U.S. bond fell 2/32 to yield 6.91 percent.

title: Heat on Bank of Canada to prop up weak dollar.
text:
TORONTO, April 2 (Reuter) - Canada's bleeding dollar will remain in intensive care unless the Bank of Canada intervenes to match a recent U.S. interest rate hike, economists said on Wednesday. 

 The Canadian dollar weakened past the key C$1.3900 (US$0.7194) level this week, setting off another round of speculation that the central bank would raise its key bank rate by 25 basis points to shore up the currency. 

 The central bank has not raised its key bank rate, which currently sits at a 35-year-low of 3.25 percent, since February 1995. 

 "What we have to see is the Bank of Canada actually signalling to markets that monetary conditions should be moving on a slightly tighter track," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. 

 Gregory said he expected the central bank to raise rates within the next week. 

 A Canadian rate hike would match a similar move by the U.S. Federal Reserve. Last week, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan raised U.S. rates 25 basis points in a pre-emptive strike amid signs of creeping U.S. inflation. 

 If U.S. growth continued its torrid pace, Greenspan would likely raise rates again when the Fed meets in May -- a move that could spell the end of the Bank of Canada's so-called "made-in-Canada" interest rate policy. 

 That policy refers to Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen's decision in 1995 to lower Canadian interest rates even while U.S. interest rates were unchanged. 

 "Markets clearly view last week's (U.S.) rate hike as the first in a series of Fed tightenings," said Stephen Wateridge, managing director of corporate foreign exchange for CIBC Wood Gundy. 

 The widening of the spread between Canadian and U.S. interest rates to 225 basis points has already triggered a stampede of Canada-dollar selling in overseas markets. 

 The Canadian dollar has lost more than 3.0 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar in the past two months. 

 Only domestic corporate buying of Canada dollars and some recent interest by Canadian exporters to hold the Canadian currency had stemmed a further collapse of the currency, Wateridge said. 

 The steady erosion of the dollar flies in the face of Canada's relatively strong economic fundamentals, which had been expected to help underpin the currency in a crisis. 

 Canada's economy was expected to grow more than 3.0 percent in 1997, while inflation should remain within the central bank's target range of 1.0-3.0 percent, according to a Reuters poll of economists. 

 But jittery equity markets and controversy surrounding junior mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd have added to the interest rate pressure on the dollar. 

 Speculation that Bre-X's Indonesian gold mine may contain much less gold than previously reported has set off a selling frenzy in mining stocks on the Toronto Stock Exchange. 

 Thiessen, however, appears unfazed by the bellowing for a quick interest rate strike. 

 The Bank of Canada has more room to maneuver now than it did before, but that should not be interpreted as a pledge not to raise interest rates, Thiessen recently told reporters.

title: Canadian dollar rallies on economic strength.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 16 (Reuter) - The Canadian dollar has soared more than two U.S. cents so far this year and could hit 75 U.S. cents this week on the way to its highest level in almost three years, currency analysts predicted on Thursday. 

 "We definitely have a shot at it," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange adviser at brokerage CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc. 

 Economists said this week's rally could propel the dollar to 75.75 U.S. cents within the next week. The dollar has not been that high since February 1994. 

 The Canadian currency was trading at 74.70 U.S. cents on Thursday after rising half a U.S. cent on Wednesday. 

 The surge comes amid heightening domestic and international investor confidence in the Canadian economy, which is expected to show much stronger growth this year. 

 "We're pretty bullish on the Canadian economy," said Doug Porter, senior economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns. 

 Nesbitt forecast that Canada's economy would grow by 3.3 percent this year versus an estimated 1.4 percent in 1996. 

 Canadian traders expected the Bank of Canada to intervene in the market to smooth the dollar's rise, but said the central bank was unlikely to cut interest rates to try to halt the rally. 

 "I don't think we're at that point in terms of the strength in the Canada (dollar) where a cut in rates is a possibility as yet," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal. 

 Some economists predicted the Bank of Canada would let the currency rise to 80 U.S. cents this year without cutting interest rates. 

 The Canadian dollar last flirted with the top of its 72 to 75 U.S. cent range on Nov. 7, 1996. The next day the Bank of Canada trimmed short-term interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point, sparking a fall in the currency over the following two months to a low of 72.69 U.S. cents on Jan. 2. 

 Economists said Canada's brighter economic outlook was restraining the Bank of Canada from a further rate cut. 

 "We're getting new evidence that maybe growth is moving to a higher level and as a result there just doesn't seem to be a need to ease overall monetary conditions," said Bank of Montreal's Ferley. 

 The stronger dollar was seen benefiting the Canadian consumer, but was less of a blessing for exporters, who have accounted for most of Canada's growth in the past two years. 

 "They've (exporters) had an easy ride from the currency for a long time now," said Anita Lauria, economist at Salomon Brothers in New York. "The question really is how quickly do manufacturers continue to respond on the cost side."
