title: FOCUS-Canadian financial markets weaken sharply.
text:
TORONTO, Dec 5 (Reuter) - Canadian financial markets weakened sharply on Thursday, with traders citing several causes for what they called a "made-in-Canada meltdown." 

 Canadian bonds, stocks and the dollar all ended the session sharply lower in a broad-based selloff. 

 "I don't think you can lay your finger on any single factor. It's a number of events that are happening in a reasonably thin market," said Mark Chandler, a senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada. "I think you can argue the genesis of it was the weakness in the currency." 

 The Canadian dollar opened sharply weaker this morning, softening past the key C$1.3600 (US$0.7353) level. The dollar's weakness prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene in the currency markets several times, buying Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars. 

 Analysts tied the markets' drop to waning expectations about another Bank of Canada interest rate cut, investors withdrawing bets that Canadian bonds would outperform U.S. issues and attempts by traders to lock in profits. 

 Dealers said the weaker currency made a near-term rate cut by the central bank highly unlikely. Many traders had expected a cut in order to loosen monetary conditions and spur economic growth in Canada. 

 Analysts said the weaker dollar achieved the same effect by making Canadian exports more competitive. 

 Weakness in the currency and waning rate cut hopes contributed to -- but were also partly caused by -- weakness in Canadian bonds, analysts said. 

 Canadian bond prices plunged by mid-morning, posting some of their largest one-day losses in more than two years. Canada's benchmark 30-year bond recovered slightly by midafternoon, but was still down C$3.10 to C$110.85 with a yield of 7.086 percent. 

 Analysts said the selling came from domestic and foreign investors, who made profits this year betting that Canadian bonds would strengthen more than those in the United States. 

 Dealers said too many investors tried to sell Canadian bonds on Thursday to try to lock in profits before year end, causing prices to erode. 

 "In Canada, when everyone runs for the door at the same time, it creates a little bit of a bottleneck," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. "It has not been a lot of players. It's just a lot of big money leaving at the same time." 

 The selloff in the bond market and waning rate cut expectations in turn hurt the Canadian stock market, analysts said. The benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 index was down more than one percent on the day, despite gains on Wall Street, which Toronto usually tracks. 

 Stocks were led lower by financial services and bank stocks, which are the most heavily weighed subgroup of the 300 index. 

 Dealers were mixed on the near-term outlook for Canadian financial markets. Although Canada's positive fundamentals, such as low inflation, remain in place, investors will be keenly studying key November employment data due on Friday. 

 "The thing to watch out for obviously is the (Canada and U.S.) payroll reports," said Goldman's Chandler. "If we get positive surprises in terms of growth there, you could get more follow-through selling."

title: Bank of Canada cuts key interest rate to 3.50 percent.
text:
OTTAWA, Oct. 28 (Reuter) - The Bank of Canada on Monday cut its key bank rate to 3.50 percent from 3.75 percent, the lowest short-term interest rate Canada has seen in 36 years. 

 The move quickly prompted five of Canada's six major chartered banks to lower their prime lending rates to 5.0 percent from 5.25 percent, their lowest level since July 1956. 

 The bank rate, which has changed in nature over past decades, is now at its lowest level since August 1963. 

 It was the 10th rate cut this year by the Bank of Canada, and the 19th since the central bank began easing in May 1995. The Bank of Canada has now cut rates by 475 basis points since May 1995 in a bid to jump-start Canada's sluggish economy. 

 Through direct intervention in the money market, the central bank dropped its target range for the overnight lending rate to 3.0-3.50 percent from 3.25-3.75 percent. 

 The Bank of Canada uses the bank rate for loans it gives to financial institutions as lender of last resort. It is the top of the central bank's target range for the overnight rate. 

 Canadian Treasury bills firmed after the rate cut, while the currency and bonds traded steady.

title: Bank of Canada lowers rates independently of U.S..
text:
TORONTO, March 21 (Reuter) - In a bid to boost the sluggish economy, the Bank of Canada Thursday cut key interest rates to below comparable U.S. rates for the first time in more than a year. 

 Canada's central bank cut short-term rates independently of the U.S. Federal Reserve for the second time this year, a move that weakened the Canadian dollar. 

 "They bit the bullet and said we need lower rates," said Joshua Mendelsohn, chief economist with the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. "There are some signs of improvement (in the economy) but it's still pretty sluggish." 

 The central bank said in a statement that the relatively rare independent cut in domestic rates was consistent with the country's good inflation performance. 

 "The argument has always been that Canada's low inflation rate should allow it to have rates equal to or lower than the U.S., so you have that at work," said Mendelsohn. 

 The central bank also said the recent appreciation in the value of the Canadian dollar "contributed to a positive backdrop in financial markets for this move." 

 The Bank of Canada intervened in the money market early Thursday to lower the centre of the target range for its overnight lending rate by a quarter point to 5.0 percent -- below the U.S. overnight bank lending rate, or federal funds rate, of 5.25 percent, for the first time since December 1994. 

 The Bank of Canada had hesitated in reducing rates below similar U.S. rates because of concerns such a move would weaken the Canadian dollar. 

 But the currency fell only marginally after the rate cut, slipping to US$0.7342 from its open of US$0.7366. 

 "We have dropped interest rates remarkably and it hasn't had an adverse impact on our currency," said John Kellett, vice-president of equities with Royal Bank of Canada. "(The currency) has done very well." 

 The Canadian dollar has appreciated by almost 1 1/2 U.S. cents in the past month, providing room for the central bank to cut. 

 The currency was strengthened by positive investor response to this month's federal budget, strong economic fundamentals, and recent comments by Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard that a referendum on separation will be delayed until after a provincial election is held sometime before 1998.

title: Canadian dollar rallies after Quebec poll results.
text:
(All figures U.S. dollars unless specified) 

 TORONTO (Reuter) - The Canadian dollar soared past 75 cents Tuesday for the first time since February 1994 amid mounting confidence that Quebec voters will reject sovereignty in an Oct. 30 referendum. 

 Economists said the Canadian dollar was propelled by the latest opinion poll, released overnight and conducted by the SOM-Environics agency, which showed that 48 percent of voters in the French-speaking province opposed splitting from Canada, while 39 percent supported it. 

 "The only uncertainty that seems to be left is the margin of victory for the 'No' side," said Andrew Spence, chief economist with Citibank Canada. "More and more people are thinking that the 'No' side is going to win and they don't want to miss out on the value of Canadian dollar assets." 

 The Canadian dollar surged to 75.32 cents in the morning, prompting direct intervention from the Bank of Canada. Traders said the Bank sold Canadian dollars for U.S. currency at 75.30 cents in an effort to take some of the steam out of the rally. 

 Later profit taking took the Canadian dollar back to 75.13 cents. 

 Canada's Finance Minister Paul Martin also attributed the dollar strength to the poll results, calling them "very conclusive." He told reporters in Ottawa that his views were in line with financial market analysts. 

 Rumours that influential U.S. investor George Soros was in the market buying up to C$300 million, also helped lift the currency, although a spokesman for Soros declined to comment. 

 "It is the policy of Soros Fund management not to comment on rumours," said Soros spokesman Shawn Pattison. 

 "He (Soros) likes Canada. He's got Canada right. The turmoil in Canada over the last three weeks kept him away but now it looks as though he's back," said one New York-based economist who declined to be named. 

 Economists said the political uncertainty surrounding the Quebec referendum has so far been insufficient to keep investors from buying Canadian dollars. 

 "Politics always creates some volatility, but the lesson from the past is that it is temporary," said Clement Gignac, chief economist of Montreal-based Levesque Beaubien Geoffrion. 

 Gignac noted that while the Canadian dollar may be hit by referendum-related investor nervousness in the near term, the long-term fundamentals for the currency are very positive. 

 "Fundamentals are showing that this currency is undervalued. With the fundamentals favourable for commodity prices, favourable for the U.S. dollar and with the (government) downsizing in Canada, we have a recipe for a stronger Canadian dollar," he said. 

 Citibank's Spence agreed and predicted that the Canadian dollar is headed toward 76.62 cents after the referendum. 

 Gignac said the Canadian dollar is likely to climb even higher, reaching 77-78 cents over the next nine months to a year, irrespective of the outcome of the Quebec referendum. 

 "I am not a political expert. But based on our experience, the market will return to fundamentals after the referendum and the fundamentals are good," Gignac said, adding that an independent Quebec government would likely focus on fiscal responsibility and debt reduction. 

 Analysts also noted that a strong Canadian dollar will open the door for further interest rate cuts by the Bank of Canada. Such cuts, they said, are unlikely before the referendum is over, but once the Quebec issue has been resolved, interest rates could drop by a full percentage point over the near term. 

 "If that (the Quebec issue) gets resolved positively, I would think that short-term rates could come down probably ... by 100 basis points (1 percentage point)," Bruce Galloway, vice chairman of Royal Bank of Canada, told a treasury management conference in Calgary on Monday. 

 Canada's central bank has targeted short-term rates at a range of 6 to 6.5 percent.

title: Canada 's  central bank  to  intervene  less in the market.
text:
TORONTO (Reuter) - Canada's central bank said Thursday it will intervene less often in currency markets to influence the rate of its dollar because frequent actions have become less effective. 

 In an April 5 letter to major dealers obtained by Reuters, the Bank of Canada said Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin approved the change in policy. 

 "We expect this change in intervention tactics will result in less frequent incidents of intervention, but when intervention does take place, it is likely to be carried out in a more visible manner by intervening in larger amounts and using foreign exchange brokers more often," the letter said. 

 The Canadian dollar has suffered under frequent bouts of volatility since the Mexican financial crisis rocked North American currencies late last year. In January the Canadian dollar hit a nine-year low of 70.07 cents, but rallied back in recent weeks to its current 72.87 cents level. 

 Bank of Canada officials confirmed the contents of the letter but cautioned the tactics will not change the Bank's basic stance toward the Canadian dollar. 

 "We're just changing the technicalities of carrying out intervention," said an official at the Bank of Canada. "We're not really changing our policy toward the Canadian dollar." 

 In the letter the Bank of Canada said it will intervene after a certain amount of exchange rate movement in any given trading day, but will not necessarily continue at that same level the following day. 

 "An assessment of underlying pressures on the exchange rate will be factored into the determination of the point at which intervention will continue," the letter said. 

 It said the new strategy will mean the central bank will intervene less frequently, but will not change the bank's policy of maintaining orderly Canadian markets and smoothing out any large moves in the Canadian dollar. 

 The Bank said it will also use larger amounts in each intervention trade. 

 The changes come as the result of a recently completed review of intervention policy by the Bank of Canada, the first since the 1980s, the letter said. 

 "Such a review has recently been undertaken and the conclusions of this work support the idea that foreign exchange market intervention is most useful when used as a signalling tool," the letter said. 

 The Bank said it realised that its previous strategy had become less useful because of the growth of the market. 

 "The current system (of intervention), which could be described as one of maintaining orderly markets by leaning against the wind during periods of large or rapid exchange movements was last reviewed in the 1980s," the Bank said. 

 It said the frequency of its current intervention strategy reduces the newsworthiness of the move. 

 "Our analysis of the current intervention techniques we use is that they are not as effective as they could be in this regard," the Bank said.

title: Canada dollar tumble forces interest rate rise.
text:
TORONTO (Reuter) - The Canadian dollar plunged to a new nine-year low on growing investor jitters Tuesday, forcing the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates to near two-year highs. 

 The Canadian dollar has tumbled three-quarters of a U.S. cent in two days, reaching a low of C$1.4145 (70.69 cents) despite intervention by the central bank. 

 The Bank of Canada managed to slow the decline only by raising its target range for a key money market rate, the overnight call loan rate, by 0.5 percentage point. 

 The Canadian dollar has come under pressure due to concern about the country's debt and about the crisis in Mexico. Asian investors were cited as some of the biggest sellers, traders said. 

 "Higher budget deficits and Quebec sovereignty heating up -- there are a combination of things that are not looking favourable for Canada," one Canadian currency trader said. 

 Dealers say the Canadian dollar remains on an overall downward trend, regardless of short-term fluctuations. 

 However, ecconomists disagree whether the move in the call loan rate foreshadowed a long-term trend to higher rates in Canada or was a one-time effort to shore up the currency. 

 "We viewed it as an attempt to shore up the currency. It would not be an indication that the Bank (of Canada) is trying to tighten policy," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at the Bank of Montreal. 

 However, other economists argued that such a short-term view may lead to further weakness if speculators smell blood and savage the Canadian dollar again in the next few days. 

 "That will probably leave them exposed to further downward pressure on the currency as speculators perhaps get a sense that the Bank wants to mount a defence of the currency," said Citibank Canada economist Andrew Spence. 

 The fall in the currency prompted a 12-basis-point rise in the Bank of Canada's key lending rate, the rate that guides banks' commercial and retail rates, to 7.24 percent. 

 Royal Bank's Wright said the rate move could be the Bank of Canada's attempt to pre-empt a widely expected rise in U.S. rates by the Federal Reserve at the end of January. 

 "Today (the Bank of Canada) moved ahead of the Fed," Royal Bank of Canada economist Craig Wright said. "Last time around they waited and waited and moved after the Fed."

title: Canadian Dollar Suffers Some Spillover From Mexico Crisis
text:
TORONTO (AP-DJ)--Shock waves from the economic crisis in Mexico have helped send the Canadian dollar to almost nine-year lows against the U.S. dollar in recent trading sessions, some analysts say. 

 The Canadian dollar, already weakened by perceptions that Canadian interest rates are too low and by worries ahead of the federal budget statement in February, is also seeing some selling as a result of the recent sharp fall in Mexico's new peso, the analysts say. 

 They say there's a trend towards judging the Canadian dollar with the same criteria used on Mexican holdings - and at the moment, the market's verdict is a move to the safe haven of the U.S. dollar. 

 'We've seen a pattern where the Canadian dollar weakens with the Mexican peso. It's a sympathetic reaction; although fundamentals are different, these are two North American currencies with enormous current account deficits and political instability,' says Mark Schwartz, a foreign exchange trader at Lehman Brothers in New York. 

 On Tuesday, as the Mexican new peso plunged again, the U.S. dollar strengthened sharply against the Canadian dollar, despite reported intervention by Canada's central bank in defense of the Canadian currency.

title: Canadian dollar hits new low after weak jobs data.
text:
TORONTO, July 10 (Reuters) - Canada's limping dollar received another blow on Friday, when nervous selling sparked by surprisingly weak employment data sent the currency down to record lows. 

 Before trimming some losses, the Canadian dollar fell to a record trading low of C$1.4795 (US$0.6759) on Friday. 

 A week ago, it stood at C$1.4690 to the U.S. dollar (US$0.6807). 

 Traders, who had expected some growth in job creation, sold Canadian dollars on news that the country's employment fell for the second consecutive month in June. 

 Total employment fell by 35,900 to 14.24 million with most declines recorded in the agricultural sector, after a drop of 7,300 in May. The jobless rate was unchanged at 8.4 percent. 

 Canadians may see more weakness on the jobs front in July as the impact of the General Motors plant shutdowns in North America was not fully reflected in the latest data. 

 The Bank of Canada, the nation's central bank, has so far stood by and let the currency slide because its retreat has been fairly orderly. 

 Economists and market participants expect the bank to hold off raising its key lending rate for a while. Such a move would would be expected to lure investors into Canadian assets, boosting dollar demand. 

 Mario Angastiniotis, senior economist at Standard & Poor's MMS, said the Bank of Canada is likely to intervene in the market to sell U.S. dollars around the key psychological level of C$1.4800 (US$0.6757). 

 "As long as there's no momentum behind to push it (the U.S. dollar) to higher spot levels (against the Canadian dollar), I think the bank will basically let it ride without doing anything on the interest rate front," he told Reuters Television. 

 The only support for the Canadian dollar appears to be coming from occasional slips in the U.S. dollar's value against key currencies, such as the German mark and Japanese yen. 

 The U.S. dollar fell against the mark on Friday as the market turned more optimistic after Thursday's bearish views of Russia's economic problems. This pulled the currency down to 140 yen, albeit for a short period, from above 141 yen. 

 Financial markets remained wary because of uncertainty over the prospect of Japan's ruling party under Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto surviving the Upper House election on Sunday and delivering on promised fiscal stimulus measures. 

 The Canadian dollar is vulnerable to safe-haven capital flows to the United States. The U.S. dollar has in the past firmed against all major currencies when concerns grew over the world's troubled regions, such as Asia and Russia. 

 "The Canadian dollar story has been a global story until today. The weakness in the exchange rate was clearly reflecting the weakness in the commodities prices, which are relevant to Canada," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Bank Securities. "However, we're beginning to see signs of slowdown domestically, and the question is if that slowdown is temporary or something more permanent." 

 Technical analysts foresee further medium-term weakness in the Canadian dollar, which has been sliding since mid-March when it peaked at C$1.4073 (US$0.7106) in the current cycle. 

 Canada's bearish jobs report came on the heels of Thursday's news of a 4.6 percent drop in June housing starts, making the third consecutive month of declines. Construction industry strikes in the key province of Ontario were blamed.

title: Canada to swap bond proceeds to US dlrs-dealers.
text:
NEW YORK, June 22 (Reuters) - Canada will swap proceeds of its planned four billion mark 10-year bond offering into floating-rate U.S. dollars, according to swaps dealers in New York. 

 The floating rate U.S. dollar proceeds will be tied to the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR), according to dealers. 

 Some of the funds may be used to replenish dollar reserves Canada spent defending the Canadian dollar against the U.S. currency in the most recent round of intervention by the Bank of Canada last Monday, dealers said. 

 A part of the swapped funds will be invested in U.S. securities with maturities less than one-year, according to some traders. 

 An official at the Ministry of Finance in Canada declined to say what currency the end-proceeds would be held in. He only said that proceeds would be used for the country's foreign exchange reserves. 

 The issue will be priced off the German bunds curve rather than any one issue, dealers said. Deutsche Bank and Credit Suisse First Boston are lead-managers.

title: Canada bonds open weaker as U.S. dlr, bonds fall.
text:
TORONTO, June 18 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds opened weaker on Friday, moving in a tight range ahead of the weekend, as some funds flowed back into equities and a weaker U.S. dollar hurt the sentiment of North American bonds. 

 A fall in the U.S. dollar to 134 yen on Friday after a rebound to 138 yen on Thursday was depressing U.S. treasuries, which opened lower on profit-taking overseas. 

 U.S. bonds have gained sharply in recent weeks from the notion that economic crises in Asia and Russia would continue to drive global capital seeking a safe haven into U.S. dollar assets. 

 "We are mostly following the U.S. market today. The price action is... there's not whole a lot going on," said Jeoff Hall, managing Canadian market analyst at Technical Data in Boston. "The trend lower comes in lower volume." 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond fell C$0.37 to C$135.37 to yield 5.534 percent. 

 Its U.S. 30-year counterpart fell 12/32 to yield 5.74 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread was 21 basis points after 20 points at the previous close here. 

 Bonds are down as some expect a further fall in the U.S. dollar against the yen as deputies to the Group of Seven finance ministers gather in Tokyo to discuss a broad range of economic issues in Japan and Asia. 

 Positive statements by Summers on Tokyo's bid to jump-start its economy and implement structural reform could trigger more buying of yen versus the U.S. dollar. 

 Some nervousness stemmed from talk that two ailing Japanese banks, Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and Nippon Credit Bank, would be delisted, Hall said. The two banks denied a report of a possible merger between the two overnight. 

 Canada's five-year bond was falling ahead of U.S. two-and five-year note auctions next week. 

 When the U.S. dollar was forging ahead against all major currencies until Washington and Tokyo staged a rare joint intervention on Wednesday, it wasn't just Canada's problem. 

 But now the Canadian dollar doesn't rally when the yen rallies, and currency dealers are asking themselves what will happen to the Canadian dollar when the yen goes back down to 145 yen to the U.S. dollar? 

 And this weakness sometimes spills into Canadian bonds. 

 "Right now the Bank of Canada has really got its back up against the wall right now," Hall said. "There was a lot of consideration given to today being the day when the Bank of Canada would hike rates, and didn't happen, so the Canadian dollar was an easy target for sellers." 

 "I don't think it's a long-term phenomenon, but as we get into next week, Monday and Tuesday, I think that the rate watch vigil gets all in earnest." he predicted. 

 Hall said he did not agree with a rate increase at this stage to boost the Canadian dollar, but added that could be "a necessary evil." 

 "To be consistent with their prior action and words, then certainly it looks like a rate hike would justified," he said. 

 Canada's dollar has been under pressure from weak prices of commodities, a pillar of the nation's exports, and as capital flows into safer and more attractive U.S. assets, which provide higher returns than Canadian bonds. 

 Canada's May consumer price index (CPI) released on Friday were above the consensus forecast. 

 Overall CPI rose 1.1 percent year on year in May after a 0.8 percent rise in April, and the core rate (ex-food and energy) rose 1.4 percent from a year earlier after a 1.2 percent rise in April. 

 Economists on average had predicted a rise of 0.7 percent in all items year on year, and an increase of 1.2 percent in the core rate. 

 "I think what we are seeing is a transitory price increase, certain areas stemming from the weaker Canadian dollar, one area specifically the travel accommodation cost. That is due to increased tourism from the U.S.," said Sal Guatieri, senior economist at Bank of Montreal. 

 The U.S. dollar's gain versus the Canadian dollar in recent months gives Americans higher purchasing power. 

 "No increase in underlying price pressures. Goods inflation on a year-on-year basis is still very subdued. Even services inflation was quite tame," he said. "That of course is reflecting an ongoing slack in the economy and falling commodity prices." 

 Mark Mullins, chief economist at Midland Walwyn Capital Inc said the business travel cost, natural gas and food prices contributed to the higher inflation rate. 

 "I think we going to find these more a one-off factor than a new trend. I think we're still going to see the numbers basically below one percent annualized for the next few months," he told Reuters Television. 

 On whether higher-than-expected CPI would justify an interest rate hike by the Bank of Canada for supporting the Canadian dollar, he said: 

 "We are dealing with the situation here in Canada there is a very high degree of uncertainty. And it's more international and domestic. The (central) bank has recently reduced its forecast for economic growth. So I don't think they are in any great rush to raise rates. 

 The money market was steady to a bit weaker as the Canadian dollar remained under selling pressure. 

 The market was also watching for any G7 comments on Japan and Asia. 

 Canada's inflation rate, as shown in the CPI, is still in a good range and there's no extreme worry that the central bank would be forced to raise interest rates, one trader said. 

 "I don't think the market really expects the bank to (raise rates now), just keeping a wary eye on it," he said. "We're just sitting here on the edge of what's happening. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill traded with a yield of 4.85 percent, compared with 4.84 percent at the previous close here. 

 The Canadian dollar was moving between C$1.4732 (US$0.6788) and C$.4685 (US$0.6810) in nervous trade on Friday. 

 The Bank of Canada holds its twice-monthly T-bill auction next Tuesday.

The market was particularly jumpy before the 0900 EDT/1300 GMT window for the central bank's daily money market operations.



"People are feeling a bit under pressure, with weakness in Canada even with the yen rally, the Aussie rally, everything is rallying against the (U.S.) dollar except for Canada," another trader said. "People are viewing this as a possibility, that there might be a move by the (central) bank."



He expected the Canadian dollar to weaken again towards C$1.4750 (US$0.6780) if there is no support from a higher interest rate, which would offer a higher return on investment in Canadian assets.



The Bank of Canada has opted to intervene periodically to stem the fall in the Canadian dollar, but has not pushed up the key lending rate as the slide has been orderly.



In cross trading, the Canadian unit fell to 92.55 yen from 93.65 yen at the previous close here as the Japanese currency generally gained versus the U.S. dollar, and slipped against the German currency, quoted at 1.2154 marks after 1.2188 marks.



As the U.S. dollar was forging ahead against all major currencies until



Washington and Tokyo staged a rare joint intervention on Wednesday, the



Canadian dollar was not alone in falling.



But on Friday the Canadian dollar did not rally when the yen rallied, and


currency dealers are asking themselves what will happen to Canada when the yen



goes back down to 145 yen to the U.S. dollar?



Even commodity price-sensitive currencies were firming versus the greenback



on Friday.



The Australian dollar, though shedding earlier gains, rose to US$0.6172



from US$0.6078 on Thursday, and the New Zealand dollar was up to US$0.5230 from



US$0.5153.



Economists see Canada's inflation as still being benign.



Canada's overall consumer price index (CPI) for May rose 1.1 percent year



on year after a 0.8 percent rise in April, and the core rate (ex-food and



energy) rose 1.4 percent from a year earlier after a 1.2 percent rise in



April.



Economists on average had predicted a rise of 0.7 percent in all items year



on year, and an increase of 1.2 percent in the core rate.



"I think what we are seeing is a transitory price increase, certain areas



stemming from the weaker Canadian dollar, one area specifically, the travel



accommodation cost. That is due to increased tourism from the U.S.," said Sal



Guatieri, senior economist at Bank of Montreal.



The U.S. dollar's gain versus the Canadian dollar in recent months gives



Americans higher purchasing power in Canada.



"(There's) no increase in underlying price pressures. Goods inflation on a



year-on-year basis is still very subdued. Even services inflation was quite



tame," he said. "That of course is reflecting ongoing slack in the economy and falling commodity prices."



Mark Mullins, chief economist at Midland Walwyn Capital Inc., said the



business travel cost, natural gas and food prices contributed to the higher inflation rate.



"I think we're going to find this more a one-off factor than a new trend. I



think we're still going to see the numbers basically below one percent



annualized for the next few months," he told Reuters Television.



On whether higher-than-expected CPI would justify an interest rate hike by the Bank of Canada to support the Canadian dollar, he said: "We are dealing



with the situation here in Canada where there is a very high degree of



uncertainty. And it's more international than domestic. The (central) bank has



recently reduced its forecast for economic growth. So I don't think they are in any great rush to raise rates.



The Bank of Canada said on Friday its monetary conditions index (MCI) fell to -5.63 from -5.61 a week earlier. The MCI has been on the downtrend for the last two months.



On Thursday, Canada's central bank appeared to have stepped into the market to buy Canada from C$1.4685 (US$0.6810) to C$1.4705 (US$0.6800), but it met constant U.S. dollar buying.



On Thursday, a smaller-than-forecast surplus in Canada's international



trade weighed on the Canadian dollar as traders took it as a sign of slower economic growth.



Canada's April trade surplus had fallen to C$1.20 billion from a revised C$1.81 billion in March, below the average forecast by economists at C$1.69 billion.

title: Canada bonds end mixed, long end recovers.
text:
TORONTO, June 18 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended mixed on Thursday, with the long end of the yield curve recovering from a drop caused by a smaller-than-expected surplus in Canada's international trade for April. 

 While a rebound in the U.S. dollar against yen was prompting buying of U.S. treasuries, a weakening Canadian currency overshadowed bonds here in the morning, and was still hurting the short end by the close. 

 "Canada's long end was benefiting from the U.S. and the rest of the market is under pressure because of the (Canadian) currency," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 The U.S. dollar rebounded to a day's high of 138.22 yen on Thursday after plunging to 136 yen from 143 yen on Wednesday in the wake of a rare joint U.S.-Japan intervention in the currency market. 

 The Canadian dollar finished North American trade weaker at C$1.4707 (US$0.6799) on Thursday, shedding Wednesday's gains, which were ushered in by the joint action by the world's two biggest economies. 

 "Our currency has reacted the least favourably to the intervention package yesterday and this morning's trade number was extremely poor," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. "So those two things together weigh on the currency,, and in turn weighs on the (bond) market." 

 Canada's April trade surplus fell to C$1.20 billion from a revised C$1.81 billion in March, below an average forecast by economists of C$1.69 billion. 

 The U.S. April trade deficit rose 9.5 percent to $14.46 billion, the highest level since the current series began in January 1992. The U.S.-Japan trade gap fell 6.0 percent to $5.41 billion, while the U.S. deficit with Canada rose 44.2 percent to $1.25 billion. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond rose C$0.30 to C$135.79 to yield 5.511 percent. 

 Its U.S. 30-year counterpart rose 13/32 to yield 5.71 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread was 20 basis points after 21 points at the previous close here. 

 The Canadian dollar remained under pressure from weak prices for crude oil and other commodities as the nation depends on exports of natural resources for steady economic growth. 

 Webber said an interest rate increase by the Bank of Canada would boost the Canadian dollar, but that he did not expect the central bank to raise rates soon. U.S. treasuries were watching movements in the U.S. dollar and the equities market. 

 The Dow Jones industrial average, after rallying on Wednesday, closed down 16.45 points at 8813 on Thursday. 

 On Friday, Canada will release its May consumer price index. Economists on average forecast a rise of 0.7 percent in all items year on year after a rise of 0.8 percent in April, and an increase of 1.2 percent in the core rate (ex-food and energy) after a rise of 1.2 percent in April. 

 The government of Canada said on Thursday it will hold four bond auctions, including one real return issue, in the third quarter of 1998. The first auction, of 10-year bonds, will be on August 12, with details to be released on August 6. 

 In regional news, the province of Ontario said there was no T-bill auction on Thursday. 

 The money market was weaker, reacting to a fall in the Canadian dollar on Thursday. 

 "With the fact that the currency has weakened off, we have weakened off as well. We've seen profit-taking in some of the WI bills and in the long end," one money market trader said. 

 "Even when we improved yesterday, our clients were sitting on the sidelines. They want to see where the dollar's going," the trader said, adding that money market players are comfortable with the U.S. dollar below C$1.4640 (US$0.6831). 

 The Canadian dollar ended weaker at C$1.4707 (US$0.6799) on Thursday, despite talk of Bank of Canada intervention, reflecting the U.S. dollar's rebound against the yen. 

 "Between now and Tuesday, we're expecting to be a little cheaper here," the trader said. The Bank of Canada holds a T-bill auction next Tuesday, which comes in every two weeks. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill traded with a yield of 4.84 percent, compared with 4.77 percent at the previous close here. 

 ((Masaru Sato, Reuters Toronto newsroom (416) 941-8107, toronto.newsroom@reuters.com))

TORONTO, June 18 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended weaker around C$1.4702 (US$0.6802) on Thursday, despite talk of Bank of Canada intervention, reflecting the U.S. dollar's rebound against the yen.



Canada's central bank appeared to have stepped into the market to buy Canadian dollars from C$1.4685 (US$0.6810) to C$1.4705 (US$0.6800), but it met constant U.S. dollar buying.



"Yesterday there were (U.S.) dollar buyers, today there are dollar buyers and cross Canada selling. The market is just steadily bid and it still needs dollars," said one trader. "It's been a pretty tough trend because you just haven't had any time to buy dollars on dips."



"The market has been disappointed that the bank hasn't had anything (to say) to express concern over the currency," he said. "Probably it could have come in with a strong statement."



The U.S. dollar rebounded to a day's high of 138.22 yen on Thursday after plunging to 136 yen from 143 yen on Wednesday in the wake of a rare U.S.-Japan joint intervention in the currency market.



"As long as the yen continues to move back towards 140 (yen to the U.S. dollar), Canada will move towards C$1.4800," said Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange, at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities. "The weakness in the yen will be translated in the weakness in the Canadian dollar."



Figures showing a smaller-than-forecast surplus in Canada's international trade for April, released on Thursday, also weighed on the local dollar.



Canada's April trade surplus fell to C$1.20 billion from a revised C$1.81 billion in March, below an average forecast by economists of C$1.69 billion.



A smaller surplus could suggest slower economic growth, but it is a little too early to revise down the estimate for Canada's gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter based on this figure, said Randall Powley, senior economist at Scotia Capital Markets.



"It's only one month of a quarter. Also I'd like to see some revisions, as we've seen in the recent past, these revisions could be quite large and could change the direction of the impact on the GDP," he said.



The U.S. April trade deficit rose 9.5 percent to $14.46 billion, the highest level since the current series began in January 1992. The U.S.-Japan trade gap fell 6.0 percent to $5.41 billion, while the U.S. deficit with Canada rose 44.2 percent to $1.25 billion.



In cross trading, the Canadian unit, after plunging on Wednesday, rose to 93.65 yen from 93.23 yen at the previous close here, but fell to 1.2188 marks from 1.2217 marks.



The market is awaiting news from Tokyo, where Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers is discussing Japan's banking sector reform and plans to haul the flagging Japanese economy out of recession, a key to stabilising Asian economies and financial markets.



   The market wants to see how Summers and his team emerge from a series of



meetings in Japan early next week.



    "If they come back smiling and with big programmes that everybody believes



will save Japan, then I think that the (U.S.) dollar will continue to go down



and the yen will start to rise," Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High



Frequency Economics told Reuters Television. "But I don't think Japan can



deliver the goods and therefore I expect it (the U.S. dollar) to come back



firming... I think the mid-140s is back in everybody's sights again."



To regain investor confidence, Japan needs to implement long-term



structural reform and deregulation, which will not take place overnight.



Canada's regaining of some ground versus the U.S. dollar is giving the Bank



of Canada some breathing space, but the Canadian dollar remains vulnerable to



global market uncertainties and weak commodities prices.



On Friday, Canada will release its May consumer price index. Economists on



average forecast a rise of 0.7 percent in all items year on year after a rise



of 0.8 percent in April, and an increase of 1.2 percent in the core rate



(ex-food and energy) after a rise of 1.2 percent in April.

In London story headlined "Fed and BOJ alone on dlr/yen intervention-traders" please read in first and second paragraphs that the intervention was selling not buying. 

 A corrected repetition follows. 

 LONDON, June 17 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan  stood alone in selling (corrects) dollars for yen on Wednesday, traders said. 

 They said there was no evidence that central banks from other countries had intervened alongside the Fed to sell (corrects) dollars for yen at 139.10-15 and again with the Bank of Japan at 138.60 yen. 

 "There is absolutely no evidence that any other bank has been in the yen apart from the Fed," said one central bank salesman at a major European bank.

Foreign exchange dealers in Europe said they saw no signs of any other banks involved in the intervention amid a raft of "no comment" responses from central banks around the world. 

 "We think if this was concerted, the central banks would be making a lot more out of it, not just a bunch of 'no comments'," said one French trader. 

 In Frankfurt, traders said they saw no sign of the German central bank and the Bundesbank itself declined to comment. 

 "We don't comment on such issues, we have nothing to say," a Bundesbank spokesman said in response to a Reuters enquiry. 

 The central banks of Germany, England, France, Italy, Sweden, and Canada declined to comment on the intervention, while the central banks of Switzerland, Denmark and The Netherlands all said they had not participated.

title: Canada dlr hits new low against U.S. dollar.
text:
TORONTO, June 15 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar continued to weaken against the U.S. dollar on Monday morning, hitting another intraday weak point of C$1.4728 (US$0.6790), traders said. 

 The currency had set a new low of C$1.4715 (US$0.6796) about an hour earlier as the market tested the topside of the U.S. dollar in the absence of clear signs that Canada's central bank was intervening to defend the local dollar. 

 Traders said they expected the Canadian dollar to weaken further. 

 They reckoned the Bank of Canada would not raise its key lending rate to boost the local dollar by attracting investors through higher returns on Canadian assets. 

 "The market consensus seems to be that they (the Bank of Canada) won't do anything any time soon," said Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities. 

 Canada's central bank last raised its bank rate by 50 basis points to 5.0 percent on January 30 after the local dollar had plunged on speculative selling and spurred monetary conditions considered too loose. 

 By the bank's measure, a weaker Canadian dollar means more stimulus in the domestic economy as it lowers export prices. 

 Meanwhile, the Canadian unit firmed against the Japanese currency in cross trading, rising to 99.24 yen from 98.35 yen late on Friday here. 

 The yen has been hit by the growing concern over the stagnant Japanese economy and Asia's economic problems. 

 Against the German mark, the Canadian dollar shed earlier gains and was quoted around 1.2308 marks, down from 1.2311 marks in late North American trade on Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar continued to surge versus the yen and mark on the back of a safe-haven flight of capital to U.S. markets from Asia and part of Europe.

TORONTO, June 12 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended nervously firmer at C$1.4665 (US$0.6819) on Friday, licking its wounds after hitting a record low of C$1.4711 (US$0.6798) in active trade on Thursday.



Trading lacked direction and was confined in a tight band as players were unsure about how far the Bank of Canada will let the Canadian dollar fall as the U.S. dollar continues to firm against major currencies.



The U.S. dollar, although faced with some profit-taking, stayed afloat, quoted around 144 yen and 1.8050 marks in late North American trade.



It was a week of safe-haven buying of U.S. dollars and bonds as the global market was increasingly concerned about economic and financial difficulties confronting Asia and Russia.



The latest data confirmed Japan was deep in recession. Its gross domestic product contracted at an annual rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter after a revised annualized drop of 1.5 percent in the previous quarter.



The U.S. dollar has gained sharply also comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Thursday. Rubin urged Japan to deregulate and open markets, which he said is the key to correcting the yen's weakness.



On Friday, he said Washington was "very concerned" about the weak yen, but repeated that Tokyo should deal with its financial sector problems.



Meanwhile, the U.S. economy appears to be growing steadily without causing serious fears of inflation.



This week's data showed that retail sales rose 0.9 percent in May, stronger than expected, and producer price index came at a higher-than-expected rise of 0.2 percent in May, which was still considered moderate.



In cross trading, the Canadian unit edged up to 1.2311 marks from 1.2304 marks at the previous close here, and to 98.35 yen from 98.01 yen.



"We are getting pessimistic with respect to the commodities prices, and the currency could remain around this level throughout this year, C$1.4600 (US$0.6849) to C$1.4700 (US$0.6803)," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, macro economics at Bank of Montreal.



He expects commodities prices to stay depressed for now as the gloomy outlook for Japan's economic turnaround will remain a drag on other Asian economies.



Without sound domestic economic fundamentals - low inflation and government's effort to balance the federal budget this year - the Canadian unit could have fallen more quickly.



"There are positives out there, but in the near term they are just limiting the marked depreciation of the Canadian dollar, Ferley said.



On the central bank's policy, he said: "The weakness we've seen in the Canadian dollar reflects more of a pessimistic outlook for commodities prices... and they should stay on the sidelines and accept a sort of a weaker currency, rather than by countering it by raising interest rates."



Mark Chandler, senior economist at Goldman Sachs Canada, also urged the


central bank to hold off on raising rates just to defend the dollar.



And he predicts the Canadian dollar should recover to the C$1.4200



(US$0.7042) level in three to six months if commodities prices recover, noting

Canada's monetary policy should remain on hold for the next five months,



barring any blows to the economy.

title: Canadian markets hit by Asia woes, commodities.
text:
TORONTO, June 11 (Reuters) - Canadian equity markets racked up another day of steep losses on Thursday and the country's currency hit record lows as the Asian flu and ailing commodity prices gave investors the chills. 

 A fall in U.S. equities, hit hard by warnings about corporate profits and fears about the sinking Japanese yen, only worsened Canada's sickly performance. 

 Analysts warned the bloodletting is unlikely to end soon, although most stopped short of predicting a true bear market. 

 "It's not going to stop now. There's still some downside here and it's not going to feel good," said John Kellett, vice-president of Canadian equities at Royal Bank of Canada. "I'm not truly bearish insofar as I think the economic fundamentals are reasonably good still." 

 The Canadian dollar closed around C$1.4683 ($0.6811) after weakening to a record intraday low against the U.S. dollar of around C$1.4711 ($0.6798), traders said. 

 The previous intraday trading low of C$1.4686 (US$0.6809) was set on January 29 this year, when the currency faced strong speculative selling. 

 "The Canadian dollar is rapidly turning into the Canadian half-dollar," said Fred Ketchen, senior vice-president and director of equity trading at ScotiaMcLeod Inc. 

 The tumble in Canada's currency followed a surge in the U.S. dollar against major currencies as safe-haven capital kept on flowing from Asia into the United States. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told the U.S. Senate banking committee that while the weak yen is a global concern, the remedy lies in hands of Japanese policymakers. Traders took Rubin's comments as an indication the G7 is taking no joint action to help stem the yen's slide, although Rubin later said intervention is not off the table and U.S. intervention could come at the appropriate time. 

 Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Bernard Bonin said on Thursday that the central bank was unlikely to be lifting rates to defend the beleaguered Canadian dollar any time soon. 

 "We continue to believe that, between now and the publication of the next Monetary Policy Report, due in November, the appropriate course would be to keep monetary conditions within their recent range, provided there are no new shocks," Bonin told financial planners in Quebec City. 

 The Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's largest, came under heavy fire from investors as well. The bellwether TSE 300 Composite Index finished down 138.00 points, or 1.86 percent, at 7295.76 on Thursday. Volumes were fairly thin as alarmed investors hugged the sidelines. 

 Losses since Monday's close total more than 261 points or roughly 3.5 percent. 

 None of the TSE's 14 sub-sectors was immune to the selling but the gold and silver group was the biggest loser, falling more than five percent in afternoon trade before recovering to close 281.98 points, or 4.57 percent, lower at 5887.74. 

 In contrast to the battered currency and stock markets, Canadian bonds continued to firm with long bonds at record highs, profiting along with U.S. treasuries from safe-haven buying. 

 Weak commodity prices have bedevilled the resource-heavy Toronto stock market in recent weeks and analysts said they see little on the horizon to lift prices. 

 In London, gold melted through $290 versus a morning fix of $292.90 an ounce as buyers evaporated from the market. 

 Standard & Poor's MMS technical analyst Katherine Beattie said she sees nothing that will immediately reverse Toronto's downward trek. But she still called the fall a correction rather than a true shift of sentiment to bearish from bullish. 

 "A 400-to 500-point correction from 7800 is not a big deal," Beattie said. 

 ($1=$1.47 Canadian).

title: Canada dollar hits low,  central bank  sits back.
text:
TORONTO, June 11 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar's plunge to a new low against its U.S. counterpart on Thursday is prompting debate on what strategy the nation's central bank should use to fight currency speculators. 

 The Bank of Canada has customarily tried to defend its dollar by boosting key lending rates, which in theory will attract investors by providing higher returns. 

 But the bank has come under fire since last year for this approach because of fears it may choke off economic growth by driving up borrowing costs for consumers and businesses. 

 The Canadian dollar slipped to a new intra-day low of C$1.4710 (US$0.6798) on Thursday as the U.S. dollar powered ahead against major currencies on the back of safe-haven capital flows from Asia into the United States. 

 The central bank has so far not moved to raise interest rates to defend the dollar, and did not even appear to have intervened in the currency market on Thursday. 

 Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Bernard Bonin on Thursday said Canada's monetary policy should remain on hold for the next five months, barring any blows to the economy. 

 "We continue to believe that, between now and the publication of the next Monetary Policy Report, due in November, the appropriate course would be to keep monetary conditions within their recent range, provided there are no new shocks," he told financial planners in Quebec City. 

 He said while the most recent figures suggest that Canada's economic outlook is somewhat more favourable than anticipated a couple of months ago, "the fact remains that this outlook carries with it a larger margin of uncertainty than normal." 

 "I don't think it's sensible to block every exchange rate move every time," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Bank Securities in Toronto. "By the end of the day, the Bank of Canada is targeting inflation, not the exchange rate." 

 Canada's inflation rate is below that of the United States, and at the low end of a 1-3 percent central bank target band. 

 "If the exchange market remains relatively orderly, they will do nothing," Spence said, adding that the central bank is likely only to "moderate the overshoot" in Canadian dollar selling, instead of blocking speculative selling. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, one of the most powerful figures in the world when it comes to market intervention, has said repeatedly that no country can manipulate exchange rates for a sustained period. 

 "Should the bank react to the weakening Canadian dollar? I think the short answer is no," said Mark Chandler, senior economist at Goldman Sachs Canada. 

 It would be inconsistent for the bank to do so because it has already said in its May 13 semi-annual policy report that uncertainties from Asia's crisis will prompt wider fluctuations in the currency and monetary conditions, he said. 

 In addition, he said, a weaker currency acts as a shock absorber for natural resources exporters in Canada as cheaper export prices should partly offset softening commodities prices due to slumping Asian demand. 

 Chandler called on the bank to "keep the gunpowder dry." 

 "There are times when you want to raise rates, more so for policy reasons than for short-term currency fluctuations," he said. 

 A Canadian rate increase looks unlikely in any case because there is no sign of overheating in the domestic economy. 

 "I think the bottom line is that as long as the (U.S.) Fed is on hold, they don't want to go ahead," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 "If the Fed goes (and raises rates), that means that the U.S. economy hasn't slowed down on its own and that should spill over into strong growth in Canada, and that will give the bank reason to tighten," he said. 

 U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Wednesday that the U.S. central bank needs no tightening of monetary policy yet. 

 The Canadian dollar has come under pressure from soft commodities prices, which have also hit the Australian and New Zealand dollars. Canada's Asian exposure is more limited, but it is vulnerable to volatility in such currencies because of a perception it shares a similar dependency on commodities. 

 Canada's exports to Asia account for only 2 percent of its gross domestic product, Chandler noted. 

 The Asian exports-to-GDP ratio is 14 percent for New Zealand and 11 percent for Australia. 

 Spence said the Canadian currency's level over the last month or so "is entirely consistent with where relative commodities prices have gone."

title: Canadian markets hit by Asia wes, commodities.
text:
TORONTO, June 11 (Reuters) - Canadian equity markets racked up another day of steep losses and the country's currency hit record lows on Thursday as the Asian flu and ailing commodity prices gave investors the chills. 

 U.S. equities, hit hard by warnings about corporate profits and fears about the sinking Japanese yen, only worsened Canada's sickly performance. 

 Analysts warned that the bloodletting is unlikely to end soon although most stopped short of predicting a true bear market. 

 "It's not going to stop now. There's still some downside here and it's not going to feel good," said John Kellett, vice-president of Canadian equities at Royal Bank of Canada. 

 "I'm not truly bearish insofar as I think the economic fundamentals are reasonably good still." 

 The Canadian dollar weakened to a new all-time intraday low against the U.S. dollar of around C$1.4707 (US$0.6799), traders said. The previous intraday trading low of C$1.4686 (US$0.6809) was set on January 29 this year, when the currency faced strong speculative selling. 

 "The Canadian dollar is rapidly turning into the Canadian half-dollar," said Fred Ketchen, senior vice-president and director of equity trading at ScotiaMcLeod Inc. 

 The tumble in Canada's currency followed a surge in the U.S. dollar against major currencies as safe-haven capital flows from Asia into the United States. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told the U.S. Senate banking committee that while the weak yen is a global concern, the remedy lies in hands of Japanese policymakers. Traders took Rubin's comments as an indication the G7 is taking no joint action to help stem the yen's slide, although Rubin later said intervention is not off the table and U.S. intervention could come at the appropriate time. 

 Bank of Canada Senior Deputy Governor Bernard Bonin said that the central bank was unlikely to be lifting rates to defend the beleaguered Canadian dollar any time soon. 

 "We continue to believe that, between now and the publication of the next Monetary Policy Report, due in November, the appropriate course would be to keep monetary conditions within their recent range, provided there are no new shocks," Bonin told financial planners in Quebec City. 

 The Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's largest, was under heavy fire from investors as well. At 1340 eastern time, the bellwether TSE 300 Composite Index was down more than 127 points, or 1.72 percent, at 7306.00. Volumes were fairly thin as nervous investors hugged the sidelines. 

 Losses since Monday's close so far total 251 points or roughly 3.3 percent. 

 None of the TSE's 14 sub-sectors was immune to the selling but the gold and silver group was the biggest loser, falling more than five percent by early afternoon. 

 In contrast to the battered currency and stock markets, Canadian bonds continued to firm to record highs, profiting along with U.S. treasuries from safe-haven buying. 

 Weak commodity prices have bedevilled the resource-heavy Toronto stock market in recent weeks and analysts said they see little to lift prices on the horizon. 

 In London, gold melted through $290 versus a morning fix of $292.90 an ounce as buyers evaporated from the market. 

 Standard & Poor's MMS technical analyst Katherine Beatty said she sees little that will immediately reverse Toronto's downward trek. But she still called the fall a correction rather than a true shift of sentiment to bearish from bullish. 

 "A 400-to 500-point correction from 7800 is not a big deal," Beatty said. 

 ($1=$1.47 Canadian).

title: Canada bonds end mixed, long end up on Greenspan.
text:
TORONTO, June 10 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds ended mixed on Wednesday with the long end of the yield curve sharply firmer on comments by the U.S. central bank chief that it's not time yet for a U.S. credit tightening. 

 The short end remained weak as the Canadian dollar continued to slide against the U.S. dollar. 

 "Monetary policy might need to tighten if demand were to continue to exhibit few signs of abating noticeably," U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan told a congressional committee. 

 But he added: "We... have not perceived to date the need to tighten policy in response to strong demand." 

 In early trade, North American long bonds rose on the notion of save-haven capital flows into the United States as Asian share markets tumbled and the Australian dollar was sold overnight on growing concern over the falling Japanese yen and its impact on the region. 

 The weak yen might help Japan's exports, but that is a threat to the exports of other Asian nations. 

 The market is awaiting any sign of concerted action by the Group of Seven (G7) major nations to stem the yen's fall. 

 G7 deputy finance ministers are discussing Russia and Asia at a meeting of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in Paris this week. 

 Canada's benchmark 30-year bond surged C$0.65 to C$135.44 to yield 5.531 percent. 

 Its U.S. 30-year counterpart jumped 41/32 to yield 5.70 percent. The U.S.-Canada spread narrowed to 17 basis points from 23 points at the previous close here. 

 "We have some surprising strength related to the difficulties in Asia last night. The overnight session was quite friendly to North American treasuries, Canada's long end in particular," said Jeoff Hall, managing Canadian market analyst at Technical Data in Boston. 

 This prompted the Ontario provincial government to reopen sales of its 6.5 percent C$500 million long bond, maturing March 8, 2029, which was well received, he said. 

 Dominion Bond Rating Service said it is assigning a rating of A (high) to this bond issue. 

 "So we have a good market tone going to important data later in the week," Hall said. 

 On the strength of the U.S. economy, the market expects slightly stronger retail sales numbers for May on Thursday. Economists on average forecast a 0.7-percent rise in May after a 0.5-percent rise in April. 

 On the inflation outlook, the U.S. producer price index for May will be released on Friday. Economists on average expect both the overall and core PPI to rise 0.1 percent after a 0.2-percent rise in April. 

 The short end of the Canadian yield curve remained under pressure as the Canadian dollar was weakening. 

 The Canadian dollar ended weaker at C$1.4658 (US$0.6822) on Wednesday after rounds of intervention by the Bank of Canada dredged it back from a day's low of C$1.4675 (US$0.6814). 

 "The curve continues to flatten as investors bail out of 2-to 3-year bonds into the long end," Hall said. 

 The Government of Canada said its C$3.5 billion auction of 5.0 percent bonds due December 1, 2000 produced the average yield of 5.229, priced at 99.480. 

 The high/low gap was 14 basis points and the tail (high vs average) was 9 points. 

 The money market was weaker as the Canadian dollar continued to fall against the U.S. dollar. 

 "The T-bill yield has been relatively low recently and given the weakness of the currency and the current level of MCI, the market is perhaps looking for a Bank of Canada rate hike," one trader said. 

 The central bank would adjust money in circulation by raising interest rates if its monetary conditions index (MCI) swings widely to show excessively loose conditions. 

 Canada's three-month when issued T-bill yielded 4.83 percent after 4.73 percent at the previous close here.

title: Canadian dollar fall spurs  central bank intervention .

TORONTO, June 10 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar continued to slide on Wednesday as the currency market tested the resolve of the central bank to defend the weakening currency. 

 By the end of the day the Canadian dollar was still slouching towards its record low of C$1.4686 to the U.S. dollar (US$0.6809), marked on January 29 this year. 

 Earlier in the day it came under speculative selling by U.S. dollar bulls, who braved a wave of market intervention by the Bank of Canada. 

 This helped stabilise the Canadian unit, which closed at C$1.4658 to the U.S. dollar (US$0.6822) on Wednesday. It opened at C$1.4624 (US$0.6838), down from Tuesday's close at C$1.4588 (US$0.6855). 

 The next question is whether the central bank will be forced to raise interest rates to make the return on Canadian assets attractive enough to foreign investors. 

Central bank officials have said that before raising rates they want to see if speculative forces in the market are spurring a loss of confidence in the currency. They have said central bank will not react to daily fluctuations and is looking at overall monetary conditions. 

 Canada is not the only loser in the currency market these days. 

 The Australian dollar has been hitting 12-year lows recently, while the Japanese yen fell to 141.67 yen to the U.S. dollar and the German mark slipped to 1.7990 marks on Wednesday. 

 The U.S. dollar has been surging against major currencies because worries over economic problems in Asia and Russia have prompted renewed safe-haven buying of U.S. assets. These assets are considered safe due to the economic and military might of the United States. 

 Flight-to-quality capital flows to the United States have spilled over into Canada's long-term bonds, but have not helped the Canadian dollar. 

 With the Australian dollar and the Japanese yen at low levels, speculators have appeared to be looking for a new victim. In doing so, they have ignored Canada's fairly good economic fundamentals, steady economic growth and low inflation. 

 Also, strong U.S. job growth and relatively weak Canadian employment numbers released last Friday triggered selling of the Canadian dollar. 

 "We are better than Australia, but that's no comfort to Canadians," said a Bank of Canada source. "I do feel that the (Canadian) dollar should be worth a little bit more." 

 Australian exports are much more exposed to the economic slump in Asia than are Canada's. Less than 10 percent of Canada's exports go to Southeast Asia.

WEDNESDAY, JUNE 10



TREND: WEAKER ACTIVITY: ACTIVE



*The Canadian dollar continued to weaken towards C$1.4655 (US$0.6824), where



the Bank of Canada intervened to sell USD, trying to defend CAD. *CAD's record



low vs the USD at 1.4686 (US$0.6809) is still ahead, and the market wants to



see how determined the BOC is in defending CAD. *Market awaiting any forex


comments from G7 deputies meeting in Paris this week, and any hints for



monetary policy direction from U.S. Fed Chairman Greenspan's testimony today at



around 1100 EDT/1500 GMT. *USD was bid up to 141 yen and 1.7965 marks in



morning trade.



TORONTO, June 10 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar continued to weaken on Wednesday, and the Bank of Canada intervened to defend the depressed currency by selling U.S. dollars at C$1.4655 (US$0.6824).



The central bank's move was widely anticipated as the currency continued to weaken after opening at C$1.4624 (US$0.6838) this morning, down from Tuesday's close at C$1.4588 (US$0.6855).



The Canadian dollar hit a record low versus the U.S. dollar at C$1.4686 (US$0.6809) on January 29 this year, when it came under speculative selling.



In a prepared speech, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said the Fed has not yet seen the need to tighten its monetary policy, but that it is watching inflation closely.



He said the U.S. central bank might need to raise interest rates unless U.S. demand abates "noticeably."



Greenspan also said the U.S. economy is expanding strongly despite a strong drag on trade.



He was testifying on monetary policy and the outlook for the U.S. economy before the joint economic committee of Congress started around 1100 EDT/1500 GMT today.



In cross trading, the Canadian dollar was afloat at 1.2235 marks, up from 1.2201 marks at the previous close here, and was at 96.32 yen, up from 96.12 yen.



The U.S. dollar continued to firm to around 141.25 yen and 1.7952 marks in morning trade.



The Australian dollar was falling towards 0.58 to the U.S. dollar, but rebounded to trade around 0.5865 this morning.



   Now that the Australian dollar and the Japanese yen have been sinking to



new lows, an attack on the Canadian unit by speculators is feared.



    The market has ignored Canada's fairly good economic fundamentals, steady



growth with low inflation, and instead followed the flow of buying the U.S.



 dollar, which has been also firming against the yen and the mark.



    "We are better than Australia, but that's no comfort to Canadians," said a



Bank of Canada source. "I do feel that the (Canadian) dollar should be worth a



little bit more."



   Before taking policy action, the central bank is watching if speculative



forces in the market are taking the Canadian currency drastically down and



whether the market is losing confidence in the currency, he said.



    Market players expect the bank to raise interest rates to attract investors



with higher yields if the Canadian unit continues to drop sharply.



    Bank policymakers have pointed out they are not reacting to daily movements



and are looking at the overall monetary conditions. A weaker Canadian dollar



contributes to looser monetary conditions in Canada.



    Economic fundamentals have a tough time competing against safe-haven



capital flows into U.S. dollar-denominated assets.



    Asian sharemarkets tumbled overnight on the growing fear of a falling yen



and its impact on the Chinese currency.



    The market tends to link the image of an Aussie dollar sell-off to Canada



selling, although Australian exports are much more exposed to the economic



slump in Asia than Canada's exports to the region, which are less than 10



percent of the nation's total.



"Obviously there's stops (stop-loss orders) at C$1.4610 (US$0.6845) taken



out overnight," said one trader. "There's broad-based (U.S.) dollar buying from



Far Eastern accounts and European accounts."



"There may be some stories going around that spec guys might have a look at



Canada and now trying to have a go at it and sell Canada," he said. "There's



one or two U.S. investment types looking to sell U.S., so it's a little bit of



two-way business going on at these levels here."



   The market wants to see the resolve of the Bank of Canada to defend the



depressed currency.



    "The market looks to the C$1.4605 (US$0.6847) level to buy some U.S.



 dollars, and they will probably expect at some point to test the bank at the



C$1.4660 (US$0.68121) level today," the trader said.



    The market is also looking for comments on exchange rates from deputy



finance ministers from the Group of Seven nations meeting in Paris.



    They are in Paris for the June 9-10 meeting of the Working Party III of the



Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.



    A weak yen might help Japan's stagnant economy as it makes Japanese



exporters cheaper, but that is a threat to other exporting Asian countries.



Meanwhile, the strong U.S. dollar cuts import bills and helps curb U.S.



inflation.



On the strength of the U.S. economy, the market expects slightly stronger



retail sales on Thursday. Economists on average forecast a 0.7-percent rise in



May after a 0.5-percent rise in April.



For inflation outlook, the U.S. producer price index for May will be



released on Friday. Economists on average expect both the overall and core PPI



to rise 0.1 percent after a 0.2-percent rise in April.



The policy-setting U.S. Federal Open Market Committee will meet on June 30



and July 1. For the rest of the year, the FOMC is scheduled to meet on August



18, September 29, November 17, and December 22.

TORONTO, May 29 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar opened slightly firmer at C$1.4533 ($0.6881), gaining on the crosses overnight, particularly against the mark.



Germany's proximity to Russia's financial turmoil prompted mark selling against the U.S. and Canadian dollars.



Before profit-taking emerged this morning, the U.S. rose to touch 139 yen as worries over Japan's economy deepened.



Japan's jobless rate hit a record high of 4.1 percent in April, creeping up to the unemployment rate in the United States, which has fallen to 4.3 percent.



On the crosses, the Canadian dollar rose to 1.2300 marks from 1.2234 marks at the previous close here, and to 95.45 yen from 95.38 yen.



    The market lacked clear direction.



    "For the last day and a half, the slide (in the Canadian



dollar) has abated, but we're basically sitting here around



C$1.4540 (US$0.6878) area, waiting to see what's next," said



Reid Farrill, executive director, foreign exchange at CIBC Wood



Gundy Securities. "It's hard to say what's really going to be



the next factor to move the market."



    Canada's central bank is warning the market there's no



absolute level for the monetary conditions index (MCI), which



the market was watching for signs of bank intervention or



tightening aimed at defending its currency.



    Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen has repeatedly said



there's no target zone for the Canadian dollar.



    The Canadian dollar has not recovered from selling that was



sparked by the market perception that the the bank would leave



its accommodative monetary policy unchanged for the next six



months.



Dealers were disappointed by the May 13 release of the



bank's semi-annual policy report, which did not contain a



much-sought-after bias towards credit tightening.

ACTIVITY: MODERATE *Canada dollar ended weaker around C$1.4566 ($0.6865) after dealers tested USD's topside up to C$1.4575 (US$0.6861). *No clear direction for CAD, which opened a bit firmer, gaining on crosses overnight. *USD pared gains vs mark as worries over Russia's financial system and Germany's exposure to it receded.



TORONTO, May 29 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar ended weaker around C$1.4566 (US$0.6865) on Friday after dealers tested the topside of the U.S. dollar in early trade.



The Canadian currency was left in lackluster trading while the world focused on safe-haven flows into the United States in the face of the financial turmoil in Russia, uncertainties in Asia, heightened tension between India and Pakistan, and U.S.-Japan tolerance of a weakening yen.



The currency shed most of its earlier gains in cross trading, particularly against the mark, as worries over Russia's financial stability and Germany's exposure to it receded later.



In early trade, some players took U.S. dollar short positions against the Canadian unit. Canada's gain was limited to C$1.4525 (US$0.6885).



"Nobody really was seen buying U.S. dollars, so made into Aussie/Canada buying..., but basically there were stops at C$1.4550/55 (US$0.6873/70) and just got cleaned up.



The U.S. dollar's advance was also capped at C$1.4575 (US$0.6861).



On the crosses, the Canadian dollar pared earlier gains. It was quoted at 1.2255 marks, up a bit from 1.2234 marks at the previous close here, and at 95.22 yen, down from 95.38 yen.



"I think the market sentiment is that they expect Canada to weaken further," the dealer said. "The market is getting more fun selling Canada than buying it, testing the (central) bank's resolves to see if they are really going to do anything."



He expects the currency to trade in the range of C$1.4450-1.4650 (US$0.6920-0.6823) for the next month.



The Canadian dollar lacked clear direction.



"For the last day and a half, the slide (in the Canadian dollar) has abated, but we're basically sitting here around the C$1.4540 (US$0.6878) area, waiting to see what's next," said Reid Farrill, executive director of foreign exchange at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities.



"It's hard to say what's really going to be the next factor to move the market."



Canada's central bank has told the market that there is no absolute level for the monetary conditions index (MCI), which the market was watching for signs of bank intervention or tightening aimed at defending its currency.



Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen has repeatedly said there is no target zone for the Canadian dollar.



The Canadian dollar has not recovered from selling that was sparked by the market perception that the the bank would leave its accommodative monetary policy unchanged for the next six months.



Dealers were disappointed by the May 13 release of the bank's semi-annual policy report, which did not contain a much-sought-after bias towards credit tightening.



The U.S. dollar slipped after touching 139 yen overnight as caution over a Bank of Japan intervention eased fears Japan's deepening economic problems. Japan's jobless rate hit a record high of 4.1 percent in April, creeping up to the unemployment rate in the United States, which has fallen to 4.3 percent in the latest data.

Q1 current account deficit seen falling by C$5.51 billion after a decline of C$6.24 billion in the previous quarter.



Q1 GDP seen rising 2.3 percent after a 0.7-percent rise in the previous quarter.



Friday:



May jobless rate seen at 8.4 percent, unchanged from April.



Employment growth seen at 14,300 after 71,700 in April.

title: Canada Morning: C$ Steady In Advance Of Thiessen Speech
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar was little changed Wednesday as markets waited to see how a speech from Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen later in the day would affect the embattled currency. 

 "We did a lot of damage yesterday and people want to see if the Governor responds to that either today or in his speech tomorrow," said Avery Shenfeld, senior economist with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc. 

 The U.S. dollar traded at C$1.4557 at 10:24 a.m. EDT (1424 GMT), from C$1.4552 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and from C$1.4546 late Tuesday. 

 After trading a tight range in recent sessions, the Canadian currency took a serious tumble on Tuesday, with the U.S. dollar climbing from its Monday close of C$1.4492 to about C$1.4560 before the Bank of Canadaintervened, selling U.S. currency in an effort to contain market volatility. 

 Thiessen is scheduled to speak in Montreal at around 1:15 p.m. EDT (1715 GMT), but the text of his speech will be released around 11:45 a.m. EDT (1545 GMT). He also speaks to the House of Commons standing committe on finance Thursday morning. 

 Market watchers said the beseiged Canadian dollar was getting a respite before Thiessen's speech. "They're giving him a change to perhaps rise to the occasion and warn markets about a possible rate response if the currency gets much weaker," Shenfeld said. 

 One currency trader with a major Canadian bank said the currency was benefitting from "a consensus that he's not going to say much that's going to be that harmful to the Canadian dollar." 

 While the central bank is understandably reluctant to tighten rates in light of current economic conditions, the currency's weakness may ultimately test its patience, Shenfeld observed.
