title: World  Forex  -2: Russia  Central Bank Intervenes  For Ruble
text:
In Russia, the ruble tumbled Tuesday, forcing the central bank to intervene again in defense of its currency. Investors bailed out of bonds and stocks on concerns that the government has no emergency plan to prop up its collapsing financial markets, traders said. 

 Russian Treasury bond (GKO) prices plummeted, sending the yield on GKOs as high as 57.0% from 50.0% a day ago and fueling speculation that the central bank will raise interest rates for the third time in less than a month. Last week, Russia raised its key interest rates to 50% to shore up the ruble against a massive exodus of foreign capital. 

 Late in Moscow, the dollar for next-day delivery was at 6.184 rubles, up from RUR6.174 Monday. 

 Finance Minister Mikhail Zadornov said Tuesday that despite the erosion of Russia's financial markets over the past week, the government isn't seeking additional international aid to stabilize the markets. He also said, "there will be no devaluation." 

 "But the German currency wasn't the sole victim of Russia's troubles. In fact, fears of a ruble devaluation fueled a nervous selloff in emerging markets, with the Polish zloty and Czech koruna sustaining big losses. After a sharp decline Monday, the South African rand recovered against the dollar Tuesday." 

 The Canadian dollar also tumbled, prodding the Bank of Canada to intervene in an effort to arrest its currency's fall. Traders attributed the drop in part to soft global commodity prices and delayed pressure from the Bank of Canada's semi-annual monetary report, released weeks ago, in which the central bank said monetary conditions will likely remain steady for the next six months. 

 The U.S. currency was also changing hands at C$1.4548, up from C$1.4492.

title: Canada  Afternoon: C$ Tumbles, Bank of  Canada Intervenes
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar tumbled substantially lower Tuesday, prompting currency market intervention by the Bank of Canada in an effort to restrict market volatility. 

 The U.S. dollar traded at C$1.4546 at 3:35 p.m. EDT (1935 GMT), from C$1.4517 at 8:00 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), and from C$1.4490 late Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar jumped as high as C$1.4562 Tuesday afternoon, prompting the Bank of Canada to intervene in currency markets in an effort to restrict market volatility. The central bank sold U.S. dollars at C$1.4560 at around 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT), after which the U.S. dollar levelled off and then subsided slightly. 

 Market sources cited a number of different factors behind the renewed downward pressure on the Canadian unit, which had been trading in a broad range between U.S. dollar levels of C$1.4400 and C$1.4500 in recent sessions. 

 Several sources cited selling pressures against a number of commodity-linked currencies, such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars, and continuing negative yield spreads between Canada and the U.S. 

 The pressure stemming from the fact that Canadian yields remain lower than those in the U.S. has intensified in recent weeks after the Bank of Canada signalled in its semi-annual monetary policy report that monetary conditions in Canada will likely remain appropriate for the next six months, while fears of an impending interest rate increase from the U.S. Federal Reserve Board persist in some market circles. 

 One Toronto-based currency trade said the currency's downward spiral on Tuesday began with cross selling of the Canadian dollar against the Japanese yen in Europe.

title: Bank Of  Canada Intervenes  -2:  Currency  Levels After Action
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada intervened in the foreign exchange market Tuesday afternoon to sell U.S. dollars at C$1.4560 in an effort to smooth out trading action, said a trader in Toronto. 

 The U.S. dollar leveled off at around C$1.4554 after the intervention. The central bank's intervention came after the Canadian dollar slid substantially Tuesday morning, with the U.S. dollar climbing to the C$1.4560 level by early afternoon from its Monday close of C$1.4492. 

 The central bank's unofficial policy is to intervene in currency markets after intraday moves in either direction of 70 ticks or more in order to contain volatility. 

 The Canadian dollar has been under pressure in recent weeks from a variety of factors, including weakness in commodity prices and sustained negative yield spreads between Canada and the U.S. 

 It lost significant ground earlier in May when the Bank of Canada released its semi-annual monetary policy report. The report indicated that current monetary conditions are "broadly appropriate" for the next six months in the absence of any unexpected economic shocks. 

 Many market participants interpreted the statement as implying that the central bank would not be raising interest rates in that period, resulting in additional pressure for the Canadian currency.

TORONTO, May 14 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar shed some overnight losses to end at C$1.4470 (US$0.6911) on Thursday, but was still weaker than yesterday's closing level here.



Trading is cautious ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting meeting next Tuesday and a long weekend in Canada.



Selling of the Canadian, which broke out on Wednesday over Canada's neutral central bank policy, appeared to have lost steam.



No sign of Bank of Canada intervention was seen today as some players tested the U.S. dollar topside.



"I think they (the bank) disappointed a few people. The market was looking to try take longer at C$1.4520, but that failed to materialize," said one dealer. "People wanted to test their resolve."



"Basically corporate Canada was met by sell-Canada throughout the day," he said.



There was stop-loss U.S. dollar selling interest at C$1.4525-1.4555 (US$0.6885-0.6870), he said.



The U.S. dollar rose versus the mark, while easing against the yen on fears of Japanese intervention.



A bigger-than-expected rise in the key measure of U.S. inflation hurt the U.S. dollar slightly in morning trade. The U.S consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.2 percent overall and was up 0.3 percent the core rate.



Despite the mild inflationary uplift signaled by these numbers and the U.S. producer price index Wednesday, economists see the U.S. Federal Reserve as keeping its monetary policy on hold for the time being.



An statistics official at the U.S. Department of Labor said it was too early to say whether prices had bottomed out.



Canada's key inflation rate has stayed at the low end of the bank's 1-3 percent target band, and is unlikely to move substantially higher in the coming months, economists said.



"Inflation remains very low in Canada...It certainly isn't going to help the Canadian dollar. It basically implies that the Bank of Canada has little reason to consider an increase in rates over the near term," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at MMS International.



"So given that, and that conditions remain unsettled in Asia, and that the market believes in that environment, the Canadian dollar is going to underperform."



Unrest in Indonesia's capital of Jakarta continued, and India's nuclear tests are heightening tension with its neighbors.



"The numbers are coming in a little bit weaker than expected, so suggesting no need for policy to address an inflation problem," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, macro economics at Bank of Montreal.



"The negative tone in the Canadian dollar emerged yesterday and continued overnight. That's the risk. This could be another factor to continue to weigh on the Canadian dollar," he said.



Canada's April CPI rate of increase was lower than expected: up 0.8 percent year on year after a 0.9-percent rise in March, and down 0.1 percent month on month unadjusted for seasonal factors after a 0.1-percent rise.



The core CPI was up 1.2 percent year on year after 1.3-percent rise in March.



The Bank of Canada's neutral money policy, unveiled in its semi-annual monetary policy report on Wednesday, triggered a sell-off on Wednesday. The bank sought to stem the fall by intervening yesterday, but no sign of action was seen this morning.



    Looking ahead, Canada's March merchandise trade data due



out next Wednesday are expected to post an improvement,



possibly leading to a narrower deficit of C$5 billion in the Q1



current account balance, Palombi said.



    "So that would take us back from the three percent of GDP



in current account deficit to roughly to 2.5 percent. That



could be good news for the Canadian dollar," he said.



    "Overnight we got hit because the U.S. dollar lost ground



against major currencies as a result of Asia. But safe-haven



flows could easily go back into the U.S. dollar, provided the



trade data next week is good," he said.



    On the crosses, the Canadian dollar recovered from this



morning's levels, but was still quoted lower at 1.2287 marks



after 1.2308 marks at the previous close here. Canada also cut



some losses against the Japanese currency, but was still weaker



at 92.37 yen after 92.80 yen.

title: Canada dollar takes dive on neutral bank policy.
text:
TORONTO, May 13 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar tumbled on Wednesday after Canada's central bank telegraphed in its semi-annual monetary report that it was not looking to cool economic growth with higher interest rates this year. 

 The currency lost over one Canadian cent to the U.S. dollar before settling around C$1.4445 (US$0.6923). 

 It took a wave of intervention by the Bank of Canada, buying millions of Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars in the foreign exchange market, before the selling subsided. 

 In its semi-annual monetary policy report, the central bank said recent monetary conditions in Canada would be "broadly appropriate" for the next six months. 

 This caught many traders off guard as they had expected the bank to indicate a need to tighten the money in circulation probably by the end of the year, a move usually taken to ensure a sustainable pace of growth. 

 "The short end of the (bond) market is in a little bit of trouble because people are worried now that the Bank of Canada maybe will let the currency go a little bit weaker," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research at TD Securities Inc. "It doesn't mean that they won't ever be raising rates, but it's difficult to figure out when." 

 While the U.S. dollar is receiving underlying support from a widely expected shift to a tightening bias by the Federal Reserve, the Canadian dollar is finding no such comfort north of the border. 

 Expectations of higher interest rates usually props the currency as capital tends to move to high-yielding assets. 

 Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen at a news conference refused to discuss whether the Canadian dollar was undervalued against its U.S. counterpart. 

 But he said underlying economic fundamentals are strong for the Canadian dollar as the inflation rate is lower than in the United States and commodities prices are expected to pick up. 

 The central bank predicted the economy would grow at 3.5 percent in 1998, which is still one of the best performances among major industrial nations, but slower than 4.0 percent, forecast by the bank six months ago. 

 Canada's inflation should remain in the lower half of the target range of 1-3 percent for the next six months, the bank said. The main risks for the Canadian economy are the impact from Asia's financial crisis, particularly on the western part of the nation, and soft commodities prices. 

 Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst at MMS International, warned that the Bank of Canada's neutral position does not necessarily mean it will not act at all before the next report is published in November. 

 "If Asia doesn't weigh down the economy and the U.S. economy doesn't slow down, then there will be a reason for the bank to raise before the next monetary policy report," he said. 

 Thiessen's comment that "monetary conditions may continue to fluctuate over a relatively wide range" drew some attention in the market. 

 "This suggests that a weakening in the currency might not necessarily prompt an offsetting hike in interest rates if the weakness was thought to be transitory," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, macro economics at Bank of Montreal. 

 After this morning's sell-off, some see support for the battered Canadian unit. 

 Susan Stearns, director, foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal in New York said she would go for long positions for the Canada dollar at C$1.4465 (US$0.6913). 

 Randall Powley, senior economist at Scotia Capital Markets, said the currency should rebound and move in a relatively narrow range of C$1.4200-1.4400 (US$0.7042-0.6944) for the next two months until strong buying incentive emerges. 

 But in the very near-term, the Canadian dollar still has a tainted image. 

 "You don't want to be long Canada," said a senior dealer at a Canadian bank. "The market's still angry about the report." 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Canada's Chretien says wants rates to stay low.
text:
LONDON, May 13 (Reuters) - Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Wednesday that his government would like Canadian interest rates to stay low. 

 Chretien told reporters at a ceremony to open a newly refurbished Candian embassy building in London that he believed the country's economic fundamentals were strong and that interest rates should remain low. 

 "We would like to maintain low interest rates...because we have low inflation," Chretien told reporters in London just after Bank of Canada governor Gordon Thiessen released the central bank's semi-annual policy report. 

 Chretien gave Thiessen credit for Canada's high growth, low inflation economy. 

 "(It was) because the governor of the Bank (of Canada) said there will be 3.25 percent growth in Canada that we had close to four percent growth last year and unemployment is going down," Chretien said inside the newly refurbished Canada House. "So for me I think the Canadian story is pretty good." 

 The Bank of Canada intervened and bought Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars around C$1.4410 (US$0.6940) on Wednesday as the Canadian currency weakened sharply in the wake of the Bank of Canada's report on Canadian economic growth and inflation. 

 In its semi-annual monetary policy report, the central bank said recent monetary conditions in Canada would be "broadly appropriate" for the next six months. 

 The Bank also said Canadian economic growth in 1998 would not be as vigorous as thought before, Canada's inflation should remain in the lower half of the target range of 1-3 percent for the next six months, and that the main downside risks for Canada are Asia's financial crisis and soft commodities prices. 

 The Bank of Canada's key rate was last raised 50 basis points to five percent on January 30. The central bank has a target range for overnight lending of 4.5-5.0 percent. ((Paul Casciato, London newsroom +44 171 542 8968 fax +44 171 542 5293, uk.forex.news@reuters.com)).

title: Canadian bonds, bills open mixed, curve flattens.
text:
TORONTO, April 14 (Reuters) - Canadian bonds and T-bills opened mixed on Tuesday, with the yield curve flattening slightly, as recent weakness in the Canadian dollar weighed on the short end of the curve. 

 "The curve is definitely flattening. I think people are making a bit more of a fuss over yesterday's dollar weakness than they should given the light flows," said Hank Cunningham, director of fixed income with First Marathon Securities Ltd. 

 "Curve-flattening is the major theme here in Canada," he said. 

 Canada's 30-year bond fell C$0.06 to C$134.03 to yield 5.613 percent. 

 Its U.S. counterpart rose 6/32 to yield 5.92 percent. The negative spread between the two narrowed to 31 basis points from a record 32 basis points at Monday's close. 

 The Canadian dollar weakened sharply to $1.4350 (US$0.6968) in unusually thin trading on Monday, forcing the Bank of Canada to intervene to defend the currency. 

 The Canadian dollar opened flat at $1.4346 (US$0.6970) in light trading on Tuesday as markets continued to speculate that the Bank of Canada will soon raise interest rates, traders said. 

 That speculation especially affected the Canadian money market. Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softening to yield 4.58 percent from 4.57 percent at Monday's close. 

 "The currency weakness was a catalyst to moving rates a little bit higher," said Walter Posiewko, a money market trader with Royal Bank Investment Management Inc. 

 "There seems to be buying all the way through the piece into the weakness, and there doesn't seem to be any panic forming in this market. Apparantly there is cash in the market to be employed," he said. 

 In new issue news, the Bank of Canada plans to auction C$3.0 billion of 21-day treasury bills on April 15, the central bank said in a statement on Tuesday. 

 The bills will be delivered on April 16 and will mature on May 7, the Bank of Canada said. 

 The tender is subject to standard auction terms.

title: Canada  Central Bank /Policy -2: May Want Tighter Money
text:
But the Bank of Canada's decision not to intervene and slow down the currency's rise this month sent the reverse signal, Goldman's Kasumovich said. 

 The bank's inaction suggests it still wants to see monetary conditions tightened - its stated policy stance since last May - and it would prefer that tightening to come through appreciation in the currency rather than higher interest rates, Kasumovich said. 

 'I think it's consistent with the view that over a longer time horizon they would like to see tighter conditions, and they would perhaps like to see it through the currency,' he said. 'At the same time, they have brought forward so much of the tightening they had planned to do though '98, even if the currency were to stall, we probably wouldn't see a rate hike until the latter part of the year.' 

 Kasumovich and others point to something else that might be keeping the bank out of action when its normal intervention point comes up - an intervention by the bank on Jan. 9 that choked off an incipient rally sparked by strong employment numbers. 

 That intervention drew criticism from some currency market players, who couldn't understand why the central bank would block an upswing when the currency's weakness had clearly been a concern to bank officials. 

 Andrew Pyle, chief strategist with ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, said the Jan. 9 intervention implied the central bank had a base level for the currency. 

 'The market . . . took that as a signal and started to sell the currency aggressively,' Pyle said. The Bank of Canada wants to avoid a repeat of that scenario, and that's one reason bank officials are not responding to recent gains by the currency in the usual fashion. 

 'And I think that's quite natural - and I think it's probably very appropriate policy too.' 

 Another factor dissuading the bank from sticking too strictly to its 'normal' intervention policy is a reduced need to build foreign exchange reserves, Pyle suggested.

title: Canada Central Bank  Alters  Intervention  Policy: Analysts
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Canada may be trying to send a signal to currency markets by abandoning its normal policy for intervening in currency markets in recent weeks, some observers say. 

 But exactly what that signal is and how it should be interpreted is something those observers don't agree about. 

 Three times in March, the Bank has abstained from its normal, unofficial policy of intervening in currency markets by buying or selling U.S. dollars against the Canadian currency when the U.S. dollar moves more than 70 ticks in either direction against the Canadian dollar from the previous day's close. 

 The most recent instance occurred on Wednesday, March 25, when the currency surged from Tuesday's close of C$1.4164 to C$1.4085. The other two occurred on March 9, which witnessed a jump from C$1.4193 to C$1.4094. and March 2, where it went from C41.4239 to C$1.4160. 

 Bank of Canada officials do not comment publicly on currency market intervention. 

 But Marcel Kasumovich, an economist with Goldman Sachs, believes that by deviating from its unofficial policy, the central bank is trying to send a signal to the market. 

 'In the past, the bank used deviations from its standard, daily foreign exchange intervention rule as a signal of how they feel about the mix of monetary conditions,' Kasumovich said. 

 In December and January, the currency came under sustained negative pressure that drove it to the lowest level in its 140-year history. In those months, the central bank often intervened more frequently than its policy would dictate, selling U.S. dollars in an effort to contain the downward movement. 

 The bank was clearly signaling its disapproval of the currency's decline, according to Kasumovich and other observers.

Not all are gloomy. Warren Jestin, chief economist with the Bank of Nova Scotia, said, "You've got to remember, monetary policy is extremely geared for growth right now." title: Canada  Afternoon: C$ Up Sharply On Rate Hike,  Intervention
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--It took a 1/2-point rate increase and aggressive intervention from the Bank of Canada, but the Canadian dollar was pulled off all-time lows Friday. 

 Turning its back on news of a 0.3% drop in November gross domestic product, one many economists found disturbing, the central bank pushed the bank rate up to 5%. The move has fired up a vocal disagreement among market observers over its wisdom. 

 The U.S. dollar traded at C$1.4542 at 4:13 p.m. EST (2113 GMT), down from C$1.4625 at 8:00 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) but down from C$1.4653 late Thursday. It hit an historic high Thursday at C$1.4684. 

 'Don't sacrifice the economy to save the currency, Mr. Thiessen,' wrote Tim O'Neill, chief economist with the Bank of Montreal, in an emphatic criticism of the central bank's strategy. 

 He sees little economic justification for higher interest rates because inflation is below target at 0.7%, unemployment is too high at 8.6%, the November data suggest economic momentum may be waning, and investors had not lost confidence in Canadian-dollar assets. 

 Previous to the rate increase, bonds had enjoyed an impressive bull run, widening yield spreads to U.S. Treasurys. 

 Many currency players say they liked the move, but suggest its not enough. 'I like the idea of being long Canadian dollars now, but I don't love it,' said one big-bank trader on Bay Street. He praised the bank's decision to intervene first at C$1.4625, and again at the lower C$1.4602. 'That sent a strong signal, lowering their intervention point,' he said. 

 Some analysts agreed: 'today the bank finally stepped up to the plate and did the correct thing,' said Andrew Pyle, chief strategist with ABN Amro Hoare Govett. Nesbitt Burns' chief economist, Sherry Cooper, also applauded the move.

title: Canadian dollar threatens to touch record low.
text:
TORONTO, Jan 21 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar lumbered toward a record low on Wednesday with no relief in sight as the financial markets gave up hope that the Bank of Canada would raise short-term interest rates anytime soon. 

 The currency weakened to 69.19 U.S. cents after opening the North American trading session at 69.47 U.S. cents, a hair's breadth away from the record low of 69.13 U.S. cents established in February, 1986. 

 The Canadian dollar has now shed five percent of its value in the past three months. 

 The currency's latest slide was triggered by senior central bank officials who appeared to pour cold water on market speculation of an imminent interest rate hike. 

 Deputy Bank of Canada Governor Bernard Bonin said on Wednesday that the central bank was not uncomfortable with the current level of monetary conditions and hinted at a possible change in the bank's "less accommodative" monetary policy. 

 "It could be less tightening or it could be more easing," Bonin told reporters after a luncheon speech to Montreal financial analysts. 

 His comments triggered a rapid sell-off of the Canadian dollar, prompting the Bank of Canada to intervene and buy the currency at the 69.20 U.S. cent level. 

 Yesterday, Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said Asia's economic crisis would likely reduce the bank's growth projections in for the Canadian economy in 1998. 

 "There is no doubt that the events in Asia will dampen our earlier projections of output growth for this year," Thiessen said in a speech to the Ivey School of Business in Kitchener, Ontario. 

 Thiessen later added that Asia's crisis meant that Canada's output gap would not shrink as quickly as expected, putting off prospects of higher inflation in the Canadian economy. 

 "I think what they're trying to do is send out the signal that they are going to be on the sidelines for a while yet," said Rick Egelton, deputy chief economist with Bank of Montreal. 

 "Right now in Canada we have 0.9 percent inflation, below the lower end of the Bank of Canada's one- to three-percent target range, and unemployment is still relatively high, so I think the Bank of Canada has a fair bit of scope before it has to raise interest rates," Egelton said. 

 Attempts by both Theissen and Bonin to downplay the severity of the currency's slide against the U.S. dollar -- Thiessen underlined the Canadian dollar's relative strength against most other currencies, failed to calm jittery markets. 

 "That's like saying my fingers and toes feel fine, but it's the gunshot in my chest that's bothering me," said Jeoff Hall, economist with Technical Data in Boston. 

 Hall said the Canadian dollar could weaken to 68.02 U.S. cents during the next two months as the size of Canada's ballooning current account deficit became more apparent. 

 Along with the worldwide decline in commodity prices, the current account, which is a measure of a country's indebtedness, has been a major factor in the Canadian dollar's decline. 

 Canada's third-quarter current account deficit swelled to C$25.5 billion (US$17.6 billion) on an annualised basis. 

 Economists said trade data released on Wednesday, showing continued softness in Canada's merchandise trade surplus, could pave the way for a C$30-billion (US$20.7 billion) current account deficit in the fourth quarter and more trouble for the Canadian dollar.

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Rally Fizzles Out, Despite Strong Jobs
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--A show of strength in Canada's December labor market put some muscle on the Canadian dollar earlier Friday, but it couldn't sustain it in the face of an interventionist Bank of Canada and weak stocks. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.4300 at 4:00 p.m. EST (2100 GMT), up from C$1.4253 at 8:00 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) and from C$1.4312 late Thursday. 

 'I'm really surprised its back here after this morning's rally,' said a dealer with one of the major Canadian banks. 'Everyone got all bulled up when the U.S. dollar fell through C$1.4285 and then reached C$1.4215,' he said. But there the Bank of Canada stepped in to buy U.S. dollars, and 'I don't think anyone knows why,' he added. 

 The central bank tends to stand against intraday moves in excess of 70 ticks, but often doesn't. This time it chose to enter against the Canadian dollar at C$1.4225. 

 After a brief attempt to resume its rally, the Canadian dollar succumbed to profit taking, and eventually the move downward triggered a series of stop-loss orders to buy the U.S. dollar. 

 Statistics Canada set the agenda early with news of a huge 61,700 new jobs in December, far exceeding even the most optimistic forecasts. Excluding part-time jobs, which fell 49,100, full-time employment was up a stunning 110,800. Combined with a drop in the number of active job seekers, that knocked the unemployment rate down to 8.6%, from 9.0%, a level not seen since September of 1990. 

 Those numbers suggest the economy has entered a phase of 'sustained upswing based on income growth,' said Andrew Spence, senior economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. Just judging by robust car sales in December, it seems consumers are in a mood to spend that won't likely change should the central bank nudge interest rates still higher in the period ahead, he said. That ought to prove supportive of the currency.

title: Canada Afternoon: C$ Drops As Asia Refires Commodity Worry
text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--A resumption of the turmoil in the Southeast Asian currency markets had the Canadian dollar back under attack Tuesday, as it joined other commodity-linked currencies in sharp losses. 

 Heavy selling earlier prompted repeated intervention from the Bank of Canada, and speculation is on once again that another rate hike may be required to shore up the currency. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at C$1.4315 at 4:28 p.m. EST (2128 GMT), up from C$1.4293 at 8:00 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) and C$1.4232 late Monday. Traders say another test of C$1.4416 is possible, a level hit last week for the first time since Feb. 1986. 

 'I think the culprit is the renewed turmoil in Southeast Asia,' said Doug Porter, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns Inc. A bad day for the Indonesian rupiah and others in the region played on fears the crisis there is far from over and it could spark further losses in many commodity prices important to Canada's export-led economy. 

 The weakness in commidity prices 'is making the Canadian dollar less tolerant than it had been earlier to negative interest-rate differentials,' said Avery Shenfeld, senior economist with CIBC Wood Gundy Inc. A sharp discount in Canadian interest rates, relative to U.S. rates, has been blamed for months for the Canadian dollar's recent poor fortunes. 

 Indeed, this session the three-month treasury bill shot up 26 basis points to 4.18%, in fear that the currency weakness could eventually prompt the central bank to narrow that differential with another defensive rate increase. Even at 4.18% the treasury bill still yields 89 basis points less than the comparable U.S. bill. 

 On Dec. 12 the bank raised the key bank rate 1/2 point to 4.5%, citing currency losses to explain the move.

text:
TORONTO (Dow Jones)--The Canadian dollar's New Year rally petered out Tuesday morning and the currency has plunged to levels that prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene in currency markets by selling U.S. dollars. 

 'I think the weakness we're seeing this morning is obviously related to renewed turmoil in Asia and obviously related to the divebombing we're seeing in oil right now,' said Andrew Pyle, economist with ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.

The move was consistent with the central bank's policy of intervening in currency markets when the Canadian dollar moves 70 ticks or more from the previous day's close. 

 The bank intervened repeatedly in currency markets in December, spending US $1.94 billion and reducing its reserves to US $17.97 billion. 

 Pyle said the renewed depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah - which has lost about 30% of its value since 1998 began - and other signs of instability in Asia are roiling global markets, and affecting the Canadian dollar. 

 The decline of crude oil prices is also a factor, he said. There has been widespread selling of crude oil and related product futures in the wake of expected return of Iraqi crude oil to the market and increased production by countries in the Organization of Petroluem Exporting zCountries.

title: Canada Monetary Reserves -2: Official  Operations  Reported
text:
OTTAWA (Dow Jones)--Canada's official monetary reserves declined $805 million in December, a month when the Bank of Canada intervened heavily in the currency market to slow a decline in the Canadian dollar. 

 At Dec. 31, the Finance Department said official holdings of gold, foreign currency and other monetary assets totaled $17.97 billion, down from $18.77 billion a month earlier, and down from $20.58 billion a year earlier. All reserve figures are reported in U.S. funds. 

 Official government operations, which may include purchases and sales of foreign exchange to moderate movements in the Canadian dollar, reduced reserves by $1.94 billion in December. Currency traders reported that the central bank sold U.S. dollars and bought Canadian dollars in December when the Canadian currency came under selling pressure. Despite the intervention, the Canadian dollar declined a third of a U.S. cents against its U.S. counterpart in December.

title: Canadian dollar seen sinking near record low.
text:
TORONTO, Dec 23 (Reuters) - The ailing Canadian dollar, under siege by speculators, is expected to decline toward its all-time low in coming weeks, currency analysts predicted on Tuesday. 

 With Canada's central bank apparently loath to raise interest rates for fear of aborting an economic recovery, the Canadian dollar is seen slipping as low as 69.13 U.S. cents (C$1.4465). 

 At that level, the currency's value would match the lowest level ever reached against the U.S. dollar -- a nadir last seen on Feb. 4, 1986. 

 The dollar closed on Tuesday at 69.54 U.S. cents (C$1.4380) in North American trading. The Bank of Canada intervened in currency markets late in the session to bolster the Canadian dollar, buying it for U.S. dollars. 

 This year the Canadian dollar, known locally as "the loonie" after the picture of a wild water fowl stamped on the flip side of the coin, dropped more than 5 U.S. cents from a high of 74.85 U.S. cents (C$1.3366) in late January. 

 The currency, a barometer of Canada's export and commodity-driven economy, has been buffeted for weeks by currency speculators and further undermined by a fall in gold bullion and base metal prices to their lowest levels in years. 

 Fears that the Asian economic flu could spread to Canada have further pressured the dollar, analysts said. 

 The Bank of Canada recently has tried in vain to shore up the dollar by twice raising short-term interest rates. 

 The last time it boosted the key bank rate -- similar to the U.S. Federal funds rate -- was on Dec. 12, raising it 50 basis points to 4.5 percent. 

 The central bank has since held off from more rate hikes, leading some market watchers to speculate that it was prepared to let the unit weather the storm until most market players returned from the Christmas and New Year holidays. 

 Others have argued that the Bank of Canada should stop intervening in the currency markets, selling U.S. dollars to buy Canadian dollars, and let the unit drift lower to find a natural level supported by Canada's strengthening economy and improving fiscal picture. 

 "The speculators are testing the Bank of Canada's resolve," said Harv Kalirai, I.D.E.A. analyst in New York. "If you do get (to) C$1.44 (69.44 U.S. cents)) I think another rate hike will be sooner rather than later."
